## Decision
We will retrieve the nomsNumber on demand from community-api using CRN and will not persist nomsNumber in the court-case-service case model.

- court-case-service will accept CRN, resolve nomsNumber via community-api, then call prison-api.
- We will introduce an internal identifier lookup component with a short-lived, read-through cache (e.g. 15–60 minutes TTL) to minimise latency and load, with cache-key by CRN and negative caching for misses.
- We will not require prepare-a-case to supply nomsNumber; existing request/response contracts remain unchanged.
- We will treat nomsNumber as a derived, external identifier and avoid duplicating it in our domain model to reduce data drift, propagation overhead, and write-time coupling.
- We will handle error and reconciliation cases: missing or multiple matches from community-api will be surfaced as domain errors; changes detected (e.g. 404 then later found, or identifier reassignment) will invalidate cache entries.
- We will add metrics and alerts for lookup rates, hit ratio, latency, and error codes to monitor impact and revisit if performance or reliability becomes an issue.
- If usage patterns or SLAs later demand stronger guarantees, we will consider promoting nomsNumber to a persisted attribute via a subsequent ADR, coupled with backfill and synchronization strategy.

This approach minimises changes across clients, avoids expanding our data model with externally-owned identifiers, and provides a pragmatic path with caching to meet performance needs while keeping the source of truth in community-api.

## Decision:
We will separate responsibilities and adopt a transactional outbox pattern.

- Create two service functions:
  - CommandHandler: validates/transforms the command and persists the result to Firebase, recording a corresponding domain event in an Outbox collection/table in the same datastore as part of a single atomic operation.
  - EventPublisher: consumes Outbox entries, publishes messages to the target topic, and marks entries as dispatched (idempotently with retry/backoff).

- Encapsulate Firebase writes and outbox enqueue into a single repository port (e.g., writeWithOutbox(data, event)) so CommandHandler has only one external dependency in tests. EventPublisher has only the messaging publisher port in tests.

- Ensure atomicity using Firebase/Firestore transactions or batched writes; if unavailable, use best-effort with deduplication keys and idempotent publisher.

- Messages broadcast to other topics will be derived from the stored outbox event, ensuring reliability and decoupling write concerns from broadcast concerns.

This design reduces unit-test complexity (each function mocks at most one port), improves separation of concerns, and increases operational resilience by decoupling persistence from message delivery.

## Decision:
Deprecate lookup-name on shared components and standardize JNDI bindings to eliminate ambiguity and improve UI support.

- Standard binding:
  - All shared components are bound under comp/env/<unique-id>.
  - DatabaseConnection subclasses additionally expose a javax.sql.DataSource bound under comp/env/jdbc/<unique-id>.
- Behavior change:
  - lookup-name no longer overrides the JNDI binding for either the component or its DataSource.
  - Shared* reference properties continue to be named lookup-name for backward compatibility, but their semantics are simplified: they refer to the target component’s unique-id (UI will present a dropdown of available shared components by unique-id). At runtime, references resolve to comp/env/<unique-id> (or comp/env/jdbc/<unique-id> for DataSource consumers).
- Backward compatibility:
  - If a component specifies lookup-name and it differs from comp/env/<unique-id>, the runtime will:
    - Bind the component to comp/env/<unique-id> (authoritative).
    - Optionally bind a legacy alias to the old lookup-name when the system property interlok.shared.legacyJndiAlias=true (default false). A startup WARN will indicate deprecation and the effective binding.
  - For DatabaseConnection, DataSource is always bound to comp/env/jdbc/<unique-id>. If legacy aliasing is enabled and a historical lookup-name is present, a secondary alias for the DataSource is also bound for one release cycle.
- UI/Model updates:
  - Hide lookup-name on shared component definitions.
  - For Shared* references, present a required selection by unique-id; free-form JNDI paths are disallowed.
  - Validation enforces uniqueness of unique-id across shared components of the same type.
- Migration:
  - Mark lookup-name as deprecated in schema and docs.
  - Emit startup warnings when deprecated lookup-name is detected, including the computed authoritative binding and guidance to remove it.
  - Provide a migration tool/check that rewrites references from arbitrary JNDI names to unique-id where resolvable.
- Timeline:
  - Phase 1 (current + 1 release): dual-binding via legacy alias flag available; default off.
  - Phase 2: remove legacy aliasing; lookup-name ignored entirely.

## Decision:
Adopt Infrastructure as Code as the single source of truth for all environments and local development.

- Provision and manage cloud infrastructure with Terraform, using reusable, versioned modules that mirror environment topology. Apply changes via CI to ensure reproducibility.
- Package all applications and dependencies as Docker images. Ensure the same images are used across local, staging, and production for maximal parity.
- Provide a Docker Compose stack for local development that mirrors production service topology (services, backing stores, queues, configuration) using production-like defaults with local overrides via .env files.
- Supply seed data and bootstrapping scripts to initialize local dependencies deterministically.
- Standardize developer workflow with Make targets (e.g., make up/down/seed/test) for one-command environment setup and teardown.
- Store all definitions (Terraform, Compose, configs) in the repository, versioned and peer-reviewed.
- Validate parity continuously: CI runs docker compose config validation and terraform validate/plan; nightly drift checks against remote state.
- Document configuration contracts (required env vars, ports, data volumes) and maintain compatibility tests to prevent breaking changes.

## Decision:
Adopt a CQRS pattern with an event-sourced projection for “tides” and their per-task statuses.

- Write model: continue emitting immutable domain events for tide/run/task lifecycle (created, queued, started, progressed, succeeded, failed, canceled).
- Read model: maintain denormalized projection tables optimized for the UI:
  - tide_runs (one row per tide execution)
  - tide_tasks (one row per task within a run; latest status, timestamps, attempt, assignee/runner, dependencies, summary metrics)
  - task_events (optional short history for quick drill-down)
- Projection mechanics:
  - An idempotent projector consumes events from the event bus and upserts records using deterministic ids and monotonic sequence numbers to guarantee ordering and de-duplication.
  - Rebuild capability: projectors can rehydrate the read model from the event log on demand.
- Storage: relational DB (e.g., Postgres) for projections with targeted indexes (tide_id, run_id, task_id, status, updated_at) to support fast filtering and timeline queries. Retain full history in the event store; keep projections compact.
- Real-time delivery:
  - On each projection update, publish lightweight change notifications to a fan-out channel (e.g., Redis pub/sub or the event bus).
  - UI subscribes via WebSockets/SSE to receive near-real-time updates; HTTP/GraphQL used for initial load and pagination.
- Consistency and SLAs:
  - Aim for sub-second end-to-end latency; tolerate eventual consistency.
  - Use idempotency keys and exactly-once–effective processing; dead-letter and retry with backoff.
- Operations:
  - Backfill/reindex jobs for projection recovery.
  - Metrics on lag (event offset vs projection), projector error rates, and UI staleness.
  - Access controls applied at read model endpoints.

This provides a stable, rebuildable source of truth with a fast, UI-friendly projection that supports a detailed, real-time pipeline view.

## Decision:
Standardize all HapiJS plugin modules on CommonJS. Author and publish plugins using module.exports with the Hapi-expected shape:

- module.exports = { name, version, register }
- Consumers use const plugin = require('pkg') (no .default indirection)
- No export default in plugin packages

Implementation details:
- package.json: set "type": "commonjs" (or omit) and define "main" to the CJS build.
- If using TypeScript, compile with "module": "commonjs" and emit CJS outputs.
- Avoid hybrid/dual export patterns to prevent ambiguity for consumers and tooling.
- Where ESM consumption is required, provide an explicit ESM wrapper package or entry point that re-exports module.exports, but default to CJS for Hapi compatibility.

This removes interop friction, keeps registration straightforward, and ensures consistent consumption across all plugin packages.

## Decision:
We will migrate all ECS capacity to the ECS-Optimized Amazon Linux 2 AMI and standardize on the Docker overlay2 storage driver. Launch Templates/Configurations for ECS Auto Scaling Groups will be updated to use the AL2 ECS-Optimized AMI and a single-root-volume layout. We will size the root EBS volume to accommodate both OS and container/storage needs (default 30 GB minimum, increased per service requirements), and we will no longer maintain a separate data volume for Docker.

Rollout will be executed via new Launch Templates/Configurations and progressive ASG refresh (instance replacement) to ensure all nodes adopt the new AMI and storage driver before end-of-support for the legacy AMI. Monitoring, user-data, and Terraform modules will be updated accordingly.

## Decision:
Introduce compositional “Op Traits” as first-class reusable building blocks for op definitions, favoring composition over inheritance.

- Define OpTrait(name, [parameters]) { Inputs/Args/Outputs/TypeConstraints/Doc/Signatures } as a reusable fragment. Traits may accept parameters (with defaults) to customize names, defaults, docs, and constraints.
- Ops can include multiple traits: Include(TraitA(...), TraitB(...), …). Included members are merged into the op. Single-inheritance remains supported but is deprecated in favor of traits.
- Post-include mutability: After inclusion, all included members are addressable and editable in-place within the op (e.g., Arg("epsilon").defaultValue = 1e-5; Doc += "…"). This provides direct access and reduces boilerplate.
- Merge and override rules:
  - Members are keyed by name and merged by default. Conflicts require explicit resolution via Override(name){…}, Rename(old,new), or Remove(name).
  - Identical duplicates merge silently; non-identical duplicates without explicit resolution trigger a validation error.
  - Resolution order is explicit; Include() order is not used to implicitly resolve conflicts.
- Documentation composition:
  - Docs from traits are concatenated in include order; traits may define placeholders and op-time substitutions. Ops can append or override sections explicitly.
- Validation:
  - Detect trait cycles and ambiguous merges as errors.
  - Validate parameter bindings, required members, and signature consistency after composition.
- Discoverability and tooling:
  - Generated metadata records trait inclusions to make relationships explicit in documentation and tooling (e.g., graphs, search facets).
- Backward compatibility:
  - Existing ops can be incrementally migrated by extracting common parts into traits; behavior of non-migrated ops is unchanged.

## Decision:
Implement an Export Search Results capability that allows users to download the results of any search query in common, portable formats.

- Provide export formats: CSV (default) and JSON (NDJSON for large sets). For media/file assets, support optional bulk ZIP of referenced files plus a CSV/JSON manifest.
- Exports run asynchronously via a background job. Users trigger an export from the search UI; the system snapshots the query, filters, sort, and selected fields, then enqueues a job.
- Results are generated from the search index with consistent ordering, deduplicated, and written in batches to object storage (e.g., S3) with server-side compression (GZIP). Provide a pre-signed, time-limited download link and notify users via in-app notification and/or email when ready.
- Enforce guardrails: configurable max row/file limits, sampling option when over limit, rate limiting per user, and cancellation. Include schema/version metadata in the export.
- Access control is enforced at export time; only data the requester can see is exported. Sensitive fields are excluded by default; admins can opt-in. All export events are audited.
- API: POST /exports with query payload and format; GET /exports/{id}/status; GET link to download artifact. Exports expire and are garbage-collected.
- UX: “Export” button reflecting current search; allow field selection, format choice, and show progress.

## Decision:
Adopt a two-tier structure for feature katas to balance approachability and rigor.

- Kata tiers
  - Basics: an introductory kata that teaches the feature’s everyday usage and mental model.
  - In-Depth (Expert): a comprehensive kata that covers edge cases, spec nuances, pitfalls, and interoperability.

- Naming
  - Use the canonical feature name plus suffixes: “<Feature> — Basics” and “<Feature> — In-Depth”.
  - Keep the same group tags as peers (e.g., “Object API”), add “expert” to the In-Depth variant.

- Directory and files
  - Place both under the same topic path; use files or subfolders:
    - <topic>/<feature>/basics.spec.js
    - <topic>/<feature>/in-depth.spec.js
  - If a README/metadata exists, share a single README with a “Basics” and “In-Depth” section, or two minimal READMEs cross-linking each other.

- Scope and size
  - Basics: 5–10 tests, common patterns, no exhaustive edge cases, zero or minimal theory; estimated 10–20 minutes.
  - In-Depth: as many tests as needed for correctness (algorithm steps, errors, coercions, iterables, realm/this semantics, etc.); estimated 30–90 minutes.
  - Avoid test duplication; In-Depth may build upon but not repeat Basics.

- Cross-linking and prerequisites
  - First test (or header) of each kata links to its counterpart.
  - List prerequisites explicitly (e.g., “requires: Iterables Basics”) and optional follow-ups.

- Publishing guidance
  - Prefer releasing Basics first; In-Depth follows when ready.
  - If only an In-Depth exists, add a TODO placeholder for Basics and mark difficulty accordingly.

- Consistency rules
  - Follow existing formatting/style ADRs.
  - Use consistent tags, naming, and directory structure across ES versions and libraries.

## Decision:
We will standardize on containerization as the default packaging and runtime model for all new services and, where feasible, for migrating existing services, aligning with Hackney’s preference.

- Use OCI-compliant images as the primary deployment artifact across all environments (local, CI, test, staging, production).
- Prefer Docker/BuildKit (or equivalent OCI builders) for image creation; maintain organization-approved base images with hardened OS, consistent runtime layers, and common tooling.
- Provide guidance and tooling for local development using containers (e.g., Docker Compose or equivalent) to ensure environment parity.
- Operate containers on the chosen orchestrator (Kubernetes per prior ADRs), with supporting standards for configuration, secrets, networking, and observability.
- Integrate image provenance, vulnerability scanning, and policy enforcement in CI; store images in a centralized registry.
- Treat non-container deployments as exceptions requiring an ADR and explicit justification (e.g., vendor SaaS, specialized hardware constraints).

This decision ensures consistency, portability, and operational efficiency across Hackney’s digital services while enabling teams to adopt a common, well-supported approach.

## Decision:
Establish a mandatory, versioned Design Guidelines (DG) as the single source of truth for design rules and conventions.

- Ownership and governance: A Design Council (arch leads + senior engineers) owns the DG, approves changes, and arbitrates disputes.
- Versioning and change control: DG is stored in the repo, uses semantic versioning, and is changed via ADR-backed pull requests with impact assessment and migration notes.
- Enforcement: 
  - Mandatory design review gate for significant changes (features, interfaces, data models).
  - PR checklist links to relevant DG rules; non-compliance blocks merge unless a waiver is approved.
  - Automated checks (linters/validators/templates) where feasible; templates for diagrams and documents.
- Exceptions: Formal waiver process with rationale, risk assessment, scope, timeframe, and sunset date; tracked and revisited.
- Communication and enablement: Onboarding materials, concise rule summaries/cheatsheets, and examples; periodic refresh sessions.
- Measurement: Track compliance, waivers, and review outcomes; publish metrics to drive continuous improvement.

## Decision:
We will adopt jMolecules (and its Spring/Hibernate/Jackson integrations) as the standard library for expressing tactical DDD building blocks, replacing our custom base classes and annotations.

jMolecules will provide first-class, framework-agnostic abstractions for Aggregates, Entities, Value Objects, Repositories, Identifiers, and Domain Events via types and annotations. Its integrations allow us to map these concepts consistently to persistence and serialization layers without leaking infrastructure concerns into the domain model.

We will:
- Introduce jMolecules types/annotations (e.g., AggregateRoot, Entity, ValueObject, Identifier, DomainEvent).
- Replace custom DDD marker interfaces/base classes with jMolecules equivalents and deprecate legacy code.
- Leverage jMolecules integrations for Spring Data and Hibernate to align repository and mapping conventions, and for Jackson to serialize value objects and identifiers consistently.
- Keep domain logic and invariants in our model; jMolecules will standardize the expression and mapping of DDD patterns, not business rules.
- Establish guidelines and examples for aggregates, IDs, events, and repositories using jMolecules to ensure uniformity across modules.

This reduces boilerplate, increases interoperability with the broader JVM ecosystem, and improves maintainability by converging on a well-supported, idiomatic DDD foundation.

## Decision:
Adopt Terraform as the primary Infrastructure as Code tool to define, provision, and manage all Data Submission Service infrastructure. All cloud resources will be expressed in Terraform (HCL), organized into reusable versioned modules, and applied via a CI/CD pipeline with plan/apply workflows and peer review.

- Use Terraform providers for the target clouds (primarily AWS), enabling a consistent, provider-agnostic workflow and simplifying any future multi-cloud needs.
- Represent environments (e.g., dev, test, prod) as separate stacks with shared modules and environment-specific variables to ensure isolation and repeatability.
- Enforce standard practices: code review for all changes, terraform fmt/validate, and plan output review before apply.
- Prefer Terraform-native resources; if gaps exist, integrate provider-native templates or custom scripts via Terraform resources, encapsulated behind modules to preserve a consistent interface.
- Maintain state remotely with appropriate locking and access controls; restrict direct console changes and reconcile any drift through Terraform.

This approach provides reproducibility, traceability, and automation while minimizing cloud-vendor lock-in and manual effort.

## Decision:
We will incorporate recurring, qualitative usability studies into our development lifecycle to validate UX assumptions and identify major usability issues early.

- Conduct moderated usability studies on prototypes and early builds at key milestones and before major releases.
- Recruit 5–7 representative participants per round, covering primary user roles and accessibility needs; include at least one assistive technology user when feasible.
- Focus sessions on the highest-risk tasks and end-to-end user journeys; use think-aloud protocol.
- Default to remote sessions with secure screen/audio recording and informed consent; conduct in-person testing when context of use materially impacts results.
- Synthesize findings within 48 hours into prioritized issues, root causes, and actionable recommendations; track issues to resolution in the backlog.
- Define exit criteria: no outstanding critical (P0) usability issues for targeted journeys before moving to the next phase or release.
- Repeat testing after major UX changes to validate fixes; measure progress by reduction of critical issues across rounds and observed task success.
- Store research plans, notes, recordings, and summaries in the shared repository linked to the RFC PR; protect participant data per privacy policies.
- Complement qualitative studies with analytics and surveys where appropriate, but do not defer addressing issues surfaced qualitatively.

## Decision:
Adopt PEtab as Maud’s canonical input/exchange format and deprecate the custom TOML schema over a staged transition.

- Make PEtab the default for new projects, leveraging its tabular representation for priors, measurements, and experimental conditions to reduce complexity and file size, and to improve interoperability with existing tooling.
- Maintain read-only support for the current TOML format during a transition period, with clear deprecation notices and a migration guide.
- Provide robust import/export tooling:
  - A toml→PEtab converter covering all currently supported constructs.
  - A PEtab→internal loader that validates against the PEtab schema, reports diagnostics, and maps to Maud’s internal model.
- Define a minimal PEtab profile required by Maud plus documented, namespaced extensions (via PEtab annotations) for Maud-specific features not covered by core PEtab; upstream proposals to PEtab where appropriate.
- Integrate PEtab validation into CI and runtime checks to ensure schema compliance and early error detection.
- Align planned auto-generation pipelines (from 3D genome-scale models, raw measurements, and prior analyses) to emit PEtab directly.
- Documentation: update user guides and examples to PEtab-first, with a migration section from TOML.
- Timeline: PEtab support available immediately; PEtab set as default in the next minor release; TOML deprecated after two minor releases and removed after one major release, contingent on feature parity and user feedback.

## Decision:
Implement the data processing pipeline using serverless compute. Specifically:
- Use AWS Lambda to execute discrete processing stages (ingest, transform/enrich, and index into Elasticsearch).
- Trigger the pipeline from S3 events (object-created) with SQS as an optional buffer for throttling and retries.
- Orchestrate multi-step/longer workflows with AWS Step Functions to handle fan-out, parallelization, checkpointing, and error handling.
- Access Elasticsearch (or Amazon OpenSearch Service) directly from Lambda, using VPC integration if required.
- For exceptionally large or long-running batches that exceed Lambda constraints, run on-demand ECS Fargate tasks invoked by Step Functions as a fallback.

This serverless-first approach eliminates the need to provision or maintain VMs, scales automatically with data arrivals, and minimizes cost for the application’s periodic workload while keeping integrations limited to S3 and Elasticsearch.

## Decision:
Implement layered brute-force mitigation combining edge rate limiting and application-level throttling for the three sensitive endpoints (Actor Login, One Time Passcode, Viewer Code).

- Edge protection: Enable rate-based rules in the CDN/WAF (e.g., CloudFront + AWS WAF) to throttle abusive IPs globally. Apply conservative per-IP limits and automatic temporary blocks; exclude trusted internal ranges.

- Application throttling: Add Redis-backed sliding-window counters keyed by:
  - Per-credential subject (e.g., email/actorId for login, LPA reference for OTP, viewer code)
  - Per-IP
  Evaluate both keys; enforce the stricter outcome.

- Policy (configurable per endpoint via environment):
  - Threshold N failures within T seconds triggers a temporary lockout for L seconds for that subject and for that IP on that endpoint.
  - Exponential backoff on repeated lockouts with capped maximum.
  - Successful verification/login resets the subject counter; IP counter decays naturally.
  - Use a sliding window or token-bucket algorithm to avoid hard window edge effects.

- Behavior:
  - Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After on throttled requests; keep error messages generic (no indication which factor triggered throttling).
  - Do not increase counters on clearly invalid/malformed requests that fail validation before lookup to avoid key probing.
  - Store counters with TTL and add jitter to reduce stampedes.

- Observability and ops:
  - Emit metrics (counts, lockouts) and alerts on anomalies.
  - Provide admin override to unblock a subject.
  - Log with privacy in mind (hash identifiers), aligning with GDPR data minimization.

## Decision:
All UI screens, views, and components must adopt the UITestablePage interface for defining and managing accessibility identifiers. Legacy patterns or ad-hoc identifier assignment are deprecated and must not be used in new code. New features must implement UITestablePage from inception; existing pages should be migrated opportunistically during maintenance, with priority on high-traffic and flaky-tested areas.

Key points:
- Centralize all accessibility identifiers via UITestablePage to ensure consistency, discoverability, and testability.
- Enforce identifier naming conventions and stability through UITestablePage contracts.
- Prohibit hardcoded identifiers outside UITestablePage implementations.
- Introduce lightweight lint/CI checks to prevent non-compliant identifier usage.
- Provide a migration guide and shared utilities to streamline adoption (e.g., common prefixes/scopes, helpers).
- Mark legacy interfaces as deprecated and schedule their removal after migration coverage reaches agreed thresholds.

## Decision:
We will adopt inclusive, respectful technical language across code, documentation, UI, and communications. We will replace problematic terms with accepted alternatives, including:
- blacklist/whitelist → blocklist/allowlist
- master/slave → primary/replica or leader/follower (context-dependent)
- sane/insane → expected/unexpected or typical/atypical
- dummy → sample/example or placeholder
- grandfathered → legacy/previously exempt
- abort/kill → cancel/terminate/stop (context-dependent)

We will publish a language guide in the contributor documentation with a maintainable glossary and decision rules for selecting terms by context. We will integrate linting checks (e.g., inclusive-language linters) into CI to block new noncompliant language and provide autofix suggestions where possible. We will update templates (issue/PR, README, API docs, UI strings) to model preferred terminology.

We will migrate existing references opportunistically: for code identifiers via non-breaking deprecations (aliases, redirects, versioned APIs), and for docs/UI via immediate edits. We will review third-party dependencies for exposed terminology and prefer inclusive options when feasible.

## Decision:
We will retire the single, overloaded “environment” variable from the Jenkins shared library and replace it with a typed, explicit context. All library entry points will accept an EnvironmentContext object (or map) with the following canonical keys:
- lifecycle: dev | test | uat | staging | perf | prod (logical stage)
- subscription_id: Azure subscription GUID
- tenant_id: Azure AD tenant (optional if derivable from subscription)
- platform: aks | appservice | vm | other
- region: Azure location
- instance: free-form instance label (e.g., team/demo name, PR number)
- namespace/resource_group: platform-specific isolation scope

“env” is reserved for Jenkins’ built-in and must not carry deployment semantics.

We will:
- Update library functions to require explicit keys and fail fast with validation (schema checks, allowed values).
- Provide a compatibility shim that maps legacy environment strings to the new context for a deprecation window (two release cycles), emitting warnings.
- Publish a glossary and code examples; enforce naming via linting and PR checks.
- Remove the legacy parameter after the deprecation period and disallow multiple meanings per variable.

This decision eliminates ambiguity, enables multiple environments per subscription, improves debuggability, and increases flexibility for future topologies without changing the runtime platforms.

## Decision:
Reference upstream Yocto layers as pinned git submodules rather than forking third-party code into our repository.

- Each external layer (e.g., meta-raspberrypi) is added as a submodule at a specific tag/commit known to be compatible with our distro.
- Our customizations live in a dedicated meta-<project> layer. We integrate and override via bbappends, machine/distro configs, and patches stored in our layer, keeping upstream layers unmodified.
- Upstream contributions are submitted to the original layer maintainers; we carry temporary patches in our layer until they are merged, then drop them when we advance the submodule.
- Submodule revisions are updated intentionally via a controlled process (compatibility testing in CI, fast-forward only where possible, with a changelog entry per bump).
- The root repo includes .gitmodules and a bootstrap script to clone submodules consistently (optionally supporting kas manifests for reproducible builds and CI).
- For rare long-lived divergences or unmaintained layers, we may fork as a last resort, but only with clear ownership and a deprecation path back to upstream.

This approach preserves upstream provenance, reduces maintenance and merge burden, ensures reproducible builds through explicit pinning, and keeps our customizations isolated and reviewable within our own layer.

## Decision:
Introduce a granular, queryable Translations API and decouple integration titles from config-flow translations.

- Replace the single bulk endpoint with:
  - GET frontend/translations?lang=xx&domains=a,b,c&areas=config,options,device_automation,state
  - Defaults to no domains; clients must request only what they need.
  - Support multiple calls and partial responses.

- Move integration display names out of strings.json/config:
  - If a product name is not translated, use manifest.json title directly.
  - For integrations requiring translated titles, create a dedicated top-level titles catalog (e.g., titles.json), fetched via GET frontend/translations/titles?lang=xx[&domains=…].
  - Deprecate and remove title under config.

- Keep platform state translations but make them opt-in:
  - Allow requesting state per domain (including merged platform state) via areas=state.
  - Clients only fetch state when rendering entities that need it (e.g., moon, season).

- Server behavior and performance:
  - Apply gzip/br compression and ETags keyed by lang+domain+area version; support If-None-Match for incremental client updates.
  - Version per domain/area to enable fine-grained cache invalidation.
  - Maintain legacy frontend/get_translations for one release behind a feature flag, emitting deprecation warnings.

This reduces payloads drastically, enables lazy loading, corrects the title scoping mistake, and keeps rare state translations available without penalizing all clients.

## Decision:
- Use Domain-Driven Design to define service boundaries around Bounded Contexts with clear Ubiquitous Language and ownership by a single team per context.
- Discover domains via facilitated Big-Picture Event Storming, followed by Design-Level Event Storming to identify aggregates, invariants, and transactional boundaries.
- Produce and maintain a Context Map (contexts, upstream/downstream relations, anti-corruption layers, shared kernel only as last resort).
- Start coarse-grained: one service per bounded context initially; split only when justified by cohesion/coupling analysis, independent deployability, scaling needs, or change-frequency hotspots.
- Prefer asynchronous choreography across contexts; use orchestration only where explicit global process control, compensation, or observability demands it.
- Define canonical domain events per context; keep events business-focused, immutable, and versioned for backward compatibility. Use a schema registry and consumer-driven contracts to manage evolution.
- Encapsulate persistence per service; aggregates enforce invariants within a single service/transaction boundary. Cross-service workflows use sagas with idempotent handlers and outbox patterns.
- Establish architectural fitness functions and guardrails: dependency checks (no shared databases), coupling metrics, change lead-time, and incident blast-radius as signals for (re)partitioning.
- Adopt iterative evolution via the Strangler pattern: split/merge services based on observed domain volatility and team cognitive load; revisit boundaries after major domain changes.
- Document decisions and boundaries in ADRs; keep diagrams and context maps living artifacts reviewed at each planning increment.

## Decision:
Standardize service health reporting and orchestration integration via explicit startup, liveness, and readiness checks.

- Each service must expose:
  - /startup (or startupProbe): returns 200 only after initialization completes (migrations, warm caches, key material loaded). Prevents early restarts and false liveness failures.
  - /live (livenessProbe): fast, in-process health indicator (event loop alive, heap within bounds). Must not call external dependencies.
  - /ready (readinessProbe): indicates ability to serve traffic. May check critical dependencies (DB/broker/feature flags) with tight timeouts and circuit-breaker awareness.

- For gRPC services, implement grpc.health.v1 Health service with SERVING/NOT_SERVING states mapped to readiness; use a lightweight liveness reflection or separate ping method. For non-HTTP protocols, use TCP or exec probes as appropriate.

- Kubernetes configuration:
  - Configure startupProbe to gate liveness/readiness during boot.
  - Set probe timeouts < 2s, period 5–10s, and conservative failureThreshold to balance sensitivity vs flapping.
  - Use preStop hooks and SIGTERM handling to set readiness=false, drain connections/consumers, and complete inflight work before terminationGracePeriodSeconds elapses.

- Security and performance:
  - Health endpoints remain unauthenticated but must not leak sensitive data; include only minimal diagnostics (build/version, uptime, dependency status codes).
  - Endpoints must be cheap and constant-time; avoid heavy queries or full dependency sweeps.

- Contract:
  - HTTP 200 -> healthy, 503 -> not ready/unhealthy. Optional JSON payload: {status, version, commit, checks}.
  - Readiness may be degraded per dependency but should prefer fail-closed for critical paths defined per service.
  - Liveness must only reflect process viability to avoid restart storms due to transient downstream issues.

- Observability:
  - Emit standardized metrics and logs for probe transitions (e.g., readiness_changed, liveness_failures_total) to support alerting and SLOs.

This decision ensures orchestration systems can reliably determine startup success and ongoing health, enabling safe rollouts, autoscaling, and resilient recovery.

## Decision:
We will adopt Hapi as our Node.js web framework. Hapi’s opinionated, modular architecture (plugins, server methods, route scopes) enables clean separation of concerns and parallel development without route or middleware collisions. Its first-class features—built-in routing, validation with @hapi/joi, authentication/authorization strategies, request lifecycle controls, and caching via catbox—reduce custom boilerplate and improve consistency across services. This facilitates standardisation, code reuse, and maintainability as our team and service portfolio grow. Hapi’s configuration-over-code approach, rich ecosystem, and strong operational characteristics (input/output validation, detailed error handling, and observability hooks) help us ship secure, reliable services faster while aligning with our goal of using the best tool for scalable Node web applications.

## Decision:
We will establish and mandate a CCS Common Security Controls Baseline (CSCB) for all new and materially changed services, aligned to the HMG Security Policy Framework (SPF), NCSC guidance, and UK GDPR. The CSCB will provide a single, department-agnostic control set that suppliers and internal teams must implement and evidence.

Key elements:
- Controls catalogue: Base on ISO/IEC 27001/27002 and NCSC Cloud Security Principles, with mappings to NIST 800-53 for completeness and to common departmental profiles. Include privacy controls aligned to UK GDPR.
- Classification tiers: Define OFFICIAL and OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE overlays and optional service overlays (e.g., payment, user data, integration) to tailor assurance proportionately.
- Assurance model: Require evidence via standard artefacts (SoA, risk register, threat model, DPIA, test results), independent testing (CREST/ CHECK where appropriate), and supplier attestations (Cyber Essentials Plus minimum). Continuous assurance through policy-as-code and automated compliance checks in CI/CD and cloud (e.g., OPA, CSP native config rules).
- Secure-by-default delivery: Provide reference architectures, IaC guardrails, baseline hardened images, logging/monitoring standards, and vulnerability/patch SLAs. Mandate zero-trust principles for identity, device, and network access.
- Third-party and SaaS: Apply the same baseline using a shared due-diligence questionnaire mapped to CSCB; require evidencing of controls and contractual security obligations.
- Exceptions: Any deviation requires a documented risk acceptance by the CCS SIRO/CISO with time-bound remediation.
- Governance and lifecycle: Publish CSCB v1.0 with control mappings and assurance templates. Review at least annually or on major SPF/NCSC updates. Maintain a controls library and reusable patterns.

All consuming departments may retain additional bespoke requirements; where present, we will map and reconcile them to the CSCB to minimize duplication and enable a single assurance pack per service.

## Decision:
- Host all technical SDK documentation in the SDK GitHub repository under a /docs directory; remove or migrate any non-SDK material to the public website.
- Scope split:
  - In-repo (technical): README (landing), intro (quick start), concepts (core abstractions), guides/how-to, reference (API/godoc links), modules (per-module specs), spec (protocol/module specs), clients (CLI/REST/SDK usage), architecture (ADRs and internal design), translations, migration/upgrade notes, changelog.
  - Website (high-level): FAQs, whitepaper(s), positioning/overview, ecosystem, non-technical and cross-product content.
- Apply the same pattern to each framework/tool: each repo owns its technical docs; the website aggregates only high-level cross-cutting content and links back to repo docs.
- Website navigation sources only selected SDK sections (README, intro, concepts, clients, guides) from the repo; architecture and internal specs are excluded from the website by default but remain linkable.
- Version documentation per SDK release (e.g., docs/versions/vX.Y) with “latest” synced to the default branch; website build selects a version to surface and provides version switcher.
- Enforce docs-as-code workflow: changes via pull requests, mandatory review by CODEOWNERS per docs area, CI linting/links/structure checks, and preview builds.
- Establish deprecation/migration policy for moved content with redirects and “Moved to …” stubs to prevent link rot.
- Default to public visibility; sensitive internal runbooks remain in private repos but follow the same structure.
- Define ownership and maintenance SLAs for each section to prevent staleness.

## Decision:
We will package and deploy the application as Docker containers built via multi-stage Dockerfiles into immutable images. Images will be tagged with semantic versions plus the Git commit SHA (e.g., 2.3.0+abc123) and never use “latest” in production.

A CI/CD pipeline will build, scan, and sign images, then push them to a managed container registry. Deployments will be automated to a managed Kubernetes cluster using Helm, leveraging rolling updates by default and blue/green when schema or compatibility risks exist. Pods will define readiness/liveness probes and resource limits/requests for safe, zero-downtime rollouts.

Configuration will be injected via environment variables and secrets from a managed secrets store; images remain twelve-factor and stateless. We will enforce non-root containers, read-only filesystems where possible, and regular base image updates via automated dependency tools. Critical CVE rebuilds will be triggered automatically.

Update strategy: immutable image tags, imagePullPolicy=IfNotPresent in stable environments (with unique tags ensuring new pulls), and Always in CI/test. Rollbacks will be instantaneous via Helm version history. For local development, docker-compose will mirror production services.

This approach enables simple, repeatable, and low-risk updates through immutable artifacts and orchestrated rollouts.

## Decision:
Adopt TOML as the sole configuration format for stentor.

Rationale:
- TOML is purpose-built for configuration, with deterministic, stricter parsing that reduces ambiguity and class of errors common in YAML (implicit typing, anchors, indentation sensitivity).
- Strong cross-language ecosystem and stable spec enable reliable parsing across tools.
- Human-writable with clear semantics for primitives, tables, and arrays; nested structures remain readable with explicit tables.

Implementation details:
- Config file name: stentor.toml (default), overridable via CLI flag and environment variable.
- Enforce a minimal schema (types, required keys, allowed enums) validated at startup; provide a stentor validate command.
- Version the config with a top-level config_version field; include migration helpers (stentor migrate) for breaking changes.
- Support environment-variable interpolation for secrets and deployment-specific values, with explicit syntax and documented precedence.
- Provide a reference example and a machine-checkable schema in docs.
- Do not support YAML in core to avoid dual-format divergence; offer an optional one-time conversion tool for users preferring YAML.

This choice optimizes safety, determinism, and long-term maintainability while remaining approachable for users.

## Decision:
- Implement the frontend in TypeScript (strict mode) rather than plain JavaScript.
- Rationale: Type safety reduces runtime bugs, improves refactoring confidence, and enhances developer productivity through richer IDE support and auto-completion. It scales better for a multi-developer codebase and long-term maintenance.
- Tooling: Adopt a standard tsconfig with strict type checking, path aliases, and incremental builds. Enforce conventions via ESLint (typescript-eslint), Prettier, and type-aware rules in CI.
- Interop: Use type-safe APIs by generating TypeScript types from our backend schema (OpenAPI/GraphQL) to ensure contract consistency and reduce integration errors.
- Migration/Velocity: Permit isolated JavaScript files only for build tooling or third-party integration shims, but application code must be TypeScript.
- Onboarding: Provide a starter template with common types, utility types, and patterns (e.g., React hooks, state management) to reduce boilerplate and ensure consistency.

## Decision:
Adopt Rails ActiveStorage for image uploads and processing.

- Rationale: It is the Rails-standard, well-supported, tightly integrated with ActiveRecord (our chosen ORM), requires minimal boilerplate, supports direct uploads, and works with our target storage providers (e.g., Amazon S3). Paperclip is deprecated; Shrine offers greater flexibility but adds complexity we do not currently need.

- Implementation choices:
  - Storage: S3 in production (optionally fronted by CloudFront), local disk in development/test.
  - Direct uploads: Enable ActiveStorage direct uploads to offload app servers.
  - Processing: Use the image_processing gem with libvips for performant variants/thumbnails.
  - Backgrounding: Process variants and purges via ActiveJob/Sidekiq.
  - Security: Enforce content-type and size validations at the model/controller level; consider antivirus scanning (e.g., ClamAV) if required.
  - Performance: Avoid N+1 by preloading attachments (e.g., with_attached_* helpers); leverage CDN caching for variants.
  - Migrations/Setup: Use rails active_storage:install and environment-specific service configs.

- Future considerations: If we later require advanced upload control (pause/resume, persistent client-side cache, custom pipelines), re-evaluate Shrine for targeted components; otherwise continue with ActiveStorage as the default.

## Decision:
Adopt a Clean/Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) architecture to separate concerns and maximize maintainability.

- Layers and responsibilities:
  - Domain: Pure business model (entities, value objects, domain services), domain events, invariants. No framework or IO code.
  - Application: Use cases/interactors orchestrating domain behavior, transactions, and security rules. Defines ports (interfaces) for external services/persistence. Stateless, thin coordination layer.
  - Presentation (UI): Views/Controllers/Presenters/ViewModels responsible for rendering, input handling, and mapping to/from application DTOs. No business rules.
  - Infrastructure: Adapters implementing ports (repositories, gateways, message brokers, file/HTTP), persistence mappers, frameworks.

- Dependency rule:
  - Only inward dependencies: Infrastructure and UI depend on Application; Application depends on Domain; Domain depends on nothing. No lateral or outward calls.
  - Communication via ports (interfaces) defined in the Application layer; adapters live in Infrastructure.

- Data and mapping:
  - Use DTOs/Commands/Queries for UI↔Application boundaries.
  - Use persistence mappers to translate between Domain entities and storage models; no ORM leakage into Domain/Application.

- Module structure:
  - /domain, /application, /infrastructure, /presentation (or platform-specific UI modules).
  - Feature-first subpackages to co-locate related domain, use cases, and adapters where appropriate without breaking dependency rules.

- Cross-cutting concerns:
  - Handled via decorators/middlewares/aspects (logging, metrics, auth, caching, validation) at boundaries, not inside domain entities.

- State management:
  - UI state contained in Presentation; business state in Domain; transactional consistency managed by Application layer.

- Testing strategy:
  - Domain: fast unit tests.
  - Application: use case tests with mocked ports; contract tests for ports.
  - Infrastructure: integration tests per adapter; end-to-end tests across boundaries.

- Enforcement:
  - Dependency injection for runtime wiring.
  - Static checks (e.g., ArchUnit/module boundary rules) and CI to prevent rule violations.

## Decision:
Treat the KeySet returned by kdbGet() as the complete, authoritative dataset for the session. Lookups are strictly read-only: ksLookup must only return keys that are already present and must not create, synthesize, or compute default values. If a key is not present, ksLookup returns no result and the caller is responsible for providing defaults explicitly via separate mechanisms.

Internal maintenance (e.g., hash rebuilds) may occur during access and can affect iteration order or iterator validity. Applications must not rely on stable iteration state across lookups; reinitialize iteration as needed and avoid assumptions about ordering or pointer stability.

## Decision:
Automate the refresh of profiles-db from nightly ETL outputs with built-in validation and safe deployment.

- Nightly pipeline: On completion of the Syndication and POMI ETLs, trigger a CI/CD pipeline that consumes the generated outputs as versioned artifacts.
- Data validation gate: Before updating profiles-db, run automated validations including schema conformance, referential integrity, null/range checks on key fields, row-count deltas vs previous load, and source freshness checks. Validation results are published and stored.
- Build and publish: If validations pass, build a new immutable profiles-db artifact (e.g., container image or seed bundle) with the updated data and tag it with date and version.
- Deployment strategy: Automatically deploy to Staging first. Run smoke tests and basic read performance checks. If successful, promote to Production. If any validation or post-deploy checks fail, abort and notify; Production remains on the last known-good version with an automated rollback available.
- Observability and audit: Persist validation reports, checksums, artifact digests, and change logs; emit metrics and alerts to the monitoring stack.
- Manual override: Allow manual approval steps or freeze windows when required.
- Decoupling: Externalize configuration for artifact locations and credentials; avoid embedding data in application code to remove the need for manual repo updates.
- Security and access: Ensure least-privilege access for pipelines to read ETL outputs and write deployments.

This decision ensures daily GP data updates are reliable, validated, and low-touch, eliminating manual updates and reducing risk.

## Decision:
Adopt a ClusterTaskManager as the single logical Task API for the whole cluster, replacing per-node TaskManager ownership.

- Persist all Task definitions, metadata, and lifecycle states in a shared TaskStore (e.g., Cassandra/PostgreSQL) as the source of truth with globally unique TaskIds.
- Dispatch execution via a message broker-backed work queue (e.g., RabbitMQ). Scheduling enqueues tasks; worker executors on each node consume from the queue.
- Enforce single-run semantics with distributed locks/leases stored in the TaskStore (or broker exclusive-claim) with TTL/renewal to prevent duplicate execution and enable safe recovery.
- Implement at-least-once delivery with idempotent task handlers; use ACK/NACK and visibility timeouts to requeue on worker failure or node crash.
- Maintain cluster-wide listing, filtering, and detail retrieval by reading from the TaskStore; all state transitions (created, started, progress, completed, failed, canceled) are written atomically.
- Emit task lifecycle events onto the event bus to support cross-node await, monitoring, and UI projections; include heartbeats/progress for near–real time updates.
- Preserve existing public TaskManager API; provide a compatibility wrapper on each node that proxies to the ClusterTaskManager to avoid intrusive changes.
- Provide backpressure and fairness via prefetch limits, priority queues, and optional routing keys; support targeted execution (affinity/capabilities) by tagging tasks and binding queues accordingly.
- Add operational safeguards: deduplication keys, retries with exponential backoff and dead-letter queues, metrics/tracing, and admin controls (pause/resume/cancel).

## Decision:
Adopt the ecosystem-native dependency manager and lockfile for the project’s primary language (e.g., npm/pnpm/Yarn for Node.js, Poetry/pip-tools for Python, Maven/Gradle for Java, Cargo for Rust). Enforce deterministic builds by committing lockfiles and enabling CI checks to fail on missing/outdated lockfiles.

Automate dependency updates using Renovate (preferred) or Dependabot with policies that:
- Pin direct dependencies to exact versions; allow compatible semver ranges only where necessary.
- Batch non-breaking updates; isolate major updates behind separate PRs with automated testing.
- Schedule updates and security patches regularly.

Introduce a private package proxy/cache (e.g., GitHub Packages, JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus) to improve reliability, caching, and provenance, with provenance/attestations enabled where supported.

Codify dependency policies in code review and CI:
- Block ad-hoc edits to manifest/lockfiles outside Renovate/approved workflows.
- Run vulnerability and license scans on every PR and release.
- Generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for releases.

Document a minimal workflow for adding/updating dependencies and bootstrap scripts to ensure developers use the sanctioned toolchain consistently (including Node/Python/Java version managers as applicable). This standardizes dependency management, improves security, and ensures reproducible builds.

## Decision:
Introduce a first-class, platform-agnostic “release” capability in sfpowerscripts. We will add:
- A new CLI command: sfpowerscripts release, which orchestrates fetch → validate → deploy → post-deploy → changelog generation in a single, idempotent workflow.
- A declarative Release Definition (YAML/JSON) that describes artifacts/packages, version constraints or channels (rc/prod), target environments, approvals/gates, pre/post steps, rollout strategy, and failure/rollback policies.
- Built-in artifact resolution (from defined feeds/registries), environment-specific overrides, and support for parallel/serial stage execution.
- Automatic changelog generation tied to the resolved artifact set and commit SHAs/tags, published with release metadata (version, artifacts, environments, timestamps, outcomes) to a release registry for auditability.
- Options for dry-run, resume-on-retry, and partial-failure handling with clear exit codes for CI integration.

Existing commands (fetch, deploy, changelog) remain available but are treated as building blocks; pipelines on any CI/CD platform will invoke the single release command with a Release Definition. This unifies behavior across platforms, removes bespoke pipeline logic, standardizes release audit/provenance, and provides consistent approvals and gates regardless of the underlying CI/CD system.

## Decision:
loadStream will return a transaction-scoped readable stream whose lifecycle is bound to the ambient transaction. The stream must be fully consumed and closed before the transaction completes; any attempt to use it after commit/rollback will throw. The API requires an explicit transaction context and enforces:

- Snapshot-bound reads: the stream is backed by a cursor fixed to the transaction’s snapshot/isolation level.
- Failure propagation: any read error (e.g., stream deleted) triggers a transaction failure, ensuring atomic read-then-write flows.
- Deterministic retries: on transaction retry, previously created streams are automatically closed/disposed and new streams are created under the retried transaction.
- Resource safety: the transaction manager auto-closes any unclosed streams on commit/rollback to prevent leaks; using try-with-resources/using is recommended.
- Scope enforcement: streaming outside the transaction boundary is prohibited. Callers needing data post-commit must materialize it inside the transaction.
- Limits/guardrails: configurable caps on concurrently open streams per transaction and timeouts to avoid long-lived cursors.

This design supports safe, consistent in-transaction streaming, aligns failure domains (read errors abort the transaction), and ensures predictable behavior under retries while preventing resource leakage.

## Decision:
Run CI/CD tooling inside each programme cluster and deprecate the separate “tools” cluster. Concourse will handle both CI and CD, replacing Flux (and our fork). Pipelines will execute in-cluster and apply changes using Kubernetes service accounts scoped to their target namespace, eliminating the need to distribute cluster-modifying credentials outside the cluster.

Key elements:
- Concourse deployment per programme cluster; one Concourse Team maps 1:1 with a Kubernetes Namespace (RBAC-synced), providing least-privilege access and clear multi-tenancy boundaries.
- Pipelines use in-cluster service account tokens (projected, short-lived) with namespace-scoped Roles/RoleBindings; no cluster-admin for tenants.
- Git commit verification and provenance checks are implemented via Concourse resources/steps (GPG/Sigstore) instead of Flux; Notary image signing integrated into pipelines.
- Container registry, image scanning, and Notary services are provided from within the programme cluster or via tightly-scoped, cluster-local endpoints; credentials are namespace-scoped.
- Visibility and troubleshooting are improved by exposing deployment status, logs, and history through the Concourse UI and metrics.
- Standardized pipeline templates and tasks reduce configuration drift; per-environment differences are expressed as values/params, not pipeline duplication.
- Secure-by-default posture: network policies around Concourse, read-only SCM deploy keys, IRSA/Workload Identity for cloud access, and audit logging of apply actions.
- Migration: run Concourse CD in parallel with Flux until parity is proven, then remove Flux and revoke external credentials.

This approach reduces operational complexity, consolidates control planes, improves developer visibility, and ensures that only in-cluster, least-privilege credentials can modify cluster state.

## Decision:
Adopt PostgreSQL as the primary database and use its built-in full‑text search (FTS) for multilingual search with first‑class support for Czech.

- Use PostgreSQL FTS with per-language text search configurations. For Czech, use pg_catalog.czech where available; otherwise define a custom ispell/hunspell dictionary from system cs_CZ dictionaries to improve stemming and hyphenation handling. Configure custom stopword lists per language.
- Enable extensions: unaccent (accent-insensitive search) and pg_trgm (trigram indexes) to support “contains”/“startsWith” use cases alongside FTS.
- Store language metadata per document/field; generate and persist a tsvector column per text field using the appropriate language configuration at write time. Create GIN indexes on tsvector columns and GiST/GIN or GIN_trgm indexes on frequently filtered text fields for prefix/substring queries.
- Support synonyms via PostgreSQL synonym dictionaries bound into the language configurations (managed as versioned synonym files).
- Query pattern: combine to_tsquery/plainto_tsquery (language-specific) against tsvector columns for relevance-ranked results, with optional trigram predicates for partial matches. Apply unaccent in both indexing and querying paths to keep behavior consistent.
- This keeps the stack simple (no additional search service), provides robust Czech and broader multilingual search, and scales with proper indexing and vacuum/analyze/autovacuum tuning. If future requirements outgrow PostgreSQL FTS (e.g., advanced cross-lingual relevance or complex aggregations), we will reassess introducing a dedicated search engine.

## Decision:
Rufus will enforce encapsulation at both package and module boundaries through a combination of packaging, type-level annotations, directory conventions, and CI enforcement.

- Package boundary
  - Require package.json “exports” maps for all packages. Only declared subpaths are importable; deep paths are blocked by Node/TS resolution.
  - Provide a Rufus command to generate/validate exports maps from declared public barrels (e.g., src/index.ts and src/public/*/index.ts).
  - Disallow publishing files outside the exports map via files or .npmignore validation.

- Module boundary
  - Use explicit named exports only. Non-exported declarations are private by default.
  - Adopt TSDoc tags to classify surface: @public, @beta, @alpha, @internal. Default to @internal when absent in internal modules.
  - Integrate API Extractor to:
    - Validate that only @public/@beta/@alpha APIs are exported by public barrels.
    - Fail CI if @internal-propagated types leak into the public API (e.g., via type positions).
    - Produce trimmed .d.ts rollups containing only the public API.
  - Enable TypeScript stripInternal (or API Extractor equivalent) for declaration emit.

- Directory and export structure
  - Two-root convention: src/public and src/internal. Only src/index.ts and src/public/**/index.ts may re-export to the package surface. src/internal/** is never re-exported.
  - Re-export rules: index files only re-export immediate children; wildcard for index-to-index; explicit named lists for non-index files.
  - No default exports in public API.

- Linting and CI
  - Enforce “no deep imports” from consumers via ESLint (no-restricted-imports) and unit tests/examples that import only from the package root or approved subpaths.
  - Enforce internal access: imports from src/internal/** are only allowed within the same package; external packages cannot import them.
  - Provide a Rufus CI check that compares the built .d.ts public rollup to a committed API baseline to detect breaking changes.

- Documentation and tooling
  - Generate public API docs from the public .d.ts rollup only.
  - Provide a Rufus scaffold that creates public/internal directories, index files, and exports map stubs.

This ensures private identifiers are unreachable to consumers, keeps public surfaces explicit and reviewable, and automates enforcement in development and CI.

## Decision:
- Adopt Next.js (React + TypeScript) as the primary web framework for the web client.
- Rationale:
  - Performance and SEO: Built-in SSR/SSG/ISR, image/font optimization, and edge-ready middleware deliver fast, crawlable pages.
  - Developer experience: First-class TypeScript, file-based routing, layouts, server components, excellent docs, and a rich ecosystem of UI/tooling.
  - Scalability: Supports modular architecture, monorepos (via Turborepo), code-splitting, dynamic routing, and incremental static regeneration for large content sets.
  - Deployment flexibility: Optimized for Vercel but portable to any Node/Docker environment; supports serverless/edge runtimes.
  - Standards and longevity: React ecosystem maturity, wide talent pool, and enterprise adoption reduce onboarding and long-term maintenance risks.
  - Mobile reuse: Logic and components can be shared with React Native/Expo where feasible.
- Constraints and practices:
  - Use the App Router (stable features) with React Server Components; defer experimental Server Actions unless justified.
  - Enforce strict TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier, and testing (Vitest/Jest + React Testing Library) baselines.
  - Follow accessibility and internationalization best practices using Next’s i18n routing.
  - Implement PWA where offline capability is required using next-pwa or equivalent.
- Risk mitigation:
  - Avoid vendor lock-in by not relying on Vercel-only APIs; keep infra portable.
  - Isolate domain logic from React components to reduce framework coupling.
  - Monitor Next.js release notes for breaking changes and schedule regular upgrades.
- Alternatives considered (not chosen): CRA (maintenance/obsolescence), Remix (great routing but smaller ecosystem), Angular (higher onboarding cost for team versed in React), SvelteKit/Nuxt (smaller hiring pool, less alignment with planned stack).

- Chosen Alternative: Use ETags with If-Match for optimistic locking.

- Rationale:
  - Avoids clock skew and precision issues inherent in Last-Modified/If-Unmodified-Since.
  - Provides opaque, versioned concurrency control with minimal payload and high throughput.
  - Clear, standard HTTP semantics enable consistent client recovery flows.

- Decision Details:
  - Every GET/HEAD on a singular resource returns a strong ETag representing the current version (opaque value, e.g., incrementing row_version or hash of persisted content).
  - Mutating requests (PUT/PATCH/DELETE) MUST include If-Match with the ETag obtained from the most recent GET. Requests without If-Match are rejected with 428 Precondition Required.
  - If the ETag provided in If-Match does not match the current resource version, respond 412 Precondition Failed with a message indicating the resource has changed. Include a link or instruction for the client to refetch the resource.
  - On match, apply the mutation and return 200/204 with the updated ETag.
  - For list endpoints, return weak ETags only for caching; they are not valid for concurrency control.
  - ETag values are opaque to clients; do not encode PII or internal schema details.

- Implementation Notes:
  - Backing store should maintain a version column (e.g., bigint row_version) updated atomically on each write. Use this as the ETag source to avoid expensive hashing.
  - Enforce If-Match at the API boundary and in the service layer to prevent bypass via internal calls.
  - For partial updates (PATCH), ETag validation is identical to full updates.
  - Document client recovery: on 412, refetch resource to get the new ETag, present differences to the user, allow retry/merge.
  - Log conflict events for observability and tune UX flows.

- Consequences:
  - Slight client complexity (must echo ETag), offset by improved data integrity and user experience.
  - Eliminates “last write wins” surprises, scales well in distributed environments without synchronized clocks.

## Decision:
Adopt 1Password as the single source of truth for developer-consumed secrets needed for local EASi app development.

- Create a shared “EASi Dev Secrets” vault containing all developer-facing API keys and credentials. Access is provisioned via group membership with enforced MFA and least-privilege permissions (View only by default; Edit limited to designated maintainers).
- All secret updates and rotations must be performed in 1Password first. Email or Slack DMs must not be used to transmit secret values. Rotation announcements will be posted in the team Slack channel referencing the 1Password item (no plaintext values).
- Use 1Password item history and audit logs for traceability; include metadata (owner, rotation cadence, upstream contact/URL, last verified date) in each item. Tag items that require periodic verification and set 1Password reminders where supported.
- For engineers who prefer CLI access, allow optional use of 1Password CLI (op) with device-bound authentication; no additional infrastructure knowledge is required.
- For application/runtime secrets, continue storing and retrieving via AWS SSM/Parameter Store; where developer access is required, mirror the human-readable value in 1Password with a clear pointer to the authoritative runtime location. Do not require engineers to have AWS credentials to obtain local-only secrets.
- Establish an SLO: secret changes must be reflected in 1Password within 2 business hours of rotation detection. Break-glass procedure: on unexpected rotations, a maintainer posts a link to the updated 1Password item.
- Periodically review vault membership and item validity (quarterly). Remove stale secrets and enforce unique, scoped credentials per integration where feasible.

## Decision:
Each ml-aoi Item will reference exactly one label Item.

- Ensures a simple, predictable ingestion model: all label metadata can be copied onto the ml-aoi Item, making it a valid STAC Label Item and immediately compatible with existing label-aware tooling.
- Avoids forcing consumers to crawl catalogs or interpret multi-source “meta-label” constructs, reducing implementation complexity and failure modes.
- Keeps validation straightforward (schema: at most one label link; required mirroring of key label metadata onto ml-aoi properties).

Support for multi-class or multi-source labels will be handled via a preprocessing step that merges multiple label sources into a single STAC Label Item per ml-aoi. We will provide guidance and utilities for this merge (e.g., union of FeatureCollections or configuration-driven composition). The single referenced label may be external; data duplication is not required.

This decision preserves a clean contract for consumers today while leaving room to introduce a future, explicit “aggregate label” construct or extension if native multi-label per-item support becomes necessary.

## Decision:
We will support defects raised against either:
- a specific property (property-level), or
- a communal location within a scheme (communal-level).

Data model:
- Scheme: minimal entity created by New Build Team.
- Property: child of Scheme; when available, reference Property API/Addresses API identifiers (e.g., UPRN/PropertyId); store an address snapshot for operational use.
- CommunalLocation: child of Scheme; does not require a formal property record; includes:
  - name/type (e.g., lift, corridor, car park, roof),
  - free-text location descriptor/access info,
  - optional geo point and address snapshot,
  - optional related property references (for impact) without enforcing hierarchy beyond scheme.

Defect:
- Must reference exactly one Location, where Location is oneOf(Property, CommunalLocation).
- Stores an immutable address/location snapshot for contractor accuracy.
- May include related properties set for reporting (many-to-many) but not required for triage.

APIs:
- Expose a unified Defect resource with a polymorphic location payload (property or communal).
- Publish stable external references to Property API/Addresses API where known; otherwise use internal IDs with future upsert/migration capability.
- Do not couple to Repairs API for property data; use Property API/Addresses API when available.

Scope now:
- Manual creation of Schemes, Properties, and CommunalLocations by the team (MVP).
- No modeling of cores/blocks/sub-blocks initially due to inconsistent definitions.

Migration path:
- When Addresses API provides canonical hierarchy, we will link/migrate Scheme/Property/CommunalLocation via external identifiers, preserving existing defect-location links and snapshots.
- Maintain backward-compatible API contracts to avoid breaking dependent services.

Rationale:
- Meets user need for accurate contractor location and access.
- Minimizes technical debt by avoiding Repairs API coupling.
- Keeps defect data reusable across services while allowing future alignment to the strategic Addresses API.

We will extend the bindings API to be operation-aware and bi-directional.

- Introduce a standardized request/response contract:
  - BindingRequest: { resource (ORID/URI), operation, mode, payload, parameters, headers, correlationId, timeout }
  - BindingResponse: { status, payload/stream, metadata, headers, diagnostics, correlationId }
- Define canonical enums:
  - Operation: Read, Write, Create, Update, Delete, List, Invoke, Subscribe, Ack/Nack
  - Mode: In, Out, InOut (default inferred from Operation; Write/Create/Update/Delete=Out, Read/List/Subscribe=In, Invoke=InOut)
- Capability discovery:
  - Each binding must declare SupportedOperations and SupportedModes at init; attempting an unsupported operation returns NotSupported.
- Backward compatibility:
  - Existing one-way calls map to Operation=Write, Mode=Out when operation is omitted.
  - Responses remain optional for Out-only ops; for In/InOut ops, payload/stream is required on success.
- Transport and SDK updates:
  - gRPC/HTTP and language SDKs adopt the new envelopes; streaming responses supported for large payloads (e.g., blob reads).
  - CorrelationId propagated end-to-end for tracing and retries.
- Error and retry semantics:
  - Standardized error codes (NotFound, Conflict, Unauthorized, RateLimited, NotSupported, Transient) with retry hints in metadata.
- Resource addressing:
  - Prefer ORID/URI to decouple from physical endpoints and enable operator-driven reconfiguration without client changes.

This enables scenarios like getting a blob via BindingRequest(operation=Read, resource=blob://account/container/key) and returning a stream, while keeping existing write-only flows intact.

## Decision:
Adopt a concise, consistent, and machine-friendly repository naming convention across all GitHub organizations.

- General format: <domain|solution|platform>-<product|component>-<purpose>[-<tech>]
- Character set: lowercase a–z, digits, hyphens only; no underscores, spaces, or special characters.
- Length: <= 100 characters; prefer 15–40 characters.
- Separators: use single hyphens; no leading/trailing/multiple consecutive hyphens.
- Clarity: use meaningful words; avoid internal abbreviations unless standardized and documented.
- Versioning: do not embed versions in repo names.
- Ownership: include the owning domain/solution as the leading segment when applicable.
- Tech qualifier: add only when necessary to disambiguate (e.g., -python, -terraform, -helm).
- Type suffixes (standardized):
  - -svc: deployable service/application
  - -lib: reusable library/package
  - -cli: command-line tool
  - -ui: frontend/UI
  - -api: API definition/contract only
  - -ops: operational tooling/runbooks
  - -infra: infrastructure as code
  - -config: environment-agnostic configuration
  - -poc or -spike: experiments (short-lived)
  - -docs: documentation only
- Forbidden: customer names, secrets, environments (dev/test/prod), regions, ticket IDs, dates.
- Examples:
  - odh-data-ingest-svc
  - dat-event-schema-api
  - supplychain-order-matcher-svc
  - pricing-core-lib-python
  - retail-demand-forecast-ui
  - payments-shared-infra-terraform
  - telemetry-pipeline-config
- Cross-org alignment:
  - ODH/generic tooling: prefix odh- or dat- respectively.
  - Solution-specific: start with solution abbreviation (e.g., sc- for Supply Chain).
  - Configuration repos in config org: include related GCP project stem and end with -config.

All new repositories must follow this convention; existing repos should be migrated when touched.

## Decision:
Adopt a single, structured logging standard and API for the entire codebase and prohibit ad‑hoc logging.

- Provide a lightweight ElektraLog API with macros: ELEKTRA_LOG_TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL. Macros capture file:line, function, module, and thread id automatically.
- Prefer structured, key–value logging (message plus fields) with stable field names; support printf-style formatting for convenience.
- Default output is human-readable to stderr; support configurable sinks: syslog/journald (Unix), file rotation, and JSON lines for machine consumption. Only one dependency-free core is mandatory; platform sinks are optional plugins.
- Configure level, sink, and format at runtime (env vars and config) and at build time (compile flags). Production default is WARN and above; TRACE/DEBUG compiled out unless enabled.
- Define canonical levels and usage guidelines: TRACE for verbose internals, DEBUG for developer diagnostics, INFO for state changes, WARN for recoverable issues, ERROR for failures, FATAL for process-terminating conditions.
- Include correlation/request ids when available; never log secrets or PII. Provide redaction helpers and a denylist of keys. Logs must not change program behavior.
- Disallow logging in tight hot paths unless TRACE and compiled out; prefer assertions for programmer errors and logs for runtime diagnostics.
- Introduce a linter/convention check and code review rule: no new ad‑hoc prints, only ElektraLog; ensure consistent messages and fields. Migrate existing logs to the new API and remove unusable/inconsistent variants.

Use styled-jsx as the default styling mechanism.

- Rationale: styled-jsx scopes CSS to components by default, eliminating selector collisions and unintended cascade effects without relying on naming conventions like BEM. It is built into Next.js, supports SSR out of the box, and keeps styles co-located with components.
- Global fallbacks: When consuming external design systems (e.g., GOV.UK) or app-wide resets, use :global blocks or a dedicated global stylesheet. Keep global usage minimal and well-documented.
- Theming/overrides: Expose customization via CSS custom properties (tokens) and component props. Allow a className prop passthrough for escape-hatch overrides if necessary.
- Developer experience: Write real CSS (including media queries and pseudo-selectors) inline next to components. Enforce scoping and usage via linting (eslint-plugin-styled-jsx).
- Performance: styled-jsx compiles to scoped CSS with deterministic class names; no runtime selector collisions.

This approach meets our goals: strong isolation, baked-in defaults, controlled override surface, and optional global integration when required.

## Decision:
Yes—support runtime overrides via command line flags and environment variables with a clear precedence model and guardrails.

- Precedence: command-line flags > environment variables > config file > built-in defaults.
- Scope: only documented, whitelisted keys are overridable; unknown keys are rejected with a startup error.
- Validation: all sources pass through the same schema validation (types, ranges, enums, inter-field constraints). Startup fails fast on invalid overrides with actionable messages.
- Secrets: prefer environment variables (or secret managers) for sensitive values; flags for non-sensitive operational toggles. Never echo secret values in logs.
- Immutability: overrides are evaluated once at startup; configuration is immutable thereafter.
- Observability: on startup, log the effective configuration with source annotations per key (redacting secrets). Provide a dry-run/–validate mode to verify overrides without running the app.
- Environment controls: production defaults favor config file or env-managed secrets; flags may be disabled or restricted in production deployments.
- Compatibility: maintain backward compatibility for existing env var names; introduce deprecation warnings and migration guidance when renaming keys.
- Portability: follow 12-factor principles, enabling container/orchestrator workflows; provide example manifests for env/flags usage.

This approach enables safe, auditable, and flexible configuration while preventing drift and misconfiguration.

## Decision:
Adopt a hierarchical multi-tenant RBAC model with clear actor scopes and APIs:

- Tenancy hierarchy: Instance > Consumer Site > Organization > Author/User.
- Roles and scopes:
  - Instance Manager (instance scope): provision/disable consumer sites, global settings, quotas, observability.
  - Consumer Site Admin (consumer-site scope): register organizations, configure branding/domains, manage site-level integrations and API keys.
  - Organization Manager (organization scope): manage authors, groups, sharing rules, catalogs/playlists, org-level settings.
  - Author (organization scope): create/manage videos, assets, metadata, access controls within org and shared collections granted by org managers.
  - Viewer (video/playback scope): view videos via time- and scope-limited tokens; no persistent account required in Marsha.

Identity and authentication:
- Admin/author/manager identities in Marsha via SSO (OIDC/SAML) with the consumer site’s IdP or Marsha-native accounts where SSO is unavailable.
- Viewers authenticate to the consumer site; playback authorized in Marsha via signed short-lived JWTs issued to the consumer site by Marsha (no viewer PII in Marsha).

Authorization:
- RBAC enforced at each scope with explicit permission sets (e.g., manage_instance, manage_consumer_site, manage_org, manage_authors, manage_video, publish_video, view_video).
