- Cross-organization sharing mediated by Organization Managers through share policies; no implicit cross-tenant access.

APIs and boundaries:
- Instance Admin API: instance-level lifecycle and observability.
- Consumer Site Admin API: org lifecycle, keys, configuration.
- Organization API: author/user management, libraries, video lifecycle.
- Playback API: token exchange, manifests, DRM/key services; CDN delivery.
- All administrative APIs require OAuth2 client credentials per scope; playback uses signed JWTs bound to resource IDs, IP/geofence (optional), and TTL.

Onboarding and lifecycle:
- Instance Managers onboard Consumer Sites; Consumer Site Admins create organizations; Org Managers invite Authors; viewers flow through consumer site embedding.
- Audit logging per action at each scope; exportable to SIEM.
- Data isolation by tenant; encryption at rest; soft-delete with retention controls.

This model cleanly maps actors to responsibilities, supports federated identity, minimizes viewer coupling, and scales operationally across many consumer sites and organizations.

## Decision:
Use dedicated, single-purpose, company-managed mailboxes as the root user email for every AWS account, following a strict, collision-free naming convention and strong MFA.

- Create one mailbox per account in the corporate email domain/subdomain (e.g., aws-root-<org>-<account-alias>-<account-id>@company.com), avoiding plus-addressing and shared lists. Each mailbox must be unique, not forwarded, and used exclusively for AWS root communications.
- Manage mailbox lifecycle centrally (automation where possible) with a definitive registry mapping account ID → root mailbox in our CMDB/infra repo. Creation and deprovisioning follow a documented runbook with approvals.
- Access to each mailbox is granted only via time-bound, audited, break-glass procedures to a small cloud platform admin group; no persistent delegates. All access is SSO-enforced with phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 hardware keys) and logging.
- Configure each AWS root user with hardware key MFA; disable SMS/TOTP for root. Store recovery materials (if any) under dual-control in the corporate secrets vault. Never store root passwords in code or wikis.
- Set AWS Organizations alternate contacts (billing, operations, security) to appropriate team addresses; do not use the root mailbox for general notifications.
- Prohibit personal or uncontrolled third-party email systems for root. Enforce the convention via account-creation automation and periodic compliance checks.

This provides a secure, uniform, auditable, and collision-free mechanism for root emails aligned with least privilege and phishing-resistant practices.

## Decision:
- Use PostgreSQL as the primary relational database for game records to leverage ACID guarantees, strong relational modeling, and mature SQL for complex reporting.
- Model the OLTP schema in 3NF (e.g., games, players, sessions/matches, events, scores) with clear foreign keys and constraints to ensure data integrity and consistent joins for reports.
- Implement time-based partitioning (e.g., by day/week/month) on high-volume tables such as game_events to improve write performance and facilitate data lifecycle management.
- Create targeted composite and partial indexes aligned to key reporting dimensions (e.g., by game_id, player_id, session_id, created_at) and use covering indexes for frequent aggregations.
- Provide read replicas for reporting workloads to isolate analytics from transactional throughput and reduce contention.
- Introduce materialized views for common aggregates (e.g., daily active users, retention, score distributions) with scheduled refresh; use query planner hints/ANALYZE and statistics maintenance to sustain performance.
- Enable CDC via logical replication or Debezium to feed a downstream analytics store (optional but recommended as reporting grows), where a star schema can be maintained for advanced BI without impacting OLTP.
- Enforce schema evolution via migrations (Flyway or Liquibase) and maintain versioned DDL/DML as code.
- Ensure durability and recoverability with automated backups and point-in-time recovery; apply row-level security where needed for PII and auditing.
- For development/testing, run PostgreSQL via Testcontainers to match production behavior; use fixtures and transactional tests for reliability.

## Decision:
We will split Snippets Service into two roles:

- Admin (authoring/build pipeline): Runs the Django application with its database and cache. It is the sole component responsible for creating and publishing bundles. On publish, the admin process writes versioned bundles to S3 and triggers CloudFront cache invalidations as needed. Admin has scoped IAM write permissions to the S3 bucket.

- User-facing (serve/redirect): Production instances will be a minimal, stateless redirect layer (e.g., Nginx or a lightweight service) that performs URL parsing/manipulation and issues redirects to CloudFront URLs for the pre-generated bundles in S3. These instances do not run Django and have no dependency on DB or cache. They require no AWS write permissions.

This separation removes unnecessary runtime complexity from the user-facing path, reduces operational risk and costs, and improves scalability and latency by delegating content delivery to CloudFront/S3. The deployment pipeline will ensure bundles are pre-generated by Admin, uploaded to S3 with immutable, cache-friendly keys, and that appropriate CloudFront invalidations or versioned URLs are used. Monitoring will verify redirect correctness and bundle availability.

We will introduce explicit API versioning and adopt Semantic Versioning for all public API releases.

- All breaking changes will be released as a new major API version (v2, v3, …). We will expose versions via the URL path (/api/v{major}) and advertise them via versioned media types to support content negotiation.
- Backward-compatible changes (additive fields/endpoints) will be released as minor versions; bug fixes as patch versions. Minor/patch releases must not break existing documented behavior.
- We will maintain at least N and N-1 major versions concurrently for a minimum deprecation window (e.g., 90 days) unless security concerns require faster retirement. Deprecations will be communicated in advance with migration guidance.
- A human-readable changelog and machine-readable OpenAPI specs will be published per version; breaking changes will be clearly labeled.
- CI/CD will enforce versioning rules and contract tests to prevent accidental breaking changes in non-major releases.

This approach provides predictable upgrades for third parties and our frontend while allowing us to evolve the API safely.

## Decision:
We will implement application-level, tamper-evident audit logging around all HSM operations to compensate for the lack of native per-sign operation logs.

- Introduce a dedicated “Signing Proxy” service as the sole component permitted to access the HSM. All signing/encryption requests must flow through this proxy.
- Enforce strict request provenance: the proxy requires and validates a correlation ID set (external request ID, internal trace ID, subject/connector ID), a purpose code, and a canonical payload digest before performing any HSM operation.
- Persist an append-only audit record for every HSM use, capturing: timestamp, key identifier/alias, operation type, payload digest, caller identity, originating connector, environment, and outcome. The audit record itself will be chained (hash-linked) and signed by an audit key distinct from the operational keys.
- Ship audit records to immutable storage (e.g., S3 with Object Lock and bucket-level MFA Delete) and to the central SIEM; enable CloudWatch log integrity verification and create alerts for gaps, out-of-order chains, or unexpected volumes.
- Correlate proxy audits with platform telemetry (CloudTrail, instance access logs, VPC Flow Logs) to establish end-to-end traceability.
- Block any direct HSM access outside the proxy, enforce rate limits and per-connector quotas, and run periodic reconciliation reports to detect anomalies.

This approach provides evidential monitoring until native HSM auditing becomes available.

## Decision:
Compute and serve the “issues average age” from a cached, precomputed metric rather than fetching all issues synchronously per request. Introduce a background aggregation pipeline that:
- Hydrates an issues metadata store per repository (issue id, created/closed timestamps, state) via rate-limit-aware pagination.
- Maintains a rolling aggregate (count, sum of ages for open/closed as needed) so the average can be computed without scanning all issues.

Implementation details:
- Persist issues and aggregates in our DB; expose an endpoint that returns the latest computed average and a freshness timestamp.
- Use a job queue to perform initial hydration and periodic incremental updates (scheduled and on-demand), respecting GitHub rate limits with adaptive backoff, ETag/If-None-Match conditional requests, and page checkpoints to resume.
- Use GitHub webhooks (issues, issue_comment where relevant) to trigger fine-grained updates that keep aggregates near-real-time without full re-scans.
- For first-time repos, return 202 Accepted with a “calculating” status (or a best-effort sampled estimate if configured), enqueue the job, and update clients when ready.
- Enforce per-repo concurrency limits and global rate budgets; optionally shard across multiple tokens with fairness.
- Cache results in Redis with short TTL to absorb traffic spikes; never compute averages inline on the request path.

This approach prevents abusive API usage, provides predictable latency, and scales to very large repositories.

## Decision:
Adopt Yarn v3+ (Berry) with Workspaces and Plug’n’Play (PnP) across the monorepo to eliminate ad‑hoc yarn link usage and prevent phantom/missed dependencies.

- Use workspace protocol (workspace:*) for all intra-repo package dependencies; local packages are auto-linked without yarn link.
- Enable Plug’n’Play to remove node_modules and strictly enforce that each package declares every dependency it imports.
- Add Yarn Constraints (constraints.pro) to enforce dependency declarations and versions across packages.
- Configure TypeScript Project References and composite builds for fast, correct cross-package builds; generate types on build.
- Add linting to detect missing/unused deps (eslint-plugin-import no-extraneous-dependencies) and consolidate to a shared ESLint config.
- Standardize developer tooling via Yarn SDKs (yarn dlx @yarnpkg/sdks) for editor/TS server compatibility under PnP.
- CI/CD: use Corepack to pin Yarn, cache .yarn/cache and build outputs, and run yarn workspaces foreach for build/test; optional Zero-Install via committed .yarn/cache.
- Provide migration guardrails: prohibit yarn link, hoisting, and path-mapped imports that bypass package boundaries; document import paths and publishing strategy.

This choice improves local DX, ensures correctness by construction, reduces setup time, and provides consistent behavior in local, CI, and production.

## Decision:
Adopt GNU Make as the single entry point for all repository tasks across development, build, and CI/CD. Define a canonical Makefile per repo that orchestrates language- or tool-specific commands (npm, pip/poetry, gradle, terraform, docker, etc.) via phony targets. CI/CD pipelines will invoke the same Make targets to ensure identical behavior and reduce drift.

Key conventions:
- Standard targets: setup, bootstrap, deps, lint, fmt, test, unit, integration, security, build, package, image, run, up/down, migrate, seed, clean, distclean, generate, docs, release, deploy, verify, ci.
- make help prints a self-documented target list with descriptions.
- Targets must be idempotent, non-interactive by default, and respect environment variables (override via .env and CI-provided vars).
- Delegate complex logic to scripts in scripts/ and keep Makefile declarative and thin.
- Prefer containerized execution (Docker/Compose) for reproducibility; provide DOCKER=1 toggle and consistent images/toolchains for CI and local use.
- Cache-aware builds (e.g., build artifacts, dependency caches) are centralized under a predictable .cache/ directory to simplify cleanup.
- Platform considerations: rely on GNU Make features only; for Windows developers, run via WSL2 or containerized make.
- Security and provenance: integrate pre-commit hooks and policy checks as Make targets; centralize SBOM, signing, and attestations.
- Documentation: README includes quick-start and target catalog; CI definitions reference only Make targets (no duplicated logic).

This standard provides one command surface for all actors (developers, CI, CD), improves discoverability and consistency, and minimizes pipeline-specific scripting.

## Decision:
Adopt “where-away” as the canonical package and project name.

- Publish to npm as where-away (unscoped). If availability changes, fall back to @your-scope/where-away without renaming the repo or binary.
- Provide a CLI with the binary name where-away and an alias whereaway for ergonomic invocation.
- Use where-away as the GitHub repository name and as the homepage/docs branding.
- Optionally reserve the whereaway npm name later via a thin wrapper package that depends on where-away, if still available.
- Include clear package metadata (description: “Lightweight, keyboard-navigable bookmarks”; keywords: bookmarks, keyboard, navigation, links, launcher) to aid discovery.
- Keep the name stable across artifacts (npm, repo, docs, binary) to avoid user confusion.

## Decision:
Adopt Keycloak as the central Identity and Access Management (IAM) platform to provide authentication and authorization across Wellcome Collection services. Keycloak will act as the organisation’s Identity Provider (IdP), exposing standards-based protocols—OpenID Connect (OIDC) and OAuth 2.0 as the primary interfaces, with SAML 2.0 available for legacy integrations. WebAuthn/FIDO2 and TOTP will be enabled for MFA.

We will integrate Keycloak with the Wellcome Library’s existing pool of registered members via user federation. Where a compatible directory (e.g., LDAP) exists, we will configure direct federation. If member data resides in a custom store (e.g., RDBMS), we will implement a Keycloak User Storage Provider to authenticate and map attributes without duplicating the source of truth. For services that require local accounts (e.g., public/non-member access), Keycloak will manage those natively with appropriate policies.

Authorization will use Keycloak’s roles, groups, and resource-based permissions (UMA 2.0 where appropriate). Claims-based mappings will provide downstream services with only the attributes they require. Where provisioning is necessary, we will use Keycloak’s Admin API/webhooks; SCIM may be added via a supported extension if needed.

Keycloak will be deployed in a highly available configuration (containerised, behind a reverse proxy, with externalised database and secrets management), enabling audit logging, GDPR-aligned data retention, and configurable consent screens. This solution provides an open, standards-compliant, extensible platform that integrates with existing membership data while avoiding vendor lock-in.

## Decision:
- Preserve and propagate the full original error. Our wrappers will accept and store the original error as `cause` (using Error.cause) and never discard properties.
- Replace current wrappers with enriched, serializable errors:
  - ValidationError({ message, details?, cause? })
  - CommercetoolsError({ message, statusCode?, details?, cause? })
- Do not override stack; use native stack from the original error. Use Error.captureStackTrace where available.
- Retain retry semantics, but compute from the most reliable source: prefer `statusCode` on the wrapper, else `cause.statusCode`, else `cause.code`/network indicators. Rule remains: retry if <200, 409, or >=500, plus network/timeouts.
- Standardize structured details captured from the cause when present:
  - name, code, statusCode, requestId/correlationId, request method/url, request payload size, response body (truncated), response headers (whitelisted), errors array, service/context (notification type, payment key, pspReference).
- Provide toJSON() on both errors to emit a redacted, structured payload suitable for logging/transport, excluding secrets (authorization, tokens, PANs) and truncating large fields.
- Logging policy: always log the wrapper with { err, err.cause } and enable logger option to include cause; emit a single structured log line per failure at error level, plus a concise notification acknowledgement.
- Backwards compatibility: keep existing `retry` boolean and message shape; deprecate direct construction without cause.
- Update notification handlers to:
  - Wrap any thrown error with the appropriate wrapper including cause and context.
  - Never mutate the original error.
  - Include IDs to enable join across systems (notificationItemId, merchantReference, payment key, pspReference).

## Decision:
Implement event transformers as processors rather than backends. Transformers will be stateless, composable units that can be appended to any backend’s (router/logger) processor pipeline. This reduces configuration nesting and cognitive load, promotes reuse across multiple backends, and simplifies ordering, testing, and incremental rollout. Configuration will live alongside existing processor pipelines, avoiding separate backend blocks and custom wiring. We will define clear processor interfaces (input/output contracts and idempotency guidelines), support deterministic ordering, and provide common utilities for error handling, metrics, and tracing within the processor framework. If a transformer requires I/O or persistent state, it must encapsulate this behind well-defined processor boundaries and timeouts, or trigger a future ADR to elevate it to a dedicated component.

## Decision:
Adopt a single, explicit, authoritative Agent State as the core of the Rust architecture, with all subsystems interacting through well-defined interfaces and an event-driven, unidirectional data flow.

Key elements:
- Central state store: a single AgentState struct (thread-safe, e.g., behind Arc<RwLock<...>> or an actor) representing all persistent and transient agent data.
- Unidirectional flow: inputs (UI, network, scheduler) emit Commands; pure reducers transform AgentState and emit Events; side-effect handlers (effects) respond to Events to perform I/O (network, disk, crypto), feeding new Commands back into the system.
- Strict boundaries: subsystems expose traits/ports; no cross-module shared mutability or implicit references. All dependencies are injected via interfaces to the state or effect ports.
- Determinism and testability: reducers are pure functions; Event logs enable replay, debugging, and reproducibility. State transitions are auditable.
- Concurrency model: a small number of orchestrating actors/tasks own mutation of AgentState; other tasks communicate via message channels. This prevents races and clarifies ownership.
- Extensibility: new capabilities are added by introducing new Commands/Events and reducers/effects without coupling modules.
- P2P isolation: networking is a port/effect. Gossip, DHT ops, and validation are modeled as Commands/Events, keeping protocol details out of core state logic.
- Error and recovery: explicit state machines per domain (e.g., DHT sync, validation) encoded within AgentState; recovery proceeds from state + event replay.

This architectural rewrite eliminates implicit dependencies, reduces complexity, and balances distributed concerns with a coherent, single-agent authority over state, improving correctness, observability, and maintainability.

## Decision:
Introduce an explicit attribute to distinguish simplification axioms from definition axioms, and do not treat them interchangeably by default in function evaluation.

- Add a dedicated attribute (e.g., [simplification]) to mark axioms intended solely for term rewriting/simplification. Unmarked axioms remain definition axioms by default.
- Function evaluation will consume only definition axioms unless a backend explicitly opts into using [simplification] axioms for evaluation in narrowly specified cases.
- Simplification engines may use both kinds as appropriate, but must respect the attribute boundary when applying axioms operationally vs. definitionally.
- Maintain backward compatibility: existing axioms without the new attribute continue to behave as definition axioms. A deprecation window can encourage annotating existing simplification rules.
- This separation improves soundness, predictability, and tooling: frontends and backends can validate well-formedness, avoid unintended non-termination in evaluators, and provide clearer diagnostics and documentation.
- Backends may extend with finer-grained tags (e.g., [evaluation], [partial], [priority]) but the core distinction is normative.

This approach avoids conflating roles in evaluation code, keeps semantics explicit and reviewable, and enables targeted optimization without breaking existing definitions.

## Decision:
Adopt the dotcom model.liveblog as the canonical internal representation for liveblog rendering, and introduce/maintain an explicit adapter layer that maps CAPI responses to this abstraction.

- Frontend will no longer consume raw CAPI shapes for liveblogs; it will consume only model.liveblog.
- A dedicated transformer (owned by dotcom) will convert CAPI content into model.liveblog, insulating frontend from CAPI schema changes.
- The model.liveblog contract will be versioned and documented, with stability guarantees and migration guidance when breaking changes are necessary.
- Validation and schema tests will be added at the adapter boundary to ensure parity with CAPI and detect upstream changes early.
- Any new liveblog features will be expressed first in model.liveblog, with corresponding adapter updates, keeping frontend rendering logic simple and strongly typed.
- Direct references to CAPI types in frontend liveblog code will be deprecated and incrementally removed.

This decouples frontend rendering from CAPI, clarifies ownership and responsibilities, and reduces the blast radius of upstream changes while preserving strongly typed, component-like semantics.

## Decision:
Adopt a test pyramid with emphasis on fast, deterministic unit tests, complemented by integration, contract, and a minimal set of E2E tests. Standardize on:
- Unit testing: JUnit 5 + Spock (BDD/spec style where beneficial) with Mockito for mocking and AssertJ for fluent assertions.
- Integration testing: Spring Test (if applicable) and Testcontainers for real dependencies (DB, MQ, cache).
- Contract testing: Pact for provider/consumer API contracts.
- E2E/UI testing: Playwright for web; REST E2E via Karate or REST Assured. Use Postman/Newman only for exploratory suites.
- Coverage: JaCoCo with enforced thresholds (global line ≥80%, branch ≥70%; core/domain modules ≥90% line, ≥80% branch).
- Mutation testing: PIT with a minimum mutation score of 70% on core/domain modules.
- Static/quality gates: SonarQube to aggregate coverage, duplication, code smells, and security hotspots.

What to test:
- Unit: pure business logic, invariants, edge/error handling, serialization, mapping, feature flags.
- Integration: repositories, external integrations, message handling, configuration, and migrations using real infra via Testcontainers.
- Contracts: public API schemas, backward compatibility, and versioning rules.
- E2E: critical user journeys and release-blocking smoke paths only; keep flaky/exploratory scenarios out of CI gating.

Approach:
- Given-When-Then style; deterministic tests; no external network calls in unit tests.
- Property-based tests (jqwik) for complex parsers/algorithms.
- Golden files/snapshots for stable schemas with review.
- Test data builders and fixtures; seed datasets for integration tests.

Pre-merge/release:
- CI runs unit + integration + contract tests on every PR; enforce quality gates and coverage thresholds.
- Spin up ephemeral test environment via Docker Compose/Kubernetes; run smoke E2E and contract verification before merge.
- Nightly full E2E/regression and load tests (k6/Gatling) on staging.

Architecture checks:
- ArchUnit rules to enforce layering, module boundaries, and dependency constraints; executed in CI and treated as failing tests.

## Decision:
Introduce a pluggable XSLT assembly strategy with per-collection selection, retaining the current path-fallback mechanism and adding a new uplift-capable assembly process.

- Define a Strategy interface for XSLT assembly. Provide two implementations: (a) LegacyPathFallbackStrategy (existing behavior) and (b) UpliftBundleStrategy (new).
- UpliftBundleStrategy assembles templates from an explicit, versioned “bundle” (e.g., manifest + template set), supporting deterministic composition, dependency ordering, and lock-step upgrades.
- Select strategy via configuration at collection scope (with sensible platform defaults). Collections can be individually cut over without affecting others.
- Support hybrid overrides: allow per-collection overrides to layer atop the chosen strategy (e.g., local patch templates), with a clear precedence order: collection override > strategy output > platform baseline.
- Provide compatibility shims for shared/common templates so both strategies can reuse core transforms where feasible.
- Add validation and diagnostic outputs (effective template map, resolved include graph) to improve observability and ease migration.
- Ship a migration guide and tooling to generate bundles from existing fallback paths to accelerate adoption.
- Establish a deprecation timeline for LegacyPathFallbackStrategy only after a majority migration and performance/quality parity are confirmed.

## Decision:
Adopt workspace-managed internal packages with strict package-level boundaries and a single, consistent build/publish pipeline.

- Package layout: Each shared module becomes its own versioned package under packages/*, with no cross-package relative imports. All cross-package usage goes through the package name.
- Dependency wiring: Use the workspace protocol (e.g., "workspace:*") for internal dependencies. Disallow yarn/npm link and ad-hoc path aliases for cross-package use.
- TypeScript: Enable composite/project references for all TS packages and a root solution tsconfig to enable incremental builds and editor correctness. Each package declares "types" and emits .d.ts.
- Build artifacts: Each package builds to dist with a single toolchain (e.g., tsup or tsc -b) and defines package.json "main"/"module"/"types" and "exports" maps to control public API.
- Dev experience: Use watch mode per package and/or an orchestrator (Nx or Turborepo) to run affected builds/tests in dependency order with caching. Editors resolve types via project references; local runtime resolves built artifacts from dist.
- CI: Orchestrate affected builds/tests/lint using Nx/Turborepo with remote caching to ensure correctness and speed, honoring the dependency graph.
- Publishing/versioning: Use Changesets to manage versions and changelogs, and publish to the registry (private or public). Production consumers depend on published versions; within the monorepo, workspace:* resolves to local builds.
- Enforceability: Add lint rules and CI checks to forbid cross-package relative imports and disallow linking. Provide templates and scripts for creating new packages consistent with this standard.

This removes fragile linking, ensures local dev, CI, and production behave identically, and provides predictable, cacheable builds and reproducible releases.

## Decision:
Standardize on JUnit 5 (JUnit Platform + Jupiter) as the single unit-testing framework across the codebase. All new tests must use JUnit 5; existing JUnit 4 tests will be migrated. The JUnit Vintage engine may be temporarily enabled to run legacy JUnit 4 tests during the transition, but will be removed once migration is complete.

Rationale:
- Modern API and features (parameterized tests, dynamic tests, nested tests, tagging, improved assertions).
- Powerful and composable extension model (replaces runners/rules), better integration with Spring/Mockito/etc.
- Superior IDE/build tool support and parallel test execution.
- Active maintenance and ecosystem alignment.

Implementation:
- Update build to include junit-jupiter and remove junit-4; optionally include junit-vintage for interim compatibility.
- Enforce via build linting: disallow org.junit.Assert and org.junit.Test imports.
- Update CI to use JUnit Platform reports and enable parallelism where appropriate.
- Provide migration guidelines (annotations mapping, assertions, rules-to-extensions) and examples.
- Track migration via issue board; aim to remove Vintage within two iterations.

Scope:
- Applies to all JVM modules and services in this repository and future JVM projects to ensure consistency.

## Decision:
Persist all business-significant domain events as an immutable, append-only event log and treat this log as the authoritative source for historical timelines and audit. For referrals and interventions, every state transition and key action (e.g., referral submitted, first assessment booked, first action plan submitted) will be recorded as a domain event enriched with actor identity, timestamp, correlation/causation IDs, and entity references.

We will not rely on mutable referral state for historical queries. Instead, we will support time-based and “who did what when” queries by replaying and/or projecting events into queryable read models optimized for analytics and reporting. Events will be versioned to allow schema evolution, and published reliably using the outbox pattern to ensure exactly-once delivery semantics to downstream consumers.

Retention will be long-lived (default: indefinite, subject to legal/regulatory policy), with indexing on key dimensions (time, person, referral, supplier, event type). Projections will be maintained to a reporting store/warehouse to support performance dashboards and ad-hoc analysis without impacting operational workloads.

This approach decouples operational processing from analytics while ensuring complete, auditable history. Current state remains available for transactional flows via projections, but historical truths and timelines are derived from the event stream.

## Decision:
Adopt compile-time code generation to produce concrete interceptor-enabled wrappers for user classes instead of relying on runtime Proxy mechanisms. The generator will emit type-safe classes that preserve the original public API (constructors, methods, and signatures) while inserting interception hooks before/after target method invocations and around errors. Interceptors will be declared via lightweight annotations/metadata or a configuration file and composed as a chain with deterministic ordering.

Integration will occur in the build pipeline (generate-sources phase), producing sources/artifacts that are compiled alongside user code. No runtime reflection or dynamic proxying will be used in production, eliminating Proxy overhead and maximizing inlining and JIT/optimizer friendliness. The generated classes will be registered via factories/DI bindings so consumers transparently receive the intercepted implementations without code changes.

Key properties:
- Performance: near-native invocation costs; optimizer-visible call sites.
- Transparency: identical types/signatures; preserves generics and nullability contracts.
- Safety: compile-time validation of interceptor applicability and method coverage.
- Observability: standardized interception points (before/after/around, error) with context propagation.
- Configurability: opt-in via annotations/config; deterministic ordering; per-class/method scoping.
- Tooling: incremental generation, deterministic outputs, and source maps/doc comments preserved.

In development, we may optionally provide a runtime proxy fallback for rapid iteration, but production builds will exclusively use generated code.

## Decision:
Adopt a dedicated CLI parsing framework to handle subcommands and arguments. We will migrate to picocli, leveraging its subcommand model, annotations, type conversion, validation, defaulting, and auto-generated help.

We will:
- Define each subcommand as a separate annotated class to encapsulate options and business logic cleanly.
- Centralize the entrypoint with picocli’s CommandLine, wiring subcommands and shared options.
- Preserve current command names and options; introduce aliases where needed and mark any changes as deprecated with clear warnings.
- Enable standardized error messages, usage/help output, and exit codes; generate man pages and shell completion scripts.
- Add unit tests around command parsing and validation, and integration tests for key command flows.

This reduces boilerplate, improves maintainability and testability, and scales with future subcommands without disproportionate effort.

## Decision:
Adopt a fully managed build toolchain and retire Create React App (CRA)/react-scripts to regain control over Webpack, ESLint, and related configurations. We will migrate the client application to a custom Webpack 5 setup maintained in-repo, enabling explicit configuration of Node polyfills and other build behaviors.

Key points:
- Replace react-scripts with Webpack 5, webpack-dev-server, and webpack-cli.
- Configure required Node polyfills via resolve.fallback and provide plugins/shims (e.g., process/browser, buffer, stream-browserify, util, path-browserify).
- Own all linting and formatting config: ESLint (eslint-webpack-plugin) with our shareable config, Prettier independent of the bundler.
- Own transpilation: Babel with @babel/preset-env and @babel/preset-react, plus TypeScript via babel-loader (preset-typescript) or ts-loader.
- Maintain CSS/PostCSS pipeline (css-loader, style-loader or MiniCssExtractPlugin, postcss/autoprefixer), asset handling, and environment variable handling via DefinePlugin.
- Keep testing independent of bundler: Jest (or maintain current test runner), and Storybook for UI where needed.

Transition plan:
- Short term (bridge): If immediate fixes are required before full migration, use CRACO to inject Webpack 5 fallbacks and unblock builds without ejecting.
- Migration: Replace CRA scripts with npm scripts invoking Webpack configs (webpack.common.js, webpack.dev.js, webpack.prod.js), validate parity (build output, env handling, source maps), then remove CRA dependencies.
- Governance: Document build conventions, version lock critical plugins, and add CI checks to prevent configuration drift.

This decision eliminates the dependency on CRA’s limited extension points and release cadence, provides a clear path to apply Webpack 5 polyfills and future customizations, and reduces risk of recurring build breaks due to upstream constraints.

## Decision:
- Adopt a strict layered architecture: Application → Domain Services → Platform Services → OS Abstraction Layer (OSAL) → Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) → Board Support Package (BSP)/Drivers.
- Enforce dependency inversion: upper layers depend only on abstract interfaces; concrete RTOS, CPU, and driver implementations live in OSAL/HAL/BSP. No direct RTOS or register access outside OSAL/HAL.
- Define stable, versioned interfaces for:
  - OS primitives (tasks, timers, sync, IPC, memory, time)
  - I/O (GPIO, UART, I2C, SPI, PWM, ADC/DAC)
  - Storage (block, NVS/kv-store, files)
  - Networking (link, IP, TLS)
  - Power/clock/reset and boot
  - Logging/metrics and diagnostics
- Provide a plugin-style binding mechanism (factory/registry) to select OSAL/HAL implementations at build time, with optional runtime selection where feasible.
- Use a message/event-driven service bus and async interfaces to decouple components; prohibit cross-layer backdoors.
- Centralize configuration via:
  - Build-time descriptors (e.g., device-tree-like hardware description)
  - Runtime config service with schema validation; map to NVS and defaults
- Supply a reference BSP per platform with minimal, well-tested drivers; keep vendor SDKs confined to BSP.
- Enable host-based simulation and mocking for unit/integration tests; hardware-in-the-loop for drivers; conformance tests for each interface.
- Establish coding and API guidelines to keep interfaces small, deterministic, and zero-cost where possible; forbid dynamic allocation in hard real-time paths.
- Provide code generators/templates to scaffold adapters and drivers from interface specs; publish compatibility matrix and semantic versioning for all interfaces.
- Create CI gates to ensure no layer violations, interface stability, and portability (build on multiple targets).
- Documentation and examples demonstrate porting to a new board by implementing only OSAL/HAL/BSP, leaving upper layers reusable.

## Decision:
- Serve Meadow-authored IIIF manifests from a new, WM-controlled public origin (Meadow S3 bucket) behind our CDN (e.g., iiif.meadow.example.org), not via Donut.
- Use a distinct URL namespace/prefix that unambiguously identifies Meadow manifests. The CDN routes:
  - If the key exists in Meadow’s S3, serve it directly (long-lived Cache-Control, ETag).
  - If missing, fall back to Donut’s existing manifest origin for legacy objects, preserving backward compatibility during transition.
- Make Meadow manifests immutable and versioned at the object-key level; updates publish a new versioned key and update the record pointer. This removes the need for runtime re-caching by Donut.
- Warm caches at write time: upon manifest publication/update, enqueue a background job to push the object to S3 and prefetch through the CDN. Provide an internal, authenticated purge/rehydrate endpoint for exceptional re-cache needs.
- Remove the Donut recache proxy path for any Meadow-authored manifest URLs and update clients/link resolvers to emit Meadow URLs for Meadow records.
- Apply consistent headers (Cache-Control public, long s-maxage; ETag) and observability (CDN/S3 metrics, error rates) on the Meadow path to monitor cache effectiveness and fallback usage.

## Decision:
- Establish canonical, immutable, versioned identifiers for both QC Algorithms and QC Patterns.
  - Identifier format: URN and HTTPS URL pair.
    - URN: urn:cn:qc-alg:{uuid}:{semver} and urn:cn:qc-pattern:{uuid}:{semver}
    - URL: https://platform.cn/qc-algorithms/{uuid}/{semver} and https://platform.cn/pattern-atlas/patterns/{uuid}/{semver}
- All cross-references must use the URN as the primary key and include the resolvable URL as a secondary field for convenience.
  - Reference payload: { refUrn, href, relation, constraints? }
  - relation is one of: uses, implements, refines, supersedes, duplicates.
- References are always to a specific version; “latest” is disallowed in persisted links. Clients may resolve “latest” at read time via the resolver service.
- Introduce a Link Resolver service to validate and resolve references:
  - Validates existence, version, and access control at creation/update time.
  - Provides backlink discovery to materialize bi-directional links.
  - Supports soft redirects for deprecated versions and emits warnings.
- Enforce referential integrity in storage via foreign-key-like checks (async for cross-system links) and nightly audits with reports.
- Publish OpenAPI/JSON Schema for the reference object and add SDK helpers to create/validate links.
- Deprecation policy: versions are immutable; deprecate via metadata and “supersedes” links, never by mutating content.

## Decision:
Use PUT as the HTTP method to upsert the specified route.

- PUT will target a concrete route resource, e.g., `/vpcs/{vpcId}/route-tables/{routeTableId}/routes/{destinationCidr}`, and be defined to create or replace that route atomically across the designated custom route tables.
- The request body will include the minimal required fields (e.g., next hop/target, route type/priority, propagation flags) available from the log event; any omitted optional fields will retain existing values when replacing.
- PUT semantics provide idempotency: issuing the same request with the same URI and body yields the same final state, which is critical for log-triggered retries.
- PATCH is rejected due to its partial/merge semantics and higher ambiguity for cross-table synchronization; POST is rejected because the operation is not append-only and must be deterministic; DELETE is not applicable.
- Response codes:
  - 200 when an existing route is replaced with identical or updated values.
  - 201 when the route is newly created.
  - 409 if conflicting immutable attributes prevent replacement.
  - 404 if the referenced main route (or route table) does not exist.
- Optionally support If-Match/ETag for concurrency control; absent ETag, last-write-wins with idempotent PUT remains the default.

## Decision:
- Replace the callback-based reply mechanism with explicit, typed, bounded channels passed as part of each request event from Handle to Supervisor (CSP-style request/response).
- The Supervisor must respond exactly once by sending the result on the provided channel; the channel’s type encodes the expected response.
- Deprecate and remove the Callback abstraction; channels become the single mechanism for capturing async responses, reducing borrow/scope complexity and clarifying ownership.
- Standardize Handle APIs on a synchronous facade that internally awaits the channel response; provide async variants only where a concrete use case demands it. Existing async Handle methods are to be deprecated and will be reintroduced only with clear requirements.
- Use bounded channels to enforce backpressure and prevent unbounded memory growth; surface timeouts/cancellation at the Handle to avoid deadlocks and to enable graceful degradation.
- Establish simple lifecycle guarantees: a request carries a oneshot (or bounded) response sender; dropping the sender implies “no response,” which the Handle maps to a well-defined error.
- Codify type-safety and ergonomics: response types are statically defined per request kind; errors propagate via Result over the response channel.
- Update Supervisor and Handle contracts, tests, and instrumentation to reflect the channel-based model; callbacks are removed from public and internal APIs.

## Decision:
Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document significant technical and architectural choices for the Ditto project, including context, options considered, decision, and consequences. We will use the MADR template (https://adr.github.io/madr/) for consistency and readability.

- Location: docs/adr/ in the repository; one ADR per file, named YYYY-MM-DD-short-title.md.
- Scope: Any decision that materially affects architecture, quality attributes, data/contract shape, external dependencies, operational model, or team conventions.
- Status workflow: proposed → accepted | rejected | superseded | deprecated. Superseding ADRs will reference predecessors and vice versa.
- Process: Create a new ADR via template when a decision is being considered; collaborate via PR for review; merge when accepted by the designated tech lead/architecture group. Minor clarifications can amend an ADR with a dated “Amendments” section; semantic changes require a new ADR.
- Discoverability: Maintain an index at docs/adr/README.md. Tag ADRs with labels (e.g., security, data, api, ops) at the top.
- Tooling: Provide a repo script to scaffold ADRs from the MADR template.
- Ownership: Each ADR lists authors and approvers. All engineers are responsible for keeping ADRs current as decisions evolve.

This practice ensures the rationale behind Ditto’s architectural choices remains transparent, reviewable, and traceable over time.

## Decision:
Decouple Localization from JabRefPreferences. Preferences will only store raw, language-neutral values. Default values are defined centrally and are not localized.

- Introduce a typed PreferenceKey registry (e.g., enum or records) that defines:
  - key name
  - value type (boolean/int/string/list/etc.)
  - language-neutral default value

- For UI-facing strings:
  - Store either a neutral canonical value or a message key (e.g., dot-separated resource key) as the preference/default.
  - Resolve localization only at the usage site (UI) by translating the message key, or by mapping canonical values to localized display text.

- For non-string defaults (bool/int/dates/paths/enums), store raw values or enum names; never localized forms.

- Provide a Defaults provider (e.g., PreferencesDefaults) that returns raw defaults without invoking Localization, ensuring JabRefPreferences has no dependency on Localization.

- Callers obtain preferences and:
  - If a value is present, use it as-is (and, if needed for display, localize it).
  - If absent, apply the raw default and localize only at the presentation layer.

- Migration:
  - Add a one-time migration that detects legacy stored localized strings and maps them to canonical values/message keys where feasible.

This approach removes the Localization dependency from preferences, keeps defaults deterministic and testable, and confines translation to the UI layer.

## Decision:
Deprecate and remove the User.va_profile accessors in favor of the new, narrowly scoped getter methods that expose only the required, approved user attributes. We will:

- Introduce deprecation warnings on all va_profile-related methods immediately and document their replacements.
- Migrate all call sites to the new getters, updating serializers, presenters, and services to consume only whitelisted attributes.
- Add RuboCop lint rules (or a custom cop) to forbid new usages of va_profile and enforce the approved getter surface.
- Strengthen unit/integration tests to verify that only authorized attributes are exposed and that PII leakage does not occur.
- After migration completes, remove the deprecated methods and any direct MPI profile exposure from User.
- Update developer documentation and changelogs to reflect the new access pattern and upgrade path.

## Decision:
Adopt tag URIs (RFC 4151) as the canonical, immutable identifiers for all ODH data elements (entities and their stable versions).

Format:
- tag:<authority>,<YYYY>:<path>
- authority: the owning domain in lowercase (e.g., vwt.digital).
- YYYY: the year the authority had control of the name (e.g., 2020).
- path: a hierarchical, slash-separated business context ending in a stable business key.

Construction rules:
- Use meaningful, immutable business attributes (e.g., catalog/articleNo) to ensure recognizability and uniqueness.
- Scope paths with organizational and domain namespaces to avoid collisions (e.g., org/catalog/articles/{articleNo}).
- Percent-encode reserved characters; normalize to NFC; domain is lowercase; path segments preserve business-case where significant.
- Identifiers are permanent; if a business key changes or identity semantics shift, mint a new tag URI.
- Versioning (optional): append /v/{semver|yyyyMMddHHmmss} only when representing distinct, addressable versions; the base URI denotes the conceptual entity.
- Where no stable business key exists, use a well-namespaced surrogate key (e.g., uuid) as the terminal segment.

Resolution:
- Tag URIs are non-resolvable by design; any HTTP dereferencing endpoints are maintained separately via a registry mapping tag→URL.

Examples:
- tag:vwt.digital,2020:mycompany/catalog/articles/313
- tag:vwt.digital,2020:odh/datasets/customer/12345
- tag:vwt.digital,2020:odh/events/orders/2024/09/01/ABC123/v/20240901123000

Governance:
- Define and review namespace conventions per domain.
- Enforce uniqueness and format via validation in ingestion/publishing pipelines.

## Decision:
Adopt a High Privilege Access (HPA) model for production with just-in-time, least-privilege, and time-bound access:

- Default deny: no standing developer access to production shells, databases, or admin consoles.
- Access is requested via a tracked change/ticket with business justification, scoped resources, and a defined TTL; approval required by a production owner/incident commander.
- Grant access using ephemeral, role-scoped credentials (no long-lived keys), enforced with MFA and session constraints; maximum TTL and scope limits are automated.
- Provide read-only observability by default; elevation to write/admin actions requires explicit approval and narrowly scoped roles.
- All sessions and privilege grants are logged, correlated to tickets, and forwarded to SIEM; session commands and resource changes are auditable.
- Automatic revocation at TTL expiry or incident resolution; immediate revocation capability for responders.
- No standing membership in high-privilege groups; break-glass roles exist only for critical incidents, require post-incident review and credential rotation.
- Enforcement through centralized access pathways (e.g., bastion/SSO/PAM), policy-as-code, and periodic reviews of roles, scopes, and logs.

## Decision:
DOS will not persist descriptive metadata. It will be the system of record only for administrative (e.g., rights, provenance, technical, preservation) and structural metadata (e.g., component hierarchy, ordering, file-to-object relationships, versions).

For descriptive needs, DOS will store only stable references to authoritative sources (e.g., identifiers, source system type/URI) and resolve descriptive metadata on demand via external APIs/services. DOS may maintain an optional, non-authoritative cache or search index of descriptive fields for performance, with clear TTL/refresh rules; updates flow from the source systems, not edited in DOS.

APIs, data model, and events will explicitly separate descriptive from administrative/structural concerns, ensuring no duplication of descriptive metadata while enabling consistent retrieval and display across use cases.

## Decision:
- Introduce a channel-agnostic Notifications service with pluggable provider adapters. Messages are composed once, then dispatched via the highest-priority available channel per country/patient.
- For Bangladesh, enable Imo as the primary channel with SMS as a fallback. If Imo delivery cannot be initiated or confirmed, automatically fall back to SMS.
- Gate Imo delivery behind a country- and cohort-based feature flag to allow staged rollout and A/B testing. Default to SMS where Imo is disabled or unsupported.
- Implement provider adapters with a common interface (send, status, cancel) and delivery receipts. Persist per-attempt status to support retries, analytics, and auditing.
- Localize message templates in Bangla with per-channel variants and length/format constraints. Centralize template management with versioning.
- Enforce patient consent/opt-out and channel eligibility checks before send. Respect quiet hours and rate limits; configure per-channel retry/backoff and dead-letter handling.
- Capture metrics (send attempts, deliveries, failures, fallbacks, read/engagement where available) and surface dashboards for Bangladesh specifically.
- Secure provider credentials via secrets management; isolate provider webhooks; validate signatures and PII handling in accordance with data protection requirements.
- Keep India’s WhatsApp/SMS flows unchanged; reuse the same Notifications service and adapter pattern to minimize divergence and enable future channels (e.g., voice, RCS).
- Pilot with a limited cohort; expand based on deliverability and engagement thresholds.

## Decision:
We will build the front end with React and Next.js (App Router) using TypeScript.

- React provides a mature, component-driven model that encourages modular architecture, rich interactivity, and reusability.
- Next.js delivers first-class performance via server components, automatic code-splitting, SSR/SSG/ISR, route-level streaming, and built-in image/font optimization.
- The React/Next ecosystem offers broad, active community support, long-term viability, and a deep pool of talent, libraries, and tooling.
- TypeScript ensures safer, maintainable code and scalable APIs for shared UI primitives and domain components.
- We will leverage Vite or Next’s native tooling for local DX (depending on Next version), and adopt a design-system-first approach (tokens + component library) for consistent UX and modularity.
- State management will default to React Query/RTK Query for server cache and lightweight local state via React context/hooks; more advanced solutions only as needed.
- Performance guardrails: route-level and component-level code splitting, edge/runtime rendering where appropriate, image optimization, and analytics-driven performance budgets.
- PWA capabilities will be enabled as needed via Next plugins to support offline and installable experiences.

## Decision:
Adopt an xUnit-style testing standard across the solution, with approved language-specific frameworks and unified conventions, reporting, and coverage.

- Primary unit test frameworks by language:
  - TypeScript/Node.js: Jest (ts-jest), Testing Library for UI
  - Python: pytest
  - Java/Kotlin: JUnit 5 + Mockito
  - .NET: xUnit.net + Moq
  - Go: go test + Testify
- Integration testing:
  - Prefer Testcontainers (where applicable) for reproducible, containerized dependencies.
- End-to-end/acceptance testing:
  - Web UIs: Playwright
  - Optional BDD: Cucumber/Gherkin where business-readable specs are required
- Common conventions (apply to all):
  - Structure: co-locate tests next to source or under tests/ with mirroring tree
  - Naming: <name>.spec/test.*
  - Style: Arrange-Act-Assert (or Given-When-Then)
  - Mocks/stubs: language-appropriate libraries; avoid network/FS by default
  - Coverage thresholds: minimum 80% line/branch (service-specific exceptions require approval)
- Reporting and quality gates:
  - Test results: JUnit XML
  - Coverage: LCOV (JS/TS), Cobertura/JaCoCo (JVM), Coverage.py XML (Python), Coverage.gocov/Cobertura (Go), .NET cobertura
  - Central analysis: SonarQube (or equivalent) with enforced quality gate
- CI/CD:
  - Tests run on every PR and in main pipeline; support for sharding/parallelization
  - Caching dependencies and test artifacts to speed builds
- Documentation and scaffolding:
  - Provide project templates with configured frameworks and scripts
  - Include guidelines for writing tests and examples per language

## Decision:
Adopt event sourcing with CQRS as the primary persistence approach. The system’s source of truth will be an append-only event store capturing domain events; current state will be derived via projections into read models tailored to query needs.

Key elements:
- Event Store: Use an immutable, versioned event log with optimistic concurrency, idempotency, and per-aggregate streams. Enable snapshots for large aggregates to optimize load time.
- Projections: Build materialized views for read use cases; allow multiple projections to evolve independently as presentation needs change. Support replay and backfill to regenerate views when requirements shift.
- CQRS: Separate write (command) models from read models to keep domain logic focused on behavior and reduce coupling to storage structures.
- Schema evolution: Treat events as backward-compatible contracts; version events and projection handlers to support iterative change without data migrations.
- Operational guarantees: Accept eventual consistency between writes and reads; define SLAs for projection lag and implement monitoring, retries, and dead-letter handling.
- Testing and portability: Favor deterministic, pure-event tests. Keep the event store interface abstract to remain portable across providers; begin with a proven event store and an in-memory implementation for local/dev.
- Migration and portability of data: Use event streams to move data between environments and to support time-travel debugging, auditability, and point-in-time restore.

We will start with the most change-prone bounded contexts, incrementally introduce projections, and de-risk with feature flags and dual-write/compare where needed.

## Decision:
- Front end: TypeScript as the primary language for the web application. It leverages existing JavaScript skills while providing type safety and maintainability. It has broad, mature ecosystem support and first-class GIS libraries and tooling (e.g., OpenLayers, Mapbox GL JS, Leaflet, deck.gl, turf.js).
- Back end: Python 3 as the primary server language. It aligns with team experience and offers a comprehensive, production-proven geospatial stack (GDAL/OGR, Shapely, Rasterio, Fiona, pyproj, GeoPandas) with strong industry support. We will target FastAPI for modern, performant APIs, with optional Django for admin-heavy needs.

This combination maximizes developer productivity, matches current team skills, and ensures excellent GIS tooling and community support across both tiers.

## Decision:
Adopt a clear, consistent naming convention across the codebase and surrounding assets to accelerate onboarding and reduce cognitive load.

- Files and directories: lower-kebab-case (e.g., order-service, user-profile.controller.ts). One module/component per file; filename matches primary export.
- Source code:
  - Classes, React/Vue/Svelte components, Types/Interfaces: PascalCase (e.g., OrderService, UserCard, UserDto).
  - Functions, variables, object keys: camelCase (e.g., fetchUsers, maxRetries).
  - Constants and environment variables: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, DATABASE_URL).
  - Enums: PascalCase name; Members UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
  - Private fields: leading underscore only if required by tooling (otherwise avoid).
- Tests and tooling:
  - Test files co-located or in __tests__: same base name with .spec.ts|.test.ts (e.g., user-service.spec.ts).
  - Mocks/fixtures: suffix .mock.ts / .fixture.ts.
- APIs:
  - REST paths: kebab-case nouns, plural, versioned prefix (/v1/orders/:orderId).
  - GraphQL: Types/Queries/Mutations PascalCase; fields camelCase.
  - Events/Topics: domain.event_name in snake_case (e.g., billing.payment_succeeded).
- Database:
  - Tables: snake_case plural (e.g., user_accounts).
  - Columns: snake_case (e.g., created_at).
  - Migrations: timestamp_prefix_description (e.g., 20260123_add_user_index.sql).
  - Indexes/constraints: ix_table_columns, fk_from_to.
- Frontend specifics:
  - Component files: PascalCase.tsx; hooks use usePrefix (e.g., useAuth).
  - CSS/SCSS modules: lower-kebab-case.module.scss; CSS variables: --kebab-case.
- Packages and services:
  - NPM package names and repo folders: lower-kebab-case (scoped if needed, e.g., @org/order-utils).
  - Docker images: org/name:semver (lowercase).
- Git and releases:
  - Branches: type/short-kebab-summary (types: feat, fix, chore, refactor, docs, test).
  - Commits: Conventional Commits (e.g., feat(auth): add oauth login).
  - Tags: vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; prereleases with -alpha.-beta.-rc.
- Feature flags and configs:
  - Flags: domain.feature_name in snake_case; boolean positive phrasing (e.g., checkout.enable_express).
  - Config keys: dot.notation or snake_case consistently per system.
- Abbreviations:
  - Avoid nonstandard abbreviations; prefer full words. If used, apply consistently (id, uuid, url, api).

Document these rules in CONTRIBUTING.md and enforce with linters/formatters and CI.

## Decision:
Introduce explicit bus assignment for handlers and a single “default” bus alias.

- Each handler must declare its target bus (or buses). Multiple buses are allowed but must be explicit.
- If a handler does not declare a bus, it is registered to the default bus only.
- The current implicit behavior of registering handlers to all buses when unspecified is deprecated immediately and will be removed in the next major version.
- Add build-time validation: when more than one bus is configured, undefined bus assignment triggers a warning (now) and will become an error in the next major.
- This preserves current behavior in single-bus setups (default bus) while preventing accidental cross-bus registrations as the platform evolves.

## Decision:
Adopt Selenium WebDriver as the browser automation framework for feature and end‑to‑end tests to ensure true cross‑browser coverage and execution across all environments (local, CI, and cloud). We will write a single test suite using WebDriver’s W3C standard APIs and run it against multiple targets via configuration (e.g., local browsers/headless, CI runners, and BrowserStack for OS/browser matrices).

We will integrate WebDriver into the CI pipeline to execute smoke suites on every change and full cross‑browser suites on scheduled/nightly runs. For scalable cross‑browser/OS coverage, we will use BrowserStack (with credentials and capabilities managed via CI secrets). Locally, developers can run the same tests using Dockerized browsers or native installations.

Test configuration (capabilities, URLs, timeouts) will be externalized to avoid code changes per environment. This approach lets us author tests once, maintain a single codebase, and achieve consistent, repeatable execution across all supported browsers and environments.

## Decision:
Maintain three separate AWS accounts: Development (engineer sandboxes), Staging (production-like), and Production (stable BI/ETL). Staging will serve as the primary environment for Analysts/Engineers to build, modify, and test ETL with production-parity schemas and statistically representative data, without impacting Production.

Implement automated, recurring data replication from Production to Staging with the following controls:
- Replicate schemas, metadata, and data structures (e.g., Glue Catalog, warehouse schemas, IAM/data policies) to ensure parity.
- Apply deterministic de-identification/masking of PII and sensitive fields during replication to Staging, preserving referential integrity, keys, distributions, and lookup joinability.
- Use CDC where feasible to reduce latency and cost; supplement with periodic full refresh for drift correction.
- Enforce one-way replication (no writes from Staging to Production).

Use Infrastructure as Code to keep infrastructure parity across Staging and Production (networking, storage, compute, IAM). All platform and ETL code follows a Dev → Staging → Production promotion pipeline with automated tests in Development and Staging and manual approval gates to Production. Only tagged/released builds can deploy to Staging and Production.

Access and isolation:
- Analysts/Engineers receive build/test access in Staging; Production access is read-only for BI/reporting and operations.
- Enforce account-level isolation, VPC boundaries, scoped IAM roles, and full audit logging in all environments.

Operational parameters:
- Data refresh cadence in Staging set per domain (e.g., hourly CDC, daily full sync), documented SLAs, and data quality checks.
- Validate masking rules via automated tests and periodic audits.
- Implement cost controls in Staging (lifecycle policies, right-sized compute, ephemeral clusters) and prevent persistent PII storage.

This decision provides a safe, production-like Staging environment with realistic, privacy-preserving data for ETL development and testing, while keeping Production stable for reporting workloads.

## Decision:
Adopt an Advanced Search powered by Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Query DSL with a user-facing KQL/Lucene-like query syntax, and update index schema/analyzers to support new fields, boolean logic, prefix/substring matching, and synonyms.

- Expose an “Advanced Search” bar that supports field-scoped queries (e.g., author:"Jane Doe", created:[2024-01-01 TO *]), boolean operators (AND/OR), and grouping.
- Keep the existing simple form, routing to generated DSL; power users can input queries directly.
- Add mappings for new fields (created_at, updated_at, author, license, etc.) with appropriate types and sortable/aggregatable settings.
- Implement analyzers:
  - edge_ngram for startsWith on selected fields.
  - ngram or wildcard strategy for contains on selected fields (opt-in to limit index bloat).
  - synonym filters (managed via a versioned dictionary).
- Provide per-field keyword subfields for exact matches; text subfields for analyzed search.
- Add a synonyms management workflow (config + review process), with hot-reload or rolling reindex support.
- Ship UI assists: autocomplete for fields/operators, pill chips for tags, and validation to prevent invalid queries.

Positive consequences:
- Supports complex multi-field queries, AND/OR logic, startsWith/contains, and synonyms with fine-grained control.
- Improves recall/precision and tunability via analyzers and boosting; future-proof for new fields.
- Enables non-engineers to curate synonyms and relevance via managed configs.

Negative consequences:
- Larger index and slower indexing due to ngrams/synonyms; may require selective application and reindexing.
- Increased complexity in query parsing/validation and user education.
- Ongoing governance needed for synonyms and analyzer changes.

## Decision:
Adopt Project Lombok to generate the builder pattern and related boilerplate for EffectiveModel (and similar model classes). Specifically:
- Use @Builder on EffectiveModel (and nested/value types as needed) to provide a fluent, immutable-friendly construction API for many optional parameters.
- Combine with @Value (for immutability) or @Data (if mutability is required), plus @Getter/@With where appropriate.
- Use @Singular on collection fields to support convenient builder methods.
- Configure annotation processing in IDEs and CI; integrate Lombok via the build tool (Maven/Gradle) with version pinning and dependency checks.
- Document generated API (builder method names, defaults, nullability) and enforce validations via @NonNull and builder-level checks where necessary.
- Keep the public API stable by avoiding Lombok features that leak internal details; consider delombok in CI for source artifact generation if required by downstream tooling.

Rationale:
- Minimizes boilerplate while retaining the required builder pattern, reducing LOC and defect risk versus hand-written builders.
- Faster development and easier maintenance than manual code; avoids a language/platform shift and migration risks inherent in Kotlin adoption.
- Remains Java-first and backward compatible, with low adoption friction limited to enabling annotation processing.

Risk mitigation:
- Establish Lombok usage guidelines (approved annotations, code style).
- Add unit tests around builder defaults/validation.
- Monitor Lombok version upgrades and IDE compatibility in the toolchain.

## Decision:
Adopt Kubernetes Multi-Cluster Services (MCS) as the standard for cross-cluster service discovery and addressing, augmented with a universal, cluster-qualified DNS naming scheme.

- Establish a single ClusterSet across trusted clusters; manage membership via GitOps and signed kubeconfigs.
- Use ServiceExport/ServiceImport to publish services into the ClusterSet and expose the aggregated DNS name: <svc>.<ns>.svc.clusterset.local for any-cluster resolution.
- Introduce a cluster-qualified DNS convention to target a specific cluster: <cluster>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.clusterset.local.
- Implement CoreDNS configuration (rewrite/template plugins) to resolve cluster-qualified names to endpoints originating from the named cluster; default names remain aggregated and topology-aware.
- Enforce mTLS and authenticated east–west connectivity between clusters via mesh gateways or site-to-site networking; only authenticated clusters may join the ClusterSet.
- Tag EndpointSlices with cluster identity and propagate labels/metadata required for DNS routing and policy.
- Apply network policies and RBAC so only exported services are discoverable cross-cluster; no cross-namespace leaks.
- Provide fallbacks and health-aware routing: aggregated names exclude unhealthy clusters; cluster-qualified names return NXDOMAIN if the service is not exported by that cluster.

This yields stable, universal service names and optional cluster pinning (e.g., cluster1.serviceb.ns.svc.clusterset.local) suitable for cloud–edge and multi-region deployments.

## Decision:
Standardize the Domain API on Domain.getAgent() as the canonical method to obtain an agent instance. Reintroduce getAgent and deprecate Domain.getInstance(), maintaining it as a thin alias to getAgent for one deprecation cycle.

- Immediately: ship getAgent(); mark getInstance() as @deprecated with compiler/IDE annotations and runtime warnings in debug builds only.
- Backward compatibility: keep getInstance() functional without behavior change until the next major release; no semantic or signature differences.
- Removal plan: remove getInstance() in the next major version, after at least one minor release with deprecation notices and a published migration guide.
- Documentation: update all docs, samples, and generated API references to exclusively use getAgent().
- Tooling: provide a codemod/lint rule to automatically replace getInstance() with getAgent() and block new usages.
- Versioning: treat the deprecation as a non-breaking change; the eventual removal will be a semver-major change.
- Tests: add coverage ensuring both methods resolve identical instances during the deprecation window.

## Decision:
Adopt a mandatory, version-controlled publishing checklist and automated workflow for all crate releases to ensure consistency, quality, and traceability.

- Standardize on semantic versioning; version updated in Cargo.toml via cargo-release (preferred) or approved script.
- Require a PR using a “Crate Release” template that includes:
  - Changelog updated with user-facing changes.
  - README/docs examples verified and crate metadata (description, categories, keywords, repository, license) current.
  - MSRV and feature flags documented; public API changes reviewed.
  - Dependencies audited (cargo deny), no path/git/dev dependencies left.
  - Code formatted/linted (fmt, clippy) and tests pass across targets.
  - Security review for sensitive changes; advisories noted if applicable.
- CI gates:
  - Preflight: build, test, lint, audit, docs, minimal-versions where applicable.
  - Dry-run publish (cargo publish --dry-run) and size/license checks.
- Release execution:
  - Use cargo-release to bump version, tag (vX.Y.Z), generate changelog entry, and publish.
  - Enforce maintainer 2FA; publishing uses organization token/secrets with least privilege.
  - Supply-chain: sign tags, attach provenance (e.g., SLSA/GitHub OIDC), and attach SBOM if supported.
- Post-release verification:
  - Install from crates.io to validate.
  - Create GitHub Release with artifacts/notes, link to changelog.
  - Notify stakeholders; update downstream crates and docs.
- Rollback policy:
  - If critical issues found, yank affected versions with rationale and publish a fixed patch promptly.

Deviation from the checklist requires explicit approval from maintainers.

## Decision:
Introduce a temporary offline-first mode that persists data locally and defers server synchronization until the backend is restored.

- Implement a local persistence layer (IndexedDB/SQLite via a repository abstraction) to store:
  - Domain entities needed for read flows.
  - A durable “outbox” queue for all create/update/delete actions with payload, metadata, and timestamps.
- Default all reads to the local store; all writes are appended to the outbox and applied locally for immediate UX continuity.
- A background sync worker performs periodic health checks; when the backend is available it:
  - Replays the outbox in order with idempotent requests.
  - Pulls server updates incrementally.
  - Resolves conflicts via timestamp-based last-write-wins for immutable/append-only data; for mutable PII prefer server-authoritative with client replay or marks for manual review where necessary.
- Gate the mode behind a remotely configurable feature flag and automatic fallback if server unavailability exceeds a threshold; allow runtime rollback.
- Security and privacy:
  - Encrypt sensitive fields at rest where platform permits; never store credentials/tokens in plaintext.
  - Purge local data on sign-out and after a configurable TTL; store the minimum necessary to operate.
- Observability and resilience:
  - Add metrics for queue depth, replay success/failure, and local store errors.
  - Ensure versioned schemas and safe migrations; include recovery (truncate/reseed) path if corruption is detected.
- When server sync is fixed, disable offline-first mode, drain the outbox, reconcile, and garbage-collect local-only data.

## Decision:
- Adopt Apache Kafka as the primary messaging middleware to enable highly scalable, durable, and partitioned event streaming.
- Use Kafka topics as the canonical EDA backbone; model core EIP needs via:
  - Pub/Sub via topics and consumer groups
  - Competing consumers via partitions
  - Message routing via topic conventions and header-based filtering
  - Event reprocessing via retention and compaction
  - Dead-letter topics for error handling and retries
- Implement stream processing patterns with Kafka Streams and/or ksqlDB to cover Content-Based Router, Splitter/Aggregator, Enricher, Deduplicator, and Saga coordination where applicable.
- Standardize schemas via a Schema Registry (JSON Schema or Avro) and enforce compatibility rules to ensure evolvable contracts.
- Provide a lightweight SDK and reference components to hide boilerplate and promote consistent EIP implementations within MICO.
- Operate Kafka on Kubernetes using the Strimzi Operator (or a managed Kafka service) for elasticity, observability, and automated ops.
- Enforce security and governance: TLS-in-transit, SASL auth, ACLs per topic, topic naming conventions, quotas, and auditing.
- Configure resilience defaults: idempotent producers, exactly-once semantics where required, backoff/retry policies, and DLTs.
- Where traditional queue semantics or request/response are strictly required, complement with a thin adapter or a secondary broker only for those cases; keep Kafka as the system-of-record event backbone.

## Decision:
Do not select or persist a single “canonical” OCN at scrub time. Instead, persist the full, normalized set of OCNs provided for each holding and evaluate matches against HathiTrust items using the entire set.

- Ingest/Normalize: Accept multiple OCNs per holding. Normalize by stripping non-digits, deduplicating, and retaining all unique OCNs. Optionally enrich with known merge/alias expansions when available.
- Matching: Perform matching against HathiTrust items using the full OCN set. Matching is idempotent and order-independent.
- Re-evaluation: Recompute matches whenever repository content changes (e.g., after HathiTrust item ingests) via event-driven hooks or scheduled reconciliation jobs. Late-arriving items that match any OCN in the set will be linked automatically without requiring the member to resubmit holdings.
- Validation: Eliminate the “max OCN” check using the OCLC web widget scraping. Treat OCNs as unbounded numeric identifiers; validate only format (digits) and well-formedness. Do not reject based on a current-maximum heuristic.
- Backward compatibility: Migrate existing records by retaining any stored single OCN and augmenting with additional OCNs from subsequent submissions. Future submissions can add/remove OCNs; the persisted set reflects the latest known truth.
- Auditability: Record provenance (submitted list, normalization, expansions) and timestamps to support debugging and repeatable state reconstruction.

This decision removes order-dependent effects, preserves valid multi-OCN use cases (bound-withs, deprecated/merged OCNs), and ensures holdings-to-item matches remain correct as data evolves.

## Decision:
We will replace the deprecated Docker image with an officially maintained CryptPad flist built from upstream releases via CI. The flist will be configured to use a single data root at /var/lib/cryptpad for all application state. Since flists do not use Docker volumes, persistence will be provided by attaching a platform-native persistent mount (e.g., 0-DB/ZDB-backed filesystem) to /var/lib/cryptpad via the deployment manifest, ensuring data survives restarts and upgrades.

We will ship a one-time migration job that, on first start, imports data from an existing Docker volume backup (tarball) into /var/lib/cryptpad. Backups and restores will be performed by archiving this directory to object storage. The Docker-based deployment path is deprecated and will be removed after a grace period; documentation will guide operators through export (from Docker volume) and import (into flist deployment). Continuous delivery will publish versioned flists, with rollback supported by re-attaching the same persistent mount.

## Decision:
Do not introduce a standalone versioning scheme for HTTP App Callback endpoints at this time. Post v1.0, evolve App Callback contracts via additive, backward-compatible changes and capability negotiation.

- Maintain current callback routes (for example, /dapr/subscribe, /dapr/config) without an explicit version segment.
- Use the runtime-to-app handshake (/dapr/config) and explicit capability flags/metadata to negotiate optional features and behaviors.
- Prohibit breaking changes to existing callback shapes; introduce new optional fields with clear defaults and tolerate unknown fields.
- If a breaking change becomes unavoidable, introduce parallel, opt-in endpoints under a new prefix (for example, /dapr/v2/...) while retaining the existing endpoints through a documented deprecation window.
- Define and publish a deprecation policy (announcement, minimum support window, and removal criteria) and use response headers/metadata to communicate upcoming changes when feasible.
- Align with Dapr runtime API version cadence; the runtime selects the highest mutually supported callback contract via capability negotiation.

This balances stability for existing apps with a clear path for future evolution.

## Decision:
We will implement Hive-compatible partitioning of datasets in S3 using prefix-based “key=value/” folder structures aligned to common query predicates to improve scan performance and reduce cost for Athena and similar engines.

- Partitioning standard: Use Hive-style prefixes (e.g., s3://bucket/dataset/source=xyz/year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/), enabling predicate pushdown and partition pruning.
- Partition key selection: Choose keys based on dominant access patterns (e.g., date/time, dataset type, department, jurisdiction). Default baseline is date-based (year/month/day), with additional high-selectivity keys only when justified by query statistics.
- Catalog integration: All partitioned datasets will be registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Partitions will be added/updated automatically by ingestion jobs (MSCK REPAIR TABLE or Glue crawlers where appropriate).
- File layout: Store data in columnar formats (e.g., Parquet) with target file sizes of 128–512 MB per object to avoid small-file problems and maximize query efficiency. Implement periodic compaction.
- Governance: Define dataset-specific partition schemas in data contracts. Changes to partition schemes require architectural review to avoid partition explosion and skew.
- Access controls: Apply IAM- and S3-prefix–based policies consistent with partition keys where feasible to align security boundaries with data layout.
- Lifecycle and cost: Configure S3 lifecycle rules per prefix for tiering/retention. Avoid deeply nested or overly granular partitions that increase partition counts without selectivity benefits.
- Observability: Track partition discovery, query scan metrics, and cost to iteratively refine partition strategies.
