This standard will be enforced in ingestion/ETL pipelines and validated in CI/CD to ensure consistent, performant, and query-friendly S3 layouts.

## Decision:
We will not use the Fiscal Code (FC) as the primary key. Citizens will be identified internally by an immutable, system-generated surrogate key (UUID, v7 preferred) called citizen_id. All relational references will use citizen_id as the foreign key to ensure stability across FC changes, revocations, and collisions.

We will model FCs as attributes of a citizen with full history:
- A normalized, case-insensitive FC value with checksum validation.
- Status and validity window (active/from–to, revoked, superseded).
- A uniqueness constraint that enforces “at most one active FC value” globally, implemented as a partial unique index on active records.
- Prior FCs are retained as historical records but cannot be reassigned to a different citizen (tombstoned) to avoid ambiguity and replay issues.

APIs:
- All write operations and cross-service references must use citizen_id.
- Read/search endpoints support lookup by FC; if multiple records exist historically, only the active mapping is returned by default, with an option to query history.
- FC changes produce an audit/event (FCChanged) that consumers can process to update caches and denormalized stores.

Data store:
- citizens(id UUID PK, …)
- citizen_fiscal_codes(citizen_id FK, fc_normalized, status, valid_from, valid_to, created_at, …) with a partial unique index on (fc_normalized) where status = 'active'.

Operational rules:
- FC updates are append-only (new row), previous active entry is marked superseded; hard deletes are disallowed.
- Validation is applied but never relied upon as sole uniqueness guarantee.
- Backfills/imports resolve by active FC when present; otherwise create a new citizen_id.

This approach maximizes integrity and auditability while supporting the real-world mutability and non-uniqueness edge cases of FC.

## Decision:
Introduce an immutable “tombstone” record written at delete time to enable discovery and audit of deleted items. On deletion, we will persist a Tombstone entry containing: original_item_id, resource_type, human-friendly identifiers (e.g., title), source_metadata_id, external_ids, deletion_reason, deleted_by, deleted_at, preservation_pointer (e.g., snapshot/storage URI or archival key), and minimal lookup attributes (e.g., slug, checksum, namespace). Tombstones are indexed for admin search by title, source_metadata_id, external_ids, and deleted_at.

Tombstones do not restore items themselves; they serve as a locator to the preserved snapshot. Restoration flows will accept a tombstone ID (or query results) and use its preservation_pointer to reconstruct the item. Tombstones are immutable and access-restricted to privileged roles. We will enforce a retention policy (e.g., 12–24 months, configurable) after which tombstones may be purged if compliance allows; audit-critical fields can be retained longer via export if required.

Implementation: new tombstones table with write-on-delete transaction, background backfill for historical deletes (best effort), and admin API/console views for discovery. Add indexes on (source_metadata_id), (title trigram/full-text), (external_ids), and (deleted_at).

## Decision:
Adopt Redux as the central state management solution and use Redux Thunk as middleware for handling asynchronous and conditional logic in action creators. Redux provides a predictable single source of truth, strong type and testability characteristics, excellent devtools, and a mature ecosystem that aligns with our need to share and coordinate state across multiple components (e.g., auth). Redux Thunk enables encapsulating side effects and sequencing dispatches without coupling logic to components, keeping components presentational and tests focused. We will structure state as normalized slices, use a single store with middleware, and write async flows as thunks that can be easily mocked and tested. We reject MobX due to its implicitness around updates, reduced predictability for complex flows, smaller ecosystem fit for our needs, and less alignment with our testing and architectural preferences.

## Decision:
Use Amazon EventBridge as the eventing backbone to trigger the Archiver Lambda on “issue published” events. Tools will publish canonical IssuePublished events to a dedicated EventBridge bus with a well-defined schema (detail-type: "IssuePublished", source per tool). EventBridge event pattern filtering will route only relevant events to the Archiver Lambda target.

We will enable at-least-once delivery with EventBridge’s native retry policy and add an SQS dead-letter queue for failed invocations. The event envelope will include a deterministic idempotency key (e.g., issueId + version or an eventId) so the Archiver Lambda can enforce idempotency and handle duplicate deliveries safely.

Operational guarantees:
- Strict schema versioning via EventBridge Schema Registry; backward-compatible changes only.
- Fine-grained IAM: tools can PutEvents only to the dedicated bus; Lambda has read-only access to event payloads and write access to archival storage.
- Observability via structured logging (correlating on eventId), CloudWatch metrics/alarms, and tracing.
- Concurrency controls using Lambda reserved concurrency and exponential backoff within retries for downstream calls.
- Regional isolation; cross-account access via EventBridge resource policies if tools run in other accounts.

This approach minimizes coupling, simplifies routing and filtering, and provides built-in retries, DLQ, and governance for reliable event-driven processing.

## Decision:
- Expose a platform-wide Integration Events interface to enable event-driven communication between services and external systems.
- Standardize on CloudEvents (v1.0) for event envelope and metadata across all transports.
- Provide two transports:
  - HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 Event Gateway for ingress/egress of CloudEvents.
  - Managed message broker with pub/sub semantics (primary: Kafka; alternative: NATS JetStream or Azure Service Bus) for internal fan-out and decoupling.
- Define an Event Catalog with AsyncAPI specifications, JSON Schemas, and versioning policy (semver, additive changes preferred).
- Ensure delivery guarantees and resilience:
  - At-least-once delivery with idempotency requirements for consumers.
  - Configurable retries with exponential backoff and dead-letter queues/topics.
  - Partition/subject-based ordering where required per key/aggregate.
- Security and governance:
  - OAuth2/OIDC for producer/consumer authentication; fine-grained authorization (topic/subject ACLs).
  - TLS in transit, optional payload encryption at rest.
  - Auditing of publish/subscribe actions and schema changes.
- Operational characteristics:
  - Multi-tenant isolation via namespaces/topics and quotas.
  - Back-pressure handling, rate limiting, and flow control.
  - Observability: tracing (W3C Trace Context), metrics (delivery latency, DLQ rate), and structured logs.
  - Regional high availability and disaster recovery via replication and retention policies.
- Developer experience:
  - SDKs and connectors for major languages, EIP support (filters, routing, enrichment).
  - Self-service provisioning via CRDs/API/CLI and dashboards for subscriptions and DLQs.

## Decision:
- Standardize on UTF-8 as the canonical encoding for all CSV imports and exports.
- Import behavior:
  - Accept UTF-8 with or without a BOM; automatically detect and strip a leading UTF-8 BOM prior to parsing.
  - Normalize line endings and whitespace after BOM removal.
  - Validate encoding: if bytes are not valid UTF-8, attempt heuristic detection of common legacy encodings (e.g., Windows-1252) only to produce a clear error message with remediation steps (re-save as UTF-8), not to transcode automatically.
  - Ensure header handling is BOM-safe so the first column name is parsed correctly.
- Export behavior:
  - Provide two CSV export variants:
    - “Excel-compatible CSV” including a UTF-8 BOM to ensure Excel correctly identifies UTF-8.
    - “Standards-compliant CSV” without a BOM for downstream systems that expect strict RFC 4180 behavior.
  - Default download in the UI is the Excel-compatible variant; APIs default to the standards-compliant variant.
- UI and docs:
  - Clearly instruct users to save files as “UTF-8 (with BOM)” in Excel or to use the provided CSV template.
  - On import failure, display actionable guidance including how to re-save in UTF-8.
- Implementation:
  - Add a pre-parse step in the CSV ingestion pipeline to detect/remove BOM.
  - Add tests covering presence/absence of BOM, header parsing, multiline fields, and failure cases for non-UTF-8 input.
  - Log normalized encoding metadata for observability and support.
- Backward compatibility:
  - No breaking changes for existing files; files previously failing due to BOM in headers will now parse successfully.

## Decision:
Adopt reflection tests as the primary verification strategy for the TOSCA YAML builder.

We will author YAML service templates that embed assertion metadata describing expected object graphs of the resulting TOSCA YAML classes. A JUnit 5 test harness will discover these fixtures, invoke the builder to materialize objects, then evaluate each assertion line against the built graph.

Key elements:
- Assertion DSL: path comparator value, e.g. repositories.rp1.url = http://github.com/kleinech; supports dotted paths, map keys, list indices (e.g., node_types.ntp1.requirements.0.rqr1.capability), enums, and null checks. Comparators include =, !=, contains, size=, matches (~), and exists/absent for presence checks.
- Path resolution: reflection-based resolver with graceful handling of getters/fields, collection and map navigation, and informative failure messages (actual vs expected, resolved path prefix).
- Type coercion: convert scalar literals in metadata to target types (String, Integer, Boolean, Enum, URI) before comparison.
- Diagnostics: on failure, emit the source fixture, assertion line, resolved actual value, and a minimal diff for collections/maps to speed debugging.
- Extensibility: lightweight SPI to register custom resolvers and comparators for domain-specific types.
- Test layout: one fixture per scenario under src/test/resources; JUnit 5 parameterized tests drive all fixtures. Fast unit scope; no external dependencies.
- CI integration: run on every build; failures block merge. Manual, example-based tests are retained only for edge cases not expressible in the DSL (e.g., performance or exception semantics).

This approach provides high coverage with minimal boilerplate, keeps tests close to domain examples, and ensures the builder produces clean, valid TOSCA YAML class instances in a maintainable, declarative manner.

## Decision:
- Chosen Alternative: Springfox
- Rationale:
  - Automatically generates an OpenAPI/Swagger specification and interactive Swagger UI from Spring MVC annotations, keeping documentation in sync with the code and minimizing drift.
  - Reduces boilerplate and duplication required by manually authored Swagger files while still allowing overrides and custom model/property descriptions through annotations.
  - Produces machine-readable specs (JSON/YAML), enabling client SDK scaffolding, contract testing, and integration with API gateways.
  - Supports grouping and versioning of APIs, security schemes (e.g., JWT, OAuth2), and customizers for consistent documentation across services.
  - Markdown-only documentation is not machine-readable and cannot power tooling; it is best used as supplemental narrative guides rather than the canonical API source.
- Notes:
  - We will complement Springfox-generated docs with concise Markdown guides and examples where developer experience benefits.
  - The generated OpenAPI artifact will be published as part of the build to CI artifacts and exposed via /swagger-ui and /v2/api-docs endpoints.

## Decision:
Build the web interface as a server-rendered Node.js application using Express with Nunjucks templates and the GOV.UK Design System (govuk-frontend). This choice keeps the stack simple, prioritises accessibility and performance, and aligns with common UK government patterns and guidance. Express provides mature support for routing, middleware, and multipart/form-data handling required for secure file uploads, while Nunjucks enables reusable, accessible templates that map directly to GOV.UK components.

We will use progressive enhancement: pages will work fully without JavaScript, with lightweight client-side JavaScript added only where it materially improves usability (e.g., upload progress, chunked uploads, validation hints). We will avoid a client-side SPA framework (e.g., React/Vue/Angular) unless a clear, validated need emerges, to minimise complexity, bundle size, and maintenance overhead.

This approach enables:
- Rapid delivery with a well-understood, widely supported framework.
- Strong accessibility by default via server-rendered HTML and GOV.UK components.
- Straightforward security hardening and compliance (e.g., CSRF, input validation, headers).
- Easier operations and observability in a service-oriented environment.

If future requirements necessitate richer interactivity, we will integrate isolated, component-level JavaScript or selectively introduce a micro-frontend for specific pages without replatforming the entire application.

## Decision:
Use configuration-time service wiring to select a single implementation set. When federatedPropertiesEnabled = true, Wikibase binds all Property-related entity data access services (read, search, lookup, serialization, etc.) to the federated (API-backed) implementations; when false, the bindings point to the local (DB-backed) implementations. No runtime per-entity dispatch layer is introduced.

Rationale:
- The MVP forbids mixing local and federated Properties; therefore a binary, configuration-driven switch avoids unnecessary indirection and complexity.
- Configuration-time wiring reduces runtime overhead, avoids hot-path branching, and simplifies testing and observability.
- It minimizes failure modes during rollouts and respects the constraint that switching modes back and forth is unsupported.

Operational safeguards:
- On federated mode, registrations for creating or modifying local Properties are disabled and surface clear errors.
- Health checks verify that required remote endpoints are available before finalizing service wiring.
- Metrics/logging annotate the active mode to aid diagnostics.

This approach can later be extended (if mixed modes are supported) by introducing a dedicated dispatcher, but for the MVP we keep a simple, robust, and efficient configuration-driven selection.

## Decision:
- Adopt React with TypeScript as the primary front-end framework for Akvo DASH.
- Use Vite as the build tool and dev server for fast feedback cycles and optimized production bundles.
- Prefer ecosystem-standard libraries:
  - Routing: React Router
  - Data fetching/caching: TanStack Query
  - State management: Zustand for local/ephemeral state; Redux Toolkit if complex cross-cutting state emerges
  - Forms: React Hook Form
  - UI: Headless UI + Tailwind CSS (or MUI if a component suite is preferred). Avoid runtime-heavy CSS-in-JS for performance.
  - i18n: i18next
  - Testing: Vitest + React Testing Library; E2E: Playwright
- Enforce quality and consistency:
  - TypeScript strict mode
  - ESLint + Prettier + stylelint
  - Commit tooling (Commitlint, lint-staged) and CI checks (type, lint, test)
- Architecture:
  - Modular, feature-sliced structure with co-located tests and styles
  - Code-splitting and route-level lazy loading
  - Monorepo-ready (pnpm workspaces) to share types and utilities with backend or other clients
- Performance and UX:
  - Adopt accessibility-first guidelines (WAI-ARIA), dark mode/theming, and responsive design
  - Bundle analysis and performance budgets; image optimization pipeline
- Interop and longevity:
  - Prefer JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystem over transpiled alternatives (e.g., ClojureScript) to reduce hiring risk, onboarding time, and maintenance overhead while benefiting from broad library support (charts, maps, data grids).
- Server rendering:
  - Start as SPA; if SEO or first-paint constraints arise, plan an incremental migration path to Next.js without rewriting core UI logic.

## Decision:
Adopt a CI-agnostic, globally unique versioning scheme for source and data package RC artifacts to eliminate collisions caused by non-unique build numbers.

- RC version pattern: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-rc.<commitsSinceReleaseTag>+<runDiscriminator>
  - commitsSinceReleaseTag: count from the latest release tag on the branch (deterministic ordering).
  - runDiscriminator: a guaranteed-unique suffix chosen in this order of availability:
    1) CI run ID/execution ID
    2) Short git SHA
    3) UTC timestamp (yyyyMMddHHmmss)
- The artifact registry key will include the full pre-release/build metadata so each publish is unique even when build numbers reset.
- Pre-publish validation will check existence; on conflict, the publisher regenerates the runDiscriminator using the next available option (or a timestamp) and retries a bounded number of times.
- This scheme is applied only to source and data package RC artifacts; unlocked package versions remain managed by Salesforce.
- Provide configuration to customize the pre-release identifier (default rc) and to opt into strict determinism (disable retries, fail-fast on conflict) if required by compliance.
- Migration: existing pipelines can adopt this without changing the base MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; only RC versions gain the discriminator, avoiding mutation errors in registries.

## Decision:
Adopt Terraform as the primary Infrastructure-as-Code tool to provision and manage cloud resources external to our Kubernetes/Helm deployments, including EKS clusters, S3, Amazon MQ, and Aurora. Continue to use Helm for deploying and configuring in-cluster ACS components.

Rationale:
- Avoids vendor lock-in while enabling AWS-first delivery; supports AWS today and other providers/services (and on-prem) if needed.
- Provides a single, consistent provisioning workflow for all non-Kubernetes resources, reducing fragmentation versus CloudFormation-plus-Helm.
- Eliminates the need to build/maintain custom Kubernetes controllers and CRDs, while still allowing future selective adoption of mature controllers (e.g., AWS ACK) where they add value.

Implementation notes:
- Standardize Terraform modules for reusable AWS resources; manage remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking.
- Provision EKS and foundational networking with Terraform; delegate app/runtime config to Helm.
- Integrate Terraform into CI/CD with plan/apply gates and policy checks.
- Mitigate limited experience via training, code reviews, and initial vendor/community modules.

## Decision:
We standardize on hermetic, containerized builds. All build, test, and packaging steps run inside a Docker image, not on the host. We define a multi-stage Dockerfile with pinned base images (by digest) and pinned toolchain/dependencies via lockfiles. Builds are executed with Docker BuildKit to ensure reproducibility and caching.

Developers and CI use the same entrypoints:
- make build: docker build using the Dockerfile (multi-stage) to produce artifacts/images
- make test: run tests inside containers (docker compose/run)
- make ci: wraps build+test for CI

We prohibit non-containerized host builds to avoid environment drift. The Dockerfile sets explicit versions for OS packages and language runtimes; environment-affecting variables are fixed (e.g., SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) where supported to promote deterministic outputs.

IDE integration is facilitated via a devcontainer/.compose-based setup so editors can attach to the containerized toolchain with minimal configuration. CI validates that images are built from pinned dependencies and fails on unpinned versions.

Artifacts (images, SBOMs) are produced within the container and published by CI. This approach guarantees that any machine with Docker can build the app identically, independent of host OS or installed toolchains.

## Decision:
Adopt NetworkManager as the single abstraction for performing network requests across the codebase. The Fetchable protocol is deprecated and must not be used in new or modified code.

- Scope:
  - All new network functionality must depend on NetworkManager via dependency injection.
  - Existing modules using Fetchable will be migrated incrementally to NetworkManager.
  - Shared utilities, interceptors, retries, timeouts, caching, and logging are centralized in NetworkManager.

- Migration:
  - Introduce an adapter (FetchableAdapter) that implements Fetchable by delegating to NetworkManager for interim compatibility.
  - Update service clients layer-by-layer; remove Fetchable conformance once migrated.
  - Replace direct fetch/URLSession usage with NetworkManager calls.

- Deprecation policy:
  - Mark Fetchable as @Deprecated with guidance to use NetworkManager.
  - Disallow new references via lint rule/static analysis; add CI check.
  - Remove Fetchable after all call sites are migrated.

- Consistency and configuration:
  - Standardize request/response models, error taxonomy, and retry/backoff policy via NetworkManager.
  - Enable per-environment configuration (base URLs, headers) only through NetworkManager.
  - Centralize observability (metrics, tracing, logging) in NetworkManager interceptors.

- Testing:
  - Provide a NetworkManagerMock/Fake for unit tests and an integration test harness.
  - Update test utilities to mock via NetworkManager, not Fetchable or raw network calls.

- Documentation and ownership:
  - Update developer docs and examples to use NetworkManager APIs.
  - Code reviews must reject new Fetchable usage.
  - Assign ownership to the Platform/Networking team for maintenance and evolution.

- Backward compatibility:
  - No runtime behavior changes expected; parity maintained during migration through the adapter.
  - Any API shape differences must be addressed at call sites during migration.

## Decision:
- Remove client-side reliance on the PLAY_LANG cookie for tracking consent language selection.
- Introduce a data-language attribute (values: en, cy) as the single source of truth for the banner’s runtime language.
- Default to English when data-language is absent or invalid.
- Update MDTP/Play helpers to automatically set data-language based on the request’s resolved language (e.g. using Play’s i18n), ensuring consistent behavior even when PLAY_LANG is HttpOnly.
- Document and provide examples for classic Java services to set data-language explicitly, enabling Welsh support without requiring Play’s cookies.
- Backward compatibility: retain PLAY_LANG reading as deprecated for one transitional minor release (if present and readable, it will be used only when data-language is not set), then remove in the next major release.
- Clearly deprecate PLAY_LANG usage in release notes and migration guides; recommend making PLAY_LANG HttpOnly without affecting banner behavior.
- Align with govuk-frontend/hmrc-frontend practices by preferring data attributes for client-side configuration.

## Decision:
Decommission Neo4j and migrate to a bitemporal, open-source datastore with first-class time and full history—XTDB (formerly Crux)—as the primary persistence layer.

Rationale:
- Licensing: Adopt Apache-2.0 licensed XTDB to avoid Neo4j’s restrictive “open core” model.
- Time & history: Use XTDB’s immutable log and bitemporal model (valid-time and transaction-time) to enable time-travel queries and full auditability, which Neo4j lacks.
- Clojure-native: Leverage XTDB’s Clojure-first API and Datalog query language, eliminating the need to maintain bespoke Neo4j Clojure libraries.
- Graph-friendly: Model entities as documents and relationships as references; expose a thin graph abstraction over Datalog where needed.

Approach:
- Run XTDB with Postgres-backed or RocksDB + Kafka/LX storage depending on ops constraints; standardize via configuration.
- Introduce a persistence port with an implementation for XTDB; isolate query/mutation logic from the backing store.
- Implement read paths using Datalog and time-travel queries; implement write paths as immutable puts/deletes with valid-time semantics.
- Provide migration tooling to export Neo4j nodes/edges to XTDB documents with stable IDs and relationship refs; validate parity via query fixtures.
- Sunset Neo4j integration and libraries after cutover and stability window.

This shift removes license risk and custom driver burden, while enabling temporal analytics and full historical traceability with simpler, idiomatic Clojure infrastructure.

## Decision:
Adopt GitHub Actions as the standard CI/CD platform for the HEE National Website Platform.

- Source of truth: GitHub repositories with branch protection and required status checks.
- Build and test: Containerised builds with matrix testing across supported runtimes; caching for dependencies; artifacts stored via Actions artifacts.
- Security and compliance: Native code scanning (CodeQL), Dependabot, and SAST/secret scanning enabled across repos; provenance via build attestations (where supported).
- Secrets and identity: Use OIDC federated workload identity from GitHub to cloud providers; no long‑lived credentials in GitHub. Runtime secrets stored in cloud secret managers; minimal secrets in GitHub Environments when required.
- Deployments: Environment-based workflows (dev, test, staging, prod) with required reviewers/approvals and manual gates; progressive delivery (blue/green or canary) where the target platform supports it.
- Infrastructure as Code: Provisioning and changes via Terraform executed from Actions with policy checks (e.g., OPA/Conftest) and plan/apply segregation.
- Reusability and standardisation: Organisation-level, reusable workflows and composite actions for linting, testing, building, container image publishing, IaC plans/applies, and deployment steps; versioned and centrally maintained.
- Observability and rollback: Post-deploy smoke tests, health checks, and automatic rollback policies; emit deployment metadata to monitoring/alerting.
- Runners: Use GitHub-hosted runners by default; introduce hardened self-hosted runners for privileged tasks (e.g., private networking) with isolation and patching policies.
- Governance: Release versioning, SBOM generation, image signing (Sigstore/cosign), and mandatory review of promotion between environments.

This choice provides tight integration with our GitHub workflow, strong security posture without shared credentials, rich ecosystem support, and minimal platform overhead, while remaining cloud-agnostic for deployments. We will review suitability in 6 months and reassess if project scope or hosting constraints change.

## Decision:
We will use explicit Dependency Injection with constructor injection and a per-request scope to resolve the object graph for each Command and Query.

- Composition roots: Each module exposes a registration function that wires its handlers, services, repositories, mappers, and policies. The host/application startup composes modules and owns the container.
- Resolution: API layer constructs the Command/Query DTO and asks the container to resolve the corresponding handler interface; the container builds the full graph via constructor injection. No Service Locator, no ambient context.
- Lifetimes:
  - Scoped (per request/operation): handlers, application services, repositories, unit-of-work, Db contexts, cache contexts.
  - Singleton: stateless utilities (e.g., serializers, clock, id generators, config, mapping profiles).
  - Transient: pure mappers/validators where construction cost is negligible and no state is held.
- Factories: Use typed factories for aggregates and domain services that need runtime parameters or deferred creation; factories are resolved via DI.
- Boundaries: Cross-module dependencies must go through module-defined interfaces to keep modules independently testable and replaceable.
- Registration: Prefer explicit, code-based registrations per module; allow safe assembly scanning only for well-known conventions (e.g., IHandle<T>).
- Testing: Handlers can be constructed directly with test doubles or resolved from a lightweight test container using the same registrations.

This approach keeps object graphs explicit, testable, and isolated per module, while avoiding hidden dependencies and global state.

## Decision:
Deprecate and remove all Core integrations that directly access GPIO (including SPI and I2C) due to low usage, lack of maintainers, unstable container passthrough, and platform variability. Effective immediately:
- No new GPIO-based integrations will be accepted into Core.
- All existing GPIO/SPI/I2C integrations enter deprecation: feature-freeze and “will be removed” warnings.
- Removal will occur after a deprecation window of two stable releases (minimum 4 months), with clear breaking-change notes.

Migration path:
- Recommend ESPHome (or similar dedicated firmware projects) for sensors/actuators; integrate with Home Assistant via native ESPHome, MQTT, or other supported bridges.
- Provide concise migration guides for common devices/patterns.

Support stance:
- Home Assistant OS/Container/Supervised will not guarantee GPIO passthrough or platform-specific quirks; we will not invest in cross-platform GPIO stability within Core.
- Vendor- or community-owned GPIO functionality may live as external integrations or add-ons maintained outside Core.

Exception policy:
- Only consider reintroducing hardware-bus integrations if they meet all of: strong maintainer commitment, broad cross-platform support (upstream kernel/userspace), automated CI with hardware-in-the-loop or reliable emulation, and demonstrable high usage. Otherwise, they remain out of Core.

We will revisit this decision if a robust, portable hardware abstraction with proven maintenance emerges and usage justifies Core support.

## Decision:
- Abstract identity behind a dedicated IdentityProvider interface and remove hard-coded identity references from code paths.
- Make the active identity selectable via configuration parameters (e.g., env var IDENTITY_PROFILE and/or config file/ConfigMap), with deployment-time overrides via Helm/Kustomize.
- Store credentials for each identity profile in Kubernetes Secrets or an external secret manager; reference them by name derived from the selected profile.
- For Kubernetes/OpenShift workloads, parameterize serviceAccountName and associated Role/RoleBinding; support switching by updating the service account reference or projecting a token with the desired audience. Where applicable, support user/service-account impersonation.
- Enable safe rotation/switching by supporting hot-reload of identity configuration (e.g., via sidecar/reloader watching ConfigMaps/Secrets); if not feasible, perform a controlled rolling restart.
- Provide a default identity profile and validation at startup to ensure required credentials/permissions are present; fail fast on misconfiguration.
- Log identity profile changes and expose metrics/events for auditing.
- Document identity profiles, required permissions, and migration steps to switch identities across environments.

We will standardize on the name MultiFrameViewer and deprecate PagesViewer (providing a temporary alias with deprecation warnings for one minor release cycle). MultiFrameViewer will be implemented as a generic, extensible multi-frame subject viewer with a composable Filmstrip subcomponent.

Initial scope prioritizes transcription-oriented use cases:
- Per-frame navigation with keyboard shortcuts
- Per-frame mark filtering and per-frame positioning reset
- Lazy loading and cached prefetch of adjacent frames
- Basic drawing task support per frame
- Accessible focus management and labels for frames and filmstrip

Behavior will be configured via workflow.configuration.subject_viewer_config.multiFrame, with at minimum:
- filter_marks_per_frame: boolean
- positioning: "maintain" | "reset"

The Filmstrip will expose a stable interface (data source, selection model, prefetch hints, render delegate) to enable future features (e.g., flipbook behavior, continuous scroll, comparative layouts) without breaking changes. Performance and memory constraints will be addressed with virtualization and image tiling where applicable.

We will adopt an extension pattern for non-transcription requirements (e.g., ecology workflows), adding features behind configuration flags and maintaining backward compatibility. All public props and configuration will be documented; unit and integration tests will validate per-frame state, navigation, and drawing interactions. PagesViewer references in code and docs will be updated to MultiFrameViewer.

## Decision:
- Adopt CSS Modules for component-level styling to achieve automatic local scoping of class names and avoid global CSS collisions.
- Use Sass (SCSS syntax) as the CSS preprocessor to enable variables, mixins, and nesting with a familiar, widely adopted syntax.
- Configure the build tool (e.g., Vite/Webpack) with css-modules enabled and sass-loader to ensure minimal integration friction and fast developer onboarding.
- Centralize design tokens (colors, spacing, typography) in a small set of SCSS partials (e.g., _tokens.scss) imported into module styles as needed to standardize theming while keeping modules isolated.
- Keep a minimal global stylesheet for true globals (CSS resets, base typography), with all component styles implemented as .module.scss files.
- Provide a short style guide and sample components to accelerate adoption by future maintainers, leveraging the common industry familiarity with SCSS and CSS Modules.
- Optionally add Stylelint with a lightweight config to enforce consistency without steep learning overhead.

## Decision:
Build an internal, lightweight case-management web application to support the end-to-end accessibility monitoring workflow, prioritising open-source components and alignment with the GDS Way.

- Platform and hosting: Deploy on GOV.UK PaaS (Cloud Foundry) to minimise ops overhead and align with GDS guidance.
- Technology stack: Node.js with TypeScript and Express for the backend; GOV.UK Frontend and the GOV.UK Design System for the UI; Postgres as the primary data store.
- Authentication/authorisation: Organisation SSO via Azure AD/Google OAuth (OIDC) with role-based access (admin, analyst, viewer).
- Core features: 
  - Registry of public sector websites (CRUD, tagging, ownership metadata).
  - Work queue for triage, prioritisation, assignment, and progress tracking.
  - Test records with structured data capture and attachments.
  - Report generation from Markdown templates rendered to HTML/PDF (Puppeteer), versioned per report.
  - Email delivery and tracking via GOV.UK Notify; template variables mapped from test records.
  - Interaction logging (notes, contact history) linked to sites and reports.
- Integrations and storage: Object storage (S3-compatible) for artefacts; audit logging; optional import/export via CSV.
- Delivery and quality: GitHub for repo management; GitHub Actions for CI/CD, security scanning, and automated testing; IaC for PaaS manifests.
- Licensing and openness: MIT-licensed, public by default, to enable reuse and reduce cost.

This approach satisfies suitability, reduces ongoing costs, follows the GDS Way, and directly supports all defined operational requirements.

Decide to publish a single NPM package that exports all components.

Rationale:
- Simplifies development, consumption, versioning, and publishing while we iterate quickly.
- Modern bundlers support tree-shaking, minimizing bundled code to only imported components.

Implementation:
- Package name: @org/ui (placeholder).
- ESM-first build with CJS compatibility; mark "sideEffects": false to enable tree-shaking.
- Provide per-component subpath exports to support granular imports without multiple packages:
  - "exports": { "./Button": { "import": "./esm/Button.js", "require": "./cjs/Button.js", "types": "./types/Button.d.ts" }, "." : "./esm/index.js" }
- Avoid cross-component hard dependencies where possible; prefer composition via props/children to keep graphs lean.
- Enforce SemVer at the package level; document breaking changes clearly in release notes.
- Add CI checks for bundle size regressions and verify tree-shaking effectiveness (e.g., using size-limit).

Style guide:
- Consume the single package; showcase components via direct imports. If necessary, expose experimental components behind feature flags or “preview” exports.

Re-evaluation criteria:
- Consider splitting to per-component packages if any of the following occur: significant and recurring bundle size concerns despite tree-shaking, strong consumer demand for independent versioning, or materially divergent dependency graphs across components.
- If splitting later, plan a phased migration using Changesets/Lerna/Nx, maintain subpath export aliases for backward compatibility, and provide codemods.

## Decision:
Adopt OpenAPI 3.1 as the canonical, machine-readable API contract and the single source of truth for our HTTP API.

- Author and version an openapi.yaml in the repository (contract-first where feasible). All API changes require PR review against this spec and semantic versioning.
- Generate human-readable docs from the spec and host them at /docs using Swagger UI (interactive) and ReDoc (narrative). Provide both YAML and JSON downloads.
- Enforce quality in CI: validate the spec (openapi-cli), lint with Spectral, and detect breaking changes with openapi-diff. Require examples for all operations and schemas.
- Reuse JSON Schema components for request/response bodies and error models; include examples and explicit status codes. Document authentication, pagination, filtering, and error formats.
- Automatically generate and publish client SDKs from the spec using OpenAPI Generator for key ecosystems (e.g., TypeScript/Java/.NET), published to internal registries on release. Generated clients live in separate repos and are regenerated on each API release tag.
- Provide a Postman collection and environment derived from the OpenAPI spec and keep it in sync via CI.
- Serve the OpenAPI document from a stable URL (e.g., /openapi.yaml) and include a changelog and deprecation notices in the spec and docs.
- For backward compatibility, deprecate before removal and avoid breaking changes within a major version.

This approach yields machine- and human-readable documentation with minimal duplication and enables automated client generation and validation in the delivery pipeline.

We will adopt a lightweight, open RFC/ADR process in a single, public “architecture-decisions” Git repository.

- Proposals: Anyone may open a PR using the ADR template (problem, context, options, decision, consequences, risks, references). Each ADR is assigned an ID, owner, status, and tags; a README index keeps a centralized catalog.
- Review: Discussion occurs in the PR. A minimum review window of 5 business days applies (7 for high-impact). Decisions use lazy consensus with at least two approvals from different teams; high-impact items require three, including one from Security/SRE. If consensus fails, the Architecture Working Group adjudicates.
- Versioning: ADRs are immutable once accepted. Changes are made by creating a new ADR that supersedes the prior one; minor clarifications are edits via PR with clear changelog entries.
- Transparency: All discussion, rationale, and alternatives remain in the PR history. Meeting notes, if any, are linked in the ADR.
- Centralization and discoverability: ADRs live in the dedicated repo and are mirrored to the open web via GitHub Pages. We cross-link from relevant code repositories and documentation. Labels and tags enable search by domain and impact.
- Cadence: We hold a brief, regular architecture review to surface blockers and elevate contentious proposals; decisions are still finalized in PR.
- Compliance: All architecture-impacting changes must reference an accepted ADR in their implementation PRs.

## Decision:
We will maintain a living, versioned log of architectural decisions using Lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) stored in the repository (docs/adr). Each ADR will be a small, immutable markdown file with a sequential ID and the fields: Title, Context, Decision, Status (Proposed | Accepted | Deprecated | Superseded), Consequences, Alternatives, and Links.

Scope:
- Create an ADR for every significant architectural decision or reversal (e.g., technology choices, data model changes, cross-cutting concerns, runtime topology, deprecations), including explicit decisions to not change.

Process:
- Propose: Open a PR with a new ADR (Status: Proposed) before or alongside implementation.
- Discuss: Keep rationale and trade-offs in the PR; summarize key points in the ADR.
- Decide: A designated approver (e.g., tech lead/architect on-call) accepts the ADR; merge marks Status: Accepted.
- Implement: Link the ADR from related code changes and docs.
- Evolve: Supersede via a new ADR; never rewrite history—update Status to Superseded with links.
- Review: Quarterly cleanup to ensure indexes, statuses, and links are current.

Conventions and tooling:
- Directory: docs/adr; index file with a numbered list and short summaries.
- Template provided at docs/adr/0000-template.md; adr-tools or similar may be used but is optional.
- CI will flag “architecture-impacting” PRs to require a linked ADR.
- Tag ADRs by domain/component for discoverability.

This approach provides traceability, preserves intent over time, and reduces decision paralysis by making rationale explicit and auditable.

## Decision:
- Chosen Alternative: gin-gonic/gin

We will use Gin as our HTTP router and middleware framework. Gin offers high performance (built on top of httprouter), a mature ecosystem, and an ergonomic API for route grouping, middleware chains, and parameterized routes. It also provides first-class helpers for JSON binding/validation, structured error handling, and response rendering, which accelerates endpoint development and improves consistency.

Gorilla/mux has been archived and is no longer actively maintained, so we will not adopt it. Writing our own router or using only the standard library would slow delivery, require reimplementing common concerns (routing, middleware, recovery, logging), and increase maintenance risk.

Implementation guidelines:
- Use Gin’s route groups to organize API versions and feature areas.
- Keep business logic decoupled from Gin by defining handler interfaces and thin adapters; accept/return net/http types where feasible to limit framework lock-in.
- Centralize common middleware (logging, recovery, request ID, CORS) and error handling.
- Enable Gin release mode in production; integrate with our structured logger.
- Rely on Gin’s binding/validation with explicit DTOs; avoid implicit magic in handlers.
- Ensure graceful shutdown via net/http server with context timeouts.
- Cover routes with integration tests using httptest; unit-test handlers independently of Gin where practical.

This choice balances developer productivity, performance, and maintainability while preserving an escape hatch to replace the router in the future if requirements change.

## Decision:
We will use Jest as our unit test framework to support a fast TDD workflow and built-in mocking.

- Test runner and assertions: Jest (expect/Matchers), with watch mode (jest --watch) for rapid feedback.
- Mocking: Use Jest’s native mocking features:
  - jest.fn() for function doubles and spies
  - jest.spyOn() for spying on object methods
  - jest.mock() for module-level mocks and manual mocks via __mocks__
  - jest.useFakeTimers() for time-based code
- Project setup:
  - Co-locate tests as *.test.[jt]s?(x) next to source files
  - Default environment: node (override per test if needed)
  - Coverage reporting enabled with thresholds to maintain quality
- TypeScript projects: Use ts-jest (or babel-jest if using Babel) to run tests without a separate build step.

NPM scripts:
- test: jest
- test:watch: jest --watch
- test:coverage: jest --coverage

This setup provides fast, isolated programmer tests with robust, ergonomic function and module mocking aligned with a TDD workflow.

## Decision:
We will manage database schema changes with Flyway using SQL-based, versioned migrations stored in the application repository.

Key points:
- Tooling: Flyway Community Edition, executed via CLI/Docker in CI/CD; optional app-startup migration only in non-prod to speed developer workflows.
- Migration format: forward-only, versioned SQL files named VYYYYMMDDHHMM__short_description.sql committed to version control. Repeatable migrations (R__*.sql) reserved for idempotent reference data or views.
- Strategy: adopt an expand-and-contract approach for zero/low-downtime changes (add columns as nullable/defaulted, backfill, dual-write/read, then remove deprecated artifacts in a subsequent release).
- Rollbacks: no down scripts in production. Correct issues with new forward migrations. For non-prod, down migrations may be used for convenience but are not required.
- Environments: migrations run automatically on feature branches and main in CI against ephemeral/test databases; promoted via a dedicated CD step for staging/production with manual approval.
- Baseline: existing schema (if any) will be baselined with Flyway baseline to establish starting version.
- Access: CI/CD service account with schema-change privileges; application runtime with least-privilege (no DDL).
- Validation/quality: SQL linting in CI, required code review for migrations, and pre-deploy dry-run/validate steps. Include reversible data backfills as separate, idempotent scripts when feasible.
- Seeding: development-only seed scripts run via Make/NPM task or docker-compose; production seeding limited to essential reference data in repeatable migrations.
- Observability: Flyway info output archived in CI; database change log retained for audit.

This approach provides auditable, deterministic, environment-agnostic schema evolution, supports incremental delivery, and minimizes deployment risk.

## Decision:
- Adopt TypeScript for all new client-side code to improve confidence, readability, and self-documentation, leveraging its familiarity for JavaScript developers and strong editor support.
- Gradually migrate existing JavaScript to TypeScript, prioritizing modules with the most change risk or domain complexity.
- Enable strict type checking (strict: true, noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks) to maximize correctness; allow any as an explicit, temporary escape hatch with TODOs.
- Define public APIs, domain models, and module boundaries with explicit types/interfaces; prefer interfaces for object contracts and type aliases for unions/intersections.
- Enforce type safety in CI (tsc --noEmit) and code review; integrate ESLint with typescript-eslint for consistent code quality.
- Avoid non-standard or deprecated TypeScript patterns (e.g., namespaces, triple-slash references); use ES modules and modern ECMAScript features.
- Provide onboarding guides and examples; maintain a shared type utilities library and project tsconfig presets to reduce setup friction.
- Revisit configuration and adoption progress quarterly to ensure developer ergonomics and build performance remain acceptable.

## Decision:
Adopt a single binary with three explicit operational modes selectable via configuration or CLI: full, validator, and seed.

- Mode selection
  - config.toml: mode = "full" | "validator" | "seed"
  - CLI: --mode=[full|validator|seed]
  - Mode is immutable at runtime; switching requires restart.

- Full mode
  - Behavior: fully syncs and stays up to date; participates in P2P gossip but never signs or proposes; runs block sync/state sync, mempool (optional), and RPC.
  - Safety: refuses to start if a priv-validator key/socket is present unless --allow-privval-in-full=true (default: false). Consensus runs in non-voting mode.

- Validator mode
  - Behavior: identical to existing validator behavior—sync without voting; once caught up, participate in consensus and signing.
  - Requirements: priv-validator configured and reachable; key type supported.
  - Safety: enable double-sign risk reduction checks by default (see ADR for double-sign checks); require explicit acknowledgement to disable. Enforce only one instance per validator key by locking privval file/socket where possible.

- Seed mode
  - Behavior: lightweight peer discovery service maintaining address book; only P2P stack active (PEX on), no consensus, no mempool, no ABCI, no block execution, and RPC disabled by default (can enable minimal /net_info with --rpc.enable=true).
  - Resources: optimized for low CPU/memory; high peer limits and aggressive address book gossip.

- Defaults and derived settings
  - full: consensus=gossip-only, mempool=on, rpc=on, pex=on
  - validator: consensus=voting, mempool=on, rpc=on, pex=on
  - seed: consensus=off, mempool=off, rpc=off, pex=on
  - On startup, validate derived settings against mode; conflicting flags cause a hard error unless --force is provided (not allowed in validator mode).

- Observability and UX
  - Log and metrics include mode tag.
  - Node info advertises mode in p2p node_info and RPC /status.
  - Clear startup banners describing enabled components and any safety interlocks.

- Security hardening
  - In non-validator modes, block any signing endpoints and Sentry/PrivVal connections.
  - In validator mode, refuse to start if double-sign protection is misconfigured or disabled without --i-know-what-im-doing=true.

We will front Kibana with an authentication/authorization proxy that uses GitHub OAuth. Specifically:
- Deploy oauth2-proxy (or equivalent) in front of Kibana, configured with our GitHub OAuth app (client ID/secret) and restricted to members of our GitHub organization and/or approved teams.
- Expose only the proxy publicly (via ALB/Ingress and TLS); place Kibana behind it on a private network/security group so it is unreachable directly.
- Use short‑lived, encrypted cookies for sessions; enforce HTTPS, HSTS, and CSRF protections provided by the proxy.
- Authorize access based on GitHub org/team membership; initially grant read‑only access to approved teams. Where feasible, map teams to Kibana roles/spaces or index patterns to scope users to their application logs.
- Centralize configuration as code (GitHub team allowlists, cookie secrets, redirect URIs, headers) and automate deployment.
- Preserve flexibility to swap the upstream identity provider by using OIDC where supported; if we later adopt a central IdP (e.g., Cognito/SSO), we will reconfigure the proxy without changing the Kibana endpoint.

This provides single sign-on with GitHub, avoids managing separate Kibana credentials, and gives us a consistent, auditable access control path to application logs.

## Decision:
Standardize on a single, immutable Docker image as the deployment artifact per app and build it once per commit in CI, then promote the same image (by content-addressable digest or git-SHA tag) to both Docker Swarm and Kubernetes.

To minimize duplicated work:
- Adopt multi-stage Dockerfiles with a shared, versioned builder base image (per language/runtime) and a slim runtime base image. Update builder bases on a managed cadence.
- Enable Docker BuildKit/buildx with registry-backed cache (e.g., --cache-to/--cache-from) and cache mounts for package managers to reuse downloaded dependencies across builds.
- Structure Dockerfiles for maximal layer reuse (copy lockfiles before sources; separate dependency install from app build).
- Publish images to a single registry and reference by digest across orchestrators/environments.
- Integrate CI to perform the build once, run tests/security scans, push the image, and trigger deployments that only pull the already-built image.

This approach eliminates redundant full rebuilds, speeds pipelines via layer caching, and ensures environment parity by deploying the exact same artifact to Swarm and Kubernetes.

## Decision:
Adopt a single, enforced pattern template and lifecycle across customer-facing, integration, and other architectures.

- Canonical format: Markdown with YAML front matter; diagrams in Mermaid/PlantUML; links to OpenAPI/AsyncAPI and reference repos.
- Required front matter: id (stable slug), title, domain (customer/integration/other), owner, status {Draft, Proposed, Approved, Deprecated}, version (semver), last-reviewed, maturity {Exploratory, Validated, Proven}, tags, related, compliance areas (Security, Privacy, Reg, Ops), and decision record link(s).
- Required sections (in order): Intent, Context & Forces, Problem, Solution (Structure & Behaviors), Reference Architecture Diagram, Variants & Options, Applicability, Trade-offs & Consequences, NFRs (perf, resiliency, cost), Security & Compliance, Integration Considerations (sync/async, contracts), Operational Considerations (observability, SLOs, runbooks), Examples & Reference Implementations, Known Uses, Anti-patterns, Open Questions, References.
- Repository structure: mono-repo docs/patterns/{domain}/{pattern-id}/ with pattern.md, diagrams/, examples/, tests/ (lint), and changelog.md.
- Governance: PR-based review with named approvers per domain; mandatory checklist to verify sections; status transitions controlled via CODEOWNERS; quarterly review SLA.
- Consistency tooling: JSON Schema for front matter and section anchors; CI linters to enforce schema, link hygiene, diagram validity; template generator (CLI) for new patterns; docs site auto-publishes with search and cross-linking.
- Consumption: patterns referenced by ADRs and solution designs by id and version; deprecation notices with migration guidance; backward-compatible updates favored, breaking changes require new major version.
- Measures: track adoption, freshness (time since review), and coverage by domain to drive continuous improvement.

## Decision:
We will implement the browser-based visualization in TypeScript (transpiled to JavaScript). TypeScript’s class-based, object-oriented syntax and static typing align with the team’s OO background, reduce onboarding time amid frequent team changes, and improve maintainability through stronger tooling (IDE autocompletion, refactoring, and type checking). The code will target modern browsers via ES modules and a standard bundler, allowing us to use the broader JavaScript ecosystem while retaining OO-friendly ergonomics.

## Decision:
We will move the mymove repository outside of $GOPATH and rely on Go modules. Developers should clone the repo to any directory not under $GOPATH; the module path remains github.com/transcom/mymove.

We will stop forcing GO111MODULE=on. For local development we will use GO111MODULE=auto (or the Go default behavior for versions where modules are enabled outside $GOPATH). CI/CD and tooling will assume module mode and no longer depend on a GOPATH-based project layout.

We will:
- Remove build/test scripts and documentation that require $GOPATH.
- Ensure Makefile, pre-commit hooks, and other tooling invoke go in module mode without setting GOPATH.
- Keep $GOPATH/bin in PATH for installed tools, but not use GOPATH for source.
- Update onboarding docs to reflect module-first workflows (go mod download, go build/test, etc.).

This supersedes ADR0003 and aligns local development with our CI/CD configuration and pre-commit tooling.

## Decision:
Adopt a risk-based, test-pyramid approach that maximizes confidence per unit of maintenance.

- Strategy:
  - Unit tests: broad coverage of business logic, domain invariants, edge cases, and pure functions. Prefer property-based tests for algorithmic code.
  - Integration tests: focus on service boundaries (DB, queues, external APIs), data contracts, and critical workflows across modules.
  - End-to-end (E2E): minimal, stable “happy path” user journeys for top business-critical flows only.

- Always test:
  - Critical user journeys (E2E, smoke).
  - Public contracts: API schemas, events, and version compatibility (contract tests/consumers).
  - Core business rules, calculations, and authorization rules (unit/integration).
  - Bug regressions (add a failing test before the fix).
  - Migrations and feature flags behavior at boundaries.

- Avoid testing:
  - Implementation details and trivial code.
  - Fragile UI specifics and broad snapshots; prefer accessible selectors and behavior-oriented assertions.
  - Redundant tests covering the same logic at multiple layers without added value.

- Quality gates and targets:
  - Code coverage: minimum 80% for domain libraries, 70% for services/UI, with rationale required when lower. Branch coverage emphasized on complex logic.
  - E2E count capped to essential paths; add only with explicit risk justification.
  - New/changed code must include tests at the appropriate layer and a brief “test scope” note in the PR.

- Maintenance and reliability:
  - Quarantine flaky tests immediately; fix or delete within an agreed SLA.
  - Prefer deterministic test data and hermetic environments; mock only at service boundaries.
  - Periodic review of test suite for redundancy and brittleness.

This balances breadth (confidence) and cost (maintainability) by pushing most checks down the pyramid, safeguarding critical flows at the top, and enforcing disciplined test selection in PRs.

## Decision:
Adopt an action-oriented, RPC-style endpoint to model the operation explicitly, rather than forcing it into a canonical REST resource URI.

- Endpoint: POST /route-tables:sync-route
- Semantics: “Synchronize a single specified route from the main route table to eligible custom route tables (add or replace).”
- Request body (minimal, log-friendly):
  - destinationPrefix (CIDR, required)
  - nextHop or target (as available; optional if derivable)
  - operation: upsert (default) | add | replace
  - constraints/filters (optional: target table tags, tenancy/scope)
  - idempotencyKey (optional but recommended)
- Behavior:
  - Server derives the main route table and resolves target custom tables per policy.
  - Upserts the route in each target table.
  - Returns a correlationId and per-table status (async-safe; may be eventually consistent).
- Rationale:
  - The action has workflow semantics and cross-resource side effects that do not map cleanly to a single resource URI.
  - POST to an action endpoint avoids overloading PUT/PATCH semantics while enabling a concise payload from limited log data.
- Consistency:
  - Use the :action suffix pattern for similar cross-resource operations (e.g., /route-tables:reconcile, /routes:propagate).
  - Enforce idempotency by idempotencyKey and the tuple (destinationPrefix, scope) to tolerate log replays.

## Decision:
Adopt Flyway as the standard tool for database versioning and safe migrations across all services.

- Store all migrations in the application repo under db/migrations, committed and code-reviewed. Use SQL-first migrations where possible for transparency and portability; allow Java/Kotlin callback migrations only when SQL is insufficient.
- Use versioned migrations (V{yyyyMMddHHmmss}__description.sql) for schema/data changes and repeatable migrations (R__*.sql) for views, functions, and seed reference data.
- Enforce forward-only migrations. Rollbacks are performed by creating new migrations that revert changes; destructive operations require explicit backups and confirmation gates.
- Run flyway validate on every commit and before deployment; run flyway migrate via CI/CD in a controlled pre-release step per environment. Disable auto-migrate on application startup in production.
- Require backward-compatible, zero-downtime patterns:
  - Expand-and-contract (add nullable columns, backfill, dual-read/write, then drop old).
  - Use transactional DDL where supported; otherwise schedule during low-traffic windows.
  - For large/locking operations, use DB-native online features (e.g., CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, partitioning strategies) or approved online schema tools specific to the engine.
- Provide dry-run and checksum validation in CI to detect drift; require baselining for existing databases.
- Parameterize environment-specific values via Flyway placeholders; manage secrets via the deployment pipeline, not in scripts.
- For long-running backfills, implement idempotent, chunked scripts/jobs invoked alongside migrations, with progress metrics and retry safety.
- Maintain migration runbooks and dashboards (applied version, status) per environment.

This standardizes versioning, improves safety, and integrates with delivery pipelines while supporting zero/low-downtime changes.

## Decision:
Implement a single, modular monolith backend that serves both “Hungry Person” (web/mobile) and “Ghost Kitchen” web clients through a unified public API with role-based access control (customer, kitchen-operator/admin). Expose a REST API (with simple pagination/filtering) to minimize client complexity and operational overhead at the projected scale (~1,000 active customers). Use a clean modular boundary inside the monolith (accounts/discounts, menu/catalog, inventory/reporting, feedback) to allow future extraction if scale or teams require it.

Leverage a managed identity provider (OIDC/OAuth2) for authentication, sessions/refresh tokens for mobile/web, and enforce authorization via centrally defined policies. Integrate with external billing/POS only for verification of purchase (for feedback eligibility) and reporting correlation; do not implement payment flows.

Use a managed relational database as the system of record and build simple reporting endpoints (and scheduled aggregates) for inventory and purchase reports. This approach optimizes for low cost, low latency, faster delivery, and a clear path to evolve into BFFs or services later if needed.

## Decision:
Adopt dual representations with clear domains:

- Sample-accurate (canonical for audio processing): positions and durations are represented as 64-bit integers in sample frames (interleaved across all channels). All DSP, slicing, buffer indexing, and file I/O use frame counts paired with an explicit sample rate.
- Time-oriented (for UI, scheduling, and metadata): positions and durations are represented as 64-bit integers in milliseconds. Floating-point seconds are permitted only at API boundaries and immediately converted; they are not persisted.

Conversion rules (centralized in a utility module):
- time(ms) -> frames: frames = floor(ms * sampleRate / 1000) for start positions; frames = ceil(ms * sampleRate / 1000) for end positions/durations to preserve inclusion of complete frames. Clamp to media bounds.
- frames -> time(ms): ms = round(frames * 1000 / sampleRate).
- All conversions require an explicit sample rate; upon sample-rate changes, recompute frame-based positions from time-based sources where applicable.

Persistence and interchange:
- Persist and exchange time metadata in integer milliseconds; never persist floating-point time.
- Persist processing-state positions in frames with the associated sample rate when needed to ensure deterministic playback/editing.

Additional constraints:
- Frames always imply samples from all channels; no channel-dependent indexing.
- Avoid mixing single/double time floats to prevent drift; use integers and deterministic rounding as specified.
- Provide helper types for strong typing (e.g., FrameCount, Milliseconds) to prevent unit mix-ups.

## Decision:
Measure uptime as user-experienced availability using both external synthetics and internal telemetry, reported over a rolling 30-day window.

- SLI definitions:
  - Request availability (APIs): successful requests / total requests. A request is successful if it returns 2xx/3xx within latency threshold; 5xx, timeouts, and connection errors are failures. Treat 429 as failure for SLA.
  - Good-minute availability (web/app): a minute is “good” if error rate <1% and p95 latency is within defined thresholds for key endpoints/journeys. Uptime = good minutes / total minutes.

- Measurement sources and frequency:
  - External synthetic probes from ≥5 geographic regions, every 30–60 seconds, covering:
    - Health/ready endpoints
    - Critical user journeys (login, checkout, core API calls)
  - Internal metrics from edge/load balancers and services (errors, latency, saturation) to corroborate and root-cause.

- Scope and aggregation:
  - Report per product and per critical user journey; roll up service uptime as the minimum of its critical dependencies (first-party services included). Third-party dependencies count toward downtime if they impact the user journey.
  - Weight multi-endpoint APIs by traffic or declared criticality.

- Maintenance policy:
  - Exclude only pre-announced maintenance within agreed windows and caps; unannounced or over-cap maintenance counts as downtime.

- Reporting and compliance:
  - Publish monthly uptime and error-budget burn; trigger alerts on fast-burn rates and SLI breaches.
  - Keep versioned SLOs/thresholds (e.g., p95 latency, error-rate cutoffs) per service and review quarterly.

This approach provides objective, user-centric uptime aligned to SLAs and actionable feedback for improvement.

## Decision:
Name the “global MADRs” Architecture Option Catalog (AOC) entries.

- We will maintain a centralized Architecture Option Catalog (AOC) that captures problem-space issues and their solution options with global, context-agnostic pros/cons and selection guidance.
- Each item in the catalog is an AOC entry (also referred to as an Architecture Option Record, AOR).
- Project-specific decisions continue to use MADR-based ADRs (“local MADRs”) in the solution space; these ADRs will link to the relevant AOC entries for traceability.
- This naming clearly separates reusable, organization-wide guidance (AOC) from concrete project decisions (ADR), avoids overloading “ADR/MADR,” and aligns with the issue/alternative semantics from the problem/solution space model.
- Repository structure: /aoc/<topic>/<option>.md for AOC entries; /adr/ for local MADRs.

## Decision:
Adopt a dedicated analytics store with pre-aggregated, partitioned summary tables fed by an incremental ELT pipeline, and deprecate application-database materialized views for dashboards.

Concretely:
- Replicate OLTP data to a columnar analytics database (e.g., BigQuery/Redshift/ClickHouse/Snowflake) via change data capture or scheduled batch loads.
- Build denormalized, partitioned (monthly/quarterly) fact tables with rollups for the dashboard domains, maintained by incremental transformations (e.g., dbt or equivalent).
- Expose dashboards exclusively from these aggregate tables to ensure predictable latencies and isolation from OLTP load.
- Define stable semantic layer contracts (metrics and dimensions) to decouple report definitions from raw schemas and enable reusability across reports.
- Schedule incremental refreshes (hourly/daily) with backfill support; maintain idempotent jobs, checkpointing, and data quality checks.
- Keep minimal, targeted materialized views only where necessary within the analytics store, not the OLTP database.
- Establish SLAs (freshness, accuracy), monitoring, and cost controls (partition pruning, clustering, query caching).

This approach simplifies the reporting stack, improves scalability and stability, reduces query complexity, supports evolving monthly/quarterly summaries, and isolates analytical workloads from the primary application database.

We will migrate from AngularJS to Angular and adopt NgRx for application state management.

- Replace all AngularJS $rootScope-based shared state with a single source of truth in the application store. During the transition, bridge legacy broadcasts only as needed via an adapter service, but do not introduce new event-bus patterns.
- Standardize on NgRx (Store, Effects, Selectors) for Angular components to align with Angular’s change detection, leverage community tooling, and reduce risks of cyclic updates and memory leaks.
- Migrate existing plain Redux slices incrementally to NgRx. Provide temporary interoperability by:
  - Creating adapter selectors/actions to read from and dispatch to legacy Redux where immediate migration is not feasible.
  - Routing all new Angular features through NgRx; no new Redux code will be added.
- Define store module boundaries per domain to keep feature modules isolated and testable. Co-locate actions, reducers, selectors, and effects with their feature modules.
- Deprecate $rootScope usage and remove it as each feature is migrated.
- Provide developer onboarding and linting/codegen scaffolds (e.g., schematics) to minimize learning curve and ensure consistency.

This approach secures ongoing browser/security support, aligns with Angular best practices and ecosystem support, and improves maintainability and performance while enabling a safe, incremental migration path.

## Decision:
Adopt Ruby on Rails as the default framework for building new applications, leveraging the team’s familiarity and its widespread use within MOJ. Exceptions will require a documented justification where Rails cannot meet specific technical or non-functional requirements.

## Decision:
Adopt GOV.UK One Login with Integrated Identity Verification (IPV) as the sole mechanism for claimant authentication and identity proofing. We will:

- Use One Login for authentication and MFA, requiring a “High” strength session for any payment-related actions.
- Rely on One Login’s IPV to achieve evidence- and fraud-check-based identity assurance (GPG45), consuming verified attributes (name, DOB, address) via the One Login/Fraud and Identity APIs and storing only identifiers and signed assertions, not raw evidence.
- Implement step-up verification for sensitive operations (e.g., bank detail changes, new claim submission, large payment releases) and re-check session strength before execution.
- Apply risk-based checks (e.g., mismatched attributes, rapid device/account changes, velocity rules) and route high-risk cases to manual review.
- Use bank account ownership verification via an approved third-party service (e.g., Open Banking/Confirmation of Payee) before first payment and on change events.
- Establish a fall-back assisted digital path for users who cannot pass online verification, with strict audit and least-privilege operator controls.
- Maintain end-to-end audit trails (pseudonymised where possible), rotate keys, and perform replay/anti-tamper validation on received assertions.
- Align data retention to business need and legal requirements, purging identity data promptly and caching tokens minimally.
- Enforce this as a hard dependency in the architecture; no local credential stores or bespoke IDV flows will be implemented.

## Decision:
Disable command echoing by default to reduce log noise, and introduce explicit, user-controlled echo toggling.

- Default behavior:
  - Echoing is disabled unless the ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG secret is enabled.
  - At the start of each step, the echo state is initialized from ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG and does not persist across steps.

- User control:
  - Introduce two workflow commands:
    - ::echo::on — enables echoing for the remainder of the current step (until ::echo::off or step end).
    - ::echo::off — disables echoing for the remainder of the current step.
  - These commands are no-ops in non-interpreted contexts and are ignored in composite/container boundaries where not applicable.

- Error handling:
  - If a command fails to process or returns an error, its raw input and resulting output are echoed regardless of the current echo state to aid troubleshooting.
  - Secret masking continues to apply to all echoed content.

- Implementation:
  - Maintain a per-runner, per-step echo flag in the command processor.
  - The parser captures raw command lines and structured parameters; logging emits either when echo is enabled or on error.
  - Ensure that any echoed values pass through existing redaction/masking pipelines.
  - Unit and integration tests will cover default-off, ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG, toggling behavior, and error-forced echo.

- Backward compatibility and docs:
  - Document the new default and provide guidance to use ::echo::on to restore legacy behavior.
  - Note that ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG=true implicitly enables echoing for the step.

## Decision:
We will replace the single (e a v) tuple input with a catalog of named, typed relations per source, each with its own source-local time (and watermarks) and an optional logical timestamp mapping for cross-source coordination. Data will be ingested via adapters (Datomic, Kafka topics, file batches, etc.) that normalize inputs into these relations.

We will introduce a unified arrangement/materialization manager governed by a cost-based optimizer. The optimizer selects which computations and indices (e.g., keyed joins, group-bys, attribute lookups) to maintain as shared arrangements across all sources and derived relations. The current DB and ImplContext hardcoded indices will be deprecated and reimplemented as optimizer-selected arrangements when beneficial.

We will adopt schema-aware layouts to reduce tuple overhead, favoring attribute-grouped structs or columnar vectors for hot attributes, with pluggable projections. The generic EAV view will remain as a derived compatibility projection rather than the primary storage shape.

APIs and query plans will operate over logical relations and keys, not on a single EAV stream, enabling efficient joins and filters per attribute and per source. Time alignment across sources will be explicit via watermarks/capabilities in the dataflow engine. This design improves multi-source ingestion, optimizer-driven reuse, and data layout efficiency while preserving backward compatibility via the derived EAV view.

## Decision:
Establish a single source of truth for the project version and inject it into all deliverables at build time.

- Canonical version source: Git tag (SemVer-compliant). If no tag is present, derive a pre-release/build metadata form (e.g., MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-branch.sha) for non-release builds.
- Build integration:
  - C++: Generate a version header via the build system (e.g., CMake configure_file) named version.hpp containing constexpr string/integers (MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH, PRERELEASE, BUILD, FULL).
  - MATLAB: Generate a version function file (e.g., +project/version.m or project_version.m) returning the same FULL version string and structured parts.
- Runtime access:
  - C++: expose Project::version::full() and component accessors.
  - MATLAB: expose project.version() and component accessors.
- Consistency guarantees:
  - CI/CD validates that release builds are performed from an annotated SemVer tag and that generated artifacts embed the exact tag.
  - Non-tag builds are clearly marked as pre-release and include short commit SHA for traceability.
- Distribution:
  - Embed the version in package metadata (MATLAB toolbox/package, C++ library SONAME/rc resource where applicable).
- Developer workflow:
  - Version bumps occur by creating a new SemVer tag; no manual edits to code files are required.

## Decision:
- Adopt re-frame as the single source of truth for application state, deprecating the Redux store and action creators.
- Define a normalized app-db schema with clear domain namespaces (e.g., auth, user, ui, entities), using IDs and references for collections and maintaining derived data via subscriptions rather than storing duplicates.
- Establish a stable public API around re-frame events (for writes) and subscriptions (for reads), exposed through a thin facade namespace to decouple UI components from internal data layout and ease future refactors.
- Use pure event handlers (reg-event-db) for synchronous state transitions and effectful handlers (reg-event-fx) for side effects (HTTP, storage, navigation), encapsulating effects/coeffects and centralizing IO logic.
- Implement memoized, composable subscriptions (reg-sub) to derive view-ready data, avoiding recomputation and ensuring performance parity with selector patterns used in Redux.
- Introduce naming and versioning conventions for events/subs (e.g., :auth/login, :entities/user-by-id) and document the schema and API in-code and ADRs.
- Provide a migration layer that bridges legacy Redux to re-frame during transition: mirror critical state into app-db, wrap legacy dispatches to trigger re-frame events, and progressively replace reducers/selectors with re-frame handlers/subs.
- Add integration tests around the facade API (dispatch/subs) and property tests for pure event-db handlers; validate schema with spec/malli in dev and during migrations.
- Handle persistence via fx (e.g., localStorage, server sync) and initialize app-db with reg-event-fx on app start; use interceptors for cross-cutting concerns (auth, tracing, validation).
- Remove Redux and related middleware once feature parity is reached, keeping dev tooling with re-frame-10x for inspection and performance profiling.

## Decision:
- Default to command tests. Tests that exercise a single command’s behavior, validation, branching, and error handling using fakes/mocks or in-memory adapters belong in command/<version>. These are the primary source of behavioral coverage and should capture most edge cases.

- Use integration tests only for cross-component concerns. Place tests in integration/<version> when they:
  - Traverse multiple components or services (e.g., command → domain → persistence → messaging).
  - Depend on real infrastructure or realistic adapters (DB, message bus, HTTP).
  - Verify wiring/config, transactions, migrations, auth/permissions across boundaries, idempotency across retries, observability, or performance characteristics.
  - Validate end-to-end workflows or contracts that cannot be meaningfully mocked.

- Avoid duplication. No test should exist in both locations. If an integration test already covers a scenario adequately, do not replicate it as a command test, and vice versa. Prefer command tests for detailed branching and edge cases; integration tests for a minimal set of happy-path and critical cross-cutting scenarios.

- Promotion rule. Start new coverage as a command test. Promote to integration only when correctness depends on real integration or multi-component behavior.

- Operational guidelines:
  - Command tests must be fast, deterministic, and run on every PR.
  - Integration tests may be slower and run in a separate CI job or schedule.
  - Name tests to reflect scope and use build tags or directories to separate suites.
  - Refactor existing overlap by moving tests to command unless they meet the integration criteria above.

We will adopt fabric8 Kubernetes Assertions for end-to-end validation of generated Kubernetes manifests. This provides type-safe, fluent, and maintainable assertions directly in our JVM-based test suite, integrates cleanly with JUnit, and reduces brittleness compared to shell-driven checks. Using fabric8’s model and assertion DSL lets us validate schema, ownership, selectors, labels/annotations, container specs, probes, RBAC, and networking constructs with clear failure messages and minimal boilerplate. Tests will execute against an ephemeral cluster (kind/minikube) to exercise server-side defaults and admission behavior, with kubectl only for ancillary smoke checks/log collection when necessary. This approach accelerates feedback, improves developer ergonomics, and remains portable across CI without introducing vendor lock-in or scripting complexity.

## Decision:
