- Validate each incoming sentence (checksum, length, required fields). Immediately drop malformed/truncated fragments and record metrics/logs; do not propagate errors.
- Key fragment groups by (talker/source, fragment ID, channel) and track expected fragment count and received sequence numbers.
- Reassemble only when all fragments of a group arrive and pass validation; otherwise, the group remains pending in the cache.
- Apply a configurable TTL (default: 60–120 seconds) to incomplete groups. On TTL expiry, evict and discard the fragments, emitting a “fragment group expired” metric and debug log; do not fail the pipeline.
- Bound memory with a configurable max incomplete groups per source and global cap; apply oldest-first eviction on pressure, with the same non-fatal discard behavior.
- Ensure idempotency: ignore duplicate fragments; tolerate out-of-order arrival; reject fragments with conflicting counts/IDs.
- Surface observability: counters for dropped malformed fragments, expired groups, successful reassemblies, and cache evictions; optional sampling of payloads for diagnostics.

This keeps the pipeline robust by letting go of perpetually incomplete fragment groups in a controlled, transparent manner while preserving valid traffic throughput.

## Decision:
[decision]: #decision

We will introduce Events as a first-class content type alongside Places/Initiatives/Companies, reusing the existing CRUD, tagging, moderation, versioning, and notification pipelines.

We will define a minimal Event schema for MVP: title, description (optional), start_datetime (required), end_datetime (optional, defaults by duration policy), timezone (required), all_day (optional), location (optional free text), optional relation to a Place entry, tags (existing tagging system), visibility/moderation fields (as for entries), creator/last editor, and audit fields. Recurrence is out of scope for MVP.

We will expose Events via the same API patterns and permissions as entries: authenticated users can create and edit; anonymous contributions follow existing moderation rules; users who opt in are notified on subsequent changes. Copyright/licensing acceptance follows existing user registration flow. Footers and attribution behave as with entries.

We will render Events in list and map views like other entries; tags drive discovery and filtering uniformly. Past events will remain accessible and be excluded from default “upcoming” views by date filters.

We will prepare for NTH features by:
- normalizing temporal fields (ISO 8601, IANA timezones) and storing start/end as UTC with original timezone preserved,
- introducing an Event projection suitable for calendar views (aggregated by day/week/month),
- designing an ICS/CalDAV-compatible read model gated by tag-based permissions and user auth, enabling read-only feeds initially and extensible to write where the user is authenticated and is an admin for the relevant tags.

We will add API pagination/sorting by start date and tag filters, and enforce validation (end ≥ start, timezone required unless all_day). We will keep URLs and slugs consistent with existing entry routing, namespaced under /events.

## Decision:
Datasets and versions are independently editable via their respective APIs, but publication is coordinated and validated to ensure consistency.

- Editing:
  - Datasets can be created and updated without existing versions.
  - Versions can be created/updated independently, referencing a dataset by ID.
  - Optimistic concurrency (ETags/If-Match) is required on both resources.

- Publication:
  - A dataset cannot be published unless it has at least one publishable version (meets validation and completeness criteria).
  - Publishing a version automatically updates the dataset’s published state and search index in a single transactional operation.
  - Publishing operations are idempotent and order-independent: re-running publish yields the same result.

- Collections constraint:
  - Business rule “an item can belong to only one collection at a time” is enforced at the version level; dataset-level collection is derived from its latest published version.
  - Attempts to assign multiple collections to a single version are rejected.

- Immutability:
  - Published versions are immutable; changes require creating a new version.
  - Dataset-level published metadata that is derived from versions is read-only and recalculated on publish.

- Validation:
  - Cross-resource referential integrity is enforced (no orphan versions; no publish without valid version).
  - Consistency checks run on publish; failures do not partially commit.

This preserves editing flexibility while guaranteeing coherent, order-independent published state.

## Decision:
Enhance macondo build to deterministically generate repository YAML descriptors as a first-class build artifact.

- Scope: During macondo build, emit one YAML per repository (as defined by ADR-0003) capturing canonical metadata: name, url, vcs, defaultBranch, revision/ref, path, submodules, sparse/monorepo mapping, dependencies, and schemaVersion. Secrets/tokens are never serialized.
- Location: Write to .macondo/repositories/*.yaml by default. Support flags: --repos-output <dir>, --no-repos (disable), --repos-only (skip other build steps), and --force (overwrite hand-edited files).
- Determinism: Stable field ordering and normalized values; idempotent regeneration produces identical files when inputs unchanged. Include a generated-by header and content hash to detect drift.
- Inputs and merge rules: Source data from remote repository config, lockfiles/pins, and resolved build graph. Precedence: build lock/pin > explicit repo config > discovery. Exclude transient build-time values unless pinned.
- Validation: Validate against a published JSON Schema; build fails on validation errors. Provide macondo repos validate for CI.
- Backward compatibility: If existing YAML is unmanaged (no generated header) and --force is not provided, skip with a warning. Otherwise update in place.
- Consumption: Make repository YAMLs part of build artifacts and attach to release bundles; downstream tools can consume them for reproducible builds and provenance.
- Documentation: Add schema, examples, and migration notes; deprecate any ad-hoc repo listing outputs in favor of these YAMLs.

## Decision:
Implement a reusable FEM VideoPlayer component that wraps HTML5 video using Video.js as the core playback engine, exposed through a thin, typed React component. This balances cross-browser reliability and rich customization with a mature plugin ecosystem.

Key points:
- Foundation: Video.js for consistent controls, captions/subtitles (WebVTT), keyboard accessibility, fullscreen/PiP, playback rate, and robust media error handling.
- Streaming: Use videojs-http-streaming (HLS/DASH) with native HLS on Safari; support MP4 progressive sources by default. Allow optional hls.js adapter if needed for edge cases.
- React API: Provide a controlled component with props and an imperative ref (play, pause, seek, setRate, mute, setTextTrack). Emit standardized events (timeupdate, durationchange, seeking/seeked, ratechange, ended, error) for tool synchronization.
- Customization: Support slot/children render props for overlay layers (e.g., annotation canvases, temporal tools), custom control bars, theming via CSS variables, and plugin registration. Maintain separation of rendering layers so interaction tools can receive pointer events independent of the video element.
- Performance: Avoid unnecessary React re-renders by delegating playback to Video.js and synchronizing state via lightweight event bridges. Lazy-load player/vendor chunks to minimize initial bundle size.
- Accessibility: WCAG-compliant controls, captions, focus management, hotkeys, and screen reader labels. Support multiple audio/text tracks.
- Extensibility: TypeScript definitions, stable interface, and adapter pattern to swap/extend the underlying player if future requirements demand alternate engines.
- Browser support: Evergreen browsers and Safari; graceful degradation to native controls when required.

## Decision:
Introduce a synchronous facade over an internal, bounded-concurrency Git operation queue backed by a local mirrored cache and incremental fetch strategy.

- Synchronous API: The adapter exposes blocking methods that only return when the requested state is fully materialized, preserving immediate consistency and a simple consumer interface.
- Internal queue with backpressure: All remote-touching Git operations are funneled through a prioritized, rate-limited work queue (per-repo fairness). This prevents thundering herds, ensures predictable latency under load, and caps IO/CPU.
- Local mirrors and persistent caches: Maintain a bare local mirror per remote on fast storage. Use incremental fetches (e.g., refspec targeting, shallow/partial clone with blob filtering) to minimize network/IO. Persist commit/graph metadata indexes to avoid re-walks.
- Request coalescing and deduplication: Concurrent identical operations (same repo/ref/range) are coalesced to a single in-flight task; followers await the same result, reducing redundant fetches.
- Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers: Apply conservative timeouts with exponential backoff and jitter for remote calls. Trip per-remote breakers on repeated failures to protect the system; surface actionable errors to callers.
- Concurrency controls: Use read-optimized locks around local mirrors and indexes; serialize destructive Git operations per repo while allowing concurrent reads.
- Resource quotas: Enforce per-tenant/repo concurrency and bandwidth limits to guarantee fairness across users.
- Observability: Instrument queue depth, wait/exec times, cache hit rates, and remote error rates to tune limits and detect regressions.

This design preserves immediate consistency for consumers while containing IO cost and ensuring system-wide performance under heavy Git workloads.

## Decision:
Use YAML front matter at the top of each Markdown document as the single source of truth for structured field values; reserve the Markdown body for human-readable narrative. Field name convention: kebab-case.

Type representation in YAML front matter:
- string: UTF-8 scalar; use folded (>-) for multi-line; no Markdown parsing assumed.
- number: YAML numeric scalar (integer or float).
- boolean: true | false (lowercase).
- date | datetime: ISO 8601; dates as YYYY-MM-DD, datetimes as UTC YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ (or with explicit offset).
- enum: string matching one of the allowed values (case-sensitive).
- array:
  - of scalars: YAML sequence (- item) or inline [a, b, c].
  - of objects: YAML sequence of mappings.
- object: YAML mapping; nesting allowed.
- null: null (unquoted).
- identifiers/refs: strings; URIs kept as strings; link rendering may occur in body.
- binary: not embedded; store externally and reference via link.

Authoritative data is only in the YAML block delimited by ---; any tables or lists in the Markdown body are non-authoritative summaries. Rich text fields (e.g., context, decision, consequences) live in the body as Markdown and are not parsed for typed fields.

## Decision:
We will handle writes via a command-oriented application layer with per-use-case Command Handlers invoked synchronously from the API.

- API layer: maps HTTP requests to immutable Command DTOs, performs basic request validation and authorization, and invokes the corresponding Command Handler via an in-process command bus (simple dispatcher).
- Application layer: Command Handlers orchestrate use cases, load aggregates via repositories, call domain methods to enforce invariants, and commit using a Unit of Work within a single transactional boundary per command.
- Domain layer: encapsulates business rules and raises domain events.
- Infrastructure: implements repositories, transaction management, optimistic concurrency (aggregate version/version check), and the Outbox pattern to persist and asynchronously dispatch domain/integration events to read-model projectors and external integrations.

Additional policies:
- Validation: input and authorization checks at API/Application boundaries; business validation in domain.
- Idempotency: support optional idempotency keys for externally retried commands; handlers must be side-effect safe under retries.
- Long-running/slow commands: submit to background workers and return 202 Accepted with a correlation ID; otherwise execute synchronously.
- Return values: commands do not return data; when necessary they may return generated identifiers of newly created resources (per ADR).
- Error handling: map domain/application errors to appropriate HTTP status codes; on concurrency conflicts return 409 with guidance to retry.
- Observability: log command intent/result, correlate with events, and emit metrics around success, latency, and retries.

## Decision:
- Implement a hybrid component model: complex EIP patterns are delivered as generic, MICO-owned components that orchestrate flow, with well-defined, minimal extension points executed via FaaS.
- Define strict contracts for extension points (typed payload schemas, determinism/idempotency guidance, side-effect boundaries, error semantics), with versioning and deprecation policy.
- Prefer declarative configuration to compose pattern topology and bind extension points to functions; ship safe defaults for all extension points to enable zero-code operation.
- Provide an SDK and templates for FaaS extensions (validation, schema helpers, retries, metrics, tracing), plus a local test harness/emulator and contract tests.
- Enforce operational guardrails at extension boundaries: timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, concurrency limits, payload size caps.
- Ensure safe failure modes: default/fallback behavior when extensions are absent or failing; explicit dead-letter paths and compensating actions.
- Deliver end-to-end observability: structured logs, metrics, and distributed tracing spanning generic components and FaaS executions; correlate via contextual headers.
- Secure execution: least-privilege IAM, network isolation, payload sanitization, and input/output validation at the boundary.
- Support progressive delivery: versioned extension contracts, side-by-side deployments, canary/ramp-up, and rollback.
- Maintain backward compatibility for existing components and patterns; adoption is opt-in and incremental.
- Package and publish patterns as reusable bundles with reference implementations and documentation for each extension point.

## Decision:
Adopt Elasticsearch (or AWS OpenSearch Service) as the enterprise search index and expose a dedicated Search API service over a denormalized, read-optimized document model replicated from the RDBMS.

Rationale:
- Purpose-built full‑text search, relevancy tuning, facets, and aggregations outperform direct RDBMS queries for enterprise-wide search.
- Mature ecosystem, managed offerings (AWS OpenSearch) for operations, scaling, backups, alerting, and security.
- Analyzer/boosting configuration enables better ranking without code changes; non-engineers can adjust via Kibana/OpenSearch Dashboards under guardrails.
- Decouples operational databases from search workloads, removing contention with the source application.

Implementation decisions:
- Replicate data from the RDBMS to Elasticsearch via Change Data Capture (e.g., Debezium -> Kafka -> OpenSearch Sink) for near‑real‑time indexing; bootstrap via batch ETL. Start with scheduled ETL if CDC isn’t immediately feasible.
- Define versioned indices per major domain (e.g., common-data-v1), denormalizing related entities into a single document to optimize query performance.
- Use index aliases for zero‑downtime reindexing and schema evolution; implement blue/green index rollout.
- Establish analyzers per field (e.g., standard + ngram for partial match, keyword for exact, edge-ngram for autocomplete) and field-level boosts aligned to business relevance.
- Expose a Search API microservice that encapsulates query construction, authorization filtering, pagination, and result shaping; prohibit direct client access to the cluster.
- Enforce security and compliance: field- and record-level filtering for PII via tokens/claims; store only necessary attributes; encrypt at rest/in transit; implement data retention policies.
- Observability: capture query and indexing metrics, slow logs, and relevance telemetry to iterate on ranking.
- Governance: maintain index mappings and relevance configuration as code; provide controlled UI access for business tuning where appropriate.

Solr was considered but not chosen due to operational overhead and lack of a first-class managed service in our target environment compared to OpenSearch. This decision enables scalable, configurable, and maintainable enterprise search while protecting source systems.

## Decision:
- Do not introduce broad implicit conversions that automatically wrap primitive/simple types (e.g., String) into nested component structures. Hidden, ambient conversions reduce readability, hinder discoverability, and increase ambiguity and maintenance risk.
- Provide explicit, discoverable helper APIs to remove boilerplate:
  - Add factory/constructor overloads and companion object helpers with sensible defaults (e.g., Legend.h1(messageKey), Fieldset.withLegendH1(messageKey), GovukRadios.withLegend(messageKey, size = Large, isPageHeading = true)).
  - Offer extension methods (syntax) as opt-in imports for common patterns (e.g., messageKey.asLegendH1, radios.withLegend(messageKey)), implemented via implicit classes/extension methods rather than implicit conversions.
  - Supply curated presets for frequently recurring configurations (e.g., LegendPresets.PageHeadingLarge).
- Keep helpers pure-presentational and independent of request/context; rely on existing i18n mechanisms (Messages) passed explicitly.
- Ensure naming and packaging favor discoverability and avoid collisions; helpers should be the default-recommended path in documentation and examples.
- Maintain backward compatibility; wrappers/overloads are additive and non-breaking.

## Decision:
Adopt ECMAScript Modules (ESM) as the standard module system across the codebase. Each source file is a module with explicit, scoped imports/exports; there will be no reliance on globals or implicit side effects.

- Use named exports by default to improve discoverability, refactoring, and tooling support. Default exports are discouraged and allowed only when interop or framework constraints require them.
- Keep modules cohesive and focused; prefer smaller, composable modules over large multipurpose files.
- Avoid circular dependencies; refactor shared contracts into dedicated modules when cycles are detected.
- Side-effect-only modules are prohibited except for well-documented entry points (e.g., polyfills), which must be explicitly named and isolated.
- All imports must be explicit and path-resolved; avoid dynamic require patterns. Dynamic import() is allowed for code-splitting or lazy loading with clear boundaries.
- Re-exports may be used to define stable public surfaces; avoid “barrel” files that introduce hidden coupling or impede tree-shaking.
- For Node.js packages, configure ESM via "type": "module" (or .mjs) and provide CommonJS compat only when required by consumers via dual publishing or conditional exports.
- Enforce conventions via lint rules (e.g., no default exports, no extraneous dependencies, import order) and CI.

This standardizes code organization, improves maintainability, and aligns with modern JavaScript tooling and ecosystem practices.

## Decision:
Discontinue build-time code generation for error macros. Replace it with a compile-time, Rust-native approach that is cross-compilation friendly:

- Introduce a small, self-contained proc-macro crate (e.g., ockam_core_derive) that provides #[derive(OckamError)] and lightweight attributes to declare error domains, codes, and messages. The derive will implement std::error::Error (or core-compatible traits under no_std), Display, and Into<ockam_core::Error>.
- Provide a minimal set of macro_rules! helpers for common patterns (e.g., err!(), into_err!()) that do not require code generation or build scripts.
- Remove any external tools and build.rs-based generators. No non-Rust tooling is required, ensuring deterministic, reproducible builds and seamless cross compilation.
- Keep the error surface ergonomic: library authors define simple enums with #[derive(OckamError)], and users receive consistent ockam_core::Error values via Into conversions.
- Ensure portability: the derive crate has no heavy dependencies and supports no_std + alloc where possible; feature flags gate std-specific behavior.

This preserves the agility of adding new errors, improves portability across targets, and maintains convenience for both library developers and users without relying on fragile code generation.

## Decision:
Chosen option: MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records), template version 2.1.2, because

- It is lightweight, Markdown-based, and easy to adopt within code reviews and the repo.
- The structure is clear, consistent, and proven in many teams, which improves maintainability and onboarding.
- It supports a simple lifecycle (proposed, accepted, rejected, deprecated, superseded) and explicit links between ADRs.

Format and structure to follow:
- Location: docs/adr/
- Filenames: zero-padded sequential number + short-kebab-case title (e.g., 0001-use-madr.md)
- One decision per file; numbers never change; superseding ADRs link to predecessors.
- Sections (in order): Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Considered Options (or Alternatives), References.
- Index: docs/adr/index.md maintained to list ADRs in order.
- Editorial conventions: concise, rationale-focused, avoid duplication, prefer links to external specs.
- Process: create as “proposed,” review via PR, update to “accepted” or “rejected,” later “deprecated/superseded” as needed.
- Optional tags: add front-matter tags (e.g., area, component) if helpful; keep core MADR sections intact.

## Decision:
Use the OpenCage Geocoding API for reverse geocoding browser-provided coordinates to a country. OpenCage offers reliable global coverage, clear usage limits, a sustainable free/paid path, and returns structured results including ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes (components.country_code), which we will standardize on for downstream logic.

Implementation details:
- Perform reverse geocoding exclusively on the server to avoid exposing API keys and to limit third‑party access to precise user coordinates. The client sends lat/lon to our backend, which proxies the OpenCage request.
- Cache successful lookups (e.g., keyed by 4–5 decimal lat/lon rounding) for 24 hours in our server cache to reduce latency, costs, and rate limit pressure. Add server-side rate limiting and circuit breakers.
- Extract and return only the minimal fields needed (country code and country name) to the client.
- Provide a resilient fallback: if OpenCage is unavailable or quota is exceeded, determine the country via an offline point-in-polygon check against a simplified Natural Earth/geojson dataset (using turf.js or a server-side equivalent). This ensures continuity and reduces border-case failures.
- Log and monitor hit rates, failures, and cache effectiveness; alert on elevated error/timeout rates.

Rationale: this balances accuracy, cost, compliance with OSM/Nominatim usage policies (no public heavy use), privacy (server-side proxy), and operational resilience.

## Decision:
Standardize on Codeception with Gherkin (BDD) for all end-to-end and acceptance tests, deprecating the legacy “Cept” syntax and browser-based JS e2e tests. We will:

- Use Codeception + Gherkin feature files as the single authoring style for UI/acceptance flows across repositories.
- Consolidate step definitions and helpers (e.g., WPBrowser/WebDriver) in shared modules to ensure reuse and consistency.
- Migrate existing Cept tests to Gherkin scenarios and port the current JS e2e coverage into Codeception steps where applicable.
- Keep unit tests in their native ecosystems (PHPUnit for PHP, Jest for JS) but reserve all cross-page/UI workflows for Codeception Gherkin.
- Enforce the standard via CI (fail builds on new Cept files), provide migration guides and examples, and add linting/formatting for Gherkin.
- Establish a deprecation schedule for Cept and JS e2e suites, with parallel runs during transition to mitigate risk.

## Decision:
Adopt Prettier as the single, canonical formatter for all JavaScript/TypeScript and related frontend files, and enforce it via programmatic tooling rather than IDE settings. We will:

- Add a project-wide .prettierrc and .prettierignore to centralize configuration.
- Provide npm scripts: `format` (writes changes) and `format:check` (verifies formatting).
- Run Prettier automatically on staged files via lint-staged in a Husky pre-commit hook.
- Enforce formatting in CI using `format:check` to prevent inconsistent merges.
- Disallow per-developer overrides of Prettier settings in IDEs; IDE integration is optional, but the programmatic tooling is the source of truth.

This ensures consistent formatting across contributors and environments, independent of IDE configuration.

## Decision:
Adopt a docs-by-repo model and restructure Cosmos SDK documentation accordingly:

- Technical, SDK-specific documentation will live in the cosmos/cosmos-sdk repository. Other frameworks/tools (e.g., Gaia/Hub, Lotion) will keep their technical docs in their respective repos. Non-technical, ecosystem-wide materials (FAQs, whitepaper, high-level Cosmos content) will live on the public website.
- Remove or relocate non-SDK materials from the SDK repo to their appropriate repos or to the website.

Restructure the SDK repo documentation as:

docs/
├── README.md                  (landing page + navigation)
├── intro/                     (what is the SDK, quickstart, prerequisites)
├── getting-started/           (install, scaffolding, first app)
├── concepts/                  (core abstractions: baseapp, store, tx, gas, modules)
├── modules/                   (per-module overview + link to spec and GoDoc)
├── spec/                      (runtime/specs, state machines, ADR references)
├── clients/                   (CLI, gRPC/REST, light client, service providers)
├── tooling/                   (dev tooling, codegen, testing)
├── architecture/              (arch overviews, ADRs, internals)
├── migration/                 (upgrade guides, changelogs, deprecations)
├── translations/              (community translations)
└── references/                (links to GoDoc, protobuf API, examples)

Website navigation will surface only:
- README (landing), intro, getting-started, concepts, clients, and selected references/tutorial links.
- Architecture and internal specs will not appear on the website sidebar but remain discoverable via deep links.

Process and governance:
- Documentation changes follow the same PR review workflow as code; each folder has clear ownership.
- Versioning aligns with release branches (e.g., release/x.y docs); website links “latest” and “stable” to the appropriate branches.
- Cross-repo docs link via canonical URLs; avoid duplications by referencing rather than copying.

## Decision:
We will prevent blind acceptance or reversal of architectural choices by maintaining a lightweight, versioned log of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) that explicitly capture motivation and consequences.

Key practices:
- Every architecturally significant change requires an ADR with mandatory Rationale and Consequences sections; no change will be merged without a linked ADR or an explicit reference to an existing ADR.
- ADRs will be short (1–2 pages), numbered sequentially, stored in the repository (docs/adr/), and written in Markdown.
- ADRs will include: Title, Status (proposed/accepted/deprecated/superseded), Context, Decision, Rationale (including explored options), Consequences (positive, negative, neutral), References (issues, PRs, docs), and Date/Authors.
- Supersede instead of edit: previous ADRs remain immutable; new ADRs reference and supersede older ones when context changes.
- Cross-linking: ADRs must link related ADRs and relevant tickets to preserve traceability across time and components.
- Review gate: ADRs are reviewed with the same rigor as code; acceptance requires sign-off from designated architecture owners.
- Discoverability: maintain an index (docs/adr/README.md) with tags (e.g., security, performance, data, integration) and summaries to speed onboarding and audits.
- Onboarding: new team members read the ADR index first; significant features link to relevant ADRs from their README or module docs.

This decision institutionalizes rationale capture, enabling informed change while minimizing paralysis and regression risk.

## Decision:
- Standardize on Apple’s XCTest as the sole testing framework for unit tests across the codebase, eliminating the third‑party unit test library.
- Shift focus from predominantly behavioral/integration-style tests to true unit tests that validate a unit’s public API and state, with clear Given/When/Then organization in XCTest methods.
- Use protocol-oriented design, dependency injection, and lightweight fakes/stubs to isolate units; avoid runtime patching/swizzling and global singletons.
- For async code, adopt XCTestExpectation and async/await tests; avoid third-party async helpers.
- Establish a test pyramid: majority unit tests, limited integration tests where necessary, and minimal end-to-end UI tests via XCUITest.
- Incrementally migrate: for each module touched, port existing tests to XCTest, replace behavioral tests with targeted unit tests, and delete redundant overlapping tests.
- Enforce conventions: one SUT per test class, clear Arrange/Act/Assert, deterministic tests without timing sleeps, and stable naming (test_<unit>_<behavior>_<expected>).
- Integrate with Xcode build and CI (xcodebuild / xctest), enable code coverage, and add pre-commit/CI gates to require XCTest-based tests for new code.
- Provide a small internal utilities package (if needed) for common test fakes/builders, kept free of external dependencies.

## Decision:
We will architect all archetypes-rules software as independently buildable, testable, and releasable modules, each with a single, clearly bounded responsibility and a minimal public API. Modules will be interchangeable via explicit contracts and dependency inversion, enabling reuse across applications and teams.

- Package-per-capability: each module encapsulates one capability; no cross-module internal imports; interaction occurs only through stable interfaces.
- Contracts first: define module boundaries with language-agnostic contracts (e.g., OpenAPI/JSON Schema/Protobuf) or interface types where language-specific; provide reference adapters to enable plug-and-play composition.
- Plugin model by default: extension points (ports) are declared in core modules; optional features ship as plugins that register via configuration or discovery without modifying cores.
- Release “minimally reusable products”: once a module fulfills its responsibility in isolation with tests, docs, and examples, it is released.
- Independent versioning and SemVer: each module is versioned and released independently; strict backward-compatibility for public APIs; documented deprecation windows and migration guides.
- Minimal dependencies and clear layering: prefer pure domain logic; infrastructure behind interfaces; composition over inheritance.
- Small, approachable units: keep modules small to lower contribution barriers; publish templates, scaffolds, and exemplars to standardize structure.
- CI/CD per module: contract checks, security scans, and compatibility tests guard releases; dependency update automation preserves supply-chain health.

This approach maximizes reusability and community contribution while keeping complexity localized and change impact small.

## Decision:
We will introduce a production-like staging environment and PR-based preview deployments served via path-based routing on fixed, pre-provisioned hostnames (no wildcard subdomains).

- Create a dedicated “staging” namespace that mirrors production configuration (env vars, secrets, build flags, CDNs) and builds Next.js with production settings (NODE_ENV=production, basePath/assetPrefix set).
- For each open PR, CI will build and push a production image tagged with the PR number and deploy a preview instance addressable under:
  - https://staging.zooniverse.org/front-end/<app>/<pr-number> (or equivalent per app)
- Ingress will route by path rather than host; Traefik rules will be pre-defined to accept path prefixes, avoiding wildcard DNS. Next.js will be configured with basePath and assetPrefix to serve correctly from a subpath.
- A stable “staging” deployment per app (tracking the main branch) will be available at a fixed path for design reviews and integration checks.
- CI/CD workflow:
  - On PR label “staging” (or manual trigger), build production assets, deploy a namespaced release with path-scoped ingress.
  - Run smoke tests against the staged URL.
  - On PR update, redeploy; on PR close/merge, auto-teardown the preview release and ingress path.
- Resource controls: limit concurrent previews per app and apply TTL to auto-expire inactive previews.
- Production deploys remain gated and occur only after validation on the stable staging deployment or a PR preview.

This provides production-like validation without wildcard subdomains, reduces regressions from production-only build differences, and supports both design review and pre-merge functional testing.

## Decision:
- Introduce a first-class Region model to represent hierarchical geographic groupings for reporting, sync, and authorization.
  - Region(id, name, slug, description, parent_id, region_type_id, active, path/ancestry).
  - RegionType(id, name, kind) to define taxonomy (e.g., country, state, district, block, facility).
- Facilities become leaf Regions:
  - Each Facility is linked to exactly one Region (region_type = facility).
  - Non-facility Regions do not replace Facilities; they organize Facilities and aggregate data.
- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Migrate existing FacilityGroups to RegionType = district with proper parentage (e.g., state -> district -> block -> facility).
  - Preserve existing identifiers; add stable slugs for URLs; backfill slugs and ancestry.
  - Deprecate direct FacilityGroup usage in new code; maintain read compatibility via views/adapters until removal.
- Authorization, reporting, and sync:
  - Replace FacilityGroup scoping with Region scoping; users are granted access at any Region node; access cascades to descendants.
  - Reporting queries accept a Region and aggregate over its descendant Facilities.
  - Mobile sync radius is defined by a Region; server returns data for patients associated with Facilities under that Region.
- API and contracts:
  - Expose Regions and RegionTypes via API (list/read with ancestry, slugs).
  - All patient- and appointment-scoped APIs accept region_id/slug for filtering; facility_id remains supported for leaf targeting.
- Admin UI:
  - Add Region management (CRUD, nesting, reparenting with validations).
  - Replace FacilityGroup views with Region views; show breadcrumbs via ancestry.
- Data integrity and performance:
  - Enforce single-parent tree, unique slug per RegionType scope, and active flags for soft deprecation.
  - Add ancestry/path indexing for efficient descendant queries.
- Documentation and governance:
  - Establish taxonomy per deployment (seeded RegionTypes); changes require data migration review.
  - Provide migration playbooks and monitoring for correctness of aggregates and sync sizes.

We will isolate all HSM-interacting workloads (e.g., Translator and any signing components) onto dedicated Kubernetes worker nodes that are not shared with public-facing services. On GSP this will be implemented as a separate node pool (or separate cluster where feasible) with:
- Strict scheduling controls (taints/tolerations, nodeSelectors) to ensure only HSM-capable workloads run on these nodes
- Dedicated subnets/security groups and network policies allowing only least-privilege, mTLS-enforced traffic from Gateway via approved paths
- Distinct IAM roles and instance profiles; no container co-location with internet-exposed pods
- Runtime hardening (read-only root FS, seccomp/AppArmor, dropped Linux capabilities, non-root, restricted egress)
- Image provenance enforcement (signed images), admission controls, and continuous vulnerability scanning
- Enhanced audit logging and alerting for cross-segment traffic, node access, and HSM usage

Gateway and other public-facing components will be confined to separate nodes and cannot schedule onto HSM nodes. No direct inbound from the internet to HSM nodes is permitted.

RE will provision and operate the isolated capacity; Application teams will adapt deployments to comply with scheduling and policy constraints; Cyber Security will review and monitor. This physical and logical segregation reduces lateral-movement risk and limits the blast radius of a compromised Gateway while maintaining GSP compatibility.

## Decision:
Adopt a service-first directory structure with language as a secondary dimension. Concretely:
- Root organizes by service, not language.
- Each service contains language-specific implementations and shared assets.
- Example:
  - services/
    - orders/
      - js/
      - java/
      - python/
      - shared/ (specs, examples, docs)
    - billing/
      - js/
      - java/
      - shared/

Rationale:
- Facilitates side-by-side consumption and comparison of different language clients of the same service.
- Keeps service artifacts co-located (specs, docs, tests), independent of language.
- Simplifies tooling for multi-language generation and testing per service.

Generator changes:
- Generators output to services/<serviceName>/<language>/ by default.
- Flags: --service <name> and --language <lang> are required or inferred from input; --flat remains available to write directly into the target path.
- When generating multiple languages from one spec, the tool nests outputs under the same service directory.

Versioning and publishing:
- Language-specific packaging follows language norms while remaining under the service directory.
- Optional version subfolders for concurrent major versions: services/<service>/<language>/v<major> (used only when needed).

Migration:
- Provide a script to relocate existing language-first layouts to the new structure and update build paths.

## Decision:
- For all V3 JSON responses, the following common top-level keys MUST appear last and in this exact order:
  1) relationships
  2) metadata
  3) links
- When one or more of these keys are absent, the remaining keys MUST preserve the relative order above. Example: if metadata is omitted, the order is relationships, then links; if relationships is omitted, the order is metadata, then links.
- Only top-level keys are in scope; ordering within nested objects or arrays is not prescribed by this decision.
- This ordering rule applies only to JSON object responses for V3 endpoints; non-JSON responses or prior API versions are out of scope.
- Implementations MUST configure serializers/encoders to enforce this ordering deterministically across endpoints.

## Decision:
We will adopt OpenAPI 3.0.x as the canonical, single source of truth for defining and sharing the DOS API endpoints.

- Format: YAML is preferred; JSON allowed for generated artifacts.
- Location: Each service maintains a versioned openapi.yaml at the repo root (and /docs for generated artifacts). Specs are part of PRs and code reviews.
- Versioning: Semantic versioning of the API (x.y.z) encoded in the spec; breaking changes require a new major version and must be exposed under a new base path (e.g., /v2).
- Compatibility: Only additive, backward-compatible changes are permitted within a major version (e.g., new optional fields, new endpoints).
- Reuse: Common schemas, parameters, responses, and security schemes are defined under components and shared via a central library where feasible.
- Security: Define OAuth2/OpenID Connect security schemes in the spec; all operations declare applicable security requirements.
- Quality gates: Linting (e.g., spectral) and validation enforced in CI; examples are mandatory for request/response bodies and error objects; schemas reference JSON Schema (OAS 3.0 dialect).
- Documentation: Human-friendly docs auto-generated from the spec and published to the internal developer portal on each merge to main.
- Mocking and tests: Contract-first workflow with mock servers generated from the spec; provider/consumer contract tests verify conformance.
- Lifecycle: Deprecated fields and operations are marked with deprecation notices in the spec and changelog, with timelines for removal.
- Discoverability: The spec is discoverable via a /openapi endpoint and via service catalogs.

This aligns with our API-first principle, leverages existing tool support, and ensures consistency with other DLS APIs already specified in OpenAPI.

## Decision:
We will upgrade all UI apps and libraries to React 17 and update semantic-ui-react to its latest compatible version. To mitigate the removal of the Responsive component and avoid an immediate ecosystem-wide breaking change, we will:

- Introduce react-responsive as the alternative for device-size-based rendering.
- Provide a new, first-class API in the UI library:
  - Components: <ShowAt>, <HideAt> (e.g., “mobile”, “tablet”, “desktop”)
  - Hooks: useMediaQuery and useBreakpoint
  - Centralized breakpoints token (exported from the UI library)
- Ship a temporary, deprecated Responsive shim inside the UI library that preserves the previous API surface but is implemented on top of react-responsive and our breakpoints. This enables incremental adoption without blocking upgrades.

Migration strategy:
- Mark Responsive as deprecated with clear console warnings and documentation.
- Provide examples and a codemod to move from Responsive to ShowAt/HideAt or useMediaQuery.
- Establish a deprecation timeline: remove the shim in the next major UI library release after a minimum 1 release cycle (e.g., 3 months) and once downstream apps have migrated.

Versioning and compatibility:
- Publish a minor (or premajor) release containing React 17 and the shim to enable smooth upgrades.
- Enforce React 17 via peerDependencies across all UI packages.
- Add ESLint rule and CI check to prevent new use of the deprecated Responsive.

This approach unblocks the React 17 migration, provides a better long-term API, and limits immediate breaking changes.

## Decision:
Replace render-props with a component-slots API backed by React Context, and move scale/cursor computation into memoized container hooks.

- Consumers will pass components (not inline functions) for extensibility: e.g., rowAxisComponent, columnAxisComponent, cellComponent. Components can freely use hooks.
- Introduce PivotGridContext providing read-only access to root data, pivoted frame, measures layout flags, and stable helpers (getCursor, getMeasureCursor, getAxisCursor). All substructures expose cursor helpers to eliminate “root data” prop plumbing.
- Compute scales and other derived values in container components with useMemo/useCallback and memoized selectors; pass them via context or lightweight props. We will not optimize by avoiding discriminants or clever inference—prefer explicit tags and pattern matching for readability.
- Deprecate render-props for axes/cells/headers. Keep a thin compatibility layer that wraps render-props into slot components, but mark as legacy.
- Remove premature low-level “optimization” that avoided pattern matching; use explicit discriminants and small, well-typed variants to reduce confusion.
- Prioritize correctness and clarity; rely on React’s memoization and React.memo to control recalculation rather than bespoke caching. Recompute scales as needed; optimize only if profiling shows hotspots.

This unifies API shape across PivotGrid parts, enables hooks where needed, eliminates prop-drilling, and simplifies mental model via explicit component slots and discriminated variants.

## Decision:
- Adopt clear, role-oriented names and verbs:
  - Commands: point-to-point “send”
  - Events: fan-out “publish”
  - Timeouts/Timers: delayed “schedule”
- Standard interface set:
  - CommandSender.send(Command)
  - EventPublisher.publish(Event)
  - TimeoutScheduler.schedule(Timeout, dueAt|delay)
  - CommandHandler<TCommand>.handle(command, context)
  - EventHandler<TEvent>.handle(event, context)
  - TimeoutHandler<TTimeout>.handle(timeout, context)
- Message model:
  - Message is a marker implemented by Command, Event, Timeout
  - Envelope<TMessage> wraps Message with Headers (immutable key/value) and Correlation/Conversation IDs
  - Address identifies destinations; Topic is a named fan-out subject
- Routing/dispatch:
  - CommandRouter routes to a single CommandHandler
  - EventDispatcher fans events to zero-or-more EventHandlers
  - Subscription and SubscriptionId model handler registrations
- Serialization and transport:
  - MessageCodec (serialize/deserialize)
  - TransportProducer (send to Address/Topic)
  - TransportConsumer (receive from Address/Topic)
  - Adapters translate between Transport and {CommandSender, EventPublisher, TimeoutScheduler}
- Persistence patterns:
  - OutboxStore and InboxStore for exactly-once/at-least-once patterns
- Naming rules:
  - Avoid ambiguous “Bus”, “Broker”, “Client”
  - Use role suffixes: Sender, Publisher, Scheduler, Handler, Router, Dispatcher, Codec, Producer, Consumer, Store
  - Methods are verb-first: send, publish, schedule, handle, route, dispatch, serialize, deserialize, produce, consume
- Renames (deprecate old names for one minor release with shims):
  - CommandBus -> CommandSender
  - EventBus -> EventPublisher
  - MessageBus -> MessageRouter (if routing only) or remove in favor of explicit Router/Dispatcher
  - TimerService -> TimeoutScheduler
  - Serializer -> MessageCodec
- Consistency:
  - Do not overload “publish” for commands or “send” for events
  - Reserve “topic” for events; “address/queue” for commands
  - Keep interfaces transport-agnostic; transport-specific types live under *.transport.* packages.

## Decision:
We will adopt OpenAPI 3.1 as the single source of truth for all service API specifications and follow a contract-first approach.

- Specification format: OpenAPI 3.1 (YAML), using JSON Schema 2020-12 for models. Files will live in repo under /apis/<service>/openapi.yaml with shared reusable components under /apis/_shared.
- Style: Resource-oriented REST over HTTPS, JSON payloads (application/json). Errors use RFC 7807 (application/problem+json) with a shared error schema.
- Versioning: Semantic Versioning of the contract. Major versions via path (/v1), minor/patch via spec version and are backwards compatible. Deprecations signaled with Deprecation and Sunset headers and x-deprecated in schemas.
- Consistency: Common conventions for pagination (page[size], page[number]), filtering (filter[<field>]), sorting (sort=field,-field), and standard headers (Idempotency-Key for unsafe endpoints).
- Security: OAuth2/OIDC (Authorization Code and Client Credentials) with scopes defined in the spec’s securitySchemes and applied per operation. All endpoints require TLS.
- Documentation: Publish human-readable docs via Redoc/Swagger UI from the OpenAPI file; examples included for all operations and error cases.
- Tooling/QA: Lint with Spectral (org ruleset) and validate in CI; generate mock servers (Prism) for early integration; optional codegen for clients/servers where appropriate; contract tests gate releases to ensure implementation matches the spec.
- Discoverability: Provide an index document and /openapi endpoints per service to serve the current spec; maintain a catalog in the developer portal.

## Decision:
We will support both paradigms, with typed entry as the primary flow and map interaction as a first-class enhancement.

- Primary: Destination input fields provide address/place autocomplete backed by our geocoding provider. Results return a canonical place ID, name, and lat/lon. We’ll debounce keystrokes, highlight top matches, and allow pasting raw lat,lon. Keyboard-only operation and screen-reader labels ensure accessibility. Selecting a suggestion drops/updates a marker on the map.

- Secondary: Users can click/tap the map to add or reposition a marker. On drop/drag end we reverse-geocode to produce a readable label and store lat/lon. If reverse geocode fails, we keep coordinates and prompt for a custom label. Markers are draggable; the list view reflects map changes and vice versa.

- Unified model: Both inputs populate the same Destination entity {id, label, lat, lon, source, placeId?}. Reordering and removing stops is done in the list; map reflects order via numbering.

- Performance/quotas: Geocoder queries are rate-limited and debounced; reverse-geocode only on drop, not during drag. Cache recent queries and nearby reverse-geocode results.

- Validation: Require a resolved lat/lon before saving a stop. Ambiguous text requires explicit selection from suggestions.

- Mobile: Large touch targets for markers, long-press to add, and sticky confirm sheets.

This approach maximizes usability and precision while keeping a single, consistent data flow.

## Decision:
Use a bare Git repository with $HOME as the work-tree so files remain in place and continue to be read/modified by external programs.

- Initialize a bare repo at $HOME/.dotfiles (or ~/.cfg) and set an alias:
  - alias dot='git --git-dir=$HOME/.dotfiles --work-tree=$HOME'
- Configure to hide untracked files (prevents noise from all of $HOME):
  - dot config status.showUntrackedFiles no
- Track only intended files (e.g., .bashrc, app configs) with dot add ~/.bashrc etc., and commit/push to a remote (e.g., GitHub).
- Use a .gitignore in the bare repo’s info/exclude or use global excludes to avoid accidental tracking of transient files.
- Handle secrets using encryption:
  - Prefer git-crypt or git-secret/age with .gitattributes to transparently encrypt designated files.
- Provide a bootstrap script for new machines:
  - Clone bare repo to ~/.dotfiles
  - Check out into $HOME (dot checkout), resolving conflicts by backing up existing files
  - Apply machine-specific overlays via a local-only include config (e.g., ~/.gitconfig.local) ignored by Git.
- For multi-host differences, use conditional includes (based on hostname) or directory-specific configs.
- Avoid symlinks to minimize breakage from programs that overwrite files.
- Establish a workflow: external changes appear as working tree diffs; review and commit as needed.

## Decision:
Establish a centralized analytics data warehouse to integrate publishing-related data from all source applications, preserving both current state and full history. We will implement an ELT approach: ingest raw data from each system into a landing/raw layer via change data capture and event streams where available, then model curated, conformed datasets in a warehouse using dimensional schemas (star models) with Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 2) to maintain historical context. We will define conformed dimensions (e.g., content item, taxonomy, organisation, user, workflow state) and shared identifiers to reconcile records across systems. Transformations will be managed as versioned, testable code (e.g., dbt), with data quality checks and documented lineage. The warehouse will serve as the single source of truth for analytical reporting and KPIs, decoupled from operational systems to avoid performance impact. We will expose curated marts optimized for reporting tools and ad-hoc analysis, and enforce governance via a data catalog, access controls, and SLA-backed refresh schedules. We will start by onboarding the highest value sources in the publishing workflow, iterating towards full coverage, and deprecate bespoke point-to-point reporting jobs once equivalent metrics are available from the warehouse.

## Decision:
We will standardize on Mock Service Worker (MSW) for all HTTP/GraphQL request mocking across unit, integration, and (where applicable) local e2e tests.

- Handlers will be defined with MSW’s express-style API in a shared mocks package (e.g., tests/mocks/handlers.ts) with per-domain files and reusable fixtures.
- Unit/integration (Node) tests will use msw/node (setupServer). The server starts in test setup, resets handlers after each test, and stops after all tests.
- Browser-based tests will use msw/browser (service worker). The worker starts before tests and is reset after each test.
- We will not mock fetch/axios directly. MSW will intercept network calls, ensuring realistic behavior and preventing API-surface coupling.
- Unhandled requests:
  - Unit/integration: throw on unhandled to catch missing mocks early.
  - e2e/dev: default to passthrough with explicit opt-in to fail on unhandled when needed.
- Handlers may be overridden per test via server.use/worker.use. Tests must clean up overrides.
- Support both REST and GraphQL (msw/graphql). Type-safe request/response fixtures are encouraged.
- Provide utilities (test-utils) for starting/stopping servers/workers, resetting handlers, and loading scenario-specific handler sets.
- CI runs will use the same configuration to ensure determinism and isolation. Real network access is disabled unless explicitly whitelisted.
- Documentation will cover patterns (auth flows, error cases, pagination), handler organization, and when to prefer MSW vs. higher-level API spies (rare).

This unifies request mocking, improves reliability, and simplifies test authoring across environments.

## Decision:
Adopt a single, reusable Terraform module to define the infrastructure, and instantiate it separately for dev, uat, and prod by passing environment-specific inputs.

- Create one module (in modules/core or similar) with no environment-specific branching or hard-coded values. All variability is via input variables with sensible defaults where appropriate.
- Define separate root configurations per environment (e.g., envs/dev, envs/uat, envs/prod) that call the module and supply tfvars for each environment.
- Use isolated remote state per environment (e.g., separate S3 bucket prefixes and DynamoDB lock tables or separate backends) to guarantee strict state segregation; do not rely on Terraform workspaces for isolation.
- Enforce consistent naming and tagging conventions incorporating the environment (e.g., name prefixes/suffixes and tags like Environment=dev|uat|prod).
- Pin provider and module versions; promote changes by updating the pinned module version per environment (e.g., dev → uat → prod), using Git tags/releases for traceability.
- Run environment-specific CI/CD pipelines: plan on pull requests, and apply only on approved merges to designated branches or via manual promotion per environment.
- Source secrets and dynamic parameters from environment-specific stores (e.g., AWS SSM Parameter Store/Secrets Manager) via module inputs, not embedded in code.
- Provide input validation and policy checks (terraform validate, tflint, tfsec/conftest) in CI to prevent unsafe changes before apply.

This approach maximizes reuse, minimizes drift, and makes promotion between environments deterministic and auditable while keeping each environment’s state, configuration, and credentials strictly isolated.

## Decision:
- Standardize on Emory Shibboleth (SAML2) as the sole authentication mechanism for both Lux and Curate in production; no alternate identity providers or local credentials will be supported in prod.
- Reuse Curate’s approved Shibboleth attribute contract for both applications, treating it as the canonical attribute set. Require identical attribute release for prod, test, and arch endpoints across both apps.
- Implement a shared SSO adapter to parse Shibboleth headers, normalize attributes, create sessions, and map roles/entitlements consistently in both applications.
- Lux will support just-in-time user provisioning: on first successful Shibboleth login, create a local user record from the received attributes (no in-app registration flows or password management). Curate retains its existing flow without new-user onboarding.
- Authorization in both apps will be derived from Shibboleth-provided attributes (e.g., unique identifier, affiliation/entitlements). Absent or insufficient attributes will result in minimal access and/or denial, per policy.
- Maintain separate Shibboleth endpoints per app and environment (prod, test, arch), with consistent configuration and attribute release across environments.
- For non-production only, allow a developer-friendly fallback (mock Shibboleth headers or a secondary dev-only provider) gated by environment and feature flag, to enable local testing without institutional SSO.
- Enforce centralized session lifecycle aligned with Shibboleth SSO (respect session timeout/renewal), and record audit logs of login, logout, and provisioning events.

## Decision:
Adopt RFC 4122 UUIDs as Meadow’s primary identifiers to preserve DONUT compatibility. All migrated DONUT UUIDs will be retained verbatim (no rekeying). New Meadow records will also use UUIDs (version 4 preferred) for consistency and uniqueness.

- Identifier type: UUID (RFC 4122), version 4 for newly created IDs.
- Storage/format: canonical hyphenated lowercase string (8-4-4-4-12), validated as UUID; database columns use native UUID type where available.
- Constraints: global uniqueness enforced via database uniqueness constraints and application validation.
- Migration: existing DONUT UUIDs are imported as-is; no transformation or mapping required.
- ULIDs: not used as primary keys; if needed for sorting or external interoperability, they may be added as optional secondary attributes without affecting the primary identifier strategy.

## Decision:
We will include and honor payloads for non-200 HTTP responses and require clients to process them.

- Server behavior:
  - For all responses except those explicitly body-less by HTTP spec (e.g., 204, 304), the server may return a payload following our prescribed response format, including for 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx statuses.
  - Error responses will carry structured metadata (e.g., codes, messages, validation details, correlationId) and may include optional data when beneficial (e.g., conflict resolution hints, canonical state).
  - Rate limiting and retry semantics (e.g., 429) will include standard headers (Retry-After, rate-limit headers) and matching fields in the payload.
  - 409/422 will include field-level validation details; 401/403 will include authentication/authorization context where safe; 5xx will include correlationId and minimal diagnostics appropriate for clients.
  - Gateways and proxies in our control must not strip response bodies for non-2xx statuses.

- Client/SDK behavior:
  - Clients must not assume empty bodies for non-2xx responses; they must attempt to parse the payload using the prescribed format for any status other than 204/304.
  - SDKs will expose non-2xx responses as typed results preserving status, headers, and parsed body (or throw typed exceptions that retain the full response), enabling callers to access useful data and metadata.
  - Redirects (3xx) will be followed per client policy while still exposing any returned payload if present.
  - Clients should surface actionable information to users (validation errors, retry guidance) and use metadata for control flow (e.g., backoff on 429 using headers/payload).

This decision ensures valuable information is not lost on non-200 responses and keeps server and client behavior consistent across the platform.

## Decision:
[decision]: #decision

We will associate every new or edited entry with the authenticated user making the change. By default, the acting user will be auto-subscribed to future change notifications for that entry; an explicit checkbox on the create/edit form will allow opting out before saving and can be changed later in entry notification settings.

We will persist copyright/license acceptance at registration; authenticated users will not be asked to re-accept on each entry.

We will show attribution in each entry’s footer as “Last edited by <display name>” (falling back to user ID if no display name). If the editor account is deleted or anonymized, we will show “Former user” with an anonymized identifier. All edits will be retained in an audit log.

We will provide an optional per-entry moderation flag (“Require approval for anonymous edits”). If enabled, edits from unauthenticated users will be stored as pending and will not be publicly visible until approved. The entry’s owner or authorized moderators (RegPi/ThemPi) can approve or reject via a signed, expiring link in a distinct notification email with a unique subject indicating “Awaiting approval: <entry name>.” Approved changes become visible and trigger standard notifications; rejected changes remain logged but not published.

Authenticated user edits will publish immediately (bypassing this moderation) but still generate notifications.

Security and privacy:
- All moderation and approval actions will be authenticated or performed via time-limited, single-use, signed links and fully logged.
- Notification preferences are per-user/per-entry with unsubscribe links.
- Display names will respect user privacy settings; we will not expose email addresses.

Nice-to-haves (deferred): a “Show only changed entries” filter for logged-in users, and a red pin marker for entries awaiting approval.

## Decision:
Reject the proposal at this time. The submission lacks sufficient context, analysis, and stakeholder input to justify a change. No clear problem statement, goals/non-goals, alternatives considered, impact assessment, or migration strategy were provided, and there was no documented discussion with affected teams.

We will maintain the current approach and architecture unchanged.

For reconsideration, a revised ADR should include:
- Clear problem statement and scope
- Objectives, success metrics, and non-goals
- Alternatives with trade-offs (including “do nothing”)
- Impact on users, operations, security, compliance, and cost
- Migration/rollout plan, timeline, and rollback strategy
- Risks, mitigations, and ownership
- Evidence of stakeholder consultation and consensus

Once the above is provided, we will re-evaluate and schedule a decision.

## Decision:
We will not expose Datalabs services to the public internet. All access will be via the JASMIN tenancy using a JASMIN-managed VPN and a hardened bastion/jump host. Runtime services will be published only on private networks using internal load balancers/private endpoints and private DNS. Kubernetes NetworkPolicies and cloud firewall rules will default-deny inbound from outside the JASMIN network and restrict east–west traffic to required flows.

Administrative and troubleshooting access will occur through the bastion using SSH with MFA, short-lived credentials, IP allowlisting, session recording, and audited commands/port-forwarding as needed. Any exceptions to expose a service externally will require a formal security review, time-bounded rules, and WAF/proxy placement. All ingress/egress paths will be logged and monitored.

## Decision:
Adopt a “one component, one file” convention to make Terraform components self-describing and discoverable.

- Structure:
  - Each component is defined in a single file named <component>.tf within its stack/project.
  - Cross-cutting files at the stack root only: versions.tf (required_version, required_providers) and providers.tf (provider configuration). No per-component variables.tf or outputs.tf.
  - Optional README.md per component for extended context and examples.

- File layout (in-order) within <component>.tf:
  1) Header comment: purpose, high-level resources created, dependencies, owners.
  2) Variables: all inputs declared with type, description, and sensible defaults where applicable.
  3) Locals: naming, tags, and derived values to standardize conventions.
  4) Data sources: clearly separated from resources.
  5) Resources and/or module calls: grouped with brief comments explaining intent.
  6) Outputs: only what consumers need, each with a clear description.

- Naming and tagging:
  - Enforce standardized naming and mandatory tags via locals and/or a shared tagging module.
  - Consistent resource name prefixes based on stack/environment.

- Documentation and validation:
  - Every variable and output must have a description.
  - Include example usage in README.md where non-obvious.
  - Apply terraform fmt and tflint; pre-commit hooks enforce formatting and basic rules.

This keeps everything required to understand a component in one place, while centralizing only common, non-component-specific boilerplate.

## Decision:
- Decompose the monolith into a multi-module, published set of artifacts with a minimal, dependency-light core:
  - riptide-core: essential APIs, execution model, and SPIs; no optional/transitive integrations.
  - Feature modules: riptide-{jackson,metrics,retry,circuitbreaker,logbook,tracing,spring-boot-starter,…}, each isolated and with clearly scoped dependencies.
- Introduce a BOM (bill of materials) to align versions across modules and simplify consumption. Consumers can import the BOM and select modules à la carte without managing versions per artifact.
- Enforce strict dependency hygiene:
  - Core forbids optional/third-party integrations.
  - Feature modules must not re-export transitive dependencies; mark them as implementation/internal where possible and shade only when unavoidable.
  - No feature-to-feature hard dependencies; depend only on core or shared SPIs.
- Provide stable extension points via SPIs and Java ServiceLoader (or equivalent) to discover optional features at runtime without coupling.
- Publish a “batteries-included” aggregate (riptide-all or a platform starter) for convenience, but keep it separate from core.
- Establish module boundaries, semantic versioning, and deprecation policy to evolve features independently while preserving core stability.
- Update documentation to present features as composable modules with clear compatibility matrices and minimal examples per module.

## Decision:
- Unit and component testing: Spock as the primary framework (readable BDD style, powerful data-driven tests). For legacy modules, continue with JUnit 4 + AssertJ until migrated.
- Mocking/Stubbing: Spock built-ins as default; Mockito for JUnit-based tests.
- Spring/Java integration tests: Spring Boot Test with Testcontainers for ephemeral infra (Postgres, Kafka, Redis, etc.).
- API testing: RestAssured for HTTP-level tests; WireMock/MockServer for HTTP stubs; Pact or Spring Cloud Contract for consumer-driven contracts.
- End-to-end/UI: Cypress or Playwright for browser E2E; Karate for service-level E2E where UI is not required.
- Architecture rules: ArchUnit to enforce architectural constraints in CI.
- Coverage and quality gates: JaCoCo for coverage reporting integrated with SonarQube; PIT (Pitest) for mutation testing on critical modules.
- Performance and reliability: Gatling or k6 for load/perf tests; Toxiproxy for resilience/chaos at the network layer.
- Test data management: Testcontainers’ reusable containers, Fixture Factory/FactoryBoy-like patterns, and Liquibase/Flyway test migrations.
- Developer productivity: Local Docker Compose for full-stack smoke tests; parallel test execution in CI; deterministic seeds for flaky-test reduction.

## Decision:
Adopt a standardized schema taxonomy and access model to guide database development and enforce least-privilege access.

- Schema taxonomy:
  - reference: curated, rarely changing shared data (code sets, lookups); read-only to apps.
  - core: normalized operational data; owned by app team.
  - stage: transient/raw ingestion landing; truncated/rotated routinely.
  - transform: intermediate processing artifacts (cleansed, conformed).
  - marts: reporting/analytics schemas optimized for read (star/snowflake, aggregates).
  - audit: immutable change logs and event trails.
  - util: migration/versioning metadata and operational helpers.
  - sandbox: isolated per-user/team exploratory area; no upstream dependencies.

- Ownership and DDL:
  - One owner role per schema; DDL only by owner via CI/CD migrations.
  - No cross-ownership DDL; no PUBLIC grants; all access via roles.
  - Objects must be schema-qualified; synonyms discouraged (only for backward compatibility with sunset plan).

- Access patterns:
  - Applications write only to core (and stage if ingest), read from approved views in core/reference/marts.
  - Reporting users read marts and approved views; no direct write.
  - Transform jobs read stage/reference/core, write transform/marts.
  - Audit is append-only via controlled procedures.

- Governance and safety:
  - Enforce access with role tiers: OWNER, RW, RO per schema; temporary elevated roles via break-glass.
  - Use views/materialized views to expose only necessary columns/rows; apply RLS where supported.
  - Naming conventions and linters enforced in CI; migrations versioned and reversible.
  - Data retention and PII policies per schema class (e.g., no PII in stage/marts unless justified).

* Provide a Welsh-translated HMRC footer by adopting hmrc-frontend’s hmrcFooter with a Scala/Play wrapper in play-frontend-hmrc that wires language via Play’s i18n (Messages) and request context.
* Do not rely on client-side cookies for language; determine language server-side via Play (e.g. MessagesApi/request2Messages) to ensure compatibility across services and avoid HttpOnly constraints.
* Centralise all footer copy in platform-maintained message bundles (messages.en/messages.cy) within play-frontend-hmrc; ensure complete cy coverage and English fallback for missing keys.
* Make footer links language-aware: generate URLs via platform helpers that resolve to the correct Welsh/English endpoints or append the appropriate language parameter (e.g. ?lang=cy) for services like tracking-consent-frontend, contact-frontend, and accessibility-statement-frontend.
* Ensure correct accessibility semantics in Welsh: set lang attributes appropriately on the document and ensure no mixed-language fragments without explicit lang tagging; maintain identical structure and ARIA across locales.
* Expose a simple Scala API for services to supply optional overrides (e.g. service name, additional links) while defaulting to platform-standard Welsh/English links and copy.
* Provide automated tests: unit tests for message resolution and URL generation, integration tests rendering Welsh footer, and visual/accessibility regression checks.
* Document usage and migration guidance; recommend adopting the Play wrapper over direct Nunjucks usage. Release as a minor, non-breaking change and deprecate bespoke footers lacking Welsh support.

## Decision:
Adopt Quart as the HTTP framework for the FlowKit API.

Rationale:
- ASGI-native and asyncio-first, enabling high concurrency, better performance, and straightforward WebSocket support for future real-time features.
- Lightweight with minimal boilerplate, avoiding the legacy and heaviness of Django and the sync-first constraints of Flask.
- High compatibility with the Flask ecosystem, allowing reuse of many Flask extensions and patterns.
- Clear migration path: if Quart becomes stagnant, its close API parity with Flask reduces switching costs; alternatively, the ASGI architecture eases migration to FastAPI/Starlette if needed.

Implementation notes:
- Run under Hypercorn (preferred) or Uvicorn as the ASGI server.
- Where FlowKit operations are blocking, isolate them via asyncio.to_thread/executors to preserve event-loop responsiveness.
- Prefer Flask-compatible extensions verified to work under Quart; otherwise, select native ASGI middlewares.

This choice balances immediate simplicity with performance and future capabilities, while containing long-term framework risk.

## Decision:
Standardize fragment menus on the AndroidX MenuHost/MenuProvider pattern.

- Every fragment that exposes a menu must register a MenuProvider in onViewCreated, scoped to viewLifecycleOwner and Lifecycle.State.RESUMED:
  - (requireActivity() as MenuHost).addMenuProvider(provider, viewLifecycleOwner, Lifecycle.State.RESUMED)
- Menus are defined via XML under res/menu with feature-scoped filenames and stable, namespaced IDs (e.g., menu_article_details.xml, id: action_article_share).
- Fragments implement onCreateMenu(Menu, MenuInflater) to inflate their menu and onMenuItemSelected(MenuItem) to handle actions, returning true when handled.
- Activities must not override onCreateOptionsMenu/onOptionsItemSelected for fragment-owned items. Activity-level menus use their own MenuProvider to avoid collisions.
- Fragments that own a Toolbar set it as the activity’s supportActionBar in onViewCreated; the MenuProvider remains the single mechanism for menu inflation/handling.
- Visibility and enablement changes occur in onPrepareMenu(Menu) within the same MenuProvider.
- Navigation actions from menu items should use the fragment’s NavController where applicable.

To enforce consistency and reduce boilerplate, provide a small helper:
- registerMenu(menuRes, onCreate: (Menu) -> Unit = {}, onPrepare: (Menu) -> Unit = {}, onSelect: (MenuItem) -> Boolean)
- This helper internally adds the MenuProvider to the activity’s MenuHost with the correct lifecycle.

This approach removes Activity coupling, ensures lifecycle-correct menu visibility, supports multiple fragments contributing menus, and provides a single, consistent pattern across the app.

## Decision:
We will require each deployable image to declare its sidecar dependencies explicitly and immutably, and we will drive deployment from that declaration.

- Declaration mechanism: standardize on OCI image labels carrying a JSON manifest under key: org.example.sidecars (e.g., [{ "name": "metrics", "image": "ghcr.io/org/metrics@sha256:...", "required": true }]).
- Version pinning: production dependencies must be pinned by image digest (image@sha256). Mutable tags (e.g., :latest, :1) are allowed only in non-production and will be blocked by policy in prod.
- Tooling: CI will validate the manifest (schema, existence, digest pullability), lock images to digests, and surface the sidecar list as build artifacts. Our Helm/Kustomize templates consume these artifacts to render the sidecar containers with exact refs.
- Change management: updating a sidecar requires a code change to the producing image (or its sidecar manifest file) and a new image release, ensuring traceability and reproducibility. Each application release thus captures a complete Bill of Materials.
- Compatibility: producers are responsible for verifying compatibility with pinned sidecars. If compatibility constraints are needed, add optional fields (e.g., "versionConstraint": "^2.3", "minKube": "1.27").
- Backward compatibility: existing services may opt-in incrementally; once opted-in, mutable tags in prod are disallowed by policy.
- Observability and SBOM: the manifest is included in the image labels and published alongside SBOMs to support audit and incident response.

This approach makes sidecar versions portable with the image, reproducible across environments, and predictable during deploys.

## Decision:
Adopt a fully declarative Infrastructure as Code approach for all environments. All infrastructure will be defined as desired state in version-controlled repositories and applied via automated CI/CD pipelines. Imperative, manual changes in cloud consoles or ad-hoc scripts are prohibited and will be blocked via least-privilege IAM and auditing.

We will standardize on reusable modules, environment-specific overlays, and parameterization to ensure consistency and reduce drift. Changes will be made exclusively through pull requests, with mandatory code review, plan output visibility, and automated policy-as-code checks (e.g., security and compliance rules) before apply.

Drift detection and reconciliation will be enabled to continuously compare live state with declared state and remediate deviations. State management will use a secure, remote backend with locking and versioning. Sensitive values will be referenced from a central secrets manager rather than embedded in code or state.

This approach increases reliability, repeatability, and auditability; reduces configuration errors (e.g., unintended public exposure); and accelerates safe change by making all modifications testable, reviewable, and reproducible.

## Decision:
Leverage ParserCache for a single “default” Termbox v2 SSR variant and bypass ParserCache for user‑customized variants.

- Cacheable default: HTML produced for (entity id, entity revision, interface language) with:
  - preferred languages equal to the interface language
  - default “more languages” toggle state
  This fragment is embedded into ParserOutput and stored in ParserCache as today.

- Customized variants: When a request indicates non‑default preferred languages and/or a non‑default toggle state (via logged‑in preferences or session/cookies), MediaWiki bypasses ParserCache for the Termbox fragment only and requests SSR directly from the Termbox service at render time. The page remains otherwise cacheable as usual.

- Service‑side mitigation: The Termbox service maintains an internal short‑TTL cache keyed by (entity id, entity revision, interface language, normalized preferred languages list, toggle state) to absorb repeated customized requests without inflating MediaWiki’s ParserCache key space.

- Eligibility detection: On each request, determine eligibility for the default variant from user/session state. If eligible, use the ParserCache fragment; otherwise, fetch customized SSR. Anonymous users without explicit settings and most logged‑in users whose preferred languages match their interface language will hit the cached default.

- No marker round‑trip: We avoid placeholder/marker injection across services; the SSR service returns complete fragments per variant it controls.

This maximizes ParserCache hit rate for the dominant traffic, limits cache key explosion, keeps SSR authoritative for what to render, and contains the cost of personalized variants to the Termbox service with bounded, service‑local caching.

## Decision:
- Adopt a snapshot-first strategy: extract complete datasets on a fixed schedule (daily baseline, ad-hoc bursts during known update windows) and persist raw HTML/JSON plus normalized records with extraction_time.
- Treat transaction timestamp as a best-effort attribute with provenance: store fields {transaction_timestamp, transaction_timestamp_source, extraction_time, source_page_asof, confidence_score}. Allow null transaction_timestamp when unavailable; never drop records.
- Implement multi-pass enrichment: re-scan recently ingested records (e.g., last 30–90 days) to backfill or correct timestamps as districts/treasuries update data.
- Maintain an update-schedule registry per district/treasury (empirical, auto-learned) to prioritize crawls when likelihood of fresh data is highest and reduce futile requests.
- Use differential detection: compare successive snapshots to infer transaction windows (first_seen_time, last_seen_time) and derive bounded timestamps where exact values are missing.
- Build a temporal validation pipeline that:
