  - Cross-checks totals across Grant-wise and DDO-wise hierarchies for the same period.
  - Flags regressions, out-of-order dates, and large deltas for manual review.
  - Assigns confidence tiers (Exact, Bounded, Inferred, Unknown) to each temporal field.
- Store all provenance and versions (immutable append-only fact table with slowly changing dimensions for entities); support reprocessing when better timestamps appear.
- Expose downstream SLAs and metadata: “as_of” time per dataset, coverage by district/treasury, and confidence distribution.
- Operationalize with idempotent jobs, rate limiting, retries, and circuit breakers; any temporal anomalies fail soft (record captured with low confidence) rather than failing the pipeline.

## Decision:
- Use RFC 4122-compliant UUID version 4 (random) for all Telemetry identifiers requiring global uniqueness.
- Rely exclusively on platform-standard or well-maintained, security-reviewed libraries that use cryptographically secure RNG:
  - Java: java.util.UUID.randomUUID()
  - Node.js: crypto.randomUUID()
  - Python: uuid.uuid4()
  - Go: github.com/google/uuid (uuid.NewRandom) or github.com/gofrs/uuid (uuid.NewV4) using crypto/rand
  - Rust: uuid crate (v4) with OsRng
- Do not implement custom UUID generators; any new language/runtime must propose a library meeting RFC 4122 compliance, CSPRNG usage, small footprint, permissive license, and active maintenance.
- Enforce a single canonical representation at API boundaries: lowercase, hyphenated 36-char string (8-4-4-4-12). Internally prefer 16-byte binary storage when supported by the datastore; otherwise store as canonical string with normalized collation.
- Provide a shared utility wrapper per language that:
  - Generates UUIDv4, validates inputs (format and variant/version bits), and normalizes to canonical form.
  - Centralizes dependency choice to ease upgrades and audits.
- Add static analysis/linting and schema constraints to prevent non-canonical or non-RFC UUIDs.
- Backward compatibility: accept uppercase on input but normalize to lowercase; reject non-RFC variants.
- Security and quality gates: pin library versions, enable dependency scanning, and include tests verifying randomness source and RFC bit layout.

## Decision:
We will capture architecturally significant decisions as small, lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) created just-in-time and maintained alongside the code.

- Scope: Any decision affecting architecture, quality attributes, external interfaces, data models, security, runtime topology, or major dependencies requires an ADR.
- Format: One decision per ADR using a concise Markdown template with sections: Context, Decision, Status (proposed/accepted/deprecated/superseded), Consequences, and References. Target length is 1–2 pages.
- Repository: Store ADRs under docs/adr/adr-{NNNN}-{kebab-title}.md with monotonically increasing numbers. Keep superseded ADRs for traceability and link related ADRs bidirectionally.
- Workflow: New or changed architectural decisions are introduced via pull request. At least one architect/tech lead reviews; product/security reviewers added as relevant. Merging signifies “accepted.”
- Traceability: Reference ADR IDs in commit messages, issues, and code comments where decisions are enacted. Major features or dependency introductions must reference an ADR.
- Maintenance: Periodically review ADRs for relevance; supersede rather than edit historical decisions. Tag ADRs by domain/component to aid discoverability and link from the project README.
- Practicality: Aim for time-boxed authorship (15–30 minutes) to ensure ADRs remain lightweight and kept up to date. Avoid large, monolithic documents in favor of modular records.

## Decision:
Do not merge Kafka Key and Value into a single row schema by default. Instead, expose a fixed, stable, tabular schema with separate columns for metadata, Key, and Value:

- Metadata columns (fixed order): topic, partition, offset, timestamp, timestamp_type, headers
- Payload columns: key (VARBINARY/BLOB), key_format, key_schema_id, key_size; value (VARBINARY/BLOB), value_format, value_schema_id, value_size

SELECT * returns the columns above in the exact order listed, ensuring deterministic name/index mapping for JDBC consumers.

Field-level access is opt-in:
- Provide UDFs/TVFs to extract fields from key/value given a format or schema (e.g., json_extract(value, '$.x'), avro_extract(value, 'field', schema_id)).
- Provide a table function EXPAND_KAFKA(topic, expand_key, expand_value, prefix_key, prefix_value) that generates a widened, prefixed schema (key_*, value_*) using the schema registry or provided schemas. Name collisions are resolved via prefixes; expansion is explicit and discoverable.

No implicit default value calculation or schema merging occurs. Users must explicitly request expansion or field extraction. This preserves intuitive behavior, avoids ambiguous column indices, and remains compatible with JDBC’s tabular model while allowing rich access to engine-returned metadata. A legacy compatibility mode for merged schemas, with strict prefixing and documented ordering, may be offered but is not the default.

## Decision:
Adopt a lightweight, open ADR + RFC process in a single, public repository to author, discuss, approve, and evolve architectural decisions.

- Repository and discoverability:
  - Create a public archetypes-rules/architecture repo as the single source of truth.
  - All ADRs live under /adrs with stable URLs and tags; a generated index page improves searchability.
  - Mirror the index to our website/docs for web discovery.

- ADR template and content:
  - Required sections: Context, Decision, Status, Alternatives considered, Rationale, Consequences, Security/Privacy impact, Operational impact, Open questions, Review date/trigger.
  - Status lifecycle: Draft → Proposed (RFC) → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded.

- Broad-based, transparent decision-making:
  - Any contributor may open an RFC (Proposed ADR) via pull request.
  - Discussion occurs in the PR; all comments remain public.
  - Approval requires: (a) at least three reviewers, including one maintainer, and (b) documented consideration of alternatives and impacts.
  - For cross-cutting/major decisions, notify relevant channels and, when applicable, request TSC review before acceptance.

- Versionable history:
  - All changes occur via PRs; Git history is the audit log.
  - Semantically version ADRs with Status changes; add a CHANGELOG.md summarizing updates.

- Shared understanding across a distributed team:
  - Publish concise decision summaries and links in release notes and team updates.
  - Hold optional, recorded walkthroughs for major ADRs and link recordings from the ADR.

- Revisitability:
  - Each ADR includes a review date or explicit triggers (e.g., new regulations, scale thresholds).
  - Superseding ADRs must reference and close prior ones, preserving context.

## Decision:
We will provision CSI-based drivers only and expose two default StorageClasses:
- glusterfs-rwx (default): Backed by GlusterFS CSI for ReadWriteMany persistent volumes, used for most application data and shared workloads.
- local-rwo (non-default): Backed by the Local Path CSI provisioner for lightweight, single-node ReadWriteOnce development/test workloads.

Rationale:
- Aligns with our earlier choice of GlusterFS for resilient, scalable RWX storage.
- Uses CSI (not in-tree) drivers to remain supported and portable across Kubernetes versions.
- Provides a clear split between shared (RWX) and fast local (RWO) needs without over-provisioning multiple niche drivers.

Operational notes:
- Enable Kubernetes external snapshotter CRDs and controller for backups and point-in-time restores of both classes.
- Mark glusterfs-rwx as the cluster “default” StorageClass; require explicit selection of local-rwo to avoid accidental use in multi-replica apps.
- Enforce topology and anti-affinity in GlusterFS to ensure replica distribution across failure domains.
- Do not provision hostPath or NFS-subdir provisioners in production clusters.

## Decision:
Adopt Apache Tika as the primary JVM-native framework for MIME detection and text extraction across supported file types. Extract text directly from source files (not converted PDFs) to preserve fidelity and avoid conversion artifacts.

Define a pluggable Extractor SPI keyed by MIME type. Provide a Tika-based default extractor covering common formats (PDF via PDFBox, Office via POI, OpenDocument, HTML, plain text, email/mbox, etc.). Where Tika’s defaults are insufficient, add targeted extractors behind the same SPI (e.g., direct PDFBox tuning for PDFs, jsoup for HTML sanitization). For images or scanned PDFs, expose OCR as an optional adapter (e.g., Tesseract) that is disabled by default to avoid mandatory external dependencies.

Implement streaming extraction with strict resource guards (max file size, page/char limits, timeouts) and safe parsing settings to mitigate malicious documents. If extraction fails or is unsupported, fall back to metadata-only indexing and surface non-fatal errors without blocking overall processing.

Keep configuration-driven overrides to enable external tool adapters (e.g., pandoc) per MIME type when operators need better fidelity; these remain optional and isolated from the core runtime. Version-pin Tika and dependent parsers for stability, with a compatibility test suite across representative formats.

This design minimizes external components, keeps the JVM-only path first-class, supports incremental addition of new types via the SPI, and ensures the application remains functional even when certain extractors are unavailable.

## Decision:
We will use a single-artifact, environment-promotion deployment model across three environments: integration → staging → production.

- Source control: trunk-based development on main with short-lived PRs. Every merge to main triggers a versioned build (Semantic Versioning) and creates an immutable, signed artifact/container image stored in the registry.
- Integration: auto-deploy latest successful build to integration with smoke, contract, and integration tests. Failures block promotion.
- Staging: promotion-only (no rebuild). Manual approval gate after integration passes. Run end-to-end, performance, and security scans. Data resembles prod via anonymized subsets.
- Production: promotion-only with change control and mandatory approval. Blue/green or canary rollout with automatic health checks and fast rollback to last known-good artifact.
- Configuration: environment-specific config via Helm/Kustomize overlays (or equivalent), with secrets in a managed secrets store. No environment-specific code; only config differs.
- Database: forward-only, idempotent migrations applied with each promotion; feature flags used to decouple schema and code rollout.
- Observability: uniform logging, metrics, and tracing; SLO-based deployment guards and post-deploy verification.
- Access control: environment-specific credentials/permissions; staging/prod pipelines require elevated approvers. All actions auditable.
- Rollback: promotion history retained; rollback is redeploying a prior artifact and config snapshot.

This ensures consistency, repeatability, and controlled risk across integration, staging, and production.

## Decision:
Implement first‑party, privacy‑preserving analytics using only previously approved, in‑house systems.

- Build a lightweight event collection endpoint in the application (Node.js) to receive client events (page views, link clicks, form start/submit, errors, task completion).
- Store events in the existing Postgres database on GOV.UK PaaS, using a schema that minimises/avoids PII (no full URLs with query strings, no user identifiers; hash/trim IPs if retained, and apply retention limits).
- Instrument the frontend using the GOV.UK Design System with data-attributes for declarative event tagging; send events via fetch/beacon only after user consent (cookie banner), with graceful degradation.
- Create reporting and dashboards using an approved, internally hosted tool (e.g., Metabase on GOV.UK PaaS) querying Postgres; if unavailable, provide scheduled exports for analysis.
- Exclude any external analytics or tracking services (e.g., Google Analytics) and third‑party beacons.
- Provide feature flags and sampling to control event volume; document the taxonomy (event names, properties), consent model, and retention policy.

## Decision
Adopt Relay (Relay Modern) as the client GraphQL framework for v5 and deprecate Apollo and our home-grown colocation framework.

Key elements:
- Enforce true component-level data colocation via Relay fragments and route-level queries; eliminate “fat queries” and manual data distribution.
- Use the Relay Compiler for static analysis, query compilation, artifact/code generation, and type-safety (TypeScript). This prevents runtime perf regressions and misuse.
- Align our schema to Relay conventions: Node interface with global IDs, Connections for pagination, server-defined cursors, and mutation input/payload patterns.
- Enable persisted/compiled queries and automatic normalization in the Relay store to reduce payload size, network overhead, and memory churn.
- Standardize pagination, mutations, and cache updates through Relay APIs instead of custom patterns or forks.
- Introduce lint rules and CI checks (relay-compiler as a required step) to gate schema and client changes, preventing anti-patterns.
- Remove the Apollo fork and internal GraphQL frameworks, reducing maintenance burden and upgrade risks.

Migration approach:
- Incremental route-by-route migration with an interoperability layer during transition; new features must use Relay.
- Begin with the heaviest screens to realize immediate performance wins; deprecate Apollo utilities in stages and remove once parity is achieved.
- Provide developer docs, codemods, templates, and examples to onboard contributors quickly.

Expected outcomes:
- Significant performance improvements (fewer round trips, smaller payloads, better caching).
- Reduced complexity and maintenance (no forks, less custom infra).
- Better reliability and contributor experience via strict, well-documented patterns and compiler-enforced correctness.

## Decision:
We will not align Libero Publisher’s front end with Libero Reviewer’s React/SPA stack. Instead, Publisher will adopt a server-rendered, progressively enhanced, read-optimised front end that prioritises fast first render, resilient core functionality without JavaScript, and minimal, targeted client-side enhancements.

This architecture will center on:
- Server-side rendering of semantic, accessible HTML with aggressive caching and CDN support.
- A standards-first approach (HTML/CSS), with lightweight, framework-agnostic JavaScript only where it adds clear value.
- Progressive enhancement patterns to ensure core reading experiences work reliably under constrained conditions.
- Shared design tokens, CSS utilities, and potentially framework-agnostic components (e.g., Web Components) to maximise reuse across the suite without imposing a SPA framework.

This choice acknowledges the distinct performance and resilience requirements of Publisher’s read-heavy product surface, which differ from Reviewer and Producer. It sacrifices some cross-product React component reuse to meet Publisher’s stronger needs for speed, accessibility, and robustness, while still enabling alignment in design systems, build tooling, and testing practices.

## Decision:
Extend the Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy controlling CloudHSM egress so that traffic to the HSM is permitted only when both:
- The originating Pod has label talksToHsm=true, and
- The originating Namespace has label talksToHsm=true.

Implementation details:
- Update the cluster-wide GlobalNetworkPolicy to include both a podSelector and a namespaceSelector requiring talksToHsm=true for egress to HSM subnets/ports. All other namespaces/pods remain denied by default for HSM destinations.
- Manage the namespace label exclusively via cluster-config (platform-owned), not tenant namespaces, ensuring visibility and change control via PR review.
- Retain existing credential isolation (as per ADR036) and per-namespace CryptoUser separation; this decision affects only network reachability.
- Provide a controlled enablement process: service teams request HSM access; platform team applies the namespace label and supplies namespace-scoped credentials.
- Add Gatekeeper/OPA constraints to prevent tenants from applying or mutating the protected namespace label on their own namespaces.
- Validate via integration tests that: (a) pod-only label does not grant HSM access; (b) namespace-only label does not grant HSM access; (c) both labels present grants access; (d) absence of labels blocks access.
- Document the policy and onboarding/offboarding steps; audit label changes and HSM egress via network flow logs.

This strengthens defense-in-depth by eliminating unilateral tenant escalation paths to HSM while preserving legitimate access through platform-governed controls.

## Decision:
Create a new, first-class authentication module in Panoptes.js that standardizes both the auth flow and the user experience across projects, replacing the existing auth in panoptes-javascript-client.

Key elements:
- Protocol: Adopt OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code with PKCE for public/browser clients. Remove support for implicit grant. Keep first-party session (cookie-based) login for zooniverse.org and unify both behind one API.
- UX: Ship reusable, accessible UI components and headless hooks:
  - Components: SignInButton, SignOutButton, UserMenu, RequireAuth, OAuthCallbackHandler.
  - Hooks/APIs: useAuth(), getAccessToken(), getUser(), signIn(), signOut().
- Token management: Built-in storage and rotation with secure defaults:
  - Access tokens in memory; refresh tokens only when permitted, stored in IndexedDB and rotated; fallback to sessionStorage.
  - CSRF/state/nonce verification; strict redirect URI and scope validation.
  - Automatic refresh and retry; consistent error surface and events (onAuthStateChanged, onTokenRefreshed).
- Configuration: Single config object (clientId, scopes, authServer, redirectUris, prompt), environment support (staging/production).
- Framework support: Framework-agnostic core with adapters; provide official React package first, with examples for vanilla/other frameworks.
- Reliability and QA: End-to-end tests with mocked auth server, cross-browser testing, and a local sandbox app.
- Migration: Deprecate and shim the old panoptes-javascript-client auth. Provide a migration guide and codemods where feasible. Maintain compatibility for one minor cycle, then remove old auth.

Outcomes:
- Consistent, secure login across projects.
- Reduced bugs via standardized PKCE-based flows and hardened token handling.
- Faster adoption via drop-in components and minimal configuration.

## Decision:
We will run PHP via PHP-FPM and connect Nginx to PHP-FPM using Unix domain sockets (not TCP) with one dedicated PHP-FPM pool (and socket) per application. Nginx will serve static assets directly and route only .php requests to the matching pool socket.

Key configuration decisions:
- Nginx: use try_files to prevent path traversal; only route *.php to FPM; block PHP execution in upload directories.
- FPM: per-app pool with explicit socket path, ownership, and permissions; configure process limits per app for isolation.
- Sockets: use listen = /run/php-fpm/<app>.sock with listen.mode = 0660 and listen.owner = www-data; listen.group = www-data (or the Nginx user).
- FastCGI params: set SCRIPT_FILENAME to $realpath_root$fastcgi_script_name; include standard fastcgi_params; enable PATH_INFO handling where needed.
- Timeouts and buffering: configure fastcgi_read_timeout, fastcgi_connect_timeout, fastcgi_send_timeout, and fastcgi_buffers to sane defaults; disable buffering selectively for streaming endpoints.
- Security: deny execution of PHP in writable paths; limit request body size; clear/whitelist FastCGI params; hide X-Powered-By.
- Health: optional /_health endpoint served by Nginx returning 200; FPM status/ping enabled per pool but not exposed publicly.

Example Nginx intent (per app):
- root to application public directory; index includes index.php
- location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string; }
- location ~ \.php$ { include fastcgi_params; fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $realpath_root$fastcgi_script_name; fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php-fpm/<app>.sock; }

This standardizes PHP hosting across services, improves performance and isolation versus TCP, and simplifies operational management.

## Decision:
Adopt explicit retention and automated compaction/garbage-collection for mail queue metadata and blobs:

- Enforce a fixed retention window (e.g., 30 days) for enqueuedMailsV3 and deletedMailsV2.
- Apply per-row TTLs on all new writes equal to the retention window. Align TWCS settings (time window size and compaction options) to ensure timely purge of expired data and reduce tombstone pressure. Reduce gc_grace_seconds to slightly above repair interval within the retention window.
- For existing data without TTL, run a one-time backfill purge by partition/window (delete rows older than retention based on enqueued/deleted timestamps) to avoid rewriting massive volumes with TTLs.
- Introduce a Blob Garbage Collector:
  - Maintain/compute reference counts of blobs from all referencing tables.
  - Periodically scan for blobs whose references have fully expired (or are older than retention) and delete them from the blob store after a safety delay (e.g., +7 days).
  - Idempotent, rate-limited, and metrics-instrumented; emits audit logs of deletions.
- Add S3/object storage lifecycle policies as a belt-and-suspenders to expire orphaned blobs beyond an extended window (e.g., 60–90 days) to cap storage costs.
- Provide configuration for the retention window to accommodate compliance needs, with sane defaults and per-environment overrides.
- Monitor with dashboards/alerts on table size, tombstones, compaction backlog, and blob storage footprint to validate effectiveness and detect regressions.

This approach leverages TWCS/TTL for scalable metadata cleanup, ensures privacy by bounded data lifetime, and safely reclaims blob storage without impacting queue semantics.

## Decision:
Standardize on a sha256-only naming scheme for preservation storage objects. The pairtree path will be derived solely from the object’s sha256 digest, and the leaf filename will be the full, lowercase hexadecimal sha256. No ULID or other identifier will be included in either the pairtree segments or the leaf name.

This decision supersedes and replaces ADR-18’s ULID+sha256 scheme. It aligns the ADR with actual operational practice and removes identifier-derived path components from the storage layout.

Implementation details:
- Digest: sha256 of the canonical preservation payload; represented as 64 lowercase hex characters without delimiters.
- Pairtree: derived from the sha256 (e.g., fixed-width segmenting such as 2/2/2/... per pairtree conventions); exact segmentation is specified in implementation docs and must remain consistent.
- Leaf name: the full sha256 hex string (optionally with a format-specific extension if required by the container format).
- Id-independence: logical identifiers are not encoded in the path; a registry maps logical identifiers to their current sha256.
- Collisions: treated as practically negligible; systems must verify that a computed sha256 matches the object referenced.

Backwards compatibility:
- Existing objects named with sha256-only remain valid; no migration is required.
- New writes must use the sha256-only scheme.
- Any tooling, validation, and documentation referencing ULID in storage paths will be updated accordingly.

## Decision:
Adopt OAuth 2.1 with OpenID Connect for user authentication and JWT bearer access tokens for API authorization. A centralized Identity Provider (IdP) will authenticate users via Authorization Code with PKCE (interactive) and Client Credentials (system-to-system). The Capacity Status API will validate tokens (issuer, audience, expiry) against the IdP JWKs and operate over TLS 1.2+.

Authorization will follow least-privilege, deny-by-default:
- Access requires scope capacity:write and audience matching the API.
- Role-based checks (e.g., DoSLead, ServiceProvider) are embedded in token claims (roles) or retrieved via token exchange/userinfo.
- Resource-level authorization is enforced by verifying the user’s permitted service IDs against the requested service (via an internal authorization service or policy engine). Only users assigned to the target service (or with DoSLead privilege) may update its capacity status.

Operational controls:
- Short-lived tokens (≤1 hour) with automatic key rotation; no reliance on refresh tokens by the API.
- Standardized error responses: 401 for missing/invalid tokens; 403 for insufficient permissions.
- Comprehensive audit logging (subject, scopes, roles, service ID, decision, correlation ID) without recording secrets.
- Rate limiting and replay protections (nonce/PKCE) delegated to the IdP; API applies per-identity throttles on write endpoints.
- Support for future federation by trusting additional IdPs via configured issuers and JWKS endpoints.

This approach ensures strong authentication, fine-grained, service-scoped authorization, and secure, auditable updates to Capacity Status.

## Decision:
Adopt commercetools Payment.key as the canonical identifier for merchantReference and deprecate the custom field.

- For all newly created payments, set payment.key = merchantReference (optionally prefixed/suffixed with merchantAccount to guarantee uniqueness if merchantReference is not globally unique).
- In the Adyen notification handler, resolve the payment by key via GET /payments/key={key}. This replaces the custom(fields(merchantReference=...)) query.
- Maintain backward compatibility during a transition period: if a lookup by key misses, fallback to the legacy custom field query and emit a deprecation warning/metric.
- Migrate existing payments by backfilling key from custom.fields.merchantReference (with merchantAccount scoping if needed). Perform this via a batched job and handle key collisions by a deterministic namespacing scheme.
- Stop writing the custom merchantReference field for new payments and mark it deprecated; remove the fallback and field usage after migration completes.
- Validate constraints: ensure merchantReference conforms to key limits (length ≤ 256, recommended ASCII), and define a normalization strategy if required.
- Update documentation and integration guides to instruct clients to populate Payment.key with the merchantReference at creation time.

Rationale:
- Native key is unique, indexed, and retrievable via fast by-key lookup, improving performance and reliability.
- Eliminates dependence on custom fields and complex queries.
- Simplifies idempotency and debugging by aligning identifiers across Adyen and commercetools.

## Decision:
Expose CHIP via a resource‑oriented JSON-over-HTTP REST API as the primary interface, documented with OpenAPI and designed for additive, backward‑compatible evolution (no URL versioning; use media types and deprecation headers when needed). Implement the API as a thin transport layer over a hexagonal (ports-and-adapters) domain, keeping business logic independent of the web framework and serialization concerns. This separation allows us to add or swap interfaces (e.g., GraphQL, gRPC, or async events) without rewriting the core, and to iterate quickly on features while maintaining stability for clients.

## Decision:
Introduce a composable logging pipeline with a small set of first-class, opt-in primitives around a minimal Handler interface.

- Define Handler as the sink abstraction (e.g., file, stdout, HTTP).
- Introduce Processor as a middleware/decorator applied before handlers to implement cross-cutting concerns.
- Logger emits Entries to a Pipeline: [Processors…] -> Handler.
- Provide built-in processors:
  - ContextEnricher: injects process/thread/fiber IDs, correlation/trace IDs, request metadata; supports explicit context passing and fiber-local storage for propagation.
  - Filter/Sampler: predicate- or rate-based filtering to reduce noise.
  - Formatter: transforms Entry to serialized form (JSON/line), separate from the sink.
- Provide built-in handler decorators:
  - MultiHandler: fan-out/tee to multiple handlers with isolated failure domains.
  - AsyncHandler: bounded in-memory queue + worker(s) for non-blocking emission; configurable backpressure policy (block, drop-oldest, drop-newest, error).
  - RetryHandler: transient-failure retries with jittered backoff.
- Ordering and fault tolerance:
  - Processor order is explicit and preserved.
  - MultiHandler isolates failures; one sink error does not affect others unless configured.
  - AsyncHandler preserves per-logger ordering within a worker.
- Configuration:
  - Pipeline is constructed explicitly and injected; no globals.
  - Sensible defaults (context enrichment + stdout JSON formatter).
  - Metrics and internal event hooks for drops, queue depth, retries.

This design cleanly separates concerns, enables reuse across all sinks, and allows teeing, enrichment, and async buffering without coupling application code to specific handlers.

## Decision:
Use a hierarchical folder structure based on type/namespace/id.

- Rationale:
  - Satisfies human readability: paths and filenames convey meaning and allow manual navigation, grepping, and code review in VCS.
  - Ensures machine processability: deterministic, schema-driven layout enables straightforward parsing, validation, and tooling without content-address resolution.
  - Namespacing prevents collisions across domains/vendors while keeping IDs concise and stable.
  - Works well with diff-based workflows, partial checkouts, and content ownership per subtree.

- Structure (conceptual):
  - <type>/<namespace>/<id>/
    - metadata.(yaml|json)
    - artifacts/
    - relations/
    - README.md (optional)

- Conventions:
  - Normalize and percent-encode/escape characters in namespace and id to be filesystem-safe; define a single canonical encoding.
  - Enforce case policy (e.g., lowercase) to avoid cross-platform issues.
  - Limit path length and segment length; validate on write.
  - Maintain an optional index (e.g., index.json) for faster lookup and reverse mappings without making it authoritative.

- Trade-offs:
  - Slightly more overhead than a flat, hash-based store but meets the human-readable requirement.
  - Deduplication can be handled at the artifact level (e.g., content-addressed files in artifacts/) while preserving readable entity paths.

This layout balances discoverability, maintainability, and robust automation for Winery’s filesystem backend.

## Decision:
We will record architectural decisions for this project using the MADR template (current version at project start).

Rationale:
- Making assumptions and trade-offs explicit improves shared understanding, onboarding, and change traceability.
- MADR is lightweight, readable in Markdown, widely adopted, and easy to maintain in Git workflows.
- It offers a clear, consistent structure while remaining flexible for different levels of detail.

Structure and conventions:
- Location: repository/docs/adr/
- Naming: YYYYMMDD-short-title.md and incremental index (e.g., 0001-use-madr.md). Keep an index.md linking all ADRs.
- Template sections: Title; Status (proposed | accepted | rejected | deprecated | superseded by <id>); Date; Context; Decision; Considered Options (with pros/cons); Consequences; References.
- One ADR per decision; do not rewrite history—create a new ADR to supersede previous ones and cross-link.

Process:
- Create an ADR for decisions with lasting architectural impact (runtime, data, security, compliance, cost, operability, team/process affecting architecture).
- Propose via pull request; discuss asynchronously; approve with standard review rules. Record dissent and alternatives considered.
- Update Status upon decision; tag releases to snapshot ADR state when relevant.
- Revisit ADRs during major milestones; use “superseded” to evolve safely.

Tooling (optional):
- adr-tools or equivalent scripts to init, list, and supersede ADRs.
- CI check to ensure each ADR has required sections and links are valid.

Expected outcomes:
- Durable decision history, improved governance and audits, faster onboarding, and clearer rationale for future changes.

## Decision:
* Use a mature, extensible OSS editor framework as the core: ProseMirror
* Model transcript as a schema-driven document:
  - Paragraph/turn nodes for speaker segments (attrs: speaker id/name, start/end)
  - Token/word nodes or inline marks with start/end timestamps and confidence
  - Optional annotation marks (entities, corrections, comments)
* Maintain timing integrity via transaction guards and schema constraints (e.g., prohibit edits that orphan or reorder time-aligned tokens without corresponding time updates)
* Implement features via plugins, not schema mutations:
  - Media sync plugin drives a playback cursor and live word highlight via decorations
  - Selection↔time mapping plugin (caret/range to timestamp and vice versa)
  - Search, diff, spellcheck, and annotation plugins as decorations/marks
  - Undo/redo integrated with timing-aware constraints
* Use decorations for ephemeral UI (playback position, search hits) to avoid document churn; throttle decoration updates for performance during playback
* Provide import/export converters for WebVTT/SRT/JSON; store canonical doc as ProseMirror JSON with timing attrs
* Expose a typed API surface:
  - Commands (jumpToTime, splitTurn, retimeRange, mergeTokens, assignSpeaker)
  - Events (onTimeChange, onSelectionTime, onAnnotation)
  - Read-only selectors (getWordAtTime, getRangeTimestamps)
* Integrate with React via prosemirror-view; keep editor state internal, expose controlled props for media time and external annotations
* Performance: incremental updates only, avoid full re-renders; virtualize very long documents; debounce expensive plugins; cap decoration density
* Accessibility: ARIA roles, keyboard-first commands for navigation/editing, screen-reader-friendly rendering of timing metadata
* Rejected alternatives: Slate/Quill/Draft.js due to weaker schema guarantees and/or plugin model for complex time-aligned text; TipTap acceptable as a thin ProseMirror wrapper but core remains ProseMirror

## Decision:
We will pin explicit AMI IDs in Terraform for long‑lived and manually curated workloads to prevent unexpected instance replacement. AMI IDs will be provided via variables (per environment) and stored in version-controlled configuration, requiring an intentional change (PR/release) to update. Automated or ephemeral workloads may continue to use the aws_ami data source to select the latest image within a major version.

For pinned stacks:
- AMI upgrades will be executed through a planned change process, including testing and rollout steps, to accommodate required manual deployment steps.
- We will document the current AMI lineage and update cadence, and track required post-AMI actions.
- Optionally, we may reference AMI IDs via SSM Parameter Store aliases to centralize updates while still gating changes via code.

This approach minimizes drift and surprise replacements in legacy deployments while retaining flexibility to auto-track latest images where appropriate.

We will implement a lightweight, embedded rule engine tailored for our Data Process pipeline, using a compact JSON-based expression DSL parsed with ANTLR (inspired by JsonQuery.g4). The engine will support the listed operators (eq/ne/lt/le/gt/ge/co/sw/ew/in/pr/not) with clear null/empty semantics and short-circuit boolean evaluation.

Key aspects:
- Parsing and validation: ANTLR grammar -> AST -> typed predicate tree; compile-time validation against a provided schema (field existence and types).
- Execution: stateless, side-effect-free evaluators over immutable inputs; deterministic results; thread-safe and scalable via pure functions.
- Performance: rule pre-compilation and caching; constant folding; optional indexable predicates for common fields; vectorized evaluation hooks for batch processing.
- Extensibility: pluggable functions and operators with namespacing; support for date/time, numeric coercions, and locale-aware string options.
- Data access: dot-path navigation for nested fields and arrays, with safe traversal and “present (pr)” semantics; consistent “in” behavior for scalars/collections.
- Operations: versioned rule definitions, JSON schema for rule payloads, linting/validation CLI, metrics and tracing, and feature flags for staged rollouts.
- Security: sandboxed evaluation (no reflection or arbitrary code execution), resource limits, and size guards on expressions.

We will reassess adopting a full BRMS (e.g., Drools) if we require forward-chaining, complex temporal reasoning, stateful sessions, or authoring tools beyond our DSL.

## Decision:
Limit Elasticsearch usage to content requiring full‑text search and migrate non‑search document types to a transactional datastore (PostgreSQL). For the remaining search content, adopt the ES 6+ “one type per index” model with explicit index-per-entity design, managed via aliases and templates.

Key points:
- Introduce a persistence/search abstraction: a SearchRepository for full‑text documents (backed by Elasticsearch) and a DataRepository for non‑search documents (backed by PostgreSQL). This decouples storage concerns and prevents accidental expansion of ES usage.
- For Elasticsearch:
  - Create one index per document kind that needs search, with versioned index names (e.g., doc-vN), write aliases, and read aliases to enable zero‑downtime reindex/migrations.
  - Use index templates and ILM to standardize mappings/settings and manage retention.
  - Prefer keyword fields over analyzed text where full‑text is not needed, to reduce index size and complexity.
- For non‑full‑text entities:
  - Store in PostgreSQL with appropriate schema, constraints, and secondary indexes; expose query needs via SQL and, if needed, materialized views.
  - Use application-level joins between ES hits and relational metadata when necessary.
- Migration:
  - Identify non‑search types and backfill to PostgreSQL.
  - Incrementally deprecate corresponding ES types/indices, switching reads via feature flags and aliases.
  - Reindex remaining ES data into new per‑type indices.

This reduces operational overhead from many ES indices, aligns with ES 6 constraints, improves data integrity for non‑search entities, and provides a clear lifecycle for search indexes.

## Decision:
We will promote immutable build artifacts between environments using S3 as the single source of truth, avoiding rebuilds.

- Bucket strategy: Use one KMS-encrypted, versioned S3 bucket (e.g., govuk-artifacts) with block public access and object ownership enforced by bucket owner. Artifacts are stored once and referenced by immutable coordinates.
- Object layout: app/{app}/{commitSHA or semver}/{build}/{platform}.zip with sidecar files: SHA256SUMS, manifest.json (build metadata, provenance), and optional SBOM.
- Immutability: Overwrites are denied via bucket policy; object-lock (governance) may be enabled where available.
- Promotion model: A Jenkins “Promote_Artifact” job promotes by either:
  - Copying the immutable object to environment aliases: env/{environment}/app/{app}/{build}/..., and/or
  - Updating a small pointer file env/{environment}/app/{app}/current.json that references the canonical object key and checksum.
  Consumers use current.json or an explicit build coordinate; both resolve to the same object.
- Access control:
  - CI build role: write to app/* only.
  - Promotion role: read app/* and write env/* (and current.json).
  - Deployment roles (per environment): read-only for env/{their-env}/** and read-only access to referenced canonical keys.
- Integrity: Deploy steps verify SHA256 before use; checksum must match manifest.
- Retention: Lifecycle policies retain manifests indefinitely, keep last N artifact versions, and expire unpromoted artifacts after M days.
- Traceability: All uploads include commit SHA, build number, source repo, and timestamps in manifest and S3 object tags; CloudTrail/S3 access logs enabled.

This ensures deployments in Staging (and beyond) use exactly the artifact produced in Integration, with controlled, auditable, and reversible promotions.

## Decision:
Adopt an A/B, image-based update strategy with an immutable root filesystem and controlled persistence.

- Root filesystem will be built as a read-only image (e.g., SquashFS) and deployed in two slots (rootfsA/rootfsB). Updates replace the inactive slot with a new, signed, checksummed image, ensuring atomic, whole-system upgrades.

- Bootloader (e.g., U-Boot/EFI) will be configured for slot selection with one-shot boot to the updated slot. A health-check mechanism (watchdog + service readiness checks) will promote the new slot to “good” on success; otherwise, automatic rollback to the previous “good” slot occurs, satisfying the requirement to reboot into a stable version after failed updates.

- Persistence will be provided via a dedicated read-write data partition. To balance security and maintainability:
  - Use directory-scoped overlayfs only for approved paths that require runtime/user modifications (e.g., /etc, selected /var/lib subtrees), with upper/worker dirs in the data partition.
  - Use explicit bind mounts for specific files or directories where strict control is desired (e.g., device identity, network credentials, licensing keys).
  - All other paths remain read-only, minimizing drift and attack surface.

- No per-package updates are supported on the immutable rootfs; all changes ship in the next image, ensuring consistency and simplifying support.

- Update artifacts must be cryptographically signed; the updater verifies signatures and checksums before activation. Power-loss-safe installation is required (write to inactive slot only, durable metadata update at the end).

- Bootloader environment and rollback counters will be stored separately from the rootfs to survive slot switches. Logs essential for diagnostics will persist under the data partition (e.g., /data/log) with symlinks/bind mounts as needed.

This design delivers atomic, secure, and reversible system-wide updates with an immutable base, while providing narrowly scoped, durable configuration/state across releases.

## Decision:
Consume publishing events from the Publishing API via RabbitMQ and delegate document updates to Sidekiq workers.

- Bind a durable, auto-recovering queue to the Publishing API exchanges/topics relevant to content and link changes.
- Use a single consumer process (Bunny) with controlled prefetch for back-pressure and concurrency. Acknowledge messages only after successfully enqueuing a Sidekiq job (at-least-once delivery).
- Enqueue idempotent Sidekiq jobs that fetch the canonical document state from the Publishing API and update the search index.
- Use Sidekiq for concurrency, retry logic (exponential backoff), and operational visibility (failure tracking, dead job queues).
- Configure a RabbitMQ dead-letter queue for poison/invalid messages and alert on DLQ growth.
- Standardize message validation and deduplication by using message IDs/version numbers; ignore stale events.
- Keep indexing logic exclusively in workers to simplify the consumer and allow horizontal scaling independently of queue consumption.
- Provide metrics on consumer lag, Sidekiq queue depth, retry counts, and indexing latency.

This approach simplifies ingestion by treating RabbitMQ as the event transport and Sidekiq as the execution engine, meeting requirements for concurrency, failure tracking, and retries while aligning with existing team practices.

## Decision:
We will build a central Cloud Platform Dashboard that aggregates metadata and provides deep links to underlying services rather than duplicating their functionality.

Key aspects:
- Scope: onboarding and SSO setup workflows with existing identity providers; surfaced security posture with links to GuardDuty and Security Hub findings; links to operational tooling (e.g., Kubernetes console, Kibana, Prometheus); account/cluster/namespace inventory and ownership mapping.
- Access control: authenticate via our chosen IdP (initially GitHub) and authorize with platform RBAC derived from GitHub org/team membership; all actions read-only with contextual deep links to perform changes in source systems.
- Architecture: a stateless web frontend (SPA) served via CloudFront/S3 with a lightweight API (API Gateway + Lambda) that aggregates data from AWS Organizations, IAM Identity Center, Security Hub, GuardDuty, EKS, and other platform APIs; no customer data stored—cache ephemeral metadata only.
- Security and compliance: least-privilege read roles, end-to-end TLS, audit logging of dashboard access and link clicks, and explicit scopes for each integration.
- Operability: feature-flagged modules, modular “card” pattern for new integrations, and CI/CD with infrastructure-as-code to iterate safely.

## Decision:
- Chosen Alternative: Spring Framework (Spring Web via Spring Boot)
- Rationale:
  - Mature, widely adopted ecosystem with strong community support, making maintenance and onboarding easier.
  - First-class support for REST (request mapping, content negotiation, validation, exception handling) with clear conventions.
  - Seamless integration with Spring Security, Actuator, Micrometer, and persistence stacks for future needs as the API evolves.
  - Excellent testing support (MockMvc/WebTestClient) and structured application layering using dependency injection.
  - Easy API documentation via springdoc-openapi (OpenAPI 3), enabling automated, up-to-date Swagger UI.
  - Production-ready features out-of-the-box (health checks, metrics, configuration management).
- Trade-offs:
  - Higher footprint than Spark Java and steeper learning curve for micro use-cases, but offset by long-term maintainability and scalability.
- Implementation Notes:
  - Use spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-validation, springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui, and spring-boot-starter-actuator.
  - Define REST controllers with @RestController, DTOs with Bean Validation annotations, and global exception handling via @ControllerAdvice.

## Decision:
- Treat RelayState as an opaque, optional value supplied by the RP. We will not inspect, parse, or rely on it for any control flow or security decisions.
- If present on the inbound request, persist it server-side bound to the RP entityID and the request ID, and return it unchanged to the same RP in the response.
- Do not generate RelayState ourselves. If absent, proceed without it.
- Enforce defensible limits and hygiene:
  - Maximum length 80 bytes to align with SAML guidance; reject requests exceeding the limit with a clear error. Allow only printable ASCII.
  - Do not log the value; log only presence and length.
  - Sanitize at log/metrics boundaries to prevent injection.
- Integrity:
  - For HTTP-Redirect binding, require that signature verification covers RelayState as per spec; fail verification if it does not.
  - For POST binding (where RelayState is not covered by a binding-level signature), rely on the server-side binding to the request/session to prevent swapping.
- Privacy and security:
  - Treat RelayState as potentially sensitive RP data; never echo it to other parties or include it in error pages.
  - Document to RPs that RelayState must not contain PII or secrets and must not be used to drive redirects without RP-side validation.
- Backward compatibility: This pass-through approach maintains existing RP usage while keeping the service provider agnostic to RelayState semantics.

## Decision:
We will implement option 4: send a single notification email per submission that contains a secure, time-limited link to download all uploaded files at once.

Implementation notes:
- On submission, we will bundle all uploaded files into a single archive (e.g., ZIP) stored in S3 and generate a presigned, expiring URL.
- The email will include no attachments, only the download link, eliminating the SES 10MB constraint and reducing email noise.
- Links will be short-lived and scoped to the target files; access will be protected via signed URLs and server-side authorization checks prior to URL issuance.
- For very large submissions, we’ll stream/pack server-side and set appropriate lifecycle policies for temporary bundles.
- If bundling fails, we’ll retry and fall back to listing individual secure links in the email as a temporary measure.
- Longer-term, we may add an admin UI (option 3) for richer retrieval workflows.

## Decision:
Use the existing postcodes.io service to resolve both full postcodes and outcodes to latitude/longitude. For full postcodes, query the /postcodes/{postcode} endpoint to obtain precise coordinates; for outcodes, use the /outcodes/{outcode} endpoint and use the centroid coordinates returned. Normalize and validate user input (strip whitespace, uppercase, standard UK postcode format) prior to lookup; reject clearly invalid formats early.

Implement a thin geocoding adapter that abstracts the lookup provider to allow future replacement if required. Add short-term caching (e.g., 24–48 hours) of results to reduce latency and external calls, and handle rate limiting, network errors, and unknown postcodes with graceful fallbacks and clear user messaging. Store only coordinates and normalized codes; do not persist PII.

## Decision:
Adopt React with TypeScript as the primary JavaScript UI framework for building responsive, component-based web applications. We will scaffold projects with Vite for fast builds/dev experience, use React Router for client-side routing, and standardize on Redux Toolkit (or React Query for server state) for predictable state management. For projects requiring SEO-friendly rendering, internationalization at build-time, or edge delivery, we will use Next.js atop React to provide SSR/SSG/ISR as needed.

This choice balances flexibility and ecosystem maturity: React’s stable component model, broad community support, extensive library availability (forms, charts, accessibility), and first-class TypeScript support reduce delivery risk and improve maintainability. It enables progressive enhancement, responsive design, and accessibility best practices, while remaining framework-agnostic enough to integrate with existing services and design systems. The large talent pool and well-documented patterns lower onboarding and long-term maintenance costs.

Testing will use Jest and React Testing Library for unit/integration tests, with Cypress for end-to-end flows. Styling will default to CSS Modules or Tailwind CSS where appropriate, guided by the design system. This decision standardizes our frontend stack, accelerates development of device-responsive UIs, and preserves adaptability for future requirements.

Adopt GitLab CI/CD to replace Jenkins for this project and begin immediate migration of existing pipelines into a .gitlab-ci.yml, targeting full Jenkins decommission by year-end.

Implementation approach:
- Define standardized stages (lint, build, test, security, package, deploy) in .gitlab-ci.yml, aligning with patterns from basket, nucleus, and snippets-service.
- Use GitLab Runners (Kubernetes executor preferred) to execute jobs; leverage GitLab-managed runners initially, then migrate to self-hosted if needed for performance or network locality.
- Integrate with Kubernetes via GitLab’s Deployments/Environments; use Review Apps for feature branches where applicable.
- Store container images in GitLab Container Registry; use tag-based pipelines for releases and environment-specific deploy jobs with manual approvals and protected environments.
- Migrate secrets and credentials from Jenkins to GitLab CI variables and Vault integration where available; remove secrets from repos.
- Implement required checks: MR pipelines, status checks, code coverage, SAST/Dependency scanning, and artifact retention for build outputs.
- Set branch protections and approval rules to enforce quality gates before deploy.
- Plan a phased cutover: run Jenkins and GitLab in parallel, validate parity, then disable Jenkins jobs and archive Jenkins config before shutdown.

This leverages existing GitLab CI expertise, reduces operational overhead, and consolidates CI/CD tooling across projects.

## Decision:
We will remove jQuery 1.x and migrate the API catalogue to jQuery 3.x (latest stable, currently 3.7.x). Where feasible, we will eliminate jQuery usage entirely in favor of native DOM APIs to reduce dependency surface; remaining required jQuery usage will be updated to 3.x-compatible patterns.

Implementation approach:
- Replace the bundled 1.x artifact with a pinned 3.x version (exact version pin), using the “slim” build unless AJAX/Effects are required.
- Use jquery-migrate during the transition to identify deprecated APIs, then remove migrate before release.
- Update or replace any jQuery plugins to 3.x-compatible versions; remove unmaintained plugins.
- Refactor code paths relying on removed/deprecated APIs (e.g., .bind/.delegate, event shortcuts, .size).
- Run full regression and accessibility tests across supported browsers; provide polyfills only where necessary.

Security and supply-chain controls:
- Serve jQuery from our assets (not a third-party CDN) with Subresource Integrity (SRI) and strict Content Security Policy (CSP).
- Lock dependency versions via package-lock and renovate/dependabot alerts to track future advisories.
- Add Snyk/GitHub Advisory scanning to CI and fail builds on known jQuery/plugin vulnerabilities.

Operational notes:
- Document breaking changes and migration notes in the repo.
- Remove all references to the 1.x artifact and prohibit it via tooling (e.g., lint rule or CI check).
- Target completion in a single release; if phased, gate behind an environment flag and remove the flag post-verification.

## Decision:
We will use a standardized, audience-aware communication package for every release:

- Primary artifact: Release Notes in Markdown following “Keep a Changelog” categories (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security) and Semantic Versioning. Titles use imperative mood; entries are concise, user-focused, and link to PRs/issues.
- Summary tiers:
  1) Executive summary (3–7 bullets) highlighting impact and actions.
  2) Developer details in categorized sections.
  3) Upgrade/migration guidance with breaking-change callouts and step-by-step actions.
- Tone and style: plain English, active voice, inclusive language, no marketing fluff. Include code snippets only when they clarify usage. Use consistent terminology and version tags.
- Channels and formats:
  - GitHub/GitLab Release page: canonical Release Notes.
  - CHANGELOG.md in repo: synchronized with releases.
  - Blog post for major releases (x.0 or breaking changes) with narrative context.
  - Mailing list/newsletter and social media for headline summary linking back to canonical notes.
  - RSS/Atom feed where supported.
- Localization: English is the source; community translations may follow after release (non-blocking).
- Timing: Publish Release Notes concurrently with tagging. For patch/minor releases, brief notes; for major releases, include deprecation timelines and migration guide.
- Ownership and workflow: Release Manager owns content; contributors provide PR titles and labels to feed automation. CI validates changelog entries, formatting, and links.
- Templates and automation: Adopt a release-notes template with required sections (Summary, Highlights, Breaking Changes, Deprecations, Upgrade Notes, Changes by Category, Known Issues, Contributors, Thanks). Automate population from PR labels/titles; manual curation allowed for clarity.

This approach ensures consistency, minimal manual work, and clear communication tailored to both end users and developers.

## Decision:
Adopt a template-driven RSpec setup and do not invoke rails generate rspec:install during project generation.

- Ship a curated, opinionated set of RSpec configuration files (spec_helper.rb, rails_helper.rb, .rspec, support/, and standard directory structure) directly from the template to ensure deterministic, fast, and CI-friendly setup.
- Avoid executing Thor’s generate("rspec:install") to prevent intermittent hangs caused by Spring and to keep the generator idempotent and non-interactive.
- Provide an optional, documented maintenance script (or rake task) that can:
  - stop Spring (spring stop),
  - run rails generate rspec:install,
  - reconcile diffs against our curated config,
  for teams wishing to re-sync with upstream rspec-rails defaults.
- Revisit replacing the template copy with a guarded generator invocation only if we can guarantee reliability across environments (e.g., verified spring stop and timeouts) and preserve our customizations.

## Decision:
Use MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records), version 2.1.2, for documenting architectural decisions.

- Location: docs/adr/
- File naming: YYYY-MM-DD-<short-title>.md; keep a simple incremental index in an index.md
- Format: Markdown using the official MADR 2.1.2 template (context, decision, status, consequences, pros/cons, options, references)
- Status lifecycle: proposed → accepted/rejected → superseded (with cross-links)
- Scope: One decision per ADR; keep small and focused; reference related ADRs and issues/PRs
- Numbering: Optional numeric prefixes are discouraged; rely on dates and index.md ordering
- Review process: Open a PR for each ADR; require at least one reviewer from architecture owners; record review outcomes in the ADR’s Status
- Change policy: Do not edit accepted ADRs except for fixes and links; create a new ADR to change a decision and mark the old one superseded
- Discoverability: Link index.md from README; tag PRs with “adr”; include ADR ID/link in commit messages impacting architecture
- Tooling: Plain Git plus Markdown; optional adr-tools or adr-log allowed but not required
- Templates: Store template at docs/adr/_template.md; bootstrap new ADRs by copying template
- Cross-project consistency: Align with organization-wide conventions where applicable; prefer reuse of shared glossary and decision taxonomy
- Automation: Optional CI check to ensure ADR folder structure and required sections exist

Rationale: MADR is lightweight, readable, and widely adopted; it balances structure with agility and supports long-term maintainability and traceability.

## Decision:
For flattened JSON-LD emission of self-encoded dialects, we will collapse the instance document and the encoded dialect domain element into a single node keyed by the shared @id. The emitter will produce the union of triples for that @id, ensuring only one flattened node is rendered.

Precedence and conflict resolution:
- All @type values from both sources are merged.
- On property collisions, the dialect domain element’s vocabulary takes precedence. Document-specific metadata is retained under annotations/meta namespaces (e.g., amf/source maps) to avoid overwriting semantic fields.
- If a collision cannot be safely merged (incompatible ranges/cardinalities), the document-level value is emitted under a disambiguated meta property and a diagnostic is recorded.

Implications:
- Consumers get a single canonical resource for the self-encoded entity, consistent with the “same resource” semantics of shared IDs.
- No additional synthetic IDs or JSON-LD links are introduced.
- Expanded emission remains unchanged; only the flattened emitter applies the merge-by-@id rule.
- Validation will verify that self-encoded documents do not introduce irreconcilable conflicts; otherwise emission fails fast with a clear error.

This maintains the one-node-per-ID constraint of flattened JSON-LD while preserving both semantic content and document metadata for self-encoded dialects.

## Decision:
We will adopt OAuth 2.0 for API authentication and authorization, delegating authentication to a dedicated Authorization Server. Access tokens will be issued by the Authorization Server and presented with each request. Resource Servers will validate tokens without contacting the Authorization Server in the common case by verifying signed JWT access tokens using the issuer’s JWKS (rotated and cached), checking issuer, audience, expiry, and required scopes/claims. For scenarios requiring immediate revocation awareness or heightened risk, we may use opaque reference tokens with RFC 7662 token introspection.

Authorization will be enforced via scopes and fine-grained claims embedded in tokens (e.g., roles, tenant, permissions). Access tokens will be short-lived; refresh tokens will be used where needed, with rotation and reuse detection. We will avoid fixed shared secrets in favor of asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256) to enable distributed verification and key rotation without service redeployments.

Where user identity is required, we will layer OpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2.0 for standardized user info and ID tokens; user MFA and risk-based policies will be enforced by the Authorization Server. All token transport will use TLS, and tokens will not be stored in URLs or logs. This design provides stronger security, scalability, and operational flexibility than fixed secrets, while supporting distributed validation.

## Decision:
Consolidate on a single configuration mechanism: an external YAML configuration file with sane defaults. We will remove the “two ways” approach (environment-variable-driven config + embedded resource file) and deprecate the in-jar config and env-var key/value mapping.

Rationale:
- Simplicity and predictability: one authoritative source of configuration.
- Reduced cognitive load and fewer failure modes from divergent behaviors.
- Easier documentation, testing, and support.

Implementation details:
- The application will load configuration from an external YAML file.
- If no path is provided via command-line, we will search conventional locations (e.g., ./config/application.yml then ./application.yml) to avoid requiring arguments in constrained runtimes.
- No per-key environment variable overrides will be supported.
- The embedded default config file inside the jar will be removed; only code-level defaults remain for non-critical settings.
- Provide a migration guide and a deprecation period for teams currently using env-var configuration, with clear error messages if deprecated mechanisms are detected.

This decision eliminates the need to rely on platform-specific behaviors (e.g., Cloud Foundry buildpack flags) while maintaining a single, clear configuration path.

## Decision:
Provide a mobile “app version” by wrapping the existing React web app in a lightweight native WebView container (Capacitor), while keeping a single codebase. Introduce an appMode feature flag (derivable from query params, env config, or native bridge) that enables app-specific UI and behavior:

- Hide the application header when appMode=true.
- Replace the “Doe een melding” button with “Sluit venster”; in appMode it calls the native bridge to close the WebView (Capacitor App.exitApp or a host-provided close handler). On the web (appMode=false), it gracefully falls back to window.history.back or a configurable redirect.
- Support initializing the map center via:
  - Query parameters (?lat=…&lng=…&zoom=…) for deep links, and
  - A native-to-web message (Capacitor bridge event) to set or update center after load.

Implementation notes:
- Add a central AppConfig provider to read appMode and initial map params from URL, env, and native bridge.
- Gate UI changes by appMode with minimal conditional rendering; no forked codebase.
- Ensure permissions (geolocation) and analytics work in both contexts; feature parity maintained.
- Ship the same production build to web and the Capacitor shell to minimize divergence.
- Document the bridge API (closeWindow, setMapCenter) and release procedures for iOS/Android stores.

This approach meets the requirements without rewriting the frontend natively and allows incremental enhancements.

## Decision:
Adopt Trunk-Based Development with short‑lived feature branches, protected main, and tagged releases.

- Branches
  - main: single source of truth; always releasable; protected (required reviews, status checks, no direct pushes).
  - feature/*: short‑lived branches for changes; created from latest main; deleted after merge.
  - release/*-<major>.<minor>: optional, time‑boxed stabilization branches for coordinated releases; created only when needed; accept only bugfix/chore docs; deleted after release.
  - hotfix/*: emergency fixes branched from the release tag (or main if no branch); merged back into main (and active release branch if present).

- Flow
  - Start work from up‑to‑date main; rebase feature branches frequently to minimize drift.
  - Open PRs early; require at least 1–2 approvals, green CI, and passing security checks.
  - Merge strategy: squash‑merge to keep a linear main history; conventional commit PR titles.
  - Tag releases from main (or release branch) with annotated semantic version tags (vX.Y.Z). CI/CD uses tags to build immutable artifacts.

- Stability and environments
  - main deploys automatically to staging; tagged releases deploy to production.
  - Only critical fixes bypass (hotfix/*), still via PR with expedited review.

- Naming conventions
  - feature/<area>/<short-desc>, bugfix/<issue-id>-<short-desc>, hotfix/<short-desc>, release/<major>.<minor>.
  - Commit messages follow Conventional Commits to drive changelogs and semantic versioning.

- Policy
  - No direct commits to main; force pushes disabled everywhere; branch lifetimes < 5 days when possible.
  - Long‑running work uses feature flags; incomplete code must be behind flags to keep main releasable.
  - Backports are performed via cherry‑pick from main into active release/* branches when applicable.

This strategy prioritizes fast integration, clear traceability via tags, minimal branch sprawl, and a continuously releasable trunk.

## Decision:
Deprecate and remove the Clucy index and its pipeline. As per ADR-007, Elasticsearch is the sole search backend; maintaining the Clucy index offers no functional value and imposes a >1 hour processing cost that blocks deployments, creates operational risk, and consumes resources.

Actions:
- Disable all Clucy-related jobs (cron, CI, Sidekiq, Jenkins) and remove associated rake tasks and scripts.
- Delete Clucy indexing code paths and configuration, including any dual-write logic and health checks.
- Update documentation, runbooks, and dashboards to remove Clucy references.
- Migrate any residual consumers to Elasticsearch aliases/endpoints; add alerts to detect unintended access to Clucy artifacts.
- Perform a one-time cleanup of any persisted Clucy indexes/artifacts.

Rollout:
- Ship as a feature flag removal with a short deprecation window if needed; otherwise remove immediately given no active consumers per ADR-007.
- Monitor Elasticsearch indexing SLOs and search latency to confirm no regressions.

## Decision:
Adopt NHS.UK Frontend as the baseline design system and ship a precompiled global stylesheet (app.css) plus Sass sources that expose NHS.UK variables, mixins, and component partials. The prototype kit will include a curated set of generic, reusable styles and utilities (e.g., spacing, layout grid, typography, visibility, alignment, width helpers) to accelerate common prototyping needs while ensuring visual consistency with NHS services.

By default, all prototypes load the standard NHS.UK styles and the kit’s utilities via a single import in the base layout. Teams can extend or override styles by adding rules in app.scss, which compiles on build/watch, while keeping upstream NHS.UK Frontend components intact. Custom utilities must be namespaced (e.g., .nhsuk-proto-*) to avoid clashes and to make removal easy when moving to production services.

We will:
- Pin and version NHS.UK Frontend as a dependency and expose a simple upgrade path.
- Provide documented utility classes and example patterns to encourage consistent use.
- Compile Sass with source maps in development and minified CSS in production.

This approach speeds prototyping, reduces bespoke styling, and maintains a consistent look-and-feel aligned with NHS design standards.

## Decision:
- Adopt Backstage’s core entity model as the standardized taxonomy:
  - Domain, System, Component (service|library|website|tool), API (OpenAPI|AsyncAPI|GraphQL), Resource, Group, User, Location, Template.
- Define mandatory relations and constraints:
  - Component: ownedBy -> Group (required), partOf -> System (required), providesApis/consumesApis (optional), dependsOn -> Resource (optional).
  - API: ownedBy -> Group (required), definition via OpenAPI/AsyncAPI/GraphQL source, system (optional).
  - Resource: ownedBy -> Group (required), dependency targets from Components only.
  - System: partOf -> Domain (required), ownedBy -> Group (optional).
  - Domain: ownedBy -> Group (required).
  - Group hierarchy allowed (childOf -> Group). User membership required in at least one Group.
- Standardize metadata conventions:
  - Naming: namespace mandatory; name in kebab-case; stable IDs; no mutable renames without migration PR.
  - Lifecycle: experimental | production | deprecated (required for Components/APIs/Systems).
  - Tags: language, runtime, tier, data-classification (recommended).
  - Annotations: git repo URL, runtime env links, oncall (PagerDuty), incident channel (Slack), error tracking (Sentry), cloud IDs (AWS ARN), ADR link.
- Single source of truth:
  - All entities declared as YAML (catalog-info.yaml) in the owning repo; multi-entity files allowed.
  - Discovery via Locations (monorepo and org-wide) with explicit ownership.
- Quality gates and governance:
  - JSON Schema validation + linting in CI; PR checks block on violations.
  - Golden path scaffolder Templates for each kind; templates enforce required fields/relations.
  - Custom kinds require RFC and plugin alignment; prefer annotations over new kinds.
- Versioning and change management:
  - Backwards-compatible changes allowed; breaking relation/name changes require migration plan and deprecation window.
- Plugin alignment:
  - Plugins must use the standardized kinds/annotations and relations; cross-plugin contracts documented and versioned.

We will standardize on TypeScript for client-side development.

- All new browser-facing projects and modules will be authored in TypeScript with strict type-checking enabled and type-checks enforced in CI.
- We will prefer TypeScript over Flow; no new Flow code will be introduced. Existing Flow code may remain, but will be migrated to TypeScript opportunistically (when significantly modified) rather than via a big-bang rewrite.
- Build toolchain: use Babel + @babel/preset-typescript for application bundles where we already rely on Babel, and use tsc (or tsup/esbuild with type-check via tsc --noEmit) for libraries and packages where emitting declaration files is required.
- Coding standards: adopt shared tsconfig (strict, noImplicitAny, exactOptionalPropertyTypes), eslint with TypeScript plugin, and precommit type-check + lint hooks.
- Documentation and API design: use TypeScript interfaces/types to formally model domain and public APIs; ship .d.ts declarations for any published packages.
- Developer experience: provide a starter template, IDE settings, and a short internal guide to lower the onboarding curve; pair on first PRs to spread patterns.
- Exceptions: plain JavaScript may be used in small throwaway scripts or prototypes with explicit approval; otherwise TypeScript is the default.

This choice improves correctness, maintainability, and IDE-assisted productivity, aligns with industry adoption, and leverages internal experience from prior TypeScript projects.

## Decision:
- Use AWS RDS PostgreSQL for all non-local environments; use a Dockerised PostgreSQL (same major version as RDS) for local development and CI. Do not spin up a local RDS instance.
- Introduce a dedicated data-access layer:
  - Use node-postgres (pg) with Knex as the SQL query builder and migration tool.
  - Implement repository/service patterns so routes/controllers no longer manipulate JSON directly.
  - Keep SQL in the data layer; expose domain models/DTOs to the rest of the app.
- Manage schema changes with versioned Knex migrations:
  - Each migration includes explicit up and down steps.
  - Enforce backward-compatible, zero-downtime patterns (additive changes first; dual-read/write where needed; cleanup in a follow-up migration).
  - Apply migrations automatically in CI for integration tests and via the deployment pipeline for each environment.
- Seed data to replace sample JSON:
  - Create deterministic seed scripts that import existing sample JSON and map it to the relational schema (including ID mapping).
  - Provide separate dev/test seed sets; no automatic seeding in staging/production.
  - Include a command suite: db:migrate, db:rollback, db:seed, db:reset.
- Testing:
  - Use Testcontainers (or docker-compose) to run PostgreSQL in CI/local for integration tests.
  - Prefer unit tests on pure services with repositories mocked; use integration tests for query correctness and migrations.

## Decision:
- Eliminate the ./server (and associated ./client) directories and place the Go server at the repository root using a standard Go project layout.
- Require the repository to be checked out within the standard GOPATH at $GOPATH/src/github.com/transcom/mymove to align with Go tooling and dependency resolution.
- Adopt conventional Go structure:
  - cmd/mymove (or equivalent) for main entrypoints/binaries
  - internal/ for non-exported packages
  - pkg/ for shared libraries
  - migrations/, config/, assets/, etc. colocated at repo root as needed
- Update imports, builds, and tests to reflect the new paths; remove any Makefile logic that artificially sets GOPATH to ./server.
- Consolidate build and run workflows so that go build, go test, and go run work from the repository root with minimal indirection.
- Update developer documentation, CI, and code generation paths to the new layout, ensuring tools and scripts assume the repository root as the module/project root.
- This simplifies local development, reduces path-related friction, and aligns the project with common Go ecosystem conventions.

## Decision:
Relying Parties must perform strict SAML validation and fail closed. At minimum, an RP must:

- Verify XML Signature over the Assertion using the signing key published in metadata (cert pinning, valid chain, non-deprecated algorithms).
- Verify Issuer equals the MSA entity ID from metadata.
- Enforce SubjectConfirmation bearer rules:
  - Recipient exactly matches the RP ACS endpoint used (including scheme/host/path/port).
  - InResponseTo matches the RP’s original AuthnRequest ID.
  - NotOnOrAfter is in the future allowing a small, configurable clock skew; reject expired.
- Validate Conditions:
  - AudienceRestriction includes the RP entity ID.
  - Assertion lifetime does not exceed policy; reject assertions outside acceptable window.
- Validate AuthnContextClassRef meets or exceeds the requested level.
- Validate NameID format (persistent) and handle PID per RP contract.
- Enforce replay protection by recording Assertion ID (and optionally InResponseTo) and rejecting duplicates within a retention window.
- Accept only assertions delivered over TLS with hostname verification; disallow redirects or endpoints not declared in metadata.
- Reject unsigned or partially signed assertions and unsigned/enveloped reference manipulation.
- Prefer a single assertion in the Response; if multiple are present, select only the one that satisfies all checks, otherwise reject.

We will provide:
- RP validation libraries/reference middleware implementing the above.
- Conformance tests and a certification checklist gating RP onboarding.
- Operational guidance for clock skew, key rotation, and monitoring of validation failures.

Non-compliant RPs will be blocked from production until they pass conformance.

## Decision:
We will adopt TypeScript across the monorepo and centralize linting via ESLint + @typescript-eslint, replacing ad-hoc ESLint overrides and avoiding TSLint.

- Compiler: Use tsc as the compiler and type-checker. Target Node’s LTS (e.g., ES2020), module=CommonJS for server packages, “strict”: true. This removes the need for manual "use strict".
- Gradual migration: Enable allowJs and (where helpful) checkJs to permit JS files with JSDoc types during transition. Migrate package-by-package; mixed JS/TS is allowed but bounded with clear ownership per package and no cross-package circularities.
- Project structure: Use a shared base tsconfig at the repo root with package-level tsconfig extensions. Use composite, incremental, and project references for fast builds and clean dependency graphs.
- Linting: Standardize on a root ESLint config extending @typescript-eslint recommended rules, with per-package overrides only when necessary. Use types-aware rules for .ts/.tsx and JS-compatible rules for .js during migration.
- Tooling: Use ts-node (or tsx) in development/test only; produce compiled JS in build for runtime. Provide scripts to copy non-TS assets and generate type declarations where needed.
- Performance: Enable incremental builds, isolatedModules (where appropriate), and leverage build caching in CI to mitigate build times.
- Coding guidelines: Require explicit types on public interfaces and module boundaries; allow type inference internally to limit verbosity. Favor pragmatic typing (don’t over-model) to reduce maintenance overhead.
- Cypress and tooling: Configure Cypress and VS Code to consume the shared tsconfig for consistent IntelliSense and type-checking.

This standardizes strictness, improves maintainability and developer experience, and resolves the ESLint/strict-mode friction, while providing a controlled, incremental path to adoption.

## Decision:
Introduce an optional Zero Downtime Deployment (ZDD) mode for the End-To-End Tests stage of the SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Pipeline. When enabled, the pipeline will perform blue/green (or rolling, per platform capabilities) deployments to SCP Neo / SCP Cloud Foundry so the currently running instance remains available until the new version is healthy, routes are switched, and the old instance is retired. This minimizes service unavailability in shared test landscapes and reduces cross-microservice interference during concurrent deployments.

Key points:
- ZDD is disabled by default to conserve resources and avoid accidental long-lived duplicates.
- Enablement is controlled via pipeline configuration (e.g., pipeline.yml/credentials) per service/environment.
- Implementation:
  - Cloud Foundry: push new app instance with unique name, run health checks/smoke tests, map routes to the new instance, unmap from the old, then delete the old instance.
  - Neo: use equivalent blue/green or rolling mechanism where available.
- Health checks and route switching are atomic where supported. Failures trigger automatic rollback to the previous stable instance.
- Backward-compatible database/schema changes are required when ZDD is enabled; non-compatible migrations must be gated or run separately.
