- Logs and metrics from both old and new instances are retained for the duration of the cutover to aid debugging.

This option allows teams using a single shared test landscape with one instance per microservice to run E2E tests without interrupting dependent services.

## Decision:
- Parse CLI arguments first and handle --help/-h before any kdbOpen/kdbGet calls.
- If help is requested, print help and exit with success (code 0), bypassing any KDB initialization or access.
- Refactor help printing to be independent of KDB state (no reliance on opened handles, KeySets, or specifications).
- If errors occurred in kdbOpen/kdbGet but --help is present, still print help and exit 0.
- Maintain existing error behavior when --help is not requested.
- Centralize help handling in a common utility to ensure consistent behavior across all tools.

## Decision:
Store any unrecognised/invalid attributes from Apply on the ApplyApplication model, not on domain models (Trainee, Degree, etc.).

- Add a JSONB column (e.g., apply_unknown_attributes) on ApplyApplication to capture fields that cannot be mapped to Register’s schema. Structure by section (trainee, degree[n], course, diversity, contact, etc.) and include schema/version metadata to aid future migrations.
- Keep domain models free of imported invalid data to avoid conflating “unknown-from-Apply” with Register’s domain validations and states.
- Provide a presenter/service that:
  - Exposes these attributes to the UI for operator review and resolution.
  - Supports per-field reconciliation actions (map to known field, add note, discard).
  - Tracks resolution status and timestamps per attribute.
- On successful reconciliation, remove or mark resolved entries from apply_unknown_attributes and persist the canonical data on the appropriate domain models.
- Log/audit all imports and reconciliation actions; include source payload snapshots for traceability.
- Validate size/PII constraints on the JSON store; encrypt-at-rest if it may contain sensitive data.
- Offer light helper accessors for common queries (e.g., has_unknown_degree_data?) but avoid adding virtual attributes to domain models.
- If future needs require distributing data to models, introduce mappers that deliberately copy and version fields rather than relocating the store.

This preserves clear separation of concerns, maintains import traceability, and provides a consistent operator workflow without polluting domain validation semantics.

## Decision:
Adopt a TypeScript-first stack with NestJS on the backend and Next.js (React) on the frontend.

- Backend: NestJS (Node.js + TypeScript) with Fastify adapter for performance, PostgreSQL via Prisma ORM, Redis for caching/queues, REST with OpenAPI and optional GraphQL module, JWT/OAuth2 auth, class-validator/transformer for DTOs, Jest for tests, and Docker/Kubernetes-ready containerization.
- Frontend: Next.js (React 18 + TypeScript, App Router) to enable SSR/SSG/ISR for performance and SEO, React Query for data fetching/cache, React Hook Form + Zod for forms/validation, Tailwind CSS for styling, and Playwright + Jest/RTL for testing.
- Communication: REST-first with OpenAPI contract; leverage tRPC or GraphQL selectively for complex client-driven queries.
- Build/DevX: Monorepo (Nx or Turborepo) to share types and utilities, unified linting/formatting (ESLint/Prettier), commit hooks (Husky), and CI/CD with incremental builds.
- Observability/Security: Structured logging (Pino), metrics/tracing (OpenTelemetry), feature flags, and security hardening (Helmet, rate limiting, CSRF where applicable).
- Scalability: Horizontal scaling behind a reverse proxy, stateless services, background workers (BullMQ), and CDN for static assets.

This stack maximizes developer productivity, consistency, and maintainability, enables end-to-end type safety, supports strong SEO and performance characteristics, and scales effectively for future growth.

## Decision:
- We will not use React.FC (or React.FunctionComponent) for typing function components.
- Components will be declared as plain functions with explicitly typed props: function MyComp(props: Props): JSX.Element.
- We will include children only when needed, typed explicitly (e.g., children?: React.ReactNode) or via PropsWithChildren<Props> where appropriate.
- For generic components, we will prefer generic function components (e.g., function List<T>(props: ListProps<T>): JSX.Element) to enable proper generic inference for children and props.
- For forwardRef and memo, we will use the recommended patterns without FC: forwardRef<Element, Props>((props, ref) => …) and export default memo(MyComp).
- Linting and templates will be updated to disallow React.FC usage (eslint rule/regexp check in CI) and encourage explicit props typing.
- Existing usages of React.FC will be migrated opportunistically; no mass refactor is required unless they block generics or cause children typing issues.

## Decision:
Deprecate and remove embedded Ruby from the shared YAML holiday definitions and standardize on language-agnostic method references. YAML will declare custom methods by stable identifiers and inputs only (e.g., methods: { id: ch_vd_lundi_du_jeune_federal, arguments: [year] }) with no executable source. We will not pursue a generic cross-language DSL for custom methods at this time.

Establish a canonical specification for each custom method:
- A human-readable description of intent and rules
- Determinism constraints and edge-case notes
- Conformance fixtures (year → expected date) covering representative ranges and edge cases

Provide a reference implementation in the Ruby library and invite/maintain equivalent implementations in other language clients. Compliance will be validated via the shared conformance fixtures in CI across language repos.

Migration plan:
- Freeze current YAML with embedded Ruby; extract behavior into spec + fixtures.
- Strip source from YAML, replace with method identifiers and arguments.
- Release a major version of the definitions with these changes; Ruby gem remains fully functional via its in-repo implementations.
- For languages lacking an implementation of a referenced method, expose a clear “unsupported custom method” error with guidance.

Where feasible, continue to promote simple rules into existing generic YAML constructs; reserve custom methods only for cases that cannot be expressed generically.

## Decision:
Adopt a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) architecture with an API Gateway in front of shared domain services.

- Introduce one BFF per client type (e.g., web-frontend-A, web-frontend-B, mobile). Each BFF exposes client-optimized endpoints and orchestrates/aggregates data from common domain APIs.
- Keep domain services client-agnostic, exposing canonical, reusable REST endpoints. Domain DTOs remain stable; client-specific view models are shaped in BFFs.
- Define API contracts with OpenAPI. BFF APIs and domain APIs have separate specs and versioning. Use semantic versioning; prefer additive changes. For breaking changes, version via URI (e.g., /v2) at BFF level; minimize breaking changes in domain APIs.
- Apply scope-based authorization and rate limits at the API Gateway. Enforce client-specific scopes so BFFs can access only the necessary domain resources. Centralize CORS, auth, and observability at the gateway.
- Support field selection and pagination consistently. Allow BFFs to project data as needed (e.g., sparse fieldsets), avoiding over-fetching for mobile.
- Encapsulate conditional/business rules that differ by client in BFFs; shared business logic remains in domain services to prevent duplication.
- Share validation schemas between BFFs and domain APIs; BFFs perform request validation (including client-specific constraints) before calling domain services.
- Implement caching at the BFF (short-lived, client-tuned) and at the gateway (public cache for safe GETs) to optimize mobile and high-latency scenarios.
- Establish backwards compatibility policy and deprecation windows per BFF to independently evolve each client without forcing synchronized releases.
- Provide an internal client registry (capabilities/feature flags) so BFFs can toggle client-specific behaviors without impacting domain services.

This approach allows multiple frontends and a future mobile app to reuse common APIs while delivering client-specific contracts and data shapes safely and efficiently.

## Decision:
Adopt Google’s resource-oriented design and standardize on an immutable resource name field named “name” as the canonical external identifier for all resources.

- “name”: Required, immutable, globally unique within its parent scope, following a hierarchical pattern per service (e.g., projects/{project}/locations/{location}/foos/{foo}). All inter-service references, API request/response payloads, and events SHALL use “name” as the identifier.
- “uid”: Optional, server-assigned UUID (e.g., UUIDv4) that is immutable and unique across time. Returned in read APIs for efficient storage/indexing and correlation, but not accepted as a reference in external APIs.
- “displayName”: Optional, user-provided, human-readable, mutable field for usability. Renames affect only displayName and do not change “name”.
- Uniqueness: Services MUST enforce uniqueness of the terminal segment of “name” within the appropriate parent scope.
- Backward compatibility: Existing APIs that expose “id” will:
  - Begin returning “name” immediately.
  - Treat “id” as a deprecated alias where feasible (read-only projection of terminal segment or legacy ID), to be removed after a deprecation period.
  - Accept both legacy “id” references and canonical “name” during transition, with server-preferring “name” and emitting deprecation warnings/headers.
- Events: All domain and audit events MUST include both “name” and “uid”.
- Cross-service integration: Services MUST store and exchange “name” for references. Internal data stores may index on “uid” for performance but must retain “name” for referential integrity and egress.

We will not support renaming of “name.” If aliasing is needed, implement explicit, long-lived aliases that resolve to the canonical “name” without changing it.

## Decision:
We will explicitly identify and exclude automated (bot) traffic at ingestion time and in downstream analytics.

- Identification
  - All synthetic checks, CI/CD smoke tests, load tests, and external monitors must use a standardized, versioned User-Agent prefix (e.g., “OurAppBot/<tool>/<env>/<version>”).
  - Automation must include a dedicated header “X-Traffic-Class: bot” (preferred) or “X-OurApp-Automation: true”. Where headers cannot be set, we will rely on the User-Agent.
  - We will maintain an allowlist of CIDR ranges for our automation infrastructure and major third-party monitors; requests from these ranges will be tagged as bot if identifiers are present.
  - For browser-based automation, we will set a short-lived cookie (e.g., traffic_class=bot) on first request when the header is present to ensure client-side trackers also exclude events.

- Exclusion
  - Server-side instrumentation will drop or tag events with traffic_class=bot before emitting to analytics/observability stores.
  - Client-side instrumentation will check for the bot cookie or header echo and suppress emission.
  - Dashboards and reports will include a default filter excluding traffic_class=bot. Historical datasets will be reprocessed with the same rule where feasible.

- Governance and Enforcement
  - A central registry of bot identifiers (User-Agent patterns, headers, CIDRs) will be maintained in code and configuration, reviewed quarterly.
  - CI checks will fail automation configurations that omit the required header/User-Agent.
  - Feature flags will allow temporary inclusion of bot traffic for testing, defaulting to excluded.

## Decision:
We will enforce TLS with strict certificate verification for all network communications. We will use CA-based validation with hostname verification as the default, prohibiting self-signed or unverified certificates in all environments. For high-risk and internal service-to-service channels where we control both ends, we will additionally implement certificate pinning (SPKI/public key pins or CA pinning) to mitigate MITM risks, with a defined rotation procedure and overlap period to avoid outages during renewals. Certificate lifetimes will be short, issuance and renewal automated (e.g., ACME), and revocation checked where feasible (OCSP/OCSP stapling). Any request to bypass verification requires a formal security exception, time-bound, and must not be used in production. Logs and alerts will detect verification failures and pin mismatches.

## Decision:
Adopt an opinionated, minimal configuration model with strong defaults and optional overrides.

- Provide a single, simple configuration surface requiring only:
  - environment (e.g., sandbox, staging, production)
  - service/entity ID
  - callback/redirect URLs
  - signing/verification key material (path or secret reference)
- Predefine metadata and endpoint values per environment; users select an environment rather than supplying raw metadata XML/URLs.
- Supply sensible defaults for timeouts, algorithms, and clock skew; no need to configure unless deviating from defaults.
- Support configuration via:
  - one small YAML file with clear, top-level fields, and
  - environment variables that map 1:1 to those fields, with env vars taking precedence.
- Validate on startup with fail-fast, human-readable errors and suggestions; provide a “--print-effective-config” option for visibility.
- Ship a “init” command that generates a minimal, commented config skeleton tailored to the chosen environment.
- Publish a machine-readable schema (JSON Schema) for the YAML to enable IDE hints and CI validation.
- Gate advanced/legacy options behind an optional “advanced:” block; omit from basic docs. Maintain a compatibility layer to read legacy configs, emitting deprecation warnings and an auto-migrated “effective” minimal config on request.
- Keep documentation and examples focused on the minimal path; provide one-page quickstart plus a minimal example file.

This approach makes the common case trivial while preserving an escape hatch for complex deployments without overwhelming new users.

## Decision:
Introduce configurable size controls for Expanded JSON-LD emission to balance readability and payload size:
- Default: First occurrence embedding with cycle protection. We embed a node the first time it is encountered during traversal and maintain an ID-based cache; subsequent references to the same node are emitted as a minimal object containing only @id.
- Configurable limits: Support maxDepth and maxOccurrences thresholds. When limits are reached, we emit only @id to avoid exponential growth. Cycles always break to @id.
- Escape hatch: Consumers requiring strictly “pure embedded” JSON can opt into forceEmbed mode (no @id fallbacks), accepting larger payloads, while consumers prioritizing size can enable aggressive de-duplication via lower depth/occurrence limits.

Flattened emission remains unchanged for strict single-node-per-ID requirements. This approach preserves the primary benefit of expanded JSON (JSON-consumable structure) while preventing pathological payload sizes through controlled de-duplication.

## Decision:
We will standardize on Kotlin as the primary language for all new applications. Mixing Java and Kotlin within the same service is discouraged and requires an explicit ADR and approval.

Rationale:
- Kotlin offers concise, safer syntax (null-safety, data classes, coroutines) with seamless Java interop, enabling painless onboarding for Java-only developers.
- Ecosystem support is mature (Gradle Kotlin DSL, Spring, Android, Ktor), with strong tooling in IntelliJ and CI.
- Consistency reduces cognitive load, increases reuse of patterns/utilities, and simplifies hiring/training.

Guidelines:
- New modules/services: Kotlin-only.
- Shared libraries: Kotlin-first APIs with Java-friendly interop where needed.
- Existing Java code: keep as-is; migrate opportunistically (boy-scout rule) but no big-bang rewrites.
- Tooling: Gradle Kotlin DSL, ktlint + detekt, Kotlin 2.x (LTS when available), target latest supported JVM.
- Training: short Kotlin ramp-up for Java developers; provide style guide and examples.
- Exceptions: permitted for third-party constraints or performance hotspots; must be justified via ADR.

Adopt a phased, backward-compatible release strategy for Dapr binaries and configurations:

- Versioning: Use semantic versioning for all binaries, images, and config schemas. Maintain a published compatibility matrix (runtime, SDKs, components, and config schema). Guarantee N-2 minor version compatibility for configs and components.
- Artifacts: Build reproducible, SBOM-included, and signed artifacts. Publish OCI images and GitHub release binaries atomically. Never overwrite tags; keep prior artifacts available for rollback.
- Rollout order: Control plane first (placement, operator, sentry), then sidecars/runtimes, then SDKs. Helm charts/manifests reference the new release but default to “safe” values.
- Canary and phased rollout: Enable canary releases via labels/namespaces. Gradually increase adoption (e.g., 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) gated by health SLOs and error budgets. Support blue/green for control plane.
- Feature flags and config gating: Ship new behavior behind disabled-by-default feature flags. Introduce new config fields with defaults and versioned schemas; validate schemas server-side and at admission time. Provide auto-migration with dry-run and strict/lenient modes.
- Safety/rollback: Zero-downtime upgrade path; sidecar restarts coordinated with app readiness. One-click rollback via immutable previous chart/image versions. Keep last two minor versions of configs accepted by new binaries.
- Quality gates: Pre-release conformance tests across N, N-1, N-2; upgrade/downgrade tests; component e2e; perf and soak. Block GA on failing SLOs.
- Communication: Release notes include breaking-change callouts, deprecation timelines, and migration steps. Provide deprecation over ≥2 minor releases before removal.
- Incident response: Emergency yank procedure with advisory, rollback steps, and patched re-release.

## Decision:
Adopt a standardized, enforceable convention for in-code task annotations and route all substantive work to the issue tracker.

- Allowed tags and intent:
  - FIXME: Known defect that causes incorrect behavior; must have linked issue.
  - TODO: Small, incremental task tightly coupled to the nearby code; must have owner and issue link, or removal date if truly trivial.
  - NOTE: Contextual advice or rationale; no action implied.
  - DEPRECATED: Usage scheduled for removal; must link to migration plan/issue.

- Required format:
  - // FIXME(#1234, owner:@alice): concise description
  - // TODO(#5678, owner:@bob): concise description
  - // TODO(owner:@bob, remove-by:2026-03-31): trivial follow-up
  - // NOTE: rationale/context
  - // DEPRECATED(#9012): replacement XYZ; removal in v2.3

- Policy:
  - Anything larger than a trivial, localized change must be tracked as an issue; the code comment references that issue.
  - No “naked” TODO/FIXME without owner and issue (or a remove-by date for trivial TODO).
  - TODOs are short-lived; remove or convert to an issue within one release cycle.
  - FIXME indicates broken behavior and is prioritized in triage.
  - Advice and design context belong in NOTE (or ADRs for larger decisions), not as TODO.

- Tooling and enforcement:
  - Add a lint rule in CI that:
    - Fails on TODO/FIXME lacking owner and issue/removal date.
    - Flags TODO older than one release or past remove-by date.
    - Reports counts of FIXME/TODO by module for visibility.
  - IDE templates/snippets to insert the standardized format.

- Migration:
  - Audit existing TODOs; create issues where needed, convert advice to NOTE, and remove stale items.

## Decision:
Expose and require a stable, opaque, globally unique Report ID for every report via the Sirius Public API.

- Use an immutable UUIDv4 reportId generated by Sirius at creation time. It is the canonical identifier for all subsequent operations on that report.
- POST /reports returns 201 with body containing reportId; no reliance on composite natural keys (donor, year) for identity.
- Support creation of multiple reports for the same donor and reporting year; each receives a distinct reportId and is independently addressable.
- All supporting-document operations are scoped by reportId (e.g., POST /reports/{reportId}/documents). Requests referencing an unknown reportId return 404.
- Natural attributes (donor identifier, reporting year, version/sequence) are returned as metadata and may be used for search/listing endpoints (e.g., GET /reports?donorId=&year=), which return a collection of reports (each with its reportId).
- The reportId is never reused, transformed, or inferred from business data; it remains constant across the report’s lifecycle (draft to submitted to approved).
- API contracts, schemas, and webhooks/events will include reportId to ensure end-to-end traceability between Digideps and Sirius.
- Optional: support Idempotency-Key on creation to prevent accidental duplicate reports; duplicates (same idempotency key) return the original reportId.

## Decision:
We will containerize all application components using Docker (OCI-compliant images) to ensure reproducible builds, consistent deployments, and local development parity.

- Each service will have a canonical Dockerfile (using multi-stage builds, minimal/pinned base images, and non-root users). Image configuration (env vars, ports, healthchecks) will live in the image or deployment manifests as appropriate.
- Images will be built in CI using Docker BuildKit/Buildx, tagged immutably (commit SHA/semver), vulnerability-scanned, and pushed to a centralized container registry.
- Local development will use Docker Compose to stand up multi-service stacks and dependencies (e.g., databases, message brokers) with environment parity to higher environments.
- Runtime deployment will consume these images in the chosen orchestrator per ADR002 (e.g., Kubernetes), leveraging declarative manifests and environment-specific configuration.
- We will adhere to OCI image/spec standards to avoid vendor lock-in and ensure portability across cloud providers and hosting options.
- We will maintain a curated set of base images and shared build tooling to promote consistency, security, and faster builds.

This approach separates application concerns from the host OS, supports PaaS/IaaS portability, and provides a repeatable, well-understood path from developer workstation to production.

## Decision:
- Feature flags will not be supported in the SCSS compilation pipeline. SCSS is compiled once without flag awareness; no conditional compilation is introduced.
- Feature-flagged UI behavior must be controlled in templates (e.g., Twig) or JS by toggling wrapper/modifier classes or data attributes on the DOM. Styles for a flagged feature must be namespaced under such class/attribute to avoid leaking changes when the flag is off.
- Existing selectors must not be changed incompatibly behind a feature flag. Instead, create parallel, opt-in selectors (e.g., a modifier or wrapper scope) that activate only when the DOM class is present.
- Breaking changes to SCSS tokens, mixins, functions, or variables must not be done under a flag. Introduce new names (e.g., $spacing-v2, @mixin button-v2) and deprecate old ones via comments. Keep both until the feature is fully released; remove deprecated items with the flag removal MR.
- Accept that flagged styles may remain in the compiled CSS during the flag’s lifetime; prioritize safety and predictability over minimal bundle size.
- Each SCSS block tied to a feature must include a comment referencing the flag name and removal plan.
- No build-step workarounds (multiple builds per flag, dynamic imports for CSS) will be implemented.

## Decision:
- Adopt React Context to provide the edition value across the app, eliminating prop drilling for this property.
- Introduce an EditionProvider at the application root that receives the edition from server/render entry and exposes it via useEdition().
- Keep the scope minimal: use Context only for stable, app-wide configuration (e.g., edition), not for frequently changing UI state.
- Do not add a global state management library at this stage; reassess if additional cross-cutting state emerges.
- Provide strong TypeScript typing for Edition and the context; include a safe default/fallback for non-wrapped consumers only in tests/dev.
- Ensure SSR compatibility by sourcing edition on the server and hydrating with the same value on the client to avoid mismatches.
- Encapsulate access behind a small utility (EditionProvider, useEdition) to keep call sites simple and enable future refactors without churn.
- Add unit tests for the hook/provider and integration tests for representative component trees to confirm prop removal and correct rendering.
- Document guidelines: prefer props for local component needs; use Context sparingly for global, stable data; avoid nested providers unless necessary.
- Monitor render performance; memoize provider value and avoid recomputation to prevent unnecessary re-renders of consumers.
- Migrate incrementally: remove edition props from intermediate components while updating consumers to use useEdition().

## Decision:
Adopt an event-driven, streaming-first architecture with CQRS to explicitly surface distributed trade-offs and enable flexible evolution of read models. Commands are accepted via simple HTTP endpoints; domain state changes are recorded as versioned events on a lightweight broker (NATS JetStream). Read-side projections subscribe to events to build task-focused, replaceable views exposed via GraphQL/HTTP and real-time updates over WebSockets/SSE.

To make first-run frictionless, provide a single-command local environment using Docker Compose (broker, API gateway, command service, projection services, dashboard). Include a Makefile (or task runner) for up, down, logs, and reset; seed scripts to publish demo events; and hot-reload dev images for rapid iteration. Ship a devcontainer configuration for zero-setup IDE onboarding.

Define AsyncAPI for event streams and OpenAPI for commands/queries. Enforce event compatibility with versioned schemas and a lightweight schema registry (embedded in the repo for the demo). Support local durability with in-memory storage defaults and optional file-backed persistence; production uses the same stack with tuned retention and replication.

Expose the system via a single public entry (gateway) for easy deployment (e.g., Heroku/Render/Fly.io), with environment-based configuration. Provide a minimal observability bundle (structured logs, tracing headers passthrough, and a simple event stream inspector UI) to highlight latency, ordering, and replay characteristics.

This approach demonstrates non-layered, asynchronous boundaries, replayable history, and independently deployable projections while remaining trivial to run locally and straightforward to extend (e.g., adding auth or new projections) without disrupting existing consumers.

## Decision:
We will separate contracts from implementations at the artifact and feature levels, enforcing OSGi visibility and preventing dependency pollution.

- Split every functional area into discrete bundles:
  - <feature>-api: exports only public API packages.
  - <feature>-spi (optional): exports only SPI packages intended for extensions.
  - <feature>-impl: contains internal packages, exports none (or only implementation-required service components), imports <feature>-api/SPI.
  - <feature>-rest/ui/etc.: depend only on <feature>-api (and SPI if needed), never on <feature>-impl.

- Source/layout:
  - Move internal packages into dedicated modules (separate source roots) instead of co-locating with API.
  - Use bnd/Bndtools to strictly control Export-Package/Private-Package and ban accidental exports.

- Build/dependencies:
  - Maven sub-modules per bundle; ensure non-transitive compile exposure:
    - API has no dependency on IMPL.
    - IMPL depends on API/SPI; IMPL must not leak to API consumers.
  - Enforce rules with Maven Enforcer + Revapi/Bnd Baseline:
    - Forbid compile-time deps on any *-impl from other modules.
    - Guard API compatibility and versioning (Semantic Versioning).

- Karaf features:
  - Define fine-grained features:
    - openhab-<feature>-api: includes only <feature>-api (and SPI).
    - openhab-<feature>-runtime: includes <feature>-impl and its runtime deps; requires openhab-<feature>-api.
  - Extensions depend on the smallest applicable feature (usually openhab-<feature>-api or -spi), not on openhab-core-base/openhab-runtime-base.
  - Avoid umbrella features for unrelated concerns; compose higher-level features from granular ones as needed.

- Provisioning/runtime:
  - Use OSGi Require-Capability/Provide-Capability to model SPI contracts and minimize activation.
  - Keep REST and other adapters as separate bundles depending on APIs only.

This modularization decouples contracts from implementations, minimizes transitive dependency leakage, enables à la carte assembly, and reduces unintended framework activation.

## Decision:
Adopt a “docs-as-code” and standardised-repo approach to make knowledge self-serve and current, reducing synchronous handovers.

Concretely:
- Standard repository structure and templates in every service: README (what/why/how), Getting Started, Architecture Overview (C4 diagrams-as-code), ADRs, Runbook/Support, Operational Playbooks, Glossary, and Contribution Guide.
- CODEOWNERS and an Ownership file (team, contacts, domain) per repo; add system catalogue entries linking to dependencies and dashboards.
- Automated status visibility: CI/CD badges, test coverage, dependency health, deployment/environment status, uptime/error-rate links, and release notes/CHANGELOG generated on merge.
- RFC/ADR lightweight process for non-trivial changes to capture context and decisions asynchronously.
- Diagrams-as-code (e.g., Mermaid/Structurizr) committed alongside code; regenerate on CI to ensure freshness.
- Onboarding packs per service (30/60/90-minute guides, “first task” checklist, local dev scripts), plus rotation checklist and shadowing plan.
- Central developer portal (or docs index) aggregating services, ownership, runbooks, dashboards, and key ADRs.
- Enforcement via repo templates, linting checks for required docs, and CI gates that warn on missing/obsolete docs.

This makes status and intent visible by default, reduces meeting-dependent knowledge transfer, and supports fast, repeatable rotations across GOV.UK teams.

## Decision:
Adopt optimistic concurrency control with explicit versioning per aggregate/entity.

- Persist a monotonically increasing version (e.g., bigint or database rowversion) on each entity. All updates must include the expected version in the WHERE clause (update … where id=? and version=?), incrementing version atomically on success. If 0 rows are affected, treat as a concurrency conflict.
- For HTTP APIs, expose the version as a strong ETag and require If-Match on all mutating requests (PUT/PATCH/DELETE). On mismatch, return 412 Precondition Failed with a payload describing the conflict and guidance to reload and reapply changes.
- For non-HTTP/internal calls, pass the version token explicitly in command payloads and enforce the same match-and-increment semantics.
- For bulk or composite operations, define clear aggregate boundaries and perform updates within a single transaction per aggregate to avoid partial success. If multiple aggregates must change, use a saga/process manager to orchestrate retries and conflict handling.
- Provide client-side helpers to surface conflicts, reload current state, and assist users in reapplying changes; for simple fields, an “overwrite anyway” option may be offered as a subsequent, informed action with the new ETag/version.
- Log and meter conflict rates; if hot-spot entities exhibit excessive conflicts, consider tactical pessimistic locks for short critical sections or redesign aggregate boundaries.
- For create endpoints, support idempotency keys to avoid duplicate records on retries.

## Decision:
Adopt a domain-driven, modular-monolith architecture with a stable, normalized relational data model (PostgreSQL) and clear bounded contexts. Start with event-storming and context mapping workshops to identify core domains, subdomains, entities, and aggregates. Define a canonical glossary and ubiquitous language to drive naming in code and schema.

Data model:
- Use UUID primary keys, ISO timestamps, and explicit foreign keys with ON DELETE constraints.
- Prefer 3NF with selective denormalization for read performance.
- Implement soft-delete only where required by business rules; otherwise rely on true deletes with audit.
- Include auditing (created_by/updated_by) and row-level optimistic locking for aggregates.
- Use migrations (e.g., Liquibase/Flyway) with strict forward-only change management and reproducible seeds/fixtures.

Application structure:
- Organize code by bounded context and feature, not technical layer: /contexts/{context}/{domain}/{aggregate}/(model, repository, service, controller).
- Encapsulate domain logic in entities/value objects; expose use cases via application services.
- Use repositories for persistence; no data access from controllers.
- Introduce a lightweight CQRS split where beneficial: read models (views/materialized views) for complex queries, commands for state changes.
- Expose a versioned REST API (JSON) with OpenAPI contracts; reserve GraphQL for future aggregations if needed.
- Publish domain events internally (in-process) for decoupling; evaluate durable outbox only when cross-service needs emerge.

Quality and tooling:
- Enforce schema and API reviews via ADRs and PR gates.
- Add comprehensive tests: unit (domain), integration (persistence), contract (API), and migration tests.
- Apply static analysis, formatting, and secure-by-default defaults (least privilege DB roles, encrypted secrets, PII classification).
- Start as a modular monolith; defer service decomposition until clear scaling or autonomy needs justify it.

We will standardize on a lightweight, portable core error model in ockam_core, with per-crate error domains and numeric codes.

- Core type: ockam_core::Error { domain: &'static str, code: u32, source: Option<ErrorCompat> } with Result<T> = core::result::Result<T, Error>.
- Domains: each crate defines a unique static domain identifier (e.g., "ockam.transport.tcp") and an enum ErrorKind mapped to stable u32 codes. Codes are crate-local and versioned; no global registry required.
- Portability: no_std by default; optional “std” feature enables std::error::Error, Display strings, and backtraces; optional “alloc” enables owned messages. On embedded, errors remain zero-alloc by default and printable via core::fmt.
- Ergonomics: provide #[derive(OckamError)] macro to define ErrorKind -> code mappings and Display messages (gated by “std”/“alloc”). Provide error!(), err_kind!(), with_context!() macros for concise construction and propagation.
- Interop: blanket From<crate::ErrorKind> for ockam_core::Error and From<ockam_core::Error> for anyhow::Error (behind “std”). Third-party crates can adopt the same pattern by choosing their own domain string and defining ErrorKind enums.
- Stability and observability: domain+code are stable across patch releases; textual messages are non-stable and optional. Optional feature “defmt” implements defmt::Format for embedded logging.
- Guidance: bubble up ockam_core::Error at public boundaries; convert foreign errors into domain-specific ErrorKind variants. Application binaries can use anyhow for rich context; libraries must not require std.

This design meets agility (per-crate enums), portability (no_std-first, zero-alloc), and convenience (derives, macros, standard Result alias).

## Decision:
Refactor services into smaller, action-specific handlers and endpoints, without introducing a generic state machine.

- Replace the overloaded UPDATE with explicit endpoints/use-cases per transition (e.g., PATCH /system-intakes/{id}/draft, POST /system-intakes/{id}/submit, POST /system-intakes/{id}/decide).
- Implement thin controllers that delegate to application services (one per action). Each service enforces:
  - Authorization (RBAC/ABAC) scoped to the action
  - Input validation and state preconditions
  - Transactional side effects and audit logging
  - Emission of domain events for asynchronous/secondary effects (notifications, search indexing), avoiding service bloat
- Keep a simple, code-level transition policy (guards + next state) colocated with each action; no FSM framework or runtime configuration.
- Ensure concurrency safety via optimistic locking and idempotency keys for mutating endpoints.
- Introduce a shared domain service layer for reusable logic (policy evaluation, notifications) to minimize duplication.
- Maintain backwards compatibility by routing the current UPDATE endpoint to the new handlers temporarily; deprecate and remove once clients migrate.
- Provide an explicit transition matrix in API docs and verify with contract tests; add unit tests per action covering authorization, preconditions, and effects.

## Decision:
Define uniform REST endpoint behavior for this service as follows:
- Protocol and Media Types: HTTPS only. Default media type application/json; UTF-8. Support content negotiation via Accept/Content-Type. Errors use application/problem+json (RFC 9457).
- Resource Modeling: Use plural, noun-based resources (e.g., /users). Kebab-case in paths (/user-profiles), camelCase in JSON fields. Avoid verbs; use sub-resources for relations (/users/{id}/tokens). For non-CRUD actions, use action sub-resources with POST (/invoices/{id}/send).
- Methods and Semantics: GET (safe, cacheable), POST (create or action), PUT (full replace), PATCH (partial update via JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7386), DELETE (idempotent). HEAD/OPTIONS as appropriate.
- Status Codes: 200 OK, 201 Created (with Location), 202 Accepted (async), 204 No Content, 400 Validation error, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 412 Precondition Failed, 415 Unsupported Media Type, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests, 5xx server errors.
- Versioning: Prefix major version in path: /v1/..., increment on breaking changes. Minor, backward-compatible changes do not bump the path version.
- Pagination, Filtering, Sorting: Cursor-based pagination with page[size] and page[after]/page[before]. Include pagination links (first, next, prev, last). Filtering via filter[field]=value. Sorting via sort=field,-otherField.
- Consistency and Concurrency: Return ETag on GET; support If-Match/If-None-Match for conditional requests and optimistic locking. Safe/idempotent operations honored; support Idempotency-Key for POST where duplicate submission risk exists.
- Dates and Formats: Timestamps as RFC 3339 in UTC (e.g., 2026-01-23T12:34:56Z). Numbers and booleans use JSON native types.
- Headers and Observability: Require Authorization: Bearer <token> (OAuth2/JWT). Accept X-Request-ID for correlation and echo it. Provide RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset when rate limiting applies. Support gzip/br compression.
- Validation and Errors: Consistent field validation; include machine-readable codes. Problem details include type, title, status, detail, instance, and errors[] for field-level issues.
- Deprecation and Lifecycle: Mark deprecated endpoints with Deprecation and Sunset headers and include deprecation notice in responses; maintain compatibility until documented sunset date.
- Documentation: All endpoints specified in OpenAPI and kept in sync with implementation and examples for typical responses and errors.

## Decision:
Adopt S3 Presigned URLs as the primary mechanism for client uploads. The API will authenticate and authorize the client, validate intended metadata (filename, MIME type, size), and return a short‑lived presigned URL (and headers) scoped to a single PUT. For files exceeding a configurable threshold, the API will issue a multipart upload with presigned part URLs and enforce part count/size limits. URLs will expire quickly (e.g., 5–15 minutes) and include content-length and content-type constraints to mitigate abuse.

Server-side will not proxy file bytes, reducing latency, egress costs, and API workload. Uploaded objects will land in a private bucket with bucket policies restricting access; lifecycle rules, server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), and object lock (if required) will be applied. Optional post-upload processing (virus scan, metadata extraction, checksum verification) will be triggered via S3 events. The API will record object keys/checksums to bind uploads to application entities and will provide a minimal fallback proxy upload path only for clients that cannot use presigned URLs, disabled by default and rate-limited.

This approach offers superior scalability, cost-efficiency, and security versus base64 or multipart-to-API uploads, while supporting large files via S3 multipart uploads.

## Decision:
We will establish a unified, docs-as-code technical toolkit spanning all architecture spaces, governed by a shared taxonomy, common templates, and a single contribution workflow.

Key decisions:
- Canonical artifact taxonomy: goals, principles, standards, patterns, anti-patterns, reference architectures, decision records, constraints, guidelines, checklists, and playbooks. Each artifact includes mandatory metadata: owner, status (draft/proposed/approved/deprecated), version, last-reviewed, applicability (domains, platforms), dependencies, and related items.
- Standardized templates per artifact type with minimum acceptance criteria and example-filled starters.
- One source of truth: a centralized repository with CI-driven validation (linting, schema checks, link integrity, coverage of metadata), rendered to a searchable docs portal. Tagging and facets enable cross-space discovery.
- Governance and lifecycle: Architecture Review Council owns taxonomy and standards; each artifact has a named steward. Lifecycle gates: propose → peer review → council approval → publish; scheduled review SLAs and deprecation policy with migration guidance.
- Contribution model: open-by-default within the org; lightweight PR process; required reviewers include domain SME and cross-space representative. Automated CLA/CoC and contribution checklist.
- Quality and consistency: editorial style guide, example catalog, pattern testability guidance, and conformance checklists aligned to operational strategies. Periodic quality audits and metrics (coverage, freshness, adoption, issue aging).
- Adoption and enablement: champions network per delivery center, onboarding training, office hours, and internal talks. Integrations with delivery tooling (backlog templates, pipeline policy checks) to encourage usage.
- Incentives and visibility: OKRs tied to contribution and freshness; dashboards for usage, gaps, and impact.

Rollout will prioritize high-leverage artifacts (standards, patterns, checklists), followed by migration of legacy content into the unified structure.

## Decision:
Adopt a token-driven theming architecture centered on Material UI v5 (MUI System) with Emotion as the styling engine.

- Use MUI’s theme (with CssVarsProvider) to manage design tokens (color, spacing, typography, radius, elevation) via CSS variables for instant, runtime theme switching (light/dark/brand variants) and fine-grained customization.
- Manage canonical tokens in a separate package using Style Dictionary to generate platform-specific artifacts (CSS variables for web, JSON for React Native/mobile, and design files as needed), ensuring consistency across platforms.
- Leverage MUI System’s sx prop and responsive design utilities to build layout primitives and composables that are theme-aware, reducing custom CSS and improving consistency and performance.
- Base components on accessible, well-tested MUI primitives; extend via theme overrides and variants rather than ad-hoc component-level props to enforce design rules at the theme layer.
- Support brand theming via layered token sets (core → semantic → brand) to enable white-labeling and future platform expansion with minimal code changes.
- Document the system and themes in Storybook with theme switcher and visual regression tests to guarantee adherence and ease onboarding.

This approach balances DX, scalability, performance, accessibility, and cross-platform reuse while aligning with modern “theme-first” design system best practices.

## Decision:
Pin the toolchain to a mutually compatible set of versions until the ESLint TypeScript plugin supports ≥3.5.0.

- Set TypeScript to 3.4.5 in package.json across the repo.
- Align @typescript-eslint/parser and @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin to the matching compatible release line.
- Enforce versions via lockfile and (if using Yarn) "resolutions" or (npm) shrinkwrap to prevent inadvertent upgrades by transitive deps.
- Add a CI check that verifies tsc -v and npm ls @typescript-eslint/* to fail on mismatches.
- Document the constraint and create a dependabot/renovate rule to notify us when the plugin adds support for newer TypeScript so we can lift the pin.

Rationale: preserves linting fidelity with minimal disruption, avoids disabling rules or forking configs, and provides a clear upgrade path once ecosystem support lands.

## Decision:
Adopt resolvable, canonical HTTPS URIs as the global identifiers for all resources. URIs will conform to RFC 3986 and be hosted under our organizational domain to ensure persistence and governance.

- Base: https://api.example.org/
- Structure: https://api.example.org/{resource-collection}/{stable-id}[/{subresource}][?query] 
- Stable ID: a non-semantic, immutable identifier (UUIDv7 or equivalent surrogate key) to guarantee uniqueness and longevity independent of business attributes.
- Canonicalization: lowercase path segments; UTF-8 percent-encoding where required; no trailing slashes for canonical form; no file extensions; hyphen-separated tokens if needed.
- Immutability: once minted, a URI never changes or is re-assigned; tombstoned resources remain resolvable with appropriate status.
- Versioning: represent resource versions as a path segment when necessary (e.g., /v1/) for API shape; entity versioning, if exposed, uses /{id}/versions/{n}.
- Discoverability: content negotiation supports multiple representations (e.g., JSON, HTML) without changing the URI.
- Avoid PII/secrets: do not embed personally identifiable or confidential data in URIs.
- Aliases: business-friendly slugs may exist as secondary, redirecting URIs; canonical URIs remain the primary identifiers.
- Referencing: all internal and external links, events, and audit trails must reference the canonical HTTPS URI.

Example:
- Collection: https://api.example.org/customers
- Entity: https://api.example.org/customers/018f3c1a-9b6b-7c62-bb88-5a3f6b0f5c51
- Subresource: https://api.example.org/customers/018f3c1a-9b6b-7c62-bb88-5a3f6b0f5c51/addresses
- API versioned: https://api.example.org/v1/customers/018f3c1a-…

## Decision:
Deprecate and remove the GraphQL stack (graphene-django, graphene, apollo-client) and standardize on a single RESTful API using Django REST Framework (DRF).

Key elements:
- Consolidate all server endpoints in DRF; stop building duplicate GraphQL resolvers. Remove graphene(-django) from dependencies and codebase.
- Replace Apollo Client in Nimbus UI with a lightweight REST data layer:
  - Use fetch/axios plus a caching/data-fetching library (e.g., React Query or RTK Query) for request deduping, caching, retries, and mutation workflows.
  - Generate typed clients/models from OpenAPI (e.g., drf-spectacular + openapi-typescript) to ensure end-to-end type safety.
- Optimize REST for UI performance:
  - Add purpose-built endpoints that return the exact aggregates the UI needs to avoid client over-fetching and request waterfalls.
  - Support pagination, sparse fieldsets, includes/expansion, and batch endpoints where appropriate.
  - Enable server-side caching (ETag/Last-Modified), compression, and conditional requests; add CDN caching for read-heavy endpoints.
  - Profile and eliminate N+1 queries; add SELECT_related/PREFETCH_related, database indexes, and query limits.
- Improve maintainability and tooling:
  - Publish an OpenAPI spec as the single source of truth; integrate automated contract tests and client generation in CI.
  - Introduce API versioning and deprecation policy; provide a short-lived GraphQL compatibility facade only if external consumers require it, then sunset.
- Migration plan:
  - Phase 1: Freeze GraphQL feature development; build missing REST endpoints.
  - Phase 2: Migrate UI screens incrementally to REST client; run dual-read/compare where needed.
  - Phase 3: Remove GraphQL schemas, resolvers, and Apollo; delete unused code paths and tests.
- Observability: Add endpoint-level metrics, tracing, and SLIs to validate performance gains and prevent regressions.

This consolidation reduces overhead, improves performance, simplifies testing and CI, and lowers long-term maintenance cost.

## Decision:
We will formalize decision-making by adopting Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) across the project. ADRs will use the MADR template, be stored under docs/adr with incremental numbering (e.g., 0001-...), and be maintained in version control. Every architectural change (affecting runtime behavior, quality attributes, dependencies, data models, build/deploy, or interfaces) requires a new ADR with Status (proposed/accepted/deprecated/superseded), Context, Decision, Consequences, and Alternatives Considered. ADRs will be authored via pull requests, reviewed by at least one architect and one domain owner, and linked from related code changes and tickets. Supersessions will be explicit, preserving history rather than editing accepted records. For traceability, each ADR must specify owners, affected components, and measurable acceptance criteria. We will provide templates and a CLI helper (adr-tools or equivalent) to ensure consistency, and integrate ADR presence checks in CI for significant changes (label-based). Public-facing ADRs will exclude secrets and follow our disclosure policy.

## Decision:
Avoid truthy/falsy checks for defaulting or flow control when valid values could be falsy (0, "", false, NaN). Instead:
- Use nullish coalescing for defaults: const speed = n ?? 50; and speed ??= 50;
- Prefer explicit comparisons in conditions:
  - Numbers: if (count !== 0) … or if (count > 0) … as appropriate
  - Strings/arrays: if (str.length > 0) …, if (arr.length === 0) …
  - Booleans: if (isEnabled === true) … when ambiguity exists
- For optionals: if (value == null) { … } to target null or undefined only; otherwise be explicit about the exact values you’re testing.
- Only use || for defaulting when the domain intentionally treats all falsy values as “unset,” which should be rare and documented.

Tooling and linting:
- Enable @typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing to prefer ?? over || for defaults.
- Enable @typescript-eslint/strict-boolean-expressions to require explicit checks for non-boolean values in conditions.
- Optionally enable unicorn/no-unreadable-iife and no-implicit-coercion to discourage terse coercion patterns (e.g., !!value) unless justified.

Rationale:
- Preserves valid falsy values (0, "", false) and reduces hidden bugs.
- Makes intent explicit, improving readability and refactor safety.
- Aligns with TypeScript’s type-aware analysis for safer code.

## Decision:
Introduce an explicit primary person reference on Household.

- Add column Household.primary_person_id referencing Person(id).
- Enforce that primary_person_id must point to a Person who is a member of the same Household (via FK + application-level check or a partial constraint if using a HouseholdMember join).
- Enforce at most one primary per household by design (single FK); for households without a determined primary, allow null during migration; make it required for new/active households thereafter.
- Update APIs/queries to expose and consume primary_person_id for routing and UI. Add fast path lookups by indexing primary_person_id.
- Provide commands/UI to set/change the primary; reassigning updates primary_person_id atomically (no cascading deletes).
- Validation rules: the primary must be active (not removed/deceased) and part of the household; if the primary is removed, require immediate reassignment or allow temporary null with audit.
- Migration plan: backfill primary_person_id using existing heuristics (e.g., designated head-of-household field if present, oldest adult, or first registrant), flag conflicts for manual resolution.
- Optional future extension: keep HouseholdMember.role enum to support additional roles (e.g., caregiver) without changing the primary designation mechanism.

## Decision:
Adopt Taurus as the primary load-testing orchestrator to generate high-volume requests against the cluster. Tests will be authored in Taurus YAML and executed using JMeter as the underlying engine for HTTP/API workloads, with optional Selenium-driven scenarios for end-to-end flows. We will standardize execution via a pinned blazemeter/taurus Docker image to ensure reproducibility, ease of setup, and portability across developer machines and CI agents.

Taurus will collect and export artifacts (JTL/CSV, console/logs, aggregated stats) suitable for import into JMeter, and for downstream analysis in Jupyter notebooks or other BI tools. We will integrate Taurus into CI/CD to enable automated smoke/perf runs and scheduled benchmarks; larger-scale tests will run on dedicated load-generator nodes sized to avoid client-side bottlenecks.

We will avoid hard dependency on BlazeMeter SaaS; tests must run offline. Where Taurus abstractions limit access to advanced JMeter features, we will embed/raw-include JMX and custom plugins as needed. If specific scenarios demand alternate engines (e.g., Gatling), Taurus may orchestrate them, but JMeter remains the default.

Versioning, test data, and result retention will be codified in the repository with templates for common scenarios, environment parameterization, and clear SLIs/SLOs for consistent reporting.

## Decision:
Adopt a new, extensible type system centered on a shared abstract base class while preserving source and wire compatibility where feasible.

- Introduce AbstractBaseType implements Type and provides:
  - Extensible attributes/context (immutable, copy-on-write map) for metadata (security context, source id, priority, etc.).
  - Standard equals/hashCode/toString/serialization semantics.
  - Common utilities (type conversion, parsing, formatting).

- Retain interfaces Type, Command, State as markers; all concrete types must extend AbstractBaseType.

- Replace enum-backed types (e.g., OnOffType, UpDownType) with final classes exposing public static singletons (e.g., OnOffType.ON, OnOffType.OFF). Keep legacy enums as deprecated adapters that delegate to the new singletons; register bidirectional parsers/formatters to maintain text compatibility.

- Replace inheritance from java.lang.Number with NumberType extends AbstractBaseType. DecimalType, QuantityType extend NumberType. Prohibit instanceof Number; add Types.isNumber(t) and Types.asNumber(t) helpers and update framework code accordingly.

- Remove ComplexType and PrimitiveType abstractions.

- Compatibility strategy:
  - Provide a v1-to-v2 adapter layer: legacy enum instances map to new singletons at boundaries (TypeParser, State/Command bus, persistence, automation).
  - Preserve canonical toString()/parse() values and serialization identifiers.
  - Mark legacy enums and Number-based APIs as @Deprecated with migration hints.
  - Offer codemods and compile-time checks to replace instanceof Number and enum exhaustiveness with utility predicates and new constants.

- Migration and rollout:
  - Phase 1 (compat mode default): both legacy and new types accepted; log deprecation.
  - Phase 2 (opt-in strict mode flag): reject legacy enums at module boundaries.
  - Phase 3: remove adapters in a major release.

- Performance and footprint:
  - Use singletons and small immutable attribute maps; avoid per-event allocations where possible (reuse withAttribute for derived copies).

This decision enables consistent enrichment of Type values with contextual metadata, reduces boilerplate, and provides a clear path to evolve the model without breaking existing bindings.

## Decision:
Adopt a permission-request flow that never blocks the system permission dialog behind a rationale on first request, and only shows rationale after a prior denial.

- Trigger point (upload action):
  - If permission is granted → performUpload().
  - If not granted:
    - If shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) == true → show non-blocking rationale (snackbar/dialog), then immediately request permission.
    - Else → request permission immediately (covers first run and cases where the user did not select “Don’t ask again”).

- Post-request handling:
  - If granted → performUpload().
  - If denied and shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) == false → treat as “Don’t ask again” or policy-restricted; show guidance UI with a button to open app Settings (ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS) to grant permission manually.
  - If denied and shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) == true → user denied once; allow retry with rationale.

- Implementation details:
  - Use the Activity Result API (registerForActivityResult(RequestPermission)) instead of deprecated onRequestPermissionsResult.
  - Preserve current check:
    when (ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(...)) { GRANTED → performUpload(); else → proceed as above }
  - Do not show the rationale before the first permission request; shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns false on first call by design.
  - Optional “educational” pre-permission screen may be shown once per install (tracked in prefs) but must not block the immediate request on first attempt.

- Android version nuance:
  - API 33+ request the narrow READ_MEDIA_* permissions instead of READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, based on media type(s) required by upload.
  - API 29+ adhere to scoped storage; avoid requesting broad storage if not needed.

This flow ensures:
- System permission dialog appears on first request.
- Rationale is shown only after a prior denial, per platform guidance.
- Clear path for “Don’t ask again” via Settings deep link.
- Minimal friction while remaining compliant with Android UX best practices.

## Decision:
Introduce an identity broker service that integrates with ORCID via OAuth2 and issues first‑party tokens to our applications. The broker will: 
- Act as the OAuth2 client for ORCID (PKCE, state/nonce), handle consent, token exchange, refresh, and scope control, then mint short‑lived JWTs for our apps. 
- Persist the ORCID iD as the stable external identifier, along with encrypted access/refresh tokens, granted scopes, and a timestamped snapshot of the ORCID record for provenance.
- Normalize ORCID data into a canonical “Researcher Profile” domain model with source attribution and field‑level provenance to support future merging with additional sources (e.g., Crossref, institutional SSO). 
- Provide APIs to: sign in with ORCID, link/unlink ORCID to an existing local account, fetch the unified researcher profile, and emit events/webhooks for profile changes.
- Implement a provider‑agnostic adapter interface so additional identity/data providers can be added without changing consuming apps.
- Run background jobs to periodically refresh ORCID records within allowed scopes and to reconcile changes into the canonical profile using deterministic merge rules.

Security and compliance:
- Use least‑privilege scopes, encrypt tokens at rest, rotate secrets, audit all consent and linking actions, and support account deletion/data export.
- Issue short‑lived app JWTs with refresh via the broker, not by exposing ORCID tokens to client apps.

This approach enables Journal (and other apps) to adopt ORCID quickly while laying the foundation for scalable identity federation and multi‑source researcher data integration.

## Decision:
Decommission the Discourse forum and consolidate user discussions and support into existing channels (Slack for conversations; documentation site for persistent guidance).

- Rationale: The forum is not used; discussions naturally occur in person or on Slack; documentation pages suffice for long-lived information.
- Actions:
  - Take a final snapshot/backup of Discourse content and export for archival.
  - Disable new posts and set the instance to read-only for a short sunset period (e.g., 2 weeks), then shut it down.
  - Redirect the forum URL to the documentation landing page (and/or a support page describing how to get help via Slack).
  - Update links in docs, onboarding materials, and automated messages to point to Slack and the documentation site.
  - Record this change in the service catalog/asset inventory and remove associated monitoring and costs.
  - Review after 3 months to ensure support needs are met; consider a lightweight, searchable Q&A pattern in docs if gaps emerge.

## Decision:
Expose the Ingress controller via a Service of type=LoadBalancer and place a layer-4 external load balancer in front of it. The external LB (cloud-provider managed where available: AWS NLB, GCP TCP LB, Azure SLB; or MetalLB on bare metal) forwards TCP ports 80/443 to the Ingress controller pods (via NodePorts/cluster IPs as managed by the Service). TLS terminates at the Ingress controller (nginx-ingress by default, Ambassador optionally), enabling cert-manager to issue and rotate certificates and to perform ACME HTTP-01 challenges over port 80, with automatic HTTP→HTTPS redirection handled at the Ingress layer.

DNS A/AAAA records for each hostname point to the external LB address. For multi-tenancy or segmentation, additional IngressClasses may be provisioned, each with its own LoadBalancer Service and external LB, enabling traffic and blast-radius isolation as needed.

The external LB performs only L4 pass-through (no TLS termination, no HTTP routing), preserving source IP where supported. Health checks target the Service’s NodePorts. This design keeps certificate lifecycle centralized in Kubernetes, satisfies encryption-in-transit requirements, minimizes cloud-vendor coupling at L7, and remains compatible with both nginx-ingress and Ambassador.

## Decision:
Offer the template primarily as a LaTeX class file (.cls) distributed via CTAN, with a public GitHub repository that mirrors the CTAN release and provides a convenience ZIP.

Rationale:
- A document template is best modeled as a class (.cls), enforcing document-level conventions (layout, structure, defaults) while allowing users to include additional packages as needed. Packages (.sty) are better suited for reusable functionality orthogonal to document class behavior.
- CTAN distribution ensures discoverability, trust, and frictionless installation/updates via TeX Live/MiKTeX package managers across platforms.
- Versioning and dependency management are handled by TeX ecosystems; users receive consistent, vetted releases without manual download steps.
- The .cls can internally depend on (or bundle) a small .sty for reusable macros if needed, preserving extensibility while keeping the user-facing entrypoint simple.

Implementation notes:
- Maintain a single source repo with CI to build and validate TDS-compliant archives, run l3build checks, and publish to CTAN on tagged releases.
- Follow semantic versioning and provide a CHANGELOG and documentation (PDF + source).
- Provide a GitHub ZIP for users without CTAN access and to facilitate issue tracking and contributions; the GitHub main branch may contain unreleased changes while CTAN tracks stable tags.

Trade-offs:
- CTAN submission has an approval/review cycle and some overhead, but this is offset by reliability and user convenience.
- Users strictly needing ad-hoc local changes can still vendor the .cls from GitHub ZIPs; official support targets CTAN-installed versions.

## Decision:
Implement an RDF export pipeline that produces CIDOC CRM–aligned data using a provisional SDBM application profile, designed to be re-mappable once the MMM unified model is finalized.

Key elements:
- Mapping layer: Define a versioned, external mapping spec (YAML) from SDBM entities/fields to RDF predicates and classes. This allows rapid iteration as MMM modeling decisions evolve without touching application code.
- Vocabularies: Prefer CIDOC CRM/FRBRoo where applicable; supplement with Dublin Core Terms, PROV-O for provenance, SKOS for concept labels, and GeoSPARQL/WGS84 for places when available. Use provisional SDBM namespace for predicates/classes only when no community term exists.
- Identifiers: Mint stable, dereferenceable HTTP URIs for core entities (manuscripts, persons, works, places). Use skolemized blank nodes for transient events/items lacking persistent IDs.
- Serialization: Provide JSON-LD (with explicit @context reflecting the mapping) and Turtle; N-Triples for bulk ingestion. Preserve language tags and datatypes.
- Provenance and versioning: Attach dcterms:source, prov:wasDerivedFrom, export timestamp, and SDBM record updated_at. Group each export in a named graph per batch.
- Delivery: Offer periodic full dumps and incremental deltas keyed by updated_at. Document and publish mapping, contexts, and change log.
- Implementation: Use Ruby RDF.rb toolchain in Rails to materialize triples from read-only SQL views, enabling reproducible, testable exports independent of UI.

## Decision:
- Introduce a two-stage lifecycle: Draft and Published.
  - Draft: metadata-only records are allowed; visible only to the creator and authorized roles.
  - Published: requires at least one validated file attachment; visible to all users with read access.
- Restrict creation to authenticated users; anonymous users cannot create records.
- Enforce validation rules:
  - Creation: allow save as Draft without files.
  - Publish action: block unless at least one file is attached and passes integrity/format checks.
- Provide clear UI/API flows:
  - Separate endpoints/actions for create_draft, attach_file, and publish.
  - Return actionable validation errors when attempting to publish without files.
- Implement governance and hygiene:
  - Auto-expire or archive stale Drafts with no file attachments after N days (configurable), with prior notification to the creator.
  - Convert existing metadata-only records to Draft state; notify owners to attach files or they will be expired per policy.
- Apply role-based permissions:
  - Only designated roles (e.g., Curator/Owner) can publish; Editors can modify Drafts and attach files.
- Maintain audit trail of lifecycle transitions (created, file attached, published, expired) for accountability and traceability.

## Decision:
We will maintain a single repository containing both production code and end-to-end (E2E) tests with a clear, stable layout:

- /app: production code
- /e2e: end-to-end tests and tooling
- /shared: code shared between app and tests (publicly safe)
- /ops: internal CI/infrastructure scripts and secrets (private-only)

CI policy:
- On every PR: build + unit tests for /app and /shared; e2e smoke suite (no external secrets) using ephemeral/local services.
- On merge to main and release/*: full e2e suite against managed environments.
- Nightly: full e2e regression.
- Path-based CI triggers ensure changes only run relevant pipelines.

Community mirror (per ADR 4):
- Mirror main and release/* branches, including only: /app, /shared, LICENSE, README, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG, CODEOWNERS.
- Exclude from mirror: /e2e (internal environments, data), /ops, any secret-bearing or org-internal content.
- Provide public stubs/dev harness under /shared/dev to allow community to build and run unit/integration tests without internal infra.

Governance:
- CODEOWNERS split by path to enforce appropriate reviews.
- Versioning and tagging occur at the root; release notes include test coverage status.
- Any future relocations must preserve these top-level paths to keep mirror rules and CI stable.

## Decision:
Adopt environment-variable–based proxy configuration for self-hosted runners. The runner runtime will recognize and propagate the following variables to all runner components, child processes, and job containers: http_proxy, https_proxy, and no_proxy.

- Canonical variables: We will standardize on lowercase http_proxy, https_proxy, and no_proxy.
- Backward compatibility: Uppercase variants (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY) will also be read. If both cases are present, lowercase takes precedence.
- Propagation: These variables will be injected into:
  - The runner service/agent process
  - All job execution environments (shells, containers, and tools spawned by the runner)
  - Pre/post job hooks and setup scripts
- Configuration sources: Variables can be set via service configuration (e.g., systemd environment files, container env, or runner config), and the runner will pass them through unchanged unless overridden at job-level configuration.
- Security: Proxy URLs may contain credentials; they will be supported but treated as secrets. We will:
  - Avoid logging values
  - Mask these variables in any diagnostic output
  - Store them only in encrypted/secret stores where available
- Validation & diagnostics: On startup, the runner will validate proxy URLs and emit clear, non-sensitive warnings for malformed values. We will provide a lightweight self-test to verify egress via the proxy.
- Defaults for no_proxy: By default, we will append localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, and well-known metadata endpoints (e.g., 169.254.169.254) to no_proxy if not already present, while allowing administrators to fully override.
- Documentation: Provide guidance on typical configurations, precedence rules, and examples, noting that some tools may behave differently but generally honor these variables.

## Decision:
Adopt Changesets for automated versioning and release management across the Origin SDK monorepo, integrated with workspace tooling (pnpm or Yarn Workspaces).

- Use workspaces to define all SDK packages and maintain a single lockfile.
- Introduce Changesets to:
  - Track changes per package via change files.
  - Automatically determine and apply semver bumps.
  - Propagate dependent version bumps when an internal dependency changes.
  - Generate aggregated changelogs per package.
- Configure Changesets’ “linked”/“dependent” behavior to ensure transitive packages are bumped and published consistently.
- Establish a CI workflow (e.g., GitHub Actions) to:
  - Validate changesets on PRs.
  - On merge to main, run changeset version to update package versions and changelogs.
  - Publish changed packages to the registry using changeset publish.
  - Optionally tag releases and create GitHub releases.
- Enforce constraints via tooling (e.g., workspace protocol, publishConfig, and private flags) to avoid accidental cross-version drift.
- Optionally complement with Nx (or native workspace tooling) to compute the dependency graph and run affected builds/tests before releasing.

This decision removes manual dependency updates, ensures consistent version propagation across the SDK, and standardizes an auditable, automated release pipeline.

## Decision:
Establish a unified Event Contract and conventions for all Shopware events.

- Event contract: all events must implement a common ShopwareEvent interface/base DTO providing:
  - name (string), version (int), occurredAt (UTC ISO-8601), aggregateType (string), aggregateId (string), payload (opaque object), metadata (map).
  - context: salesChannelId, languageId, currencyId, appId/pluginId, tenant/shopId if applicable.
  - actor: userId/system identifier (optional).
  - correlationId, causationId, traceId/requestId, idempotencyKey (optional but recommended).

- Naming convention: Domain.Aggregate.Action.vN (e.g., Checkout.Order.Placed.v1). Event names are immutable; only version increments on breaking changes.

- Payload rules:
  - Only include data necessary for consumers; no PII unless explicitly classified and documented.
  - Reference related entities by IDs; include snapshots only when required and marked as such.
  - Strongly typed fields; stable keys; no domain logic in payloads.

- Versioning and compatibility:
  - Non-breaking additions allowed within same version.
  - Breaking changes require new version; previous versions maintained until deprecation window ends.
  - Deprecations are announced and flagged; adapters provided when feasible.

- Immutability and delivery:
  - Events are immutable, side-effect free descriptors of facts.
  - At-least-once delivery; consumers must be idempotent using idempotencyKey and aggregateId+version.
  - Ordering guaranteed per aggregateId only.

- Validation and discoverability:
  - Each event version has a JSON Schema stored in an Event Registry; CI validates events against schema.
  - SDKs/codegen can be produced from the registry.
  - Documentation includes purpose, schema, examples, privacy classification, and lifecycle.

- Publishing and subscriptions:
  - Unified publisher API; domain modules emit events only through it.
  - Subscribe via a standardized handler signature receiving the event and context.

This contract and conventions apply to all existing and new events; legacy events are mapped or wrapped to comply progressively.

## Decision:
- Adopt hashicorp/go-metrics as the SDK’s unified telemetry abstraction to minimize vendor lock-in and friction for adding/removing metrics.
- Enable telemetry as an opt-in feature via application configuration; when enabled, register a default in-memory sink that supports counters, gauges, histograms/timers for lightweight, zero-external-dependency usage.
- Provide a configurable Prometheus sink as the first external sink. When enabled, metrics are exposed via the API server at /metrics?format={text|prometheus}. The default format is text; prometheus format adheres to Prometheus exposition standards.
- Support multiple concurrent sinks (fan-out) to allow operators to combine in-memory with Prometheus (and future sinks) without code changes.
- Define consistent metric naming and labeling conventions:
  - Namespace: cosmos, Subsystem: module name, Metric: operation/outcome (e.g., cosmos_tx_check_total, cosmos_store_commit_duration_seconds).
  - Standard labels: module, result/status, error_code (if applicable), chain_id (configurable), and other bounded-cardinality tags. Prohibit unbounded-cardinality labels (e.g., tx_hash).
- Provide simple SDK helpers/middleware to register and record metrics within modules (scoped to module name), minimizing boilerplate and ensuring thread-safe usage.
- Ensure low overhead and safety-by-default:
  - No-ops when telemetry disabled.
  - Efficient hot paths (preallocated metric handles, minimal allocations).
  - Bounded histogram buckets aligned with Prometheus best practices (seconds for durations).
- Expose configuration for:
  - enable flag, global sampling rate, histogram buckets, enabled sinks, Prometheus listen address/path, basic auth/TLS (if fronted), and allowed labels.
- Make telemetry lifecycle-managed by the app: initialize sinks at startup based on config; expose metrics endpoint via existing API server; flush/close sinks gracefully on shutdown.
- Preserve backward and forward compatibility by treating metric names and labels as a public surface; changes require deprecation periods and compatibility notes.
- Leave room for future sinks (e.g., StatsD, OTLP) via go-metrics adapters without altering module code.

## Decision:
Adopt Apache License 2.0 as the default license for all archetypes-rules code repositories to maximize adoption, enable commercial and open-source reuse, and encourage contributions through clear permissions, patent grants, and explicit “AS IS” warranty disclaimers.

- Every repository must include a LICENSE file (Apache-2.0), a NOTICE file when applicable, and SPDX headers in all source files (e.g., “SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0”).
- Contributions are accepted under the same license via Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) sign-off (Signed-off-by in commits) to reduce friction while ensuring provenance. A separate CLA is not required unless mandated by a downstream integrator.
- Third-party dependencies must be license-compatible with Apache-2.0; copyleft (e.g., GPL) dependencies are disallowed unless isolated behind clearly optional adapters with no linking at build/runtime.
- Documentation defaults to CC BY 4.0; examples and snippets embedded in docs are dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 and CC BY 4.0 for ease of reuse.
- Artifacts that include data sets or schemas will specify their own SPDX identifiers when not Apache-2.0, with a strong preference for permissive licenses.
- Repositories must publish a clear LICENSE scope in the README (what is covered, exclusions), and maintain a machine-readable license metadata file (e.g., .reuse/ per REUSE specification).

This licensing policy prioritizes modular reuse, broad community and enterprise adoption, and legal clarity for security-focused components.

## Decision:
Replace bare sleeps with deterministic synchronization primitives and observable completion signals.

- Provide explicit completion signals from the SUT:
  - Expose operation status endpoints (correlated via request/operation IDs) and/or domain events (e.g., message bus topics) that indicate completion, failure, or timeout.
  - For background jobs, persist and query a status record keyed by correlation ID.
  - For UI/E2E, wait on specific network responses/state transitions rather than timers.

- Standardize a test-waiting utility:
  - Introduce a shared Await helper (e.g., Awaitility or equivalent) that polls for domain predicates with bounded timeouts, exponential backoff + jitter, and rich diagnostics on timeout (last observed state/log excerpts).
  - Provide domain-specific “awaitXyzCompleted(correlationId)” functions to encapsulate predicates and reduce duplication.

- Enforce and automate:
  - Ban Thread.sleep()/fixed waits in tests via lint/static analysis and code review checklists; allow a single escape hatch with justification.
  - Define default timeouts and polling cadences per class of operation (UI action, API write, async job) with sane global defaults and overridable per-test settings.

- Observability for test determinism:
  - Emit structured events/logs with correlation IDs at start/finish/error.
  - Surface health/readiness of async subsystems to fail fast when infrastructure is unavailable.

- Backward compatibility/migration:
  - Incrementally refactor flaky tests to use the new waits; prioritize high-flake and P1 suites.
  - Where SUT changes are infeasible short-term, use resilient polling against existing read models while scheduling SUT instrumentation as a follow-up.

Success = zero bare sleeps in tests, reduced flakiness, and reproducible completion detection aligned with domain semantics.

We will standardize all React applications on a common scaffold and enforce consistency via automation, using npm as the package manager.
