- Minimum footprint: maintain a minimum of three cells per AZ (or equivalent) to preserve disruption tolerance and rollout safety.
- Scaling cadence: reduce cell count incrementally per AZ to reach the above targets, validating after each step with one week of metrics. Reassess quarterly (or after material tenant changes) and adjust the pool to keep within targets.
- Automation placeholder: retain manual capacity adjustments for now; revisit autoscaling once feasible.

This policy reduces cost by right-sizing headroom to observed risk while ensuring resilience to a single-AZ failure and rapid weekly growth without human intervention.

## Decision:
- Introduce an explicit EXIT syscall (or HALT) as the only valid termination mechanism. Programs must invoke EXIT to finish; implicit termination is disallowed.

- Bound instruction fetches to a finite code segment. Each loaded program provides a code segment base and size; the Processor maintains PC within [base, base+size). Any fetch outside this range traps with a “MissingExit/BoundsViolation” error, terminating the program with a non‑zero status.

- The loader/linker statically validates that the program image contains at least one EXIT instruction (or syscall) and rejects images that do not. This is a structural check; reachability is not enforced.

- Remove the previous “run-off-the-end implies success” behavior. Success is only signaled by EXIT with status 0; any trap (bounds, illegal instruction, etc.) results in non‑zero termination.

- Add an optional execution watchdog (max instruction count/timeout) to guard against infinite loops that never reach EXIT, terminating with a specific non‑zero status.

- Engines/runtimes are free to implement persistence and memory models independently; the bounded code segment applies at the fetch stage and does not constrain data memory.

## Decision:
We will fix a canonical formatting standard and eliminate ongoing churn:
- The formatting conventions defined in ADR1 are the authoritative baseline.
- Prettier will be used with a pinned version and checked-in configuration. No linter-based style enforcement.
- CI will run prettier --check on changed files only; we do not mass-reformat the repository.
- Existing katas are not reformatted solely for style. A kata is reformatted only when it undergoes substantive edits, or during an intentional, versioned, repository-wide major upgrade.
- New katas must follow the current Prettier config and ADR1 conventions.
- The kata metadata will include a styleVersion field to record which formatting baseline it adheres to.
- Any change to formatting rules requires updating the Prettier config and bumping styleVersion; such changes must be rare, justified, and avoid retroactive edits.

This approach stabilizes long-lived content, enforces consistency for new work, and limits disruptive formatting-only changes.

## Decision:
Adopt a monorepo, plugin-oriented Clean Architecture with a screaming-application layout for use cases, and separate, reusable domain and adapter modules.

Top-level structure:
- domain/: bounded contexts and domain modules (entities, value objects, domain services); no dependencies on application or adapters; shared kernel when justified.
- features/: each feature as first-level directory exposing application/use-case layer (input/output ports, use-case orchestrations, DTOs, policies); no feature→feature dependencies.
- adapters/: primary (driving) and secondary (driven) adapters organized by technology (e.g., web/, cli/, db/, messaging/). Adapters may target multiple features by implementing ports; application does not depend on adapters.
- apps/: application compositions (assemblies) that select features and adapters, provide configuration/DI/wiring, and produce deployables (supports multiple app variants).
- platform/: cross-cutting technical utilities (logging, serialization, http clients) with no domain or feature knowledge.

Dependency rules:
- domain ← features ← adapters is forbidden; only inward toward domain:
  - features may depend on domain and shared kernel.
  - primary adapters depend on feature input ports.
  - secondary adapters implement feature output ports; features define outbound ports, not concrete tech.
  - apps depend on features, domain, and adapters to wire them; no module depends on apps.
- Reuse domain modules across features; never nest domain inside features.
- Adapters live outside features and may serve multiple features.
- Each module is packaged as a plugin; apps assemble plugins declaratively.

This structure preserves screaming architecture at the application layer, enforces Clean Architecture boundaries, enables multi-application assembly, and avoids artificial coupling between features via shared domain or adapters.

## Decision:
We will standardise on Ruby on Rails for building our user‑facing web applications.

Rails provides secure defaults that help prevent issues such as XSS, is widely understood within our team and the wider GDS frontend community, and is well supported by GOV.UK tooling (govuk_template, govuk_frontend_toolkit, and the future govuk-frontend) via maintained gems and engines. This choice aligns us with common GDS practice, improves maintainability and onboarding, and reduces security risk compared to lighter-weight frameworks with less secure defaults.

We will not use Sinatra for new user-facing frontends. All new web interfaces will be built in Rails and integrate GOV.UK design assets through the supported Rails packages.

## Decision:
Adopt CSS-in-JS as our primary styling approach, using tagged template literals via styled-jsx for component-scoped styles. This aligns with our Next.js stack, provides automatic scoping, colocates styles with components, and avoids additional runtime/dependency overhead. We will not adopt CSS Blocks or Stylable due to added tooling/learning complexity and divergent syntaxes, nor build a custom Webpack CSS loader due to lock-in and long-term maintenance risk. Global stylesheets remain allowed for framework-wide styles (e.g., GOV.UK). If future requirements demand cross-app theming or a design-system-oriented API that styled-jsx cannot satisfy, we will reevaluate Emotion or Styled Components; until then, styled-jsx is the default for all component-level styles.

## Decision:
We will rebuild popularity updates by creating a fresh index nightly and performing an atomic alias switch, rather than updating popularity in place.

- For each nightly run, create a new index from the current read alias with the updated popularity data applied during reindexing.
- Use Elasticsearch’s reindex/scroll pipelines with throttling and bulk sizing tuned to keep cluster load within SLOs.
- Once the new index is fully built and green (including replicas), perform an atomic alias swap to point the read/write aliases to the new index.
- Retain the previous index for a short, configurable TTL for rapid rollback, then delete it asynchronously.
- Writes occurring during rebuild continue to go to the current write alias; a dual-write shim will mirror those writes to the building index to keep them in sync until the alias swap completes.
- If dual-write fails for any batch, run a targeted catch-up sync before swapping; if health checks fail, abort and keep the current index.
- This approach avoids long-running in-place updates that touch every document, provides predictable rebuild time, eliminates index locks on the live index, and enables clean rollback.

## Decision:
Adopt OpenID Connect (OIDC) with OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code flow with PKCE for the frontend, integrated with a managed identity provider (e.g., Auth0, AWS Cognito, or Azure AD B2C). The authentication endpoints (authorize/callback/logout) will be publicly accessible over HTTPS, while application data remains protected behind authenticated sessions.

The frontend will initiate OIDC flows and receive tokens via secure redirects. Tokens will not be stored in browser storage; instead, the backend will exchange the authorization code for tokens and maintain an authenticated session using short‑lived, HTTP‑only, Secure, SameSite cookies. Refresh token rotation will be enabled to support seamless re-authentication without exposing tokens to the browser.

We will apply standard scopes (openid, profile, email) and enforce strong password policies and optional MFA at the IdP level. Logout will clear the session and call the IdP’s end-session endpoint. This approach leverages a widely adopted, modern standard, minimizes custom auth logic, supports public access, and allows future portability between providers without changing the application’s core authentication flow.

## Decision:
Adopt Cypress as the primary framework for end-to-end user journey tests. Cypress will be used for both local development (interactive runner) and CI (headless) to provide fast, reliable, deterministic tests with built-in time-travel debugging, automatic waits, screenshots, and video capture. This aligns with existing MOJ practice, reduces onboarding friction, and benefits from shared patterns and tooling.

We will:
- Standardize on Cypress for E2E suites, with parallelization in CI to control runtime.
- Stub network calls where appropriate to increase determinism, while retaining critical full-stack paths.
- Integrate with CI artifacts (screenshots/videos) and use the Cypress Dashboard if needed for flake analysis.
- Run against supported browsers (Chromium-family and Firefox) to cover primary usage.

Known constraints (multi-tab flows, cross-origin limitations, some native dialogs) will be handled via test design, plugins, or, where necessary, a small supplemental WebDriver-based suite for edge cases. Continuous review will ensure coverage and stability.

## Decision:
We will deprecate and remove the “Services” link from the search results page and make the Organisation name the single, primary navigation element to the PIMS Profile Overview page. The Organisation name will be rendered as an accessible link (including appropriate aria-labels/focus states) pointing directly to the corresponding PIMS Overview route. All references, UI copy, and help text that mentioned the Services link will be updated accordingly. Any deep links or bookmarks to the previous Services link will be audited and, where applicable, redirected to the PIMS Overview to prevent broken navigation paths. Automated tests, analytics tracking, and event schemas will be updated to reflect the new click target and to preserve/compare user engagement metrics. This consolidates navigation, reduces redundancy, and aligns with the streamlined information architecture for search results.

## Decision:
Adopt a single, human-readable “action sentence” URL style for all public-facing pages, using short imperative verbs and nouns (kebab-case), e.g.:
- /donate
- /become-a-member
- /contact
- /donation/thank-you
- /membership/confirm

Guidelines:
- Use English, kebab-case, no trailing slashes (except root), and keep paths shallow (1–2 segments).
- Prefer imperatives for entry actions (/donate), nouns for overviews (/donations), and scoped subpaths for flows and states (/donation/summary, /donation/thank-you).
- Do not expose internal operations or transport semantics (avoid /add, /get, /post).
- Use query parameters only for non-structural concerns (utm_*, tracking, optional filters).
- Reserve /api/* exclusively for API endpoints (if any), which may follow REST separately.
- Avoid locale codes in the path; handle localization via headers or app state if needed.

Migration:
- Maintain 301 redirects from all legacy routes to the new canonical paths.
- Provide a central route-alias map with tests to prevent regressions.
- Log redirect hits for a release cycle to catch missed entrants and update banners/links.

Stability and governance:
- Treat URLs as product surface; changes require review and a migration plan.
- Document each route’s purpose and ownership in the routing module.
- New routes must follow the style guide and include analytics tagging where applicable.

## Decision:
Rebuild the PaaS product pages using Next.js with static HTML export, authoring content in Markdown via MDX, and adopting the GOV.UK Design System through govuk-frontend (NPM) and shared React components.

- Content will live as Markdown/MDX files in the repo so developers and non-developers can edit via Git tooling/GUI (e.g. GitHub UI), enabling low-effort updates.
- Pages will be pre-rendered to static HTML for fast performance and progressive enhancement, then served via CDN/edge, satisfying the requirement for server-rendered output (HTML delivered from the server without client JS dependency).
- We will consume Design System assets as Node packages to ease upgrades and keep parity with ADR024 (Node alignment), enabling shared component libraries across our user-facing products.
- We will not use Gatsby due to install/runtime barriers on non-developer machines and negligible benefits for our current scope.
- The existing Ruby implementation will be decommissioned once parity is achieved and accessibility issues are addressed in the new build.

## Decision:
Adopt CoreTrackable as the single interface for event tracking across all codebases. Effective immediately:

- Freeze the Legacy Trackable Interface: no new usages are permitted.
- All new tracking code must implement CoreTrackable.
- Migrate existing implementations to CoreTrackable. Where immediate refactor is not feasible, use a LegacyTrackableAdapter that implements CoreTrackable and delegates to legacy emitters to preserve behavior.
- Enforce adoption via:
  - Lint/CI rule blocking imports/references to the legacy interface.
  - Templates and examples updated to use CoreTrackable.
  - A codemod/script to replace common legacy patterns with CoreTrackable equivalents.

Backwards compatibility:
- The adapter will maintain event schemas, identifiers, and metadata parity.
- Deprecation warnings will be emitted when the adapter path is used.
- No changes to downstream analytics contracts are expected during migration.

Rollout and removal:
- Complete migration by the defined cutoff date; remove the legacy interface and adapter in the following major release.
- Provide test guidelines and a validation checklist to ensure event parity before switching off legacy paths.

Ownership:
- The Tracking Platform team owns the interface, tooling, docs, and enforcement.

We will split Content Performance Manager (CPM) and Content Audit Tool (CAT) into independently owned applications with separate repositories, deployments, and roadmaps.

- Create two repositories: govuk-cpm and govuk-cat, each with its own CI/CD, release cadence, and on-call/ownership.
- Define clear domain boundaries and APIs for any required integration; remove implicit coupling and shared runtime dependencies.
- Extract common code (auth, UI components, analytics, utilities) into shared, versioned libraries/packages to avoid duplication while preserving autonomy.
- Separate data stores and configurations; migrate/partition existing data to app-specific schemas and revoke cross-database access.
- Establish independent infrastructure (runtime, queues, caches, feature flags, monitoring) with per-app dashboards and SLOs.
- Provide a migration plan: freeze new cross-cutting changes, tag a final monorepo release, use git filter-repo to preserve history, and cut over environments incrementally with rollback paths.
- Maintain backward compatibility during transition (API versioning, redirects), and document deprecations with timelines.
- Update documentation, runbooks, access controls, and service catalogs to reflect ownership and support paths.

This separation enables focused evolution against distinct user needs, reduces cognitive load, and allows independent scaling and delivery for each product.

## Decision:
Adopt a server-centric data access pattern with a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) that exclusively communicates with the Evidence API.

- Move critical data fetching from client useEffect to server-side (e.g., Next.js Server Components/getServerSideProps or API routes). The browser never holds API tokens.
- Introduce a BFF layer (existing proxy becomes a proper server API) that:
  - Authenticates the user (reads and verifies the ID token).
  - Derives the user’s allowed “services” from token claims/identity provider.
  - Enforces authorization by constructing and forwarding Evidence API requests with server-attached filters only. Client-supplied service filters are ignored or intersected with the allowed set.
  - Signs downstream requests with server-held credentials.
- Provide a minimal client API that calls our BFF endpoints only; remove direct calls to the Evidence API.
- Improve UX by server-rendering initial data and using incremental revalidation/streaming where supported; optionally hydrate with SWR/React Query for background refresh.
- Add guardrails:
  - Schema for BFF request validation (e.g., zod) and explicit allowlists for query params.
  - Centralized authorization middleware to compute allowed services and attach them to the request context.
  - Return 403 for disallowed service requests; do not echo raw Evidence API errors.
- Optional enhancements:
  - Short-lived server cache keyed by user+filters to reduce latency.
  - Observability (structured logs, metrics) at the BFF boundary.
  - Rate limiting/throttling at the BFF to protect the Evidence API.

This change removes tamperable client-side filters, consolidates auth and policy enforcement on the server, and reduces “loading” spinners by rendering data on the server for first paint.

## Decision:
Disallow and strip all meta-based refresh/redirect mechanisms (e.g., <meta http-equiv="refresh">) from authored and user-supplied HTML. Use server- or router-level HTTP 3xx responses for redirects and explicit client logic (fetch polling, SSE, or WebSocket) for refresh behavior. Enforce via:
- HTML sanitization that removes meta refresh tags during ingestion/build.
- Static linting in CI to fail builds containing meta refresh.
- CSP navigate-to 'self' to limit document-initiated navigations, plus URL allowlists where needed.
- Documentation and code templates that standardize on 3xx redirects and client-driven refresh patterns.

Exceptions require an explicit security/accessibility review and an approved allowlist; otherwise meta refresh is prohibited across all surfaces.

## Decision:
Use OpenShift’s built-in OAuth server as the single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for all Operate First applications.

- Applications MUST authenticate users via OpenShift OAuth/OIDC. Apps that cannot natively consume OIDC MUST be fronted by an OAuth proxy (e.g., openshift/oauth-proxy or oauth2-proxy) configured against the cluster’s OAuth issuer.
- The canonical user identity is the OIDC token subject (sub); preferred_username is used for display. Applications MUST treat sub as globally unique and stable; email is optional and not a primary key.
- Authorization and tenancy are derived from token claims (e.g., groups) and OpenShift RBAC. Application roles SHOULD map to OpenShift groups to keep user management centralized. Namespaces, quotas, and sandboxing remain enforced by OpenShift; app-level RBAC augments but does not replace cluster policy.
- User lifecycle (provisioning, deprovisioning, group membership) is managed centrally in OpenShift via configured upstream IdPs (e.g., GitHub, LDAP, SAML). Applications MUST NOT store passwords or implement standalone login flows.
- Tokens MUST be short-lived; refresh handled by the proxy or OIDC client. Applications MUST validate tokens against the OpenID Provider configuration (issuer, JWKS) and enforce scopes as configured in the OAuthClient.
- MFA, password policies, and GDPR-related identity controls are enforced at the upstream IdP integrated with OpenShift; auditing is supported by propagating user, groups, and token UID in application logs.
- Each application registers an OAuthClient in OpenShift; session continuity across apps is achieved via the shared OpenShift session/token, not app-managed credentials.

This standardizes identity across applications, enables SSO, ensures unique usernames, centralizes user management, and leverages OpenShift-native authentication and auditing.

## Decision:
We will incorporate DynamoDB access into the benchmark Lambdas to mirror common real-world patterns. Each benchmark invocation will perform a DynamoDB operation representative of typical usage: GetItem (point read), Query on a partition key with optional sort key range, and an optional BatchGet path for fan-out scenarios. We will instrument and report both SDK call latency and end-to-end Lambda latency, segmented by cold/warm starts and across configurable concurrency levels.

Implementation details:
- Use AWS SDK v3; create DynamoDBClient outside the handler for connection reuse.
- Configure via environment variables (e.g., TABLE_NAME, READ_MODE=[get|query|batch], KEY_SHAPE, ITEM_SIZE, BATCH_SIZE, ENDPOINT_OVERRIDE for local).
- Provide two execution backends:
  - Local: DynamoDB Local in Docker for fast, cost-free development/CI.
  - Cloud: AWS DynamoDB on-demand tables in a dedicated benchmark stack/account for production-like runs.
- Deterministic data seeding to control access patterns (hot/cold key mixes, skew).
- Optional GSIs to benchmark index queries.
- Keep Lambdas outside a VPC to avoid network overhead; provisioned concurrency off by default with a toggle for experiments.
- IAM least-privilege policies allowing GetItem/Query/BatchGetItem and DescribeTable on the target table/GSIs only.
- Infra defined via SAM/CloudFormation with parameters to switch backend, table capacity (on-demand vs provisioned), and data scale.
- Cost and hygiene: short TTL on seeded items where applicable and automated teardown of benchmark stacks after runs.

This approach makes the benchmarks realistic while remaining reproducible, configurable, and cost-conscious.

## Decision:
- Accept and preserve unrecognized fields in metadata to maintain forward-compatibility as required by TAP 6, 10, 14, 15, and 16.
- Implement lossless round-trip parsing/serialization: parsers must capture and retain all unrecognized key–value pairs (including nested), and serializers must emit them unchanged alongside recognized fields.
- Do not modify, drop, or reorder unrecognized fields during read/write unless an explicit normalization/canonicalization mode is requested by the caller.
- Validation will treat unrecognized fields as informational (no error); emit warnings only in verbose/diagnostic modes.
- Provide an API surface to access unrecognized fields and to opt-in to normalization that may remove or reorder them (e.g., for tooling or migration use cases), disabled by default.
- Update tests and conformance requirements to ensure unknown-field round-tripping and signature-preserving behavior where applicable.

## Decision:
- Adopt Microsoft Azure as the default PaaS provider for new services requiring the specified managed capabilities, due to:
  - EU-only data residency and transfer guarantees.
  - Availability of a fully managed, geo-distributed, multi-master datastore (Azure Cosmos DB).
  - Mature, managed messaging, serverless, notifications, communications, and observability offerings.

- Core service selections (EU regions only):
  - Structured data store: Azure Cosmos DB (multi-region, multi-master, 99.999% read availability with multi-region write, configurable consistency).
  - Messaging/events: Azure Service Bus (queues/topics with transactions, sessions) and Azure Event Hubs for high-throughput event streaming.
  - Serverless: Azure Functions (consumption or premium plans; HTTP/API, event-driven).
  - Push notifications: Azure Notification Hubs (iOS, Android, browsers).
  - Email/SMS: SendGrid and Twilio via Azure Marketplace/partners.
  - Logging/telemetry: Azure Monitor (Application Insights + Log Analytics) with centralized retention, alerting, and dashboards.

- Non-functional policies:
  - All services provisioned in EU regions with explicit data residency and data-processing boundaries enforced (including private endpoints, EU-based redundancy, and traffic restrictions).
  - Target SLAs: ≥99.99% at service level; multi-region deployment for critical workloads.
  - Use managed services by default to ensure elastic scaling, lower TCO, and minimized ops overhead.

- Governance:
  - Any deviation (e.g., selecting AWS/GCP or self-managed components) requires a separate Architectural Decision with explicit justification (e.g., unique capability, regulatory mandate).
  - Review this decision in 6–12 months to validate market evolution, cost, and operational outcomes.

## Decision:
We will remove PostgreSQL from our runtime environments and deployment pipeline until there is a concrete, active use case.

Concretely:
- Stop provisioning PostgreSQL in all environments (dev, staging, prod) by removing it from Terraform/CloudFormation, Helm charts/manifests, and environment configs.
- Delete associated secrets, security groups, networking rules, users, and backups; rotate any shared credentials that referenced the database.
- Remove app-level configuration toggles and code paths that assume a PostgreSQL connection, health checks, and readiness probes tied to it.
- Update CI/CD to skip database migrations/seed steps and any checks gated on a PostgreSQL dependency.
- Adjust monitoring/alerts/dashboards to remove PostgreSQL-related signals.
- Document a reintroduction path (versioned schema management, credentials management, backups/restore, HA/DR, observability) to enable rapid reinstatement when needed.

This reduces cost, complexity, and operational surface area during the migration. If/when a component requires PostgreSQL, we will reintroduce it explicitly for that component with a dedicated ADR and production-ready posture.

## Decision:
Change the default output layout for single-spec generation to be flat: when invoking any generate-X-client command with a single spec, emit files directly into <outputDir> without creating an extra <serviceDir> level.

Retain the per-service subdirectory layout only for multi-spec generation. Provide explicit CLI switches to control layout:
- --flat (default for single-spec): write directly to <outputDir>
- --with-service-subdir <name>: force writing into <outputDir>/<serviceDir>
- --multi: when generating multiple specs, always create per-service subdirectories

Maintain backward compatibility via a deprecation period: the old single-spec behavior will be supported for one release behind a --legacy-layout flag and will print a deprecation warning. Documentation, examples, and CI scripts will be updated to reflect the new default. Generators and templates must not assume the presence of <serviceDir>; they should derive paths from the resolved layout mode. The tool will validate that <outputDir> is empty or accept --force to overwrite.

## Decision:
Adopt a NoSQL document store as the primary persistence mechanism, specifically Azure Cosmos DB (Core SQL API) in serverless or autoscale mode to keep costs low at current scale while retaining headroom for growth.

We will model domain aggregates as self-contained documents to minimize cross-entity joins, use a well-defined partition key for scalable throughput, and leverage optimistic concurrency via ETags. Default indexing will be tuned per container to control RU costs, and TTL will be used where appropriate for ephemeral data.

Cosmos DB is chosen for:
- Flexible schema to accommodate evolving data models without costly migrations.
- Managed, highly available, and globally distributable service with minimal ops overhead.
- Fine-grained cost control (serverless/autoscale, RU-based) suitable for a simple system today.
- Rich query with SQL-like syntax and change feed support for reactive processing and projections.

If future requirements demand strong relational constraints or complex cross-entity transactions that exceed reasonable document modeling, we will introduce a relational read/write side (e.g., Azure SQL or PostgreSQL) for those specific workloads while retaining Cosmos as the source for flexible aggregates and event-like histories.

## Decision:
Decouple deployment of platform applications (paas-admin, paas-billing, paas-accounts) from paas-cf and manage them as independently deployed Cloud Foundry apps. Each application will own its build/test/release/deploy pipeline and can be promoted to environments without requiring a paas-cf change or running unrelated platform steps (terraform, bosh, CF ATs).

We will stop pinning app versions in paas-cf. To retain traceability and auditability:
- Each app will use semantic versioning and publish signed releases/tags.
- Deployments will produce an immutable, auditable “deployed versions” record (e.g., a versions manifest in a separate repo or artifact store) per environment.
- Optionally, an automated job will update a lightweight manifest in paas-cf (or a dedicated “platform-app-versions” repo) with the deployed versions via a signed bot commit to preserve a clear compatibility record.

Release permissions and approvals will be controlled in the app repos via protected branches, signed merges, and pipeline approvals for production. Rollbacks are effected by redeploying a prior signed release.

Compatibility with the platform will be validated in app pipelines against a representative environment; paas-cf no longer blocks or serializes app releases.

## Decision:
Log fetch URLs in a standardized, privacy-safe, and diagnosable way at the fetch abstraction/boundary.

- Add a fetch wrapper that accepts (url, options) and generates a requestId. It:
  - Logs a “request” event before dispatch with fields: requestId, method, host, path, redactedQuery, attempt, and caller/module if available.
  - Logs a “response” event after completion with: requestId, status, durationMs, sizeBytes (if known), and error summary on failure.

- Use structured logging (key/value JSON) to enable filtering and correlation in log tools.

- Redact sensitive data:
  - By default, strip or mask query parameters and headers containing tokens, keys, auth, cookies, emails, or other PII.
  - Provide a small whitelist of query params safe to log (e.g., page, sort).
  - Truncate very long values (e.g., 256 chars).

- Provide log levels:
  - INFO: request/response with redacted URL (host+path only, redactedQuery).
  - DEBUG: optional full canonical URL with query (still redacted), request/response bodies never logged.
  - TRACE (dev only): opt-in to log full query unredacted for specific allowlisted environments and users.

- Configuration:
  - Environment flags: FETCH_LOG_LEVEL, FETCH_LOG_SAMPLE_RATE, FETCH_LOG_ALLOW_FULL_QUERY (dev-only), FETCH_LOG_WHITELIST_PARAMS.
  - Sampling on success paths to control volume; always log failures.

- Correlation:
  - Include upstream correlation/trace IDs if present; propagate requestId in headers when appropriate.

- Implementation:
  - Centralize in fetcher module (e.g., logFetchRequest/Response helpers) to ensure consistency across all fetchers.
  - Unit-test redaction and formatting; forbid ad-hoc URL logging elsewhere via lint rule.

## Decision:
- We will describe core use cases as User Stories in the “As a [role], I want [goal], so that [value]” format, each accompanied by clear acceptance criteria written in Gherkin (Given/When/Then) to ensure testability and alignment with BDD.
- We will maintain a high-level UML Use Case Diagram (PlantUML) per domain area to visualize actors, boundaries, and relationships among use cases.
- All artifacts will be stored in the repository (docs/use-cases/) as Markdown for stories and .puml for diagrams, versioned with the code and referenced from the product backlog.
- Complex flows (optional) will include lightweight sequence diagrams or BPMN sketches when needed to clarify system interactions, kept alongside the corresponding user story.
- We will enforce a Definition of Ready requiring: user story, Gherkin acceptance criteria, and (if applicable) an updated diagram, before implementation begins.

## Decision:
We will use Project Calico as the Kubernetes CNI for the cluster network.

Calico provides:
- Native Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement for fine-grained, zero-trust service-to-service controls.
- High performance, scalable L3 routing without overlays (via BGP) and flexible data planes (BGP, VXLAN, or eBPF) to fit diverse environments.
- Mature operational tooling, broad community adoption, and strong documentation/support.
- Optional in-cluster traffic encryption (e.g., WireGuard) when required, without adopting a full mesh overlay.
- Compatibility with managed Kubernetes offerings and standard cloud/network topologies.

We will not use:
- Flannel, as it lacks first-class NetworkPolicy and is less suitable for evolving security requirements.
- Weave Net, due to additional mesh complexity and overhead relative to our needs.
- “Canal,” since Calico alone now satisfies the combined functionality (routing + policy) that Canal historically targeted.

## Decision:
Adopt the updated GDS Transport webfont in place of NTA and revise our font delivery and CSS to address the identified issues:

- Consolidate to a single font per weight that includes OpenType features (e.g. tabular numbers via tnum), removing the need for separate tabular-number font files.
- Correct the font’s vertical metrics so glyphs align properly within the bounding box, allowing us to remove CSS baseline adjustments.
- Reduce payload by serving modern formats only (WOFF2 with WOFF fallback), eliminating legacy EOT/IE-specific hinted fonts and associated build steps.
- Optimise font files via subsetting to required character sets and enabling efficient compression.

This change standardises typography, simplifies CSS, reduces file size and complexity, and drops legacy browser-specific assets that disproportionately increased maintenance and bandwidth costs.

## Decision:
Place testing utilities in a separate module, dogmatest, while keeping only the core testing interfaces (if any are required for handler signatures) in dogma.

Rationale and guardrails:
- Versioning and cadence: dogmatest will follow its own release cadence to allow rapid iteration and intentional breaking changes without forcing a dogma major release. When dogma introduces breaking changes affecting the testing surface, publish a corresponding dogmatest major version. Minor/patch releases of either may occur independently.
- Compatibility contract: maintain a clear compatibility matrix in both READMEs (e.g., dogmatest vX supports dogma vY). Enforce via go.mod constraints and CI checks (matrix testing across supported versions).
- Discoverability and ergonomics: document testing usage prominently in dogma’s README with import examples (go get github.com/dogmatiq/dogmatest) and migration guidance. Provide cohesive package naming and consistent API design to minimize friction.
- Dependency hygiene: applications that do not use the testing helpers avoid pulling test-only code; production builds depend on dogma only.
- Example alignment: examples remain outside dogma per ADR-7; test examples live alongside dogmatest.

This split preserves a stable, minimal core while enabling faster evolution of test tooling, with explicit compatibility guarantees to reduce user burden.

## Decision:
Adopt a CQRS pattern with immediate writes to the transactional purchases store and asynchronous projection to summary/analytics read models, augmented by a session-scoped delta merge to reflect in-session purchases.

- Writes: Persist new purchases synchronously to the OLTP purchases table within a transaction. Use idempotency keys to ensure exactly-once behavior per client request.
- Events: On commit, publish PurchaseLogged events. Projections (summary and analytics rollups) consume these events asynchronously and are strictly idempotent.
- Reads: Summary/analytics endpoints read from denormalized read models for performance. To reflect purchases made during the current session before projections catch up, endpoints merge a small “delta”:
  - Primary: read recent unprojected purchases from a session/user-scoped write-ahead cache (e.g., Redis keyed by user/session).
  - Fallback: if cache is unavailable, query OLTP for purchases for that user since the read model’s last processed offset/timestamp (bounded by time/count) and merge.
- Reconciliation: Once the projection has incorporated a purchase (by event offset/version), remove it from the session cache. Session cache entries have short TTLs to prevent drift.
- Consistency UX: The merged totals are authoritative and reflect all persisted purchases; no optimistic-only UI. Optionally display a subtle “updating” indicator while projections catch up.
- Integrity and resilience: All writes require durable store acknowledgement before acknowledging the client. Projections are at-least-once with idempotent upserts. Endpoints are versioned to include projection watermark for traceability and alerting.

This approach provides fast reads from denormalized stores, immediate accuracy via delta merge, and strong data integrity through transactional writes and idempotent projections.

## Decision:
- Feed-specific onboarding and processing logic will reside in the ETL layer; CDH will not contain feed-specific or frequently changing transformation rules.
- CDH will own cross-cutting, stable responsibilities: canonical schema definition and validation, contract enforcement, idempotency and dedup at canonical key level, lineage, auditing, access control, and ingestion APIs/queues.
- ETL will own all variability: parsing diverse feed formats, schema mapping to the canonical model, cleansing, normalization, enrichment, dedup before canonicalization as needed, PII handling/masking prior to CDH ingestion, and feed onboarding rules (naming conventions, file layouts, schedules).
- Logic expected to change over time or differ per feed will be implemented in ETL as configuration-first with extensible code hooks, enabling rapid updates without redeploying CDH.
- Reusable generic components and libraries will be provided for ETL to minimize duplication across feeds; CDH will provide reference contracts and validation artifacts (e.g., schema registry).
- The integration boundary is a canonical ingestion interface: ETL publishes validated canonical payloads/events to CDH via defined APIs/queues; CDH rejects non-conformant payloads with actionable errors.
- Exceptions to place logic in CDH require justification that the logic is truly generic, stable across feeds, and materially benefits from centralization (e.g., uniform reference data lookups).
- This separation maximizes agility, reduces blast radius of feed changes, simplifies CDH operations, and improves testability and scalability of feed-specific processing.

## Decision:
Define explicit lifetime controls on aggregate scopes:

- Create(): Marks the aggregate instance as existing. Engines may map this to record/materialization creation (CRUD) or to a logical “begun/existing” marker (ES). Create() must be invoked before producing domain events for a previously non-existent instance. If the instance already exists, Create() must be a no-op and succeed idempotently.

- Destroy(): Marks the aggregate instance as ended. After Destroy(), the instance must be considered non-existent for all subsequent message handling; producing events or scheduling messages must be disallowed and return an error. Engines may map this to physical deletion (CRUD), tombstoning/terminal metadata or compaction hints (ES), or other persistence-specific semantics. Destroy() must be idempotent.

- Exists(): Already provided to allow domain logic to branch without side effects.

Semantics apply during command handling within AggregateMessageHandler. Engines retain freedom to implement persistence-specific behaviors for Create/Destroy while conforming to the observable contract: Create establishes existence; Destroy permanently ends it and prevents further operations on the instance.

## Decision:
Adopt a distributed background job architecture built on a durable queue with a horizontally scalable worker fleet.

- Use AWS SQS Standard queues as the primary transport, with per-priority queues (high/normal/low) and DLQs for failure isolation; optional SNS fan-out for broadcast tasks.
- Define a versioned, immutable Job Spec (type, payload, correlation ID, idempotency key, priority, timeout, max-retries, schedule, tracing context).
- Implement workers as stateless containers (ECS/Fargate or Kubernetes) subscribing to queues; autoscale on queue depth and latency SLOs.
- Guarantee at-least-once delivery; require job handlers to be idempotent. Use visibility timeouts, exponential backoff, and bounded retries before DLQ.
- Provide a Job Orchestrator service for submission, cancellation, status, and metadata; persist job state in a relational store for query/traceability.
- Support “arbitrary jobs” via pluggable handlers and, when isolation is required, dispatch to ephemeral per-job containers with resource limits.
- Include scheduled jobs via EventBridge triggering queue messages; support rate limiting and concurrency controls per job type/tenant.
- Enforce execution policies: max runtime, memory/CPU limits, timeouts, and safe serialization; validate and sign payloads for integrity.
- Provide observability: structured logs, metrics (enqueue/dequeue rate, success/failure, age, retries), traces, and DLQ inspection with replay tooling.
- Implement multi-tenant safeguards: quotas, priorities, and fair scheduling; use separate queues/namespaces where needed.
- Secure by default: IAM-scoped producers/consumers, KMS encryption at rest, TLS in transit, and secrets via AWS Secrets Manager.
- Supply SDKs/CLI to submit and monitor jobs locally, in CI, and in production, ensuring the same entry points across dev/build/CI/CD.

## Decision:
We will use EC2-backed compute for the Bare Metal rig. EC2 provides the host-level control and flexibility we require (e.g., privileged workloads, custom AMIs, kernel/eBPF tooling, GPU and NVMe local storage, tuned networking, DaemonSets/agents) that are not available or are constrained on Fargate. This choice also enables capacity strategies (Reserved/Spot/On‑Demand mix), instance right‑sizing, and placement controls for predictable performance and improved cost efficiency at sustained load.

Operationally, we will:
- Manage capacity via Auto Scaling Groups/Managed Node Groups with mixed instance policies (Spot + On‑Demand) and multiple instance families/sizes for resilience.
- Standardize base AMIs with required drivers, observability agents, and security hardening.
- Use host-level features (ENI limits tuning, enhanced networking, EBS/NVMe choices) to meet performance SLOs.

Fargate may be used selectively for isolated, bursty, or compliance-constrained workloads that benefit from its separation and zero node management, but it will not be the default for Bare Metal rig compute.

## Decision:
- Assets folder: Use docs/adr/assets with one subfolder per ADR, named by its zero-padded number, e.g., docs/adr/assets/0007/. Shared, cross-ADR assets live in docs/adr/assets/shared/. Link assets via relative paths from the ADR file.
- ADR filename pattern: Keep docs/adr/NNNN-title-with-dashes.md (zero-padded number; lowercase; ASCII; words separated by dashes; no punctuation beyond dashes).
- ADR title style: The first line is a single H1 heading with the human-readable title in sentence case, without the ADR number, e.g., "# Choose PostgreSQL for OLTP storage". The title should mirror the filename’s words with spaces, may include punctuation as needed, and should be concise and action-oriented.

## Decision:
- Maintain release notes in-repo, versioned with the code.
- For each active release branch, keep a RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y.md (Markdown) file describing all changes included on that branch since it was cut from main. Any backport to that branch must include an update to this file.
- On cutting a new release branch:
  - Copy the template from main to RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y.md on the branch.
  - On main, append the previous cycle’s RELEASE_NOTES to HISTORY.md and reset the template for the next cycle.
- The main branch always contains RELEASE_NOTES-next.md as a template/scratchpad for the upcoming branch cut.
- For WMDE intermediate tagged releases on a given release branch (e.g., -wmde.N), add a dated subsection to that branch’s RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y.md that summarizes the delta since the previous tag. If there are no changes beyond upstream, include a “No changes beyond upstream” note.
- Structure each entry with standardized sections: Breaking changes (mandatory when applicable), Upgrade notes (mandatory when applicable), Features, Improvements, Bug fixes, Security, Deprecations, and Known issues. Link to tasks/PRs.
- Every change that is user-visible or operationally relevant must include a release-notes update as part of the PR; reviewers enforce compliance.
- On tagging a release, use the corresponding section from RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y.md to populate the Git tag/Release page and Docker image description via automation.

## Decision:
- Decouple build and deploy into separate pipelines/stages to enable “build once, deploy many.”
- The Build pipeline produces immutable, versioned artifacts (e.g., packages, metadata bundles), runs tests, generates SBOM/provenance, and publishes to a centralized artifact repository.
- The Deploy pipeline consumes a selected artifact version without rebuilding, supports environment-specific configuration via variables/parameters/overrides, and can be triggered manually or via promotion rules.
- Introduce artifact promotion across environments (e.g., Dev → QA → Staging → Prod) with approvals and audit trails; rollback is achieved by redeploying a prior artifact version.
- Parameterize deployments to support configuration-only changes where applicable, avoiding rebuilds when source/binary hasn’t changed.
- Implement artifact retention policies, naming/versioning conventions (e.g., commit SHA + semantic version), and metadata tagging for traceability.
- Optimize long-running builds with caching and parallelization, but keep deploy steps fast, idempotent, and environment-isolated.
- Update CI/CD templates and documentation to reflect the new split, selection of artifact versions, and promotion workflow.

## Decision:
Switch the primary unit of measurement for performance and quality metrics from content_id to base_path for Guides and Travel Advice.

- Make base_path the primary key in metrics storage, rollups, and dashboards; retain content_id as a secondary attribute for traceability and debugging.
- Backfill the last 3+ months by regrouping existing metrics under base_path, consolidating multiple content_ids that have shared the same base_path.
- Normalize base_path (case, trailing slashes) and resolve aliases to a canonical path; attribute historical metrics to the canonical base_path.
- Handle path changes and redirects:
  - When base_path changes, migrate/merge prior metrics to the new canonical base_path.
  - Maintain a mapping table (content_id ↔ historical_base_paths ↔ canonical_base_path) to ensure consistent attribution over time.
- Update ETL pipelines and event instrumentation to emit/derive base_path at collection time; add guardrails to drop or quarantine events without a resolvable base_path.
- Revise schemas, queries, and cached aggregates to be keyed by base_path; update dashboards, alerts, and SLAs accordingly.
- Define exceptions: products outside Guides/Travel Advice may continue on content_id until validated needs emerge; support dual-key exports during the transition.
- Provide validation and reconciliation jobs to detect attribution drift between content_id and base_path, with monitoring to ensure no loss or duplication during backfill and future path changes.

## Decision:
The repository README at the root will be the authoritative entry point for onboarding and daily use. It will be concise, task-oriented, and consistently maintained, with deep links to richer documentation.

The README will include:
- Purpose and scope in one paragraph.
- High-level architecture overview with a diagram (embedded image from /docs).
- Prerequisites and a copy-paste Quick Start (single command or short sequence) to build and run locally.
- Common developer tasks: run, test, lint, format, seed data, and debug.
- Troubleshooting for first-run issues.
- Links to detailed docs: /docs site, ADR index, contribution guidelines, coding standards, release notes.
- Project status badges (build, coverage, latest release).

To ensure currency and accuracy:
- The README is the single source of truth for Quick Start; CI executes the Quick Start on every merge to validate it.
- Auto-generated sections (service table from docker-compose, CLI reference, versions) are produced by a script (e.g., scripts/update-readme.mjs) and must be run via npm run docs:readme; CI fails if the generated diff is not committed.
- A README template is shared across repos to ensure consistency but allows project-specific overrides.
- Any change that affects setup, commands, or architecture must include a README update in the same PR.

Ownership and governance:
- The Tech Lead (or designated Docs owner) is responsible for README currency.
- The README links to living docs in /docs (MkDocs) to keep the README brief; detailed guides reside there.
- The README first-run time must be ≤10 minutes on a clean machine; regressions are blocked by CI.

## Decision:
Adopt a multi-site monorepo model within dotcom-rendering, enabling teams to build and operate their sites on a shared frontend platform while enforcing strict boundaries to avoid past divergence.

- Platform-first: Centralize and own the tooling (Node/TypeScript, ESLint/Prettier, testing, bundling, release, observability) as versioned “platform” packages/configs consumed by all sites.
- Workspaces and isolation: Represent each site as an isolated workspace/package with clear ownership. Only share code via approved platform or shared libraries; prohibit cross-site imports via tooling-enforced dependency constraints.
- Standardized composition: Provide a common application shell (routing, auth, layout primitives, design tokens) to ensure consistent UX where appropriate, with site-level overrides guarded by conventions.
- Scaffolding and upgrades: Ship a site template and generators to bootstrap new sites. Manage platform changes via versioned releases, automated upgrade guides/codemods, and CI break-glass windows for coordinated migrations.
- CI/CD and quality gates: One pipeline with shared caching, artifact standards, and consistent checks (lint, type, test, bundle size). Require green platform checks for all sites; treat platform regressions as blocking.
- Governance: Define ownership and change control (RFCs for breaking changes, CODEOWNERS for platform and sites). Publish SLAs for platform maintenance and deprecation policy.
- Observability: Provide standard logging/metrics/tracing/error reporting and performance budgets enforced in CI.
- Rollout: Pilot with 1–2 candidate sites, measure build times, DX, and coupling. Proceed if complexity remains manageable; otherwise, revert to separate repos with a shared tooling distribution.

This preserves autonomy, reduces duplication, and maintains consistency through enforced platform boundaries.

## Decision:
Adopt the Serverless Framework with the serverless-offline plugin to run all Lambda functions locally, emulating API Gateway and direct invokes. Start the offline server with Node’s inspector enabled (node --inspect/--inspect-brk) to allow step-through debugging from VS Code. Provide npm scripts (e.g., sls offline start --stage local --reload) and a VS Code launch configuration to attach breakpoints. For downstream services, use local emulators (e.g., serverless-dynamodb-local) or point to localstack/AWS endpoints via environment variables to maintain parity. This enables rapid, deployment-free iteration and comprehensive local testing of all Lambdas and their event triggers.

## Decision:
We will use wrapper scripts selectively, with clear standards to retain their benefits while minimizing opacity and lock-in.

- Adoption criteria: create a wrapper only when it (a) composes multiple tools, (b) encodes repeatable SOPs, or (c) enforces security/compliance. Prefer documentation/templates over wrappers when value is marginal.
- Design principles: thin, composable, idempotent, non-interactive by default, cross-platform where feasible. Minimize external dependencies.
- Transparency: provide --verbose to echo underlying commands, --dry-run to print without executing, and --explain to show decision logic. Default to human-readable logs with optional --json output.
- Escape hatches: forward unknown args to underlying tools; support --raw or WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 to opt out. Document equivalence to underlying commands.
- UX consistency: shared flag conventions (--help, --verbose, --dry-run, --json, --yes), exit codes, and structured error messages. Autocomplete provided where practical.
- Documentation: each wrapper ships with rationale, prerequisites, examples, mapping to underlying tools, and edge cases. Keep a central catalog of wrappers and their ownership.
- Quality: enforce shellcheck, shfmt/black for language, unit/integration tests (e.g., bats), and CI. Version wrappers with SemVer; maintain CHANGELOG and deprecation policy.
- Security: default to safe operations (e.g., secret encryption with sops), avoid leaking secrets in logs, and require explicit confirmation for destructive actions (or --yes).
- Operations: keep wrappers small and maintainable; prefer libraries for shared logic. Periodically review wrappers for necessity and deprecate when tool UX improves.

This policy enables productivity and standardization while preserving flexibility and user familiarity with underlying tools.

## Decision:
We will run Terraform from Jenkins for all ongoing infrastructure changes across environments and accounts, with a one-time, minimal bootstrap executed manually.

- Bootstrap
  - Perform a single, audited manual Terraform apply from a developer machine to provision:
    - A management account Jenkins stack (compute, networking, Jenkins controller/agents)
    - Per-environment remote state (S3 buckets with versioning and encryption, DynamoDB state locks)
    - Cross-account IAM roles and policies that Jenkins will assume to manage each environment
  - Store this bootstrap Terraform in a separate repo with clear runbooks; future updates to bootstrap will be run from Jenkins once Jenkins is available.

- Ongoing operations
  - All subsequent Terraform plans/applies run in Jenkins pipelines.
  - Jenkins assumes least-privilege, cross-account IAM roles for each target environment (no long-lived user credentials).
  - Use separate Terraform states per environment/account; do not use workspaces for isolation.
  - Enforce Git-based change control: PR review required, with Jenkins executing plan on PR and gated apply on main after approval.
  - Maintain remote state in per-environment S3 buckets with DynamoDB locking; state access scoped via IAM.
  - Capture and retain Jenkins build logs and Terraform plans/applies for auditability.

- Deployment flow
  - Pipelines promote changes through environments in order (e.g., dev → staging → prod) with manual approvals where appropriate.
  - Sensitive variables managed via Jenkins credentials/Parameter Store/Secrets Manager; no secrets in state where avoidable.

This resolves the chicken-and-egg problem by limiting manual work to an initial, minimal bootstrap, after which Jenkins manages all Terraform-driven infrastructure, including its own updates.

## Decision:
We will standardize on the Mozilla IT SRE VPC module (itsre-deploy/modules/vpc) for all VPC provisioning and deprecate our prior VPC composition from ADR #5. All new VPCs and any refactors will use this module as the single source of truth.

Subnet model alignment:
- We adopt the module’s public/private subnet strategy and defaults.
- Mapping from ADR #5:
  - “Public” subnets → module public subnets (routed via IGW).
  - “Private (egress)” subnets → module private subnets with NAT enabled.
  - “Isolated (no internet)” subnets → provisioned via the module by disabling NAT for those subnets/environments (e.g., create_nat_gateways=false or equivalent variable pattern) and using separate route tables without IGW/NAT routes, where supported by the module.
- NAT gateway strategy will follow the module’s configuration:
  - Default to one NAT gateway per AZ for production-grade HA.
  - Allow single NAT gateway for non-prod to reduce cost, configured via environment tfvars.

Operational constraints:
- Subnet counts and CIDR splits will be derived from the module inputs (AZ list and base CIDR) to ensure consistency across environments.
- Standard tags (e.g., Environment, Stack, Owner, CostCenter) and Name conventions will be passed via module variables and enforced uniformly.
- IPv6, flow logs, DNS hostnames/support, and VPC endpoints will be enabled/managed per module capability and environment needs through tfvars.

Migration:
- Existing stacks will transition during scheduled maintenance by recreating subnets/route tables as needed; where immutable changes are required, blue/green VPC cutover will be used.
- ADR #5 guidance on subnet layout is superseded by this module’s approach; any exceptions must be explicitly approved and documented with module overlays or follow-up ADRs.

## Decision:
Adopt a “hamburger” architecture: a shared, consistent web experience on top; a shared, authoritative data layer for common records on the bottom; and independently deployable services in the middle.

We will establish Common Record Services (CRS) for shared entities (e.g., organisations/customers, users/contacts, suppliers, commercial agreements/frameworks, catalog items) that act as the single source of truth. Each CRS will expose versioned, well-documented APIs and publish domain events; all other services must consume these APIs/events rather than re-keying or duplicating ownership of common data.

For each common record, we will nominate a single system of record (which may be an existing SaaS such as Salesforce or a purpose-built CRS) and define canonical identifiers. Services may cache data locally for performance but must treat CRS as authoritative and reconcile via events. Point-to-point file transfers and manual re-entry for common records are to be eliminated.

All services must:
- Make their own data available via APIs and publish events for material changes.
- Use canonical identifiers for common records.
- Integrate via an event bus for propagation and eventual consistency, avoiding tight coupling.
- Conform to shared API standards (versioning, pagination, error models), schema registry, and change-control policies.
- Implement centralised authn/authz, auditing, and data protection controls aligned with the shared platform.

We will phase in CRSs for the highest-value common records first, provide migration and mapping from legacy data sources, and enforce adoption for new services. Existing systems will integrate over time through adapters until consolidation is complete.

## Decision:
- We will standardize our component prop APIs around a small, consistent set of conventions and deprecate outliers.
- Styling:
  - Keep sx as the single escape-hatch for inline theming/system styles. Type: SystemStyleObject (no unions, no implicit “any”).
  - Remove/replace all Styled System shorthands (e.g., p, m, color) with sx. Provide codemods and deprecation warnings; remove in the next major release.
  - Support className and style on all DOM-backed components; merge order: default styles < sx < style; className is appended last.
- Refs:
  - Components that render a focusable/native element or expose imperative focus/measure APIs will support ref via React.forwardRef.
  - For composites, expose explicit imperative handles where needed (useImperativeHandle).
- Passthrough and DOM props:
  - DOM-backed components accept standard HTML attributes via React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"tag"> with explicit Omit for conflicts.
  - Accept data-* and aria-* props on all components; do not blanket-spread unknown props to non-DOM children.
- Polymorphism:
  - Default to a fixed underlying element. Only introduce as polymorphism where necessary for accessibility/composition; when used, preserve typing and ref forwarding.
- Naming and semantics:
  - Boolean props prefixed with is/has; events prefixed with on and pass a single event-like argument.
  - Controlled/uncontrolled patterns follow React conventions (value/onChange; defaultValue for uncontrolled). Do not mix.
  - Avoid magic/implicit props; prefer explicit, documented options over stringly-typed flags.
- Backwards compatibility and rollout:
  - Document these rules in CONTRIBUTING and component templates.
  - Add ESLint/TS rules where feasible; provide codemods for styled-system removal and ref standardization.
  - Ship deprecations with warnings in a minor, remove in the next major.

## Decision:
Adopt Electron to package and distribute the application as an offline-first desktop app.

- Bundle the entire site (static assets and runtime) inside an Electron shell so it runs without network connectivity and without relying on GitHub Pages.
- Use a single codebase with two build targets:
  - Web: continues to build a browser version for development/demo.
  - Desktop: Electron build that loads local assets (file://) and does not require an internet connection.
- Use electron-builder to produce cross-platform artifacts (macOS .dmg/.zip, Windows .exe/.msi, Linux AppImage/.deb) and sign binaries for each platform.
- Automate builds with GitHub Actions; publish installers to GitHub Releases. Use release channels (alpha/beta/stable) mapped from branches/tags as needed to replace the prior multi-branch Pages approach.
- Enable auto-updates via electron-updater when connectivity exists; otherwise, the app remains fully functional offline using the bundled assets.
- Security hardening: disable Node integration in renderer, enable contextIsolation, use a strict Content Security Policy, load only from app:// or file://, and validate any external links/protocols.
- App data: persist user data to Electron’s userData directory; avoid local servers and prefer filesystem-backed storage/caching for offline behavior.
- Maintain a shared build system and component library to keep parity between web and desktop targets, minimizing divergence and simplifying updates to UI and dependencies.
- Versioning and release process: semantic versioning, changelogs per release; CI enforces reproducible builds.

This approach simplifies distribution, removes GitHub Pages limitations, and meets the requirement for a fully self-contained, offline-capable application while preserving an easy path for future updates.

## Decision:
Adopt Python end-to-end: use the official GOG Galaxy 2.0 Integration SDK for ecosystem integration and build the UI with Qt 6 via PySide6 and QML. This keeps integration straightforward (first-class support in Python), delivers a rich, modern-looking, cross‑platform UI with Qt/QML, and introduces a less familiar but valuable technology (QML/Qt) to learn without adding multi-language/IPC complexity.

## Decision:
- We will not write or maintain controller unit specs. They provide low confidence, are tightly coupled to implementation, and duplicate request-level coverage.
- We will test controller behaviour via request-style tests that exercise the full HTTP boundary (routing, middleware, params parsing, authentication/authorization, and rendering). In this codebase, these will use Rack::Test helpers (get/post/etc.) rather than RSpec Rails request specs (type: :request).
- We will place new tests alongside existing Rack::Test request suites and follow their conventions for helpers and argument shapes.
- We will unit-test business logic in plain objects (services, interactors, validators, query objects). Controllers should remain thin and defer to these units, which are covered by focused unit tests. This splits responsibilities: request specs assert wiring/behaviour at the boundary; unit specs assert domain logic.
- We will mock/stub only true external boundaries in request tests (e.g., external APIs, message buses, time, randomness) and avoid mocking internal controller dependencies. For domain logic, prefer real collaborators in request specs and mock them only in unit tests.
- We will deprecate existing controller specs. When touching code covered by controller specs, migrate coverage to request and unit tests and delete the old controller specs.
- We will add lightweight smoke checks for routes and serialization where appropriate in request specs to avoid duplication, asserting observable outcomes (status, headers, body) rather than internal calls.
- We will document Rack::Test argument conventions in testing guidelines to prevent confusion with RSpec Rails request spec APIs.

## Decision:
- Use DDO-wise expenditure as the primary extraction path to avoid instability in the Grant-wise pages, since both represent the same data across different hierarchies.
- Build and maintain a reliable DDO-to-Grant mapping (from official codebooks/master data) to reconstruct Grant-level aggregates post-ingestion.
- Implement resilient scraping with throttling, randomized delays, retries with exponential backoff, and checkpointing to handle intermittent crashes.
- Persist raw HTML/JSON responses and parsed normalized records with lineage metadata (source section = DDO-wise, fetch timestamp, URL, parameters) to ensure auditability.
- Validate parity by periodically sampling and reconciling reconstructed Grant aggregates against Grant-wise pages when available/stable; alert on variance beyond threshold.
- Design idempotent ingestion keyed by fiscal year, DDO code, head/subhead/month to avoid duplicates and support re-runs.
- Schedule scraping during off-peak hours with incremental updates based on “last updated” signals where available.
- Keep a controlled fallback to Grant-wise extraction only when DDO-wise endpoints are unavailable, with stricter rate limits and circuit breaker to prevent repeated crashes.
- Document hierarchy transformation logic and maintain versioned mapping to accommodate code changes across years.

## Decision:
The starter seed will remain unopinionated about state management and will not include any state-management library as a dependency by default. This avoids lock-in, reduces maintenance churn as trends evolve, and keeps the initial bundle lean.

To support teams selecting the best tool for their context, we will:
- Provide minimal, optional examples using React Context + hooks for local/global state patterns.
- Document integration guides and recipes for popular options (e.g., Redux Toolkit, Zustand, MobX, Recoil), including TypeScript patterns and testing tips.
- Expose clear extension points (prop-driven components, lifted state patterns, event/callback contracts) and a simple async data layer abstraction to be adapted to chosen libraries.
- Ensure build and lint configurations do not constrain library choice.

Projects may adopt a state library when warranted by requirements (complexity, team familiarity, ecosystem fit). The seed’s documentation will include decision criteria and migration guidance to change or remove a chosen library later.

## Decision:
Adopt quantile-based discretization of the gamma(shape, scale) distribution into K bins (default K=256) and assign categorical labels as integer bin indices. Bin edges are computed from the gamma CDF inverse (percent point function) to ensure approximately equal probability mass per bin and smooth transitions across categories. The following will be standardized:
- Parameters: shape, scale, K are explicit and versioned; random seed optional.
- Metadata: persist bin edges, parameters, K, and RNG state with outputs for reproducibility.
- Sampling: draw U~Uniform(0,1), map to bin via edges; optional intra-bin jitter (uniform within edges) when a continuous proxy is required.
- Stability: identical parameters and seed yield identical categories; monotonicity guaranteed.
- Extensibility: allow alternative binning (fixed-width, custom edges) via configuration, with defaults remaining quantile-based for smoothness.

## Decision:
Adopt Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR) as the standard format.

- Template: MADR 3.x structure with sections: Title, Status, Deciders, Date, Context and Problem Statement, Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Decision Outcome (Chosen option, Rationale, Consequences), Pros/Cons per option, Links.
- Repository layout: place ADRs under docs/adr/.
- Filenames and numbering: sequential, zero-padded, kebab-case title (e.g., 0001-use-madr.md). Keep numbers stable; superseding ADRs receive new numbers.
- Status lifecycle: proposed → accepted/rejected → deprecated/superseded. Never edit accepted ADR content except for metadata and link updates.
- Cross-references: each ADR must link to related and superseded/superseding records.
- Process: create a new ADR via pull request for any significant architectural decision or change to an accepted decision. Discussion happens in the PR; merge to accept. Minor editorial fixes may be committed directly.
- Ownership: the architecture owner curates consistency; all contributors may author ADRs.
- Automation (optional but encouraged): use adr-tools or repository templates to scaffold new ADRs and maintain an index (README.md) listing ADRs in numeric order.
- Language/style: concise, decision-focused, actionable; avoid design details that belong in design docs; record enough context to understand trade-offs later.

## Decision:
Adopt the Central Security Logging Service (CSLS) as the single system of record for audit/security events and forward all relevant GOV.UK PaaS audit logs to CSLS via Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

- Deploy and manage a CloudWatch Logs agent (or Fluent Bit with CloudWatch output) as a BOSH addon on the BOSH Director and all BOSH-managed instances to tail /var/vcap/sys/log/* audit/security logs (e.g., BOSH Director kernel audit, CredHub, UAA, CF UAA, CF Cloud Controller security).
- Emit logs in structured JSON and enrich with metadata: environment, foundation, BOSH deployment, instance group, instance ID/az, region, app/component, and log source path.
- Create per-source CloudWatch Log Groups with a consistent naming convention (e.g., /govukpaas/<env>/<deployment>/<component>) and a minimum 90-day retention (configurable by Security).
- Enable KMS encryption for log groups; restrict access via least-privilege IAM roles attached to instances/agents.
- Configure CSLS-provided subscription filters on the log groups to stream to CSLS/Splunk.
- Implement buffering and backoff in the agent to tolerate network/service disruption; monitor agent health and ingestion errors via metrics/alerts.
- Maintain a controlled allowlist of collected files and explicitly exclude non-audit or sensitive payload content where inappropriate.
- Validate end-to-end delivery with Cyber Security (field mappings, timestamps, and parsing) before enabling for production, and review quarterly.

This consolidates audit visibility, aligns with existing Cyber Security tooling, and avoids building a parallel logging stack.

## Decision:
Require PHP >= 8.2. Constrain Composer to "php: ^8.2" and run CI against the latest patch releases of 8.2, 8.3, and 8.4. We will only support PHP branches that are in active or security support per php.net/endoflife (or endoflife.date/php). When a supported PHP branch reaches EOL, we will drop it in the next minor release if doing so is non-breaking, otherwise in the next major release. New language features may be adopted as long as they are available in the minimum supported version. We will not provide compatibility shims for EOL PHP versions. The minimum PHP version may be raised only in a minor or major release with clear changelog notes and a deprecation notice at least one release in advance when feasible.

## Decision:
We will adopt continuous delivery with frequent, small, reversible releases as our default strategy.

- Cadence: Release as soon as a change meets the Definition of Done and passes all automated checks; aim for multiple releases per week (or daily) rather than batched trains.
- Batch size: Prefer small, independent changes behind feature flags/toggles to decouple deployment from release and enable safe progressive exposure.
- Rollout strategy: Use canary/gradual rollouts with automated health checks; enable fast, automated rollback/revert on failure.
- Quality gates: Require green CI (unit, integration, security, performance smoke) and passing release readiness checks. No manual sign-off unless risk-flagged.
- Compatibility: Maintain backward-compatible interfaces and use migration patterns (expand/migrate/contract) to avoid coordinated downtime.
- Observability: Instrument releases with versioned telemetry and user impact metrics; define SLO/error budgets to throttle or pause releases when breached.
- Governance: Keep release notes and changelogs automated; use semantic versioning; enforce WIP limits to prevent queuing and risk accumulation.
- Exceptions: Larger or high-risk changes must be sliced or guarded; if not possible, schedule a dedicated, mitigated release window.

## Decision:
Adopt Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0) across all deliverables to make upgrade impact clear and predictable.

- Version format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 3.4.2).
  - MAJOR: increment for any breaking change (public API, CLI, configuration, supported platforms).
  - MINOR: backward-compatible feature additions and deprecations.
  - PATCH: backward-compatible bug fixes and security updates.

- Pre-release and metadata:
  - Pre-releases use hyphen identifiers (e.g., 3.5.0-beta.1, 3.5.0-rc.2).
  - Optional build metadata uses + (e.g., 3.5.0+build.sha.abc123).

- Deprecation policy:
  - Features/APIs may be deprecated in MINOR releases with clear warnings and documentation.
  - Removals occur only in the next MAJOR release after at least one MINOR cycle of deprecation notice (or a defined timeframe, e.g., 90 days for hosted services).

- Compatibility guarantees:
  - Within a MAJOR line, MINOR/PATCH upgrades maintain backward compatibility.
  - Public artifacts (API schemas, CLI flags, file formats) are versioned and tested for compatibility accordingly.

- Release management and communication:
  - Each release includes human-readable release notes and a CHANGELOG with categorized changes (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security).
  - Git tags use vX.Y.Z and are embedded in build artifacts and package manifests.
  - Automation enforces correct version increments based on change type (e.g., via conventional commits and CI checks).

This policy standardizes expectations, reduces upgrade risk, and provides clear signaling of breaking vs non-breaking changes.

## Decision:
- Introduce a Parameter Object (e.g., PresenterConfig/PresenterDeps) to encapsulate initializer parameters; keep only truly mandatory parameters in the constructor, pass the rest via the config object.
- Provide a fluent Builder for the config object to handle optional parameters, sensible defaults, and readability.
- Centralize presenter creation behind a Factory/Assembler to minimize call-site churn and to evolve dependencies without breaking callers.
- If a DI container is available, the Factory integrates with it to resolve shared services; otherwise, the Builder remains the primary construction mechanism.
- Deprecate existing long initializers; add an overload accepting the config object and mark the long-form constructors for removal in a future release with a migration guide.
- Enforce immutability of the config once built to prevent runtime inconsistency; validate required invariants at build time.

## Decision:
Co-locate Terraform code with the services it provisions and deprecate the separate nulterra repository.

- Move each service’s Terraform into its owning repository under infra/terraform/<project> (or as defined in ADR 0010), keeping environment data and modules consistent with existing conventions.
- Reserve a separate shared repository only for reusable, environment-agnostic Terraform modules; consume them via versioned module sources. All environment- or service-specific stacks live alongside the service.
- Perform a one-time migration preserving history using git subtree or git-filter-repo into each target repo. Tag and archive nulterra as read-only with a clear deprecation notice and links to new locations.
- Update CI/CD to run terraform fmt/validate/plan/apply from the colocated paths; enforce via pre-commit hooks and CODEOWNERS for infra directories.
- Standardize repo structure:
  - infra/terraform/
    - modules/ (service-local reusable modules)
    - stacks/ (per-environment stacks referencing shared and local modules)
    - data/ (tfvars as per ADR 0010)
- Establish branch protection and mandatory reviews for Terraform changes; plans must be visible in PRs.
- Document migration steps and developer workflow in the engineering handbook.

Rationale: colocating IaC with service code reduces coordination overhead, improves code discovery and ownership, aligns changes in lockstep, and simplifies reviews and releases.

## Decision:
- Migrate the Pact Broker from Heroku to our AWS-hosted platform to align with our long-term hosting strategy and avoid free-plan constraints.
- Host Pact Broker as a containerized service within our platform (e.g., GPaaS/Cloud Foundry app or ECS), fronted by our standard ingress and observability stack.
- Use AWS RDS PostgreSQL for the Pact Broker database with Multi-AZ, automated backups, and encrypted at rest and in transit.
- Manage all infrastructure and app configuration via Terraform, including networking (private subnets, security groups), RDS, secrets, and app deployment configuration.
- Restrict access to internal networks only; expose via VPN/private ingress and enforce authentication using the same IdP as the rest of the platform.
- Implement a zero/low-downtime migration: snapshot/export Heroku Postgres, import into RDS, run schema migrations, switch DNS/endpoint with a short freeze window, and validate integrity before decommissioning Heroku.
- Set up monitoring and alerts for uptime, latency, error rates, DB health, storage, and row growth; define retention policies and pruning jobs for old pacts/verifications to control DB size.
- Decommission the Heroku app and database after a stable burn-in period and documented rollback plan.

- Provision OPG Metrics as a fully self-contained stack within the opg-management account, avoiding any shared runtime or data-plane resources with other products.
- Create a dedicated VPC (per environment) with isolated subnets, routing, NAT/IGW, security groups, and no default VPC peering; establish connectivity to other services only via explicitly approved interfaces (e.g., VPC peering/Transit Gateway) with tightly scoped routes and security controls.
- Use dedicated service components (e.g., ECS/EKS/EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, CloudFront, CloudWatch, KMS keys, SNS/SQS) with no multi-tenant clusters or shared databases.
- Manage everything with Terraform using environment-specific workspaces/state, reusable account-agnostic modules, and variable-driven configuration to enable straightforward migration to another AWS account.
