This keeps the solution within our existing Go ecosystem, avoids introducing additional infrastructure/services, and is actively maintained.

We will implement:
- Form-based PDFs: Fill AcroForms using UniPDF and flatten by default; enable a mode to skip flattening when fillable forms are required.
- Composition/merging: Use UniPDF to merge existing PDFs and raster images (e.g., PNG/JPEG) into one document.

If future layout needs exceed form templates (e.g., complex paginated layouts best authored in HTML/CSS), we will reassess introducing gotenberg as an ancillary service for HTML-to-PDF conversion; until then, we will avoid it to minimize infrastructure.

We acknowledge UniPDF’s commercial licensing; we will proceed contingent on acceptable licensing terms. If licensing becomes prohibitive, our fallback is an open-source path: pdfcpu for merging and page-level operations, combined with gofpdf for programmatic layout (with the tradeoff of higher development effort and no robust form support).

## Decision:
Capture essential host details at enrollment time instead of relying on post-enrollment distributed queries.

- Extend the enrollment flow to include a mandatory “bootstrap host snapshot” payload collected locally by the agent before/at enroll. If osquery cannot include it in the TLS enroll request, the agent must POST it immediately after enroll to a new /api/hosts/bootstrap endpoint with the same auth context.
- Minimum snapshot fields: host UUID, hostname, platform, OS name/version/build, kernel version, osquery version, hardware model, CPU model/count, memory (total), primary disk size, IPs, MACs, cloud/instance metadata (provider, instance_id, region/zone), and agent config hash. Include a schema_version and collected_at timestamp.
- Server behavior:
  - Create the host record at enroll and store the bootstrap snapshot atomically; mark the host “initialized” only after snapshot receipt.
  - If snapshot not received within a short TTL (e.g., 60s), flag host as “uninitialized,” trigger alerts, and optionally enqueue a minimal recovery query pack.
  - Validate payload size and fields, normalize and deduplicate network interfaces, and reject obviously malformed data.
- Security and reliability:
  - Use TLS with enroll secret or mTLS; sign the snapshot with the same credentials used for enroll; idempotent upserts keyed by node_key/host_uuid.
  - Enforce payload size limits (e.g., ≤128KB) and retry with exponential backoff on transient failures.
- Backward compatibility:
  - If an older agent cannot send the snapshot, enrollment still succeeds but host is flagged low-confidence and legacy distributed queries are used as a fallback.
- Observability:
  - Emit metrics for enrolls, snapshot receipt latency, and failure rates; store the raw snapshot (for audit) and a normalized projection for UI/search.

## Decision:
We will use GitHub Dependabot to keep dependencies current by enabling both security and version update PRs across all supported ecosystems in this repository. Configuration will:
- Enable security alerts and PRs daily; version updates run weekly (or more frequently for critical stacks).
- Auto-merge patch and minor updates when CI passes and required reviews are satisfied; major updates require manual review.
- Limit concurrent open Dependabot PRs to reduce noise; batch updates where supported and enable weekly lockfile maintenance.
- Apply standard labels (dependencies, security), request CODEOWNERS as reviewers, and require green CI under branch protection rules before merge.
- Define ignore rules for packages pinned for compatibility and add update groups for coordinated libraries.
- Post-merge, publish SBOM updates and trigger deployments as per normal pipeline gates.

This ensures timely, safe, and automated dependency maintenance with human oversight for breaking changes.

## Decision:
Introduce explicit Voice-Over (VO) segments in the project model and timeline, each carrying both estimated_duration and actual_duration (ms). The rough-cut estimator will sum clip durations plus VO estimated_duration until actual recordings replace them.

Estimation will default to a language-configurable speaking rate (e.g., 150 wpm) computed from script word count, with:
- Optional per-segment pace overrides (slow/normal/fast or custom wpm).
- Automatic pause modeling (e.g., 300–500 ms per sentence break, shorter for commas).
- Configurable lead-in/out padding for edit safety.
- Minimum floor per segment (e.g., ≥2 s) to avoid zero-length VOs.

When recordings exist, actual_duration replaces estimates, preserving the estimate for comparison. All durations are time-based in milliseconds and persisted in project metadata. The UI will:
- Display VO estimates on the timeline as placeholders.
- Allow direct pace and padding adjustments.
- Show aggregate rough-cut time with sensitivity analysis (+/− pace).

APIs will expose VO segments, parameters, and roll-ups; a background job can optionally refine estimates via TTS preview alignment when enabled.

## Decision:
Do not include the kernel hash in the Unit‑E block header. The proposal is rejected because committing the kernel hash in the header does not provide additional security, validation efficiency, or light‑client utility beyond what is already derivable from existing consensus data (stake input, timestamps, and randomness/entropy commitments). Adding it would bloat the header, complicate consensus upgrades, and introduce an unnecessary hard/soft‑fork surface without clear benefits.

Instead:
- Nodes will continue to compute the kernel hash on demand from already committed data.
- For observability and tooling, we will expose the kernel hash via RPC/CLI as a derived field and may include it in non-consensus block metadata (e.g., index/db) for faster lookup.
- We will revisit a header commitment only if a concrete, consensus-critical use case emerges (e.g., enabling a verifiable light-client check that cannot be achieved otherwise).

## Decision:
We will publish and consume the front‑end framework as scoped NPM packages. Public packages will be released under the organisational scope (e.g., @nhsuk/...) to the public npm registry (registry.npmjs.org) to align with existing NHS UK/NHS Digital practices and maximize discoverability. Any internal/private packages will be published to GitHub Packages (npm) under the same scope, with .npmrc registry mapping to transparently consume both sources.

We will use semantic versioning, immutable versions, and npm dist-tags (latest, next) for stable and prerelease channels. Publication will be automated via CI on signed, tagged releases, generating changelogs and attaching provenance (e.g., GitHub Actions npm provenance) for supply-chain integrity. Packages will include README, CHANGELOG, licenses, and typed entry points where applicable.

Consumption will standardize on npm as the package manager, with lockfiles committed and registry access managed via org-level tokens and SSO.

## Decision:
We will bootstrap the project from our team’s standard boilerplate template repository to accelerate setup and enforce consistent conventions. The template includes baseline project structure, environment configuration, CI/CD pipelines, linting/formatting, testing scaffolds, containerization, observability hooks, and security defaults. We will instantiate it via the GitHub Template Repository workflow (not as a fork) to enable independent evolution while allowing upstream updates to be pulled selectively. Immediately after initialization, we will remove unused modules and only keep the components relevant to this project to minimize bloat. We will track upstream changes via a monthly review and adopt updates through scripted syncs (e.g., templater/cookiecutter patches) when they provide security fixes or clear productivity gains. Any deviations from the boilerplate will be documented, with rationale, to maintain clarity and ease future upgrades.

## Decision:
We will build the backend on Node.js and use Express.js as the web framework. Express will provide a lightweight, unopinionated abstraction over Node’s HTTP module, simplifying routing, middleware composition, error handling, and request/response processing. This choice minimizes time spent on non-domain infrastructural concerns while remaining flexible for future needs. Express’s maturity, ecosystem, and extensive documentation will accelerate delivery, improve maintainability, and ease onboarding. The application will expose HTTP endpoints via Express routers, apply cross-cutting concerns (e.g., logging, security headers, parsing) as middleware, and use Express’s extensibility to integrate any additional libraries or patterns required as the project evolves.

## Decision:
- Introduce a dedicated Time Series Database (TSDB) at the edge as the authoritative store for sensor time-series data; Kafka remains an ephemeral transport/buffer.
- All analytics, historic lookups, aggregations, and graphing read from the TSDB; applications must not depend on Kafka for durable reads.
- Ingest from Kafka to the TSDB via a managed pipeline (e.g., Kafka Connect/Flink) supporting:
  - Idempotent upserts keyed by sensor ID + timestamp.
  - Handling of out-of-order/late events with a bounded lateness window.
  - Backfill/replay from Kafka offsets to recover from transient TSDB lag.
- Define clear retention and downsampling in the TSDB:
  - Hot retention for high-resolution data.
  - Tiered retention with continuous downsampling to coarser aggregates for longer horizons.
- Kafka retention may be shorter than TSDB; eventual consistency is acceptable. In case of discrepancies, the TSDB is the source of truth; reconcile by replay within Kafka’s retention window, otherwise accept TSDB state.
- Adopt a schema optimized for time-series: time as primary axis, tags/labels for dimensions, append-only writes.
- Operate the TSDB with production SLOs: resource sizing, monitoring/alerts, autoscaling (where supported), and routine maintenance (compaction, retention enforcement).
- Provide backup/restore for the TSDB (periodic snapshots + WAL/transaction logs) and validate recovery via drills. Backups are the basis for DR; Kafka is not.
- Enable optional replication/export from edge TSDB to central DC for aggregation and long-term analytics (e.g., remote write or batch export), with back-pressure and bandwidth controls.
- Deploy and manage via an operator/Helm with IaC; include security (TLS at rest/in transit, RBAC), and multi-tenant isolation if needed.

## Decision:
Adopt Gherkin (Given–When–Then) as the canonical DSL for expressing acceptance tests and documenting behavior. Acceptance criteria will be captured in .feature files written in domain language, versioned alongside the code, and reviewed with stakeholders. We will implement these scenarios using Playwright via a Cucumber-compatible runner (e.g., @cucumber/cucumber or playwright-bdd) with TypeScript step definitions that call high-level domain helpers and Playwright page objects.

Conventions:
- One feature per user-facing capability; scenarios describe observable behavior, not UI mechanics.
- Use Background, Rules, and Examples for clarity; prefer scenario outlines for data variations.
- Steps must be reusable, declarative, and business-readable; avoid technical details in steps.
- Tagging for smoke, regression, critical, and locale supports selective execution.
- Keep non-acceptance tests (integration/unit/e2e-tech) in Playwright Test syntax without Gherkin.

This unifies development and documentation of acceptance tests while keeping implementation maintainable and aligned with our chosen test framework.

## Decision:
Adopt a monorepo managed with Lerna to host openchs-android, openchs-health-modules, and openchs-models in a single repository. This enables coordinated, tandem development, shared tooling, and atomic commits across packages. We will use Lerna for package management, versioning, and publishing; Yarn/NPM workspaces for hoisting and dependency sharing; and a unified CI/CD pipeline to build, test, and release all packages together or independently as needed.

## Decision:
We will reinstate and standardize the use of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) and retrospectively capture key past decisions.

- Template: Use Michael Nygard’s ADR format (Context, Decision, Status, Consequences, Alternatives, Related) with concise, self-contained entries.
- Location and naming: Store in repo at docs/adr, numbered sequentially (e.g., 0001-title.md), kebab-case filenames, immutable once accepted. Supersede decisions with a new ADR referencing prior ones.
- Scope: Require an ADR for any cross-cutting or significant decision (architecture, data model, infrastructure, security, dependencies, patterns). Minor implementation details do not require ADRs.
- Retroactive backfill: Create a prioritized backlog of past significant decisions since 2017. For each, write a “retro ADR” with status: Accepted and the original decision date where known; include links to PRs/issues/commits and a brief rationale and alternatives considered (even if inferred).
- Workflow: Propose ADRs via pull request; at least one reviewer (tech lead or architect) must approve. Discussion happens in the PR. Merge indicates acceptance. Changes require a new ADR that supersedes the old; do not rewrite accepted ADRs except for typos.
- Indexing and discoverability: Maintain an index README in docs/adr listing ADRs by number, title, status, and tags (e.g., security, data, infra, frontend, backend).
- Lightweight discipline: Keep ADRs brief (1–2 pages max), link to deeper docs as needed. Encourage drafting ADRs early in decision-making; allow “Proposed” status until decided.
- Ownership: The tech lead curates the backlog and ensures ADRs are created for new decisions; each team member is responsible for authoring ADRs for their decisions.
- Tooling (optional): Allow adr-cli or similar to scaffold files; no mandate on specific tool.

This policy takes effect immediately; we will seed the backlog within two weeks and complete high-priority retro ADRs within the next quarter.

## Decision:
We will keep generated schemas as the authoritative, compact representation of active/decided splits, and continue to perform destructive schema changes (e.g., removing retired/decided variants) to prevent unbounded growth.

To mitigate divergence when a destructive change is later undone (e.g., re‑creating a previously retired split), the schema generator will opportunistically merge definitions from available historical migration files. If prior migration data for a split/variant exists in the retained window, those definitions will be rehydrated into the generated schema; otherwise, we accept temporary divergence and require maintainers to add a new migration to reintroduce the missing variants.

Operational guardrails:
- Maintain a rolling retention window of migrations sufficient for typical rollbacks (e.g., last 90 days); older migrations may be culled.
- The generator will log non-blocking warnings when it cannot recover prior definitions; CI may surface these warnings but will not fail the build.
- Rollbacks beyond the retention window are supported via explicit, forward migrations that re-add necessary schema variants.
- We will not source schema from production state; all reconciliation derives from repo history or new migrations.

This balances correctness and operability while keeping schemas minimal and migration history maintainable.

## Decision:
We will retain Login.gov as the single authentication provider for all TDP users and halt the migration to NextGen XMS. Login.gov already satisfies TDP’s mandatory controls—MFA for all users, PIV support for internal ACF staff, FedRAMP authorization, and an existing HHS IAA—while avoiding further roadmap delays and integration risk.

To prepare for potential future adoption of an HHS‑vetted broker, we will:
- Maintain an IdP-agnostic abstraction (OIDC/SAML broker layer) to minimize switching costs.
- Enforce policy in-app for PIV as the required second factor for internal ACF users and MFA for all users.
- Implement configuration-driven IdP endpoints and claims mapping to enable rapid cutover testing.
- Monitor HHS-vetted services (including NextGen XMS) for maturity, SDK/tooling stability, SLAs, and cost.

We will re-evaluate the decision in 12 months or sooner if (a) HHS mandates a specific service, (b) NextGen XMS demonstrates production readiness with clear migration tooling and support, or (c) a material cost/compliance change arises. This approach preserves compliance and security while minimizing delivery impact.

## Decision:
We will standardize column handling by introducing a canonical schema and a column metadata registry. All pipeline steps must reference columns via a centrally defined Column enum (or constants) that encodes canonical name, semantic role, data type, and nullability. Where operations are logically driven (e.g., “primary key,” “event time,” “partition key”), steps will target semantic roles/tags resolved through the registry, not raw column names.

Key elements:
- Canonical schema per dataset with stable logical column IDs and explicit types; physical names can evolve via registry mappings.
- Column registry library providing:
  - Column enum/constants and role/tag lookups.
  - Helpers for Spark/Pandas to resolve to framework-specific column objects.
  - Schema validation utilities (required/optional columns, type checks).
- Linting and CI rules prohibiting ad-hoc string-based column references in pipeline code.
- Backward-compatible migration: replace string literals with enum references; register aliases for legacy names; add runtime validators at stage boundaries.

Benefits:
- Eliminates duplicated, error-prone string literals.
- Enables safer refactors and dataset evolution without pervasive code edits.
- Improves readability, testability, and enforcement of data contracts across the pipeline.
- Supports column-level lineage and documentation through the registry metadata.

## Decision:
We will enforce lifecycle management for all third‑party components to reduce supply‑chain risk.

- Maintain an SBOM (CycloneDX) per service and artifact; publish and store with builds.
- Pin exact versions for all dependencies (no floating ranges); commit lockfiles; prefer LTS, well‑maintained libraries with clear release cadence.
- Source all artifacts via an internal, authenticated repository proxy (e.g., Artifactory/Nexus/GitHub Packages) with allowlisted sources, checksum/signature verification (Sigstore/cosign) and provenance (SLSA) when available.
- Automate updates: security updates are created immediately by a dependency bot (e.g., Renovate/Dependabot); non‑security updates are grouped and proposed weekly.
- Scan at multiple stages:
  - CI: software composition analysis and license compliance; fail builds on known vulnerabilities at or above a defined severity threshold (e.g., Critical/High).
  - Image/build pipeline: scan base images and OS packages on every build and nightly.
  - Runtime: continuously scan deployed images and alert on new CVEs.
- Establish remediation SLAs: Critical ≤24h, High ≤3 business days, Medium during next scheduled release, Low in quarterly maintenance.
- Track EOL/abandonment of dependencies; replace before EOL; remove unused dependencies quarterly.
- Require code owner approval for adding new dependencies; evaluate security posture, maintenance activity, license, and footprint.
- Maintain a rapid rollback path and feature flags for dependency upgrades; test via staging and canary deployments.
- Record provenance and SBOM with build artifacts; attestations are verified in deployment gates.
- Document exceptions with time‑bound risk acceptance and mitigation plans.

We will standardize on Kustomize for Kubernetes manifest management to eliminate duplication and reduce environment drift. Each service will maintain a single canonical “base” set of manifests with environment/region/cloud–specific overlays. The overlays will patch only the deltas (e.g., image tags, replica counts, resource limits, ingress hosts, storage classes, node selectors, cloud-specific annotations), while the base captures shared definitions (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, RBAC, NetworkPolicies).

Key elements:
- Repository layout: services/<service>/k8s/{base,overlays/<cloud>/<region>/<env>}
- Use strategic merge/JSON patches, ConfigMap/Secret generators, and common labels/annotations in Kustomize.
- Prohibit duplicating full YAML per target; changes must land in base with minimal overlay patches.
- Deploy via CI/CD using kubectl kustomize or a kustomize-aware controller, rendering each overlay per target cluster.
- Versioning and promotion: promote by updating image tags/params in overlays or via automated image update pipelines, ensuring identical base across environments.
- Provide shared “platform overlays” for cross-cutting concerns (e.g., logging, sidecars, PSP/PodSecurity, ingress class) to be composed with service overlays.
- Add validation (kubeval/kubeconform), policy (OPA/Conftest/Kyverno), and diffs (kubectl diff) in CI to detect unintended drift before apply.

This approach keeps a single source of truth, improves readability and operability, and enables safe, automated multi-cluster deployments without repeating manifests.

## Decision:
We will capture significant technical and architectural choices for Ockam using Lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), following Michael Nygard’s format.

- Repository and location: Store ADRs in the Ockam monorepo under docs/adr/, one Markdown file per ADR.
- Format: Each ADR includes Title, Status (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded), Context, Decision, Consequences, and Links.
- Numbering and naming: Sequential numbering (e.g., 0001-…), kebab-case short titles, immutable filenames.
- Scope: Required for decisions that affect system architecture, protocols, security posture, public APIs, cross-cutting concerns, or long-term maintenance; optional for minor/internal implementation choices.
- Lifecycle: ADRs start as Proposed via PR, reviewed by maintainers/architecture reviewers, and become Accepted on merge. Changes are made by creating a new ADR that Supersedes prior ones; existing ADRs are not edited post-acceptance except to update Status and add Superseded links.
- Process: Every substantial design PR references an ADR; code and docs link back to relevant ADRs. Releases/changelogs may reference newly Accepted ADRs.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (optional) or simple templates to create and manage ADRs.
- Visibility: Encourage concise, decision-focused writing to keep ADRs searchable, reviewable, and durable over Ockam’s evolution.

## Decision:
Adopt a pluggable Command Source strategy for all controllable entities.

- Define an ICommandSource interface (e.g., GetNextCommand(Actor, WorldState, CancellationToken) -> Command) that encapsulates decision-making for an actor.
- Each actor with a Controllable component holds a reference to its current ICommandSource. The scheduler requests a Command from that source when the actor’s turn arrives.
- Support hot-swapping ICommandSource at runtime (e.g., InputCommandSource ↔ FleeingCommandSource) to reflect status effects, possession, scripts, or AI state changes.
- Provide minimal initial implementations:
  - InputCommandSource (player input, with optional timeout/fallback).
  - SimpleAICommandSource (basic heuristics/idle).
  - FleeingCommandSource (panic/terrified behavior).
  - ScriptedCommandSource (for cutscenes/testing).
- Use composition over inheritance: behaviors live in ICommandSource implementations; actors remain simple data/abilities holders.
- Start lean: no heavy DI; use a lightweight factory to construct sources and a small registry on the Controllable component for swapping.
- Keep commands serializable and deterministic (seeded RNG provided by scheduler) to support replay/save/load.
- Selection rules: allied plants default to InputCommandSource when under player control; otherwise they use their configured AI source. Temporary effects override with higher priority sources (e.g., fear → Fleeing), then restore previous source.
- Telemetry/testing: ICommandSource can be decorated for logging/replay; unit tests target sources in isolation.

This achieves player choice in combat, enables future control of other entities, and limits complexity by delivering a minimal, extensible core.

## Decision:
- Defer introducing Redux. Continue with React local state, Context, and custom hooks until clear evidence demonstrates the need for a centralized state manager.
- Manage server cache/state with React Query; use useReducer for complex component-local state; expose shared app state via narrowly scoped Contexts wrapped by feature-focused hooks (e.g., useAuth(), usePreferences()).
- Establish adoption criteria for Redux:
  - Cross-cutting state spans multiple routes/features and requires coordinated updates.
  - Prop drilling or “Context sprawl” (≥3 nested contexts frequently combined) degrades ergonomics or performance.
  - Need for time-travel debugging or deterministic replay to diagnose defects.
  - Complex async workflows or optimistic updates require global orchestration.
  - Normalized caching of entity graphs becomes necessary beyond React Query’s scope.
- Prepare for optional migration by maintaining a state access façade:
  - All components consume state via hooks (facade) that can later be reimplemented atop Redux without refactors.
  - Keep events/intents domain-oriented (e.g., auth/loginRequested) to map directly to future Redux actions.
- If criteria are met, adopt Redux Toolkit with Thunks:
  - Use RTK slices per domain, RTK Query (if it replaces React Query) or continue React Query otherwise.
  - Enable Redux DevTools for observability; keep middleware minimal (thunk, logger in dev).
- Review criteria at each release; migrate incrementally feature-by-feature.

## Decision:
Adopt Docker as the canonical build toolchain for the containerized application, using a single multi-stage Dockerfile as the source of truth for builds.

- Use Docker BuildKit/Buildx to enable deterministic, cache-efficient, and cross-platform builds.
- Pin base images by digest and lock application dependencies (e.g., via language-specific lockfiles) to ensure reproducibility.
- Provide a lightweight Makefile (or Taskfile) to wrap common build/run/test/publish commands, minimizing installation and IDE configuration.
- Include a .dockerignore and apply reproducible build practices (explicit ARGs/ENV, fixed locales/timezones, consistent UID/GID).
- Optionally supply a devcontainer and/or Docker Compose for local development parity without bespoke IDE setup.
- Standardize CI/CD to run the same Make/Task targets and Docker build commands used locally, ensuring parity across environments.

## Decision:
Adopt PostgreSQL as the primary persistent data store, provisioned as a managed service (e.g., Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, AWS RDS, or Cloud SQL) to ensure reliability, scalability, and operational simplicity.

- Use a relational schema for core domain entities to benefit from ACID guarantees, strong consistency, and mature query capabilities.
- Leverage JSONB columns selectively for semi-structured/fast-evolving data to accommodate future feature growth without heavy migrations.
- Standardize on automatic daily backups with point-in-time recovery, multi-AZ high availability, and read replicas for scale-out reads when needed.
- Manage schema changes with versioned, automated migrations (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase or the framework’s native tooling) integrated into CI/CD.
- Employ connection pooling (e.g., PgBouncer) to support API concurrency and control resource usage.
- Plan for growth using native features: indexing (including GIN/GIN on JSONB), full-text search, partitioning for large tables, and extensions (e.g., pg_trgm, PostGIS if needed).
- For development and testing, use a Dockerized Postgres instance to mirror production settings.

This choice balances simplicity and power, is widely understood, and provides a clear path from today’s lightweight needs to future scale and complexity.

## Decision:
Chosen option: Use docs/adr/NNNN-title-with-dashes.md as the storage layout, because:
- Aligns with the widespread adr-tools ecosystem, easing interoperability and contributor familiarity.
- Zero-padded numeric prefix ensures stable chronological and lexicographic ordering in shells, editors, and code reviews.
- Human-readable slug in filename improves discoverability, searchability, and URL sharing.
- The docs/ directory is a common convention and integrates well with static site generators and GitHub browsing.

Positive consequences:
- Predictable, sortable filenames and paths.
- Easier cross-repo contribution due to common conventions.
- Better readability in PRs and repository navigation.

Negative consequences:
- Requires title slugification and potential filename changes if titles change (tooling should handle renames).
- Slightly longer filenames and path than minimal alternatives.

## Decision:
We will institute lightweight but continuous architecture governance and “architecture as code” to keep microservices, domains, and bounded contexts under control.

- Single source of truth:
  - A central architecture repository with C4/Context Maps (Structurizr DSL) representing bounded contexts, upstream/downstream relationships, and integration patterns.
  - A service catalog (Backstage) listing each service’s owner, domain, context, APIs (OpenAPI), events (AsyncAPI), SLAs, data stores, dependencies, and runtime endpoints.

- Domain rigor:
  - Contract-first design for APIs/events with schemas versioned in a shared registry; breaking-change checks enforced in CI.
  - Context Boundary Definition template required for new/changed services (purpose, capabilities, invariants, integration, data ownership).
  - Ubiquitous language glossary per context, curated in the repo.

- Change control:
  - ADRs per service and cross-cutting ADRs in the central repo; changes via PRs linking diagrams, schemas, and ADRs.
  - Lightweight Architecture Review (30-min) required for new services or boundary changes; checklist to justify service creation and avoid over-fragmentation.

- Automated guardrails:
  - Architectural fitness functions (ArchUnit/NetArchTest/depcruise) to prevent illegal dependencies and enforce layering.
  - Contract tests/consumer-driven tests; schema diff gates in CI/CD.
  - Observability-based topology (tracing/metrics) to detect unintended couplings and drift.

- Cadence and visibility:
  - Monthly architecture sync to review the context map and service catalog.
  - Versioned releases of the architecture model; diagrams generated automatically in pipelines.

This approach ensures boundaries are explicit, discoverable, and verifiable, enabling safe evolution of microservices without losing architectural control.

## Decision:
Build an offline-first Progressive Web App (PWA) as a static site. Deliver a single-page application composed of one HTML file with embedded/minimal JS/CSS and versioned static content (JSON/markdown) bundled at build time. Use a simple Service Worker (workbox or hand-rolled) to precache all assets and data, enabling full offline functionality with a cache-first strategy and a lightweight update flow (cache bust via versioned filenames).

This approach:
- Satisfies offline availability with no runtime network dependency.
- Runs on mobile and desktop via any modern browser and supports “Install App” (Add to Home Screen) through a web manifest; optional wrapping with Capacitor/Tauri can be added later if store distribution is required.
- Minimizes code and infrastructure: static hosting only (e.g., GitHub Pages/S3/CloudFront), no backend or CMS at runtime.

Content updates are released by publishing a new build (bumping the cache version). The app checks for updates on load and prompts users to refresh when a new version is available.

## Decision:
We will standardize identifiers across all API responses as follows:
- Primary identifier field: id
  - Type: string
  - Format: UUIDv4, lowercase, hyphenated (canonical textual representation).
  - Semantics: opaque, globally unique, immutable.
- Human-readable field: displayName (optional)
  - Type: string
  - Semantics: mutable label intended for UI; not an identifier and not guaranteed unique unless explicitly documented.
- Foreign keys in composite/embedded objects: use <resource>NameId (e.g., userId, projectId) to disambiguate multiple references; never mix id and uuid in the same payload.
- JSON field casing: camelCase; never use ID, Id, UUID, uuid, or identifier as field names for primary keys.

New and updated endpoints must:
- Return id on all resource representations.
- Use id consistently in list, get, create, update, and delete responses.
- Accept and return only UUIDv4 in fields defined as identifiers.

Migration plan for existing inconsistencies:
- Introduce id alongside legacy fields (e.g., uuid, identifier, resourceId) and mark legacy fields as deprecated in OpenAPI with clear sunset dates.
- Maintain read-only mirrors for legacy identifier fields for at least two release cycles; no new writes will populate legacy fields beyond mirroring id.
- Provide response headers and changelog entries documenting deprecations and timelines.
- Update SDKs, examples, and documentation to prefer id; add linters/contract tests to prevent regressions.

Exceptions (e.g., externally mandated identifiers) require ADR and explicit documentation, but must still include id as the canonical key.

## Decision:
Adopt content negotiation with explicit per-request versioning via media types. Clients must specify the desired resource version in the Accept header; the server will respond with the matching Content-Type and an API-Version header.

- Request: Accept: application/vnd.hmpps.basm.moves.v2+json
- Response: Content-Type: application/vnd.hmpps.basm.moves.v2+json; charset=utf-8 and API-Version: v2

Policy:
- Per-resource versioning: versions are scoped to a resource (e.g., moves v2, people v1) to allow independent evolution.
- Defaulting: if Accept is omitted, the server serves the stable default version for that resource and returns API-Version to make the choice explicit.
- Negotiation: if an unsupported version is requested, return 406 Not Acceptable with supported versions enumerated.
- Deprecation: include Deprecation and Sunset headers and changelog links; maintain at least one prior major version for a defined window.
- Forward/backward compatibility: clients must be tolerant readers (ignore unknown fields); servers must not break existing optional fields and should add fields as optional.
- Discovery: expose supported versions per resource via a capabilities endpoint and in response headers (API-Versions: v1,v2).
- Transitional support: continue global URI versioning where it exists; the Accept header takes precedence per request. A temporary query param ?version=v2 may be supported for debugging but is not part of the public contract.

## Decision:
Use a GitHub App with read-only repo access and fetch short‑lived installation tokens at runtime via Vault, injected into the Nomad task.

- Create a GitHub App scoped to the Axiomatic org with read-only access to the configuration repositories.
- Store the App’s private key in HashiCorp Vault and enable the Vault GitHub App secrets engine to mint installation tokens with short TTL (e.g., 1 hour).
- Configure the Nomad job with Vault integration (per-task policy limited to the specific GitHub App installation) and a template stanza to render a transient .netrc (or GIT_ASKPASS script) containing the token.
- Have dir2consul clone/fetch over HTTPS using the token; the credential file lives in the task’s ephemeral alloc dir with 0600 permissions and is removed on task exit.
- Enforce egress only to GitHub endpoints and log only non-secret metadata. No credentials are embedded in job specs, images, or repos.
- Rotate tokens per run; rely on TTL expiry and Vault revocation on job termination.

## Decision:
- Adopt Java 17 and Spring Boot as the primary backend technology to leverage its mature ecosystem, opinionated auto-configuration, production-readiness (actuators, metrics), and strong community support. This aligns with enterprise requirements for reliability, security, and long-term maintainability.
- Standardize on JUnit 5 (Jupiter) as the unit testing framework for its modern API, parameterized tests, and rich IDE/build tool integration.
- Use Mockito for mocking/stubbing collaborators in unit tests to isolate components and drive fast feedback.
- Use AssertJ for fluent, readable assertions.
- Use Spring Boot Test slices (e.g., @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) to optimize test scope and speed while maintaining realism.
- Use Testcontainers for integration tests to run dependent services (e.g., PostgreSQL, Kafka) in disposable containers, ensuring parity with production environments.
- Enforce code coverage with JaCoCo (minimum 80% line coverage, with critical modules targeted at 90%) as a quality gate in CI.
- Structure tests with a consistent package mirroring production code, naming convention *ClassNameTest* for unit tests and *ClassNameIT* for integration tests.
- Integrate tests into the build using Maven/Gradle with parallel execution enabled for unit tests, and integration tests executed in a separate lifecycle phase.
- Revisit this decision periodically to assess emerging frameworks or features (e.g., Loom/virtual threads, Spring Boot LTS updates) without disrupting the standardized approach.

## Decision:
Adopt a consistent, product-attributed, collision-free repository naming convention within the Libero GitHub organization.

Rules:
- Format: lowercase kebab-case, ASCII only, words separated by hyphens.
- Product attribution: every product-bound repository must start with its product slug to avoid clashes (e.g., journal-*, reviewer-*, discovery-*, platform-*).
- Structure: {product}-{domain(optional)}-{component}
  - domain is used to group related capabilities (e.g., content, workflow, identity).
  - component is the primary unit (service, app, library, infra module).
- Cross-product/shared assets use reserved prefixes without a product slug:
  - common-* (shared libraries/modules)
  - infra-* (infrastructure, Terraform, k8s modules)
  - tooling-* (developer tools, CI/CD helpers)
  - docs-* (organization-level docs, standards)
  - rfc-* (architecture/ADR/RFC repos)
  - design-* (design systems/assets)
- Technology/platform qualifiers are suffixes only when disambiguation is necessary:
  - -api, -service, -worker, -ui, -web, -mobile, -cli
  - language/runtime for libraries only: -js, -ts, -py, -go, -java, -dotnet
- Avoid ambiguous abbreviations; prefer canonical product/domain/component names.
- Do not prefix with “libero-” (redundant within the organization).
- Forks/mirrors: append -fork or -mirror plus source slug when needed for clarity.
- Experimental/prototypes: prefix with exp-; archived: archive-; upon promotion/archive, rename or transfer accordingly.
- Keep names concise (<= 50 chars where possible) and stable; favor discoverability over brevity.
- New repos must include a short description matching the name intent and a README that expands the product/domain/component mapping.

## Decision:
Adopt the existing, maintained target as the default and deprecate our custom target, contingent on a short evaluation spike.

- Run a timeboxed spike (1–2 days) to validate functional parity, CI compatibility, performance, and output correctness.
- If the existing target meets requirements, switch all pipelines and local workflows to it, update docs, and mark our custom target as deprecated (read-only, no new features).
- Keep our custom target only as a fallback during a short transition window; remove it after one release cycle if no regressions are found.
- Only consider re-implementing or extending a custom target if we have a validated need for nontrivial “fancy formatting” or capabilities not supported by the existing target; prefer contributing upstream over forking.
- Establish acceptance criteria: same inputs/outputs, stable CLI/API, deterministic results, good maintenance cadence, and compatible licensing.
- Provide a thin wrapper (if needed) to maintain backwards compatibility for callers.
- Document migration steps and differences in formatting behavior, and update developer onboarding.

This approach reduces maintenance burden, aligns with community standards, and avoids reimplementation unless there’s proven value in advanced formatting.

## Decision:
Introduce a high-level, one-shot API as the default usage for the algorithm. Provide Sesopenko.DiamondSquare.generate/2 (or run/2) that accepts size/params (e.g., n, seed, roughness/options) and returns the completed grid plus metadata. Retain step/1 and step_to_end/1 for advanced/debug use, but mark stepwise iteration as non-default. Additionally, expose Sesopenko.DiamondSquare.stream/1 (Elixir Stream) to allow consumers to lazily observe intermediate states without manual stepping.

- Default path: generate/2 → final grid.
- Advanced paths: step_to_end/1; stream/1 for progress/visualization.
- Ensure deterministic outputs via optional seed.
- Update docs and examples to emphasize generate/2 and hide/annotate step APIs as advanced.
- Add optional progress callback or step limit to generate/2 for long runs.

This simplifies common usage while preserving fine-grained control when needed.

## Decision:
- Adopt trunk-based development: all work merges into main via short-lived feature branches and PRs.
- Create long-lived release branches per minor line: release/<MAJOR>.<MINOR>. Stabilize and backport fixes here.
- Tag every release from its release branch with immutable, signed SemVer tags: v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<PATCH>. Tags point directly to the release commit (commit SHA is thus unambiguous).
- Maintain parallel release branches for all supported minor lines to allow independent patching for networks pinned to older versions.
- Build and publish artifacts/images for each tag, labeled with both the SemVer tag and image digest.
- Per-network deployments pin to a specific release tag (or image digest). Networks can run different tags concurrently.
- Deployment URLs are versioned by major version to encode breaking changes, e.g., https://<network>.v<MAJOR>.trubudget.example.com or https://<network>.trubudget.example.com/v<MAJOR>. Non-breaking updates (minor/patch) retain the same URL; breaking updates (major) use a new URL with incremented <MAJOR>.
- Operationally, maintain a lightweight deployment manifest per network that references the chosen tag; updating the manifest to a newer patch/minor within the same major updates the deployment without changing the URL. Moving to a new major requires both manifest update and URL change.

## Decision:
Adopt a stateless, controlled-by-consumer API for all Octagon components by default.

- Components are pure view: props-in, events-out. They do not own business or persistence state (e.g., “active”, “selected”, “open”) and must render deterministically from props.
- Consumers manage state and pass it via props (e.g., <OctoNavItem active />). Components emit intent via callbacks (e.g., onSelect, onToggle) without mutating internal state.
- Internal state is allowed only for strictly ephemeral UI concerns that cannot be expressed via props and have no semantic impact on app state (e.g., focus traps, hover, transient animation timing). Such state must not affect initial render parity or reload behavior.
- If internal state is unavoidable for usability, expose a controlled/uncontrolled pattern with a strong preference for controlled:
  - Controlled: value + onChange (source of truth is the consumer).
  - Uncontrolled: defaultValue + onChange; no silent internal resets; document behavior clearly.
- Do not persist state internally (no localStorage/sessionStorage) and do not derive state from props except where memoized computations are idempotent and side-effect free.
- Public APIs must be declarative, idempotent, and SSR/hydration-safe. Initial render must match client hydration when given the same props.
- Naming conventions: value/checked/open/active for controlled props; defaultValue/defaultChecked/defaultOpen for uncontrolled; onChange/onToggle/onOpenChange for callbacks.
- Avoid hidden listeners or implicit behavior that toggles internal state; expose intent via callbacks and let consumers wire events.
- Provide optional helpers (e.g., hooks, reducers, state containers) outside the core component to simplify common state management while keeping the component itself stateless.
- Document state diagrams and prop contracts, including edge cases (disabled, loading) and precedence rules (controlled props override defaults).

This ensures predictability across reloads, preserves top-down declarative usage, and keeps Octagon a pure view layer.

## Decision:
Introduce support for ADR_EDITOR and ADR_VISUAL environment variables to allow users to choose their preferred editors for creating and editing ADRs.

- Precedence for editor resolution:
  1) Command-line flag (--editor / --visual) if provided
  2) ADR_VISUAL (when a visual editor is requested)
  3) ADR_EDITOR
  4) VISUAL (standard env var)
  5) EDITOR (standard env var)
  6) Platform default (e.g., code, notepad on Windows; nano/vi on Unix)

- Invocation:
  - If the variable value contains a placeholder {file}, it will be replaced with the ADR file path.
  - If no placeholder is present, the ADR file path will be appended as the last argument.
  - Support quoted paths and spaced arguments; run via the platform’s shell.
  - On Windows, support .exe/.cmd/.bat and PowerShell commands.

- Modes:
  - “Visual” operations (if/when the tool distinguishes them) prefer ADR_VISUAL; otherwise ADR_EDITOR is used.
  - If the resolved editor is not found or exits with non-zero status, surface a clear error and instructions to set ADR_EDITOR/ADR_VISUAL.

- Configuration and documentation:
  - Document both variables, precedence, and examples for common editors (vim, nano, code, notepad, notepad++, sublime).
  - Provide sample usage and troubleshooting tips in the project README and --help output.

## Decision:
We will add a new utility class only when all of the following are true:
- It maps to exactly one CSS declaration (no shorthands that affect multiple properties).
- It expresses a purely presentational concern (layout/spacing/typography/visibility/z-index/positioning), not component logic or state.
- Its values come from our design tokens/scales (e.g., spacing, color, font-size, z-index tiers).
- It is broadly reusable: already used (or reasonably forecast) in at least three distinct components or across multiple pages/flows.
- It is composable and side‑effect free (does not depend on DOM structure or order beyond normal cascade).
- It reduces duplication versus existing utilities and does not overlap ambiguously with them.
- It is safe across breakpoints and themes, or we can provide responsive/variant forms consistently (e.g., md:position--relative) without exploding the API.

We will not add utilities that:
- Are one‑off fixes or tightly coupled to a specific component or layout quirk.
- Encode interaction/state (hover/focus/active/JS-driven states) unless already standardized in our utilities.
- Introduce ambiguity (e.g., multiple ways to achieve the same outcome) or violate token scales.

Process:
- Propose via PR with: rationale, examples from ≥3 call sites, chosen token values, and any needed responsive/pseudo variants.
- Add docs and visual examples; include visual regression tests where applicable.
- Gate new utilities as “provisional” for one release; confirm adoption before finalizing.
- If a utility proves underused or confusing, deprecate with migration guidance.

Example: position--relative qualifies if commonly needed to anchor absolute children across multiple components and aligns with our positioning token tiers.

## Decision:
Defer building a first-class “examples” feature and community repository. Instead, prioritize clojure.spec integration and run a focused discovery phase to validate demand and shape.

Actions:
- Publish an RFC outlining problem, proposed scope, and alternatives; solicit feedback from library authors and users.
- Conduct a limited pilot with a small set of volunteer libraries to test feasibility (setup complexity, author effort) using minimal conventions (e.g., docs metadata) rather than platform changes.
- Define success criteria: author adoption (≥5 pilot libs contributing examples), maintenance burden (≤1h/month per lib), user utility (≥70% positive feedback), and low operational cost for cljdoc.
- Evaluate need for a community examples repository only if pilots show strong utility and sustained contributions; otherwise keep examples co-located with libraries.
- Reassess after pilots to decide between: (a) no feature, (b) light-weight, convention-based indexing, or (c) full feature with tooling.

This avoids committing to a large feature with uncertain impact while gathering evidence to make an informed, incremental decision.

## Decision:
- Decouple “rich” product metadata from Stripe by introducing an external Product Metadata source of truth (S3-backed JSON documents fronted by CDN or a lightweight Metadata Service API).
- Store only a compact pointer in Stripe metadata (e.g., metadata_ref = {id, version} or metadata_url) per Product/Price, staying well below Stripe limits.
- Subscription Platform will resolve the pointer at runtime:
  - Fetch and cache metadata by id/version (in-memory and Redis) with TTL and ETag-based revalidation.
  - Preload/refresh cache on relevant Stripe webhooks (product/price updates) to minimize cold-start latency.
- Provide a product-manager-friendly management path:
  - Phase 1: Git-backed JSON/YAML with JSON Schema validation and a simple admin UI for preview/publish (writes to S3).
  - Phase 2: Replace with a minimal internal UI (roles, audit, versioning) if needed.
- Ensure backward compatibility:
  - If metadata_ref is absent, fall back to existing Stripe metadata until migrated.
  - During migration, Stripe metadata can include both legacy keys and the pointer.
- Implement strict validation and versioning:
  - Define JSON Schemas for each metadata domain (checkout content, legal URLs, support options).
  - Version documents; pointer includes version to enable safe rollbacks.
- Security and reliability:
  - Prefer private S3 with signed CDN URLs or authenticated Metadata Service; no sensitive data stored publicly.
  - Add integrity (hash) in pointer for optional verification.
  - Observability with metrics for cache hits/misses, fetch latency, failures; alert on stale/invalid references.
- Operational details:
  - Blue/green publish of documents (write new version, update pointer in Stripe after validation).
  - Rate-limit and backoff on fetch failures; serve last-known-good from cache as fallback.
  - Document ownership and change workflow for PMs; engineers own schemas and platform integration.

## Decision:
Adopt stretchr/testify as the default testing utility library for the Go codebase, while continuing to use the Go standard testing package as the test runner.

Rationale and scope:
- Use testify/assert and testify/require for expressive, readable assertions; prefer require for fatal preconditions and assert for non-fatal checks.
- Use testify/suite only where setup/teardown and shared fixtures materially reduce duplication (e.g., component-level or integration-like tests). Default to table-driven tests with plain testing.T for simple cases.
- Continue organizing tests alongside the code under test with _test.go files and go test as the only runner; no custom CLI or test harness.
- Optionally use testify/mock for simple interface mocking; for complex interaction testing teams may use a more specialized mocking tool if needed, but testify/mock is the default.
- Keep tests deterministic and fast; avoid hidden state in suites and prefer explicit fixtures and helpers (t.Helper) to maintain clarity.
- Do not build or maintain a custom test suite framework.

Conventions:
- Assertions must include helpful failure messages for non-obvious expectations.
- Prefer table-driven tests for input/output permutations.
- Avoid deep reliance on suite state across tests; each test should be independently runnable.
- Limit use of global test hooks; prefer per-test setup with t.Cleanup.

This choice provides needed ergonomics (assertions, suite support, mocks) with minimal overhead, broad community adoption, and no lock-in beyond imports, while preserving standard tooling and workflows.

## Decision:
Replace the single-key CacheAwarePropertyInfoStore with a segmented, per-Property caching strategy using WANObjectCache.

- Store each PropertyInfo row under its own cache key (one key per Property ID), with a stable key prefix not tied to deploy versions to prevent cross-deploy rehashing.
- Add batch get/set APIs in PropertyInfoStore to prefetch multiple properties in a single WANObjectCache multiGet to minimize round trips.
- Introduce a small in-process request cache and an optional short-TTL APCu layer to further reduce memcached load for hot paths.
- Invalidate per-Property cache entries on Property update via precise purges (e.g., ChangeDispatch/JobQueue hooks), avoiding table-wide invalidations.
- Use reasonable TTLs with tombstoning/hot-key protection provided by WANObjectCache, and avoid caching the entire table or large aggregates.
- For operations that need “all property info,” read the list of property IDs from DB (or a lightweight index key) and batch-fetch per-Property cache entries; do not reintroduce a single giant cache blob.
- Provide a migration period where both strategies can be toggled, then remove the single-key implementation once stability and load are confirmed.

This removes the memcached hotspot, stabilizes cache distribution across deploys, and scales linearly with the number of Properties while preserving high read performance.

## Decision:
Adopt Algolia as the primary search and relevance platform for vacancies UI and job alert construction, replacing direct Elasticsearch query logic in application code. Algolia provides out-of-the-box configurable relevance (synonyms, query rules, typo tolerance, facets, boosts, personalization), query suggestions, and tools for non-engineers to manage ranking strategies via a web UI, removing routine engineering effort from indexing/relevance tuning.

Implementation outline:
- Stand up Algolia indices for vacancies and any supporting taxonomies; backfill from the source of truth and establish near–real-time sync via event-driven pipelines.
- Replace Ruby ES client usage with Algolia’s Ruby client; for UI search, leverage InstantSearch widgets where suitable; for job alerts, express saved alert criteria as Algolia filters/query rules to generate result sets.
- Enable configurable relevance via the Algolia dashboard (attributes for ranking, custom ranking on engagement, facets, synonyms, query rules, typo tolerance). Delegate day-to-day tuning to product/ops.
- Introduce analytics feedback loop (Algolia Insights) to drive continuous improvements (e.g., promote results, add synonyms).
- Retain Elasticsearch only as a transitional backend if necessary; deprecate ES-specific base client classes and centralize search access behind a small abstraction to allow future portability.

This approach delivers materially better search quality and time-to-change, reduces bespoke relevance code, and empowers non-engineering teams to iterate quickly on search and alert criteria without deployment cycles.

## Decision:
Adopt a single master workflow with per-organization whitelist/blacklist policies applied to computed permissions.

- Maintain one authoritative master workflow (all commands, roles, transitions) and compute permissions via application-permissions-view.
- Introduce an organization-specific policy layer that filters the computed permissions using explicit allow/deny lists (deny-by-default unless explicitly allowed by policy and master workflow).
- Prefer parameterized commands and role-scoped permissions over creating new command variants; create explicit command variants only when behavior or side-effects must differ materially and cannot be expressed by parameters or roles.
- Represent organization policies declaratively (e.g., version-controlled config) with schema validation, clear defaults, and migration/versioning. The default policy equals “master” (no additional restrictions).
- Apply policy filtering at runtime after permission calculation; cache results per (org, user roles, application state) to avoid performance regressions.
- Provide test fixtures for each organization policy to assert permitted/forbidden commands across key states; add contract tests ensuring that policy cannot grant commands the master does not define.
- Ensure security and auditability: policies are deny-by-default, changes require code review, and permission decisions are traceable (include effective policy and master basis in logs).
- This approach minimizes duplication versus multiple distinct workflows, keeps command logic cohesive, and supports diverse organizational constraints without proliferating handlers.

## Decision:
- We extend MADR to support explicit cross-decision relationships between records.
- Each ADR will include a Links section listing related ADRs with typed relations:
  - Follows up on: ADR-#### – Title
  - Supersedes: ADR-#### – Title
  - Superseded by: ADR-#### – Title
  - Amends: ADR-#### – Title
  - Amended by: ADR-#### – Title
  - Relates to: ADR-#### – Title
  - Deprecates/Deprecated by (optional, if applicable)
- Relations must be implemented as relative Markdown links to the target ADR files and include the ADR number and title for readability.
- When creating a relation, authors must maintain bidirectional links where applicable (e.g., if ADR-0010 supersedes ADR-0007, ADR-0007 must be updated with “Superseded by ADR-0010” and its Status set to “Superseded”).
- We adopt a stable ADR identifier scheme (e.g., ADR-0001, ADR-0002, …) to make links robust; file names should include the identifier and a slugified title.
- We add lightweight lints/checks to CI to validate that linked ADRs exist and that supersede/superseded-by links are consistent.
- This change is backward compatible: existing ADRs can add a Links section incrementally.

## Decision:
Adopt Playwright for browser automation, executed via Jest as the test runner. We will integrate Playwright using jest-playwright (preset) so the same E2E/feature tests can run locally and in CI across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, in both headless and headed modes. Provide npm scripts to run: local (headed/watch), CI (headless/parallel), and smoke subsets. Configure per-test isolation (fresh context/page), sensible timeouts/retries, screenshots/videos/traces on failure, and environment-driven base URLs. Parallelize tests via Jest and Playwright workers where appropriate, and containerize CI execution with Playwright’s bundled browsers for reproducibility. This setup remains in place until the Playwright test runner is deemed stable enough to replace Jest.

## Decision:
Implement a CI pipeline (GitHub Actions) that builds, tests, and measures code coverage on every push and pull request. The pipeline will:
- Run unit and integration tests for each supported language using standard tools:
  - Python: pytest with pytest-cov
  - JavaScript/TypeScript: Jest with Istanbul/nyc
  - Java: JUnit with JaCoCo (Maven/Gradle)
  - .NET: xUnit/NUnit with Coverlet and ReportGenerator
- Enforce minimum coverage thresholds per project; the job fails if thresholds are not met.
- Upload coverage reports to a centralized service (Codecov or SonarCloud) for trend tracking, PR annotations, and dashboards.
- Publish human-readable coverage reports as build artifacts and add a coverage badge to the README.
- Require passing CI status checks (build, tests, coverage) before merging via branch protection rules.
- Optimize with dependency caching and a test matrix for parallelization to keep feedback fast.

This makes coverage and test execution automatic, visible, and merge-blocking, eliminating manual steps while maintaining high quality.

## Decision:
Adopt Arkency’s lightweight DDD approach as the initial baseline. Concretely:
- Organize by bounded context, each with Application (commands, command handlers), Domain (aggregates as plain objects, value objects, domain services), Infrastructure (repositories, adapters), and Read Model (projections, query handlers) modules.
- Use explicit Commands and Command Handlers (application services) to orchestrate use cases; controllers map HTTP to commands/queries.
- Model Aggregates as plain objects with invariants enforced at the aggregate boundary; persist via repositories.
- Emit Domain Events from aggregates; handle them asynchronously to build/projection read models and to integrate with other bounded contexts.
- Prefer a simple Command Bus and Event Bus; if applicable, use an event store (e.g., Rails Event Store) to persist/publish events and support projections/outbox.
- Apply CQRS: write model through commands/aggregates; read model via dedicated projections and query handlers.
- Keep the stack framework-agnostic and incremental: no heavy DDD framework; evolve toward more advanced patterns (sagas/process managers, event sourcing) as needs arise.
- Establish testing strategy aligned with Arkency practices: given-when-then tests for domain, handler-level tests for application, and contract tests for adapters.

## Decision:
We will not use a multi-tenant PaaS for the core system that stores or processes sensitive data. Instead, we will deploy in an isolated IaaS environment (VPC) with private subnets and no public endpoints, running the application tier in containers on a managed container platform or VMs, and using a dedicated managed database service. Security controls will include customer-managed encryption keys (BYOK/KMS/HSM), encryption in transit and at rest, strict network policies and security groups, secrets management, least-privilege IAM, and full audit logging/monitoring.

This approach provides stronger isolation, deterministic security controls, and compliance alignment while retaining manageable operational overhead through managed building blocks. PaaS may be used for non-sensitive, auxiliary components (e.g., logging dashboards, CI/CD) where appropriate. We will reassess PaaS adoption for core workloads if single-tenant or private PaaS options with BYOK and equivalent controls become available.

## Decision:
Introduce paired message examples support in a fully backward-compatible manner.

- Parsing/ingest: Extend the parser to accept both legacy “examples” (flat list) and the new clarified form (list of payload/header pairs). When encountering the new form, normalize internally to a List<ExamplePair {payload, headers}>. When encountering the legacy form, normalize to List<ExamplePair {payload=legacyExample, headers=null}>.
- Model: Do not modify existing public model types in a breaking way. Add a non-breaking accessor getExamplePairs() and keep existing getExamples() (deprecated) which returns a flattened list of payload examples for legacy callers.
- Serialization/emit: Preserve original shape by default (round-trip). Add an opt-in emitter flag to output the new paired structure. If emitting legacy, omit header examples or include only payloads; if emitting new, include both payload and header per pair.
- Validation: Accept both shapes. When legacy is detected, emit a non-failing deprecation warning recommending migration to paired examples. Validate that each pair includes at least a payload; headers may be absent.
- Tooling/UI: Update viewers to display paired examples when available; fall back to payload-only when using legacy.
- Documentation and migration: Document the new paired structure, provide examples, and mark legacy “examples” usage as deprecated with a migration guide. No major version bump required.

## Decision:
- Replace direct use of OpenJPEG’s opj_decompress with GDAL-based conversion to a tiled, compressed intermediate (preferably Cloud-Optimized) GeoTIFF via gdal_translate, leveraging windowed decoding to cap peak memory.
- Standardize conversion flags to balance performance and size: e.g., -co TILED=YES -co COMPRESS=LZW (or ZSTD) -co BIGTIFF=IF_SAFER -co BLOCKXSIZE=512 -co BLOCKYSIZE=512, and enforce GDAL_CACHEMAX (e.g., 256–512MB) to bound memory usage.
- Execute JP2→TIFF conversion in an isolated worker process/container with strict memory and CPU limits (cgroups/Kubernetes requests+limits). Treat OOM as a retryable failure with exponential backoff.
- Introduce a queue-based ingestion pipeline with a global semaphore to cap concurrent JP2 conversions (configurable based on host resources; default 1–2 per node).
- Add size-aware scheduling: throttle or serialize conversions for large JP2s based on file dimensions/bytes.
- Health-guard the worker with timeouts and per-task resource ceilings; emit structured metrics (duration, memory, retries) and alerts on sustained failures.
- Keep libvips pipeline unchanged; consume the generated intermediate TIFF for pyramidal TIFF and thumbnail production.
- Optionally evaluate Grok (open-source JPEG 2000) as a GDAL JP2 driver for improved performance; retain OpenJPEG as fallback.
- Document operational runbooks and provide feature flag to disable JP2 ingestion if safeguards fail.

## Decision:
Adopt a layered, minimal-friction configuration model that is powerful by default and simple to override:

- Provide sane, opinionated defaults for all non-critical options; only require a minimal set of essentials (e.g., network endpoints, credentials).
- Support layered overrides in this order: built-in defaults < profile presets < configuration file (YAML) < environment variables < CLI flags. Later layers win.
- Ship curated “profiles” (e.g., local-dev, staging, production) to cover common scenarios with zero/low edits.
- Define and publish a machine-readable configuration schema (JSON Schema) to enable validation, autocomplete, and documentation generation. Fail fast with clear, actionable error messages.
- Treat secrets as first-class: never required in config files; accept via environment variables or secret managers (e.g., Docker/Kubernetes secrets).
- Offer a guided CLI “init” that generates a minimal config from prompts, plus sample configs for common integrations.
- Ensure configuration is hot-reloadable where safe (feature flags, logging levels) and restart-required for structural changes.
- Maintain backward-compatible keys for the first draft release; introduce a deprecation path with warnings and migration hints.
- Prefer descriptive, flat keys with namespacing only when necessary (e.g., database.*, api.*, auth.*) to reduce cognitive load.
- Provide container-first packaging (Docker/Helm) with overridable values, enabling one-command setup and easy CI/CD integration.

This approach enables high configurability with minimal effort, clear validation, and safe evolution without overwhelming users.

## Decision:
Remove the Skylight profiler from the application and infrastructure. This includes uninstalling the gem/agent, deleting configuration and environment variables, revoking API keys, and removing any deployment hooks. We will not invest effort to fix or reconfigure Skylight at this time. If future performance profiling is needed, we will evaluate current alternatives (e.g., New Relic, Datadog, rack-mini-profiler) and reintroduce an observability tool with clear ownership, configuration validation, and usage guidelines. Document the removal and add a runbook section outlining criteria and steps for reintroducing a profiler.

## Decision:
Adopt a small, structured SPA built with React and TypeScript, bundled with Vite, to implement the PIN login flow, gated navigation, and in-browser Zenroom (WASM) execution.

- Use React + TypeScript for predictable component/state modeling, stronger typing, and maintainability as the UX grows beyond simple forms.
- Use React Router for page-level routing and route guards to enforce PIN-authenticated access.
- Manage auth state with a minimal store (React Context or Zustand) with:
  - in-memory session as the source of truth,
  - optional persisted flag in sessionStorage with short TTL,
  - clear logout/reset actions.
- Implement the PIN entry as a dedicated form component with accessibility-first semantics and validation; surface errors and lockouts as needed.
- Integrate Zenroom via a dedicated service:
  - load the Zenroom WASM lazily on first use,
  - run Zenroom in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the UI,
  - define a typed request/response contract for invoking scripts and receiving results/errors.
- Use Vite for fast DX, WASM support, and code-splitting; configure CSP and integrity where applicable.
- Testing: component/unit tests with Vitest + React Testing Library; e2e with Playwright for the auth flow and Zenroom execution.
- Keep styling with a lightweight approach (e.g., CSS Modules or Tailwind) to minimize JS overhead and ensure responsive, accessible UI.

This approach balances simplicity and structure: it avoids jQuery-driven ad hoc code while remaining lightweight, provides clear auth gating, and safely hosts Zenroom WASM without compromising UI responsiveness.

## Decision:
Adopt Azure Cosmos DB using the MongoDB API to minimize vendor lock-in while meeting required capabilities. We will:

- Use the MongoDB API for single-document CRUD and query operations (secondary indexes, filtering, limits, ordering).
- Implement optimistic concurrency via MVCC at the application layer by adding a version field (e.g., _v) to each document and performing conditional updates/deletes with filters that include the expected version. On success, increment _v; on mismatch, return a concurrency error.
- Define required secondary indexes explicitly (including compound indexes for common sort/filter patterns) and enforce unique constraints where applicable.
- Standardize on a thin repository layer that depends only on widely used MongoDB driver interfaces, avoiding Cosmos-specific extensions, to preserve portability to managed MongoDB or other document stores.
- Target the highest Cosmos-supported MongoDB API version compatible with our drivers (e.g., 6.x), and validate behaviors for limits, sort stability, and collation where used.
- Avoid Cosmos-specific features (stored procedures, triggers, server-side scripts) to prevent coupling.

This approach satisfies CRUD, query needs, and concurrency control, while reducing proprietary lock-in and enabling future migration paths.

## Decision:
Adopt a two-tier testing strategy that maximizes automation for items #1 and #2 and uses targeted, reliable end-to-end checks for #3.

- Validation and Transformation (items #1 and #2):
  - Implement comprehensive unit tests for input validation with clear, structured error messages.
  - Ensure the HTML output is deterministic; use snapshot tests for the generated HTML (including embedded CSS/JS) with stable IDs/classes to avoid flaky diffs.
  - Include fixture-based tests to cover representative inputs and edge cases.

- Interactive Behavior (item #3):
  - Use Playwright in headless mode to load the generated HTML file directly from disk (or via a lightweight static server) and exercise a minimal set of critical interactions:
    - Assert that expected links render with correct text and hrefs.
    - Verify click navigation/handlers and keyboard interactions behave as intended.
    - Check focus management and ARIA roles where applicable.
  - Keep E2E coverage to a small, high-value smoke suite to minimize brittleness while ensuring core behavior is validated.

- Tooling and CI:
  - Provide npm scripts: test (unit+snapshots), test:e2e (Playwright), and test:ci (both, with headless/no flake retries).
  - Run unit and snapshot tests on every push; run E2E in CI with retries and video/trace on failure for diagnosis.
  - Offer a local “preview” script that generates the HTML and opens it in a browser for quick manual verification.

This approach gives fast, robust feedback for format and transformation while ensuring the resulting HTML actually renders and responds correctly, without over-investing in fragile UI test coverage.

## Decision:
Use a managed PostgreSQL database as the system-of-record for Bookit’s persistence needs.

Rationale:
- Strong relational model matches the domain (locations → bookables → bookings) and enforces data integrity with foreign keys and constraints.
- ACID transactions and row-level locking are essential to prevent double-booking and ensure consistency under concurrent access.
- Managed Postgres services (e.g., AWS RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL) provide durability, automated backups, point-in-time recovery, monitoring, and high availability across deployments.

Key choices:
- Schema with normalized tables: locations, bookables, bookings, with UUID primary keys.
- Enforce booking validity via constraints:
  - Foreign keys (bookings → bookables → locations).
  - Non-overlapping reservations per bookable using PostgreSQL exclusion constraints on time ranges (bookable_id WITH =, timeslot WITH &&).
  - Business rules (e.g., within operating hours) enforced via application and check constraints where applicable.
- Use UTC timestamps and a consistent time zone handling strategy.
- Optimistic locking (e.g., version column) on bookings to reduce contention; transactional upserts where appropriate.
- Migration and versioning via Flyway (or Liquibase) managed as part of CI/CD.
- Connection pooling via PgBouncer or application pool; parameterized queries/ORM with prepared statements.
- Backups and retention configured to meet RPO/RTO; enable PITR and regular restore drills.
- Production readiness: multi-AZ/zone HA, automated failover, monitoring/alerting on latency, lock waits, deadlocks, storage, and replication lag.

Future considerations:
- Read replicas for reporting/analytics; optional caching layer for hot reads if needed.
- Partitioning of bookings by time for long-term scale.
- Event outbox pattern for integration without compromising transactional integrity.

## Decision:
Adopt tsconfig “path aliases” and enable them at runtime and build time without relying on native ts-node support.

- Development/test: use ts-node with tsconfig-paths.
  - Start commands use prerequires:
    - node -r ts-node/register -r tsconfig-paths/register src/index.ts
  - For test runners (e.g., mocha/jest), add the same prerequires or their equivalents.

- Production: compile with tsc and rewrite aliases post-emit.
  - Build: tsc --project tsconfig.json
  - Post-build: tsc-alias (or switch to a bundler like tsup/esbuild/webpack that respects tsconfig paths)
  - Run: node dist/index.js

- Enforce consistency via NPM scripts:
  - dev: node -r ts-node/register -r tsconfig-paths/register src/index.ts
  - build: tsc && tsc-alias
  - start: node dist/index.js

This preserves required path-alias bootstrapping, avoids ts-node’s lack of native support, and ensures both fast DX and reliable production execution.

## Decision:
Adopt Scala as the primary implementation language for LaTiS.

We will target Scala 3 to leverage its improved type system, concise syntax, and safer functional constructs while retaining seamless JVM interoperability. Scala’s hybrid OO/FP model aligns with LaTiS’s requirements for composable data transformations, strong static typing, and expressive domain modeling.

We will use sbt as the build tool and maintain clear Java interoperability boundaries to allow integration with existing JVM libraries and gradual migration where needed. We will prefer the standard library and well-adopted, lightweight FP libraries (e.g., Cats, FS2) only where they provide clear value, to manage complexity and onboarding.

To mitigate learning curve and tooling friction, we will establish coding standards, provide targeted training, and supply reference implementations. Performance, compile times, and dependency footprint will be monitored with CI checks and guidance on idiomatic, efficient Scala.

## Decision:
Adopt GitHub as the initial source of truth for identity and access, implementing single sign-on across the cloud platform via GitHub OAuth/OIDC.

- Authentication: All user-facing platform services (e.g., Kubernetes dashboard/API via kubectl OIDC, Kibana via OIDC proxy, Prometheus, Concourse, platform UIs) must integrate with GitHub OIDC where native, or via a proxy that supports GitHub.
- Authorization: Use GitHub Organization membership and Teams as the canonical representation of users, teams, and roles. Map GitHub teams to platform roles (e.g., Kubernetes RBAC, AWS IAM roles, tool-specific roles) via automated sync.
- AWS Access: Provide federated access to AWS accounts/roles via OIDC/SAML brokers that consume GitHub team membership, avoiding long-lived credentials.
- Lifecycle: Provisioning, permission updates, and deprovisioning are driven by GitHub org/team changes, enforced by automation (e.g., CI/CD and controllers) and auditable via pull requests where applicable.
- Scope and exceptions: This is the default for all new services. If a service cannot support GitHub-based auth, a compliant proxy must be placed in front. Any deviations require explicit approval and a migration plan.
- Future evolution: This approach serves as the initial identity layer; we will reassess when/if a dedicated IdP (e.g., enterprise SSO) becomes advantageous, while preserving the GitHub team-to-role model for developer-facing access.

## Decision:
Adopt “MVC plus focused objects, organized by domain” to keep Rails code maintainable and navigable.

- Organize by domain (feature-first): app/domains/<domain>/{commands, queries, services, policies, serializers, presenters, value_objects}
- Keep MVC thin:
  - Models (ActiveRecord): persistence, associations, basic validations and scopes only; no multi-step workflows.
  - Controllers: parameter parsing, auth, orchestration; delegate to commands/services; no business logic.
  - Views/API: use serializers for API shaping; presenters/decorators for view-specific formatting.
- Business logic lives in:
  - Commands/Services (app/.../commands or services): single responsibility, callable (call), transactional where needed, return result objects not raw exceptions.
  - Queries (app/.../queries): encapsulate complex read concerns; return AR::Relation or read models.
  - Form Objects (app/forms or domain/forms): aggregate validation for multi-model input.
  - Policies (app/.../policies): authorization via Pundit-style policy classes.
  - Jobs (app/jobs): background work via Sidekiq/ActiveJob; jobs call commands/services.
  - Value Objects (app/.../value_objects): domain primitives with invariants.
- Conventions:
  - One class per file; clear suffixes: UserCommand, OrdersQuery, OrderPolicy, OrderSerializer.
  - Public APIs stable; private methods internal; avoid callbacks except for persistence invariants.
  - Prefer dependency injection over globals; avoid reaching across domains.
  - Explicit transactions in commands; queries never mutate.
- Testing:
  - Unit-test commands/queries/policies/serializers; request specs for controllers; minimal model tests.
- Dependency flow: Controller -> Command/Query -> Model/Repo -> DB; Presenters/Serializers only at the edges.
