- Dependency install: rely on npm ci for CI/reproducible installs and npm install for local development.
- Asset synchronisation: a postinstall (or prepare when publishing) hook will copy the required NHSUK UI kit assets and any other runtime assets into the app’s public/ directory to ensure the application can run immediately after install.
- Running the app:
  - npm start launches the production server (node server.js or equivalent).
  - npm run dev starts the app in watch mode using nodemon for automatic restarts on source changes.
- Optional utilities:
  - cross-env for portable environment variable configuration.
  - concurrently for running watch/build pipelines in parallel if needed (e.g., dev server + asset watcher).
- Example script targets (illustrative):
  - "clean": node scripts/clean.mjs
  - "assets": node scripts/sync-assets.mjs
  - "postinstall": "npm run assets"
  - "start": "node server.js"
  - "dev": "nodemon server.js"
  - "build" (if bundling is required later): integrate esbuild/rollup as dedicated scripts without changing the orchestration approach.

This approach provides a simple, dependency‑light, and cross‑platform startup workflow: npm ci/install → npm run assets → npm start (or npm run dev). It aligns with modern Node practices, reduces cognitive overhead, and keeps future extension straightforward.

## Decision:
We will fold the Advance Passenger Info (API) functionality into the drtv2 codebase and deploy it as an internal module of the drtv2 service rather than as a standalone webservice.

- The separate API project will be deprecated and archived after migration.
- We will remove support obligations for PHP drt; any transitional needs will be handled via a temporary adapter in drtv2, not by continuing the separate service.
- The integration will be implemented behind a clear internal interface (ports/adapters) to preserve the option of future extraction without coupling drtv2 to external service boundaries.
- API functionality will be exposed only internally within drtv2 processes; no external network endpoints will be created for this module.
- Configuration, secrets, and data access used by the former service will be migrated into drtv2’s configuration management, following existing conventions.
- CI/CD will be consolidated: one repository, one pipeline, one deployment artifact for drtv2 including the API module.
- Rollout will use feature flags and/or dark launches to mitigate risk; observability (logging/metrics/alerts) for API functionality will be integrated into drtv2’s monitoring.
- Documentation and runbooks will be updated to reflect the new ownership, deployment, and operational model.

This consolidation reduces operational overhead, removes duplicate integration patterns, and aligns with the decision to focus solely on v2.

## Decision:
Treat Aleph as the sole source of truth for circrequests and operate statelessly with respect to CaiaSoft outcomes.

- Submit the current complete set of holds from Aleph to CaiaSoft each run/window.
- Consider a hold “valid” only while it appears in the Aleph-provided list; remove/stop sending it once it no longer appears.
- Do not track locally which holds were previously sent to CaiaSoft or which were denied; do not auto-resubmit denied entries.
- Rely on CaiaSoft’s UI/process for staff to handle denied entries; avoid creating churn by re-sending known-denied requests.

Operational safeguards:
- Log and surface metrics for CaiaSoft denials and submission errors for observability and trend analysis, without affecting submission logic.
- Ensure submissions are idempotent where possible (e.g., by including stable identifiers) to minimize duplicate work on CaiaSoft’s side.
- Alert only on transport/processing failures (e.g., API errors), not on business denials, which are expected and managed in CaiaSoft.

This simplifies the system, avoids unnecessary resubmissions, and aligns with stakeholder guidance while keeping Aleph authoritative.

## Decision:
Adopt named exports exclusively across all authored code and public APIs. Default exports are disallowed.

- Every module exports named symbols only, even when there is a single export.
- Consumers import using named syntax (import { Foo } from 'pkg'), never default.
- Re-exports use named form. Wildcard re-exports (export *) are permitted only between index files where naming collisions are controlled; otherwise explicitly list symbols.
- React components, hooks, utilities, and types are exported as named symbols (export function Component() {}, export const useThing = …, export type Thing = …).
- CommonJS interop: do not introduce synthetic default exports. CJS consumers use require('pkg').Foo. No default export shim is provided.
- Enforce via lint rules:
  - Enable: import/no-default-export
  - Disable: import/prefer-default-export
  - Optionally enable TypeScript-specific equivalents in @typescript-eslint.
- Code generation and scaffolding templates must emit named exports.
- Exceptions (e.g., frameworks that mandate default exports like Next.js pages) are limited to boundary adapter modules, isolated from shared libraries, and must not leak default exports into package public APIs.

This decision applies to all new code and to modified files; existing default exports will be migrated opportunistically.

## Decision:
We will not publish or maintain packages for any specific OS/package manager. Instead, we will:

- Publish signed, versioned source archives and tagged releases (Semantic Versioning) with a minimal, portable installation method (e.g., make install / shell script) that requires no platform-specific packaging.
- Provide and maintain a packaging guide describing build artifacts, install locations, dependencies, license/compliance info, and recommended metadata to support downstream packagers.
- Keep the repository free of distro-specific packaging files; community packaging metadata should live in downstream repositories maintained by those communities.
- Link to community-maintained packages in documentation under a clearly marked “Community Packages” section with disclaimers (no official endorsement/support; versions may lag).
- Offer stable interfaces (CLI/FS layout), a changelog with packaging-impact notes, and pre-release announcements to help downstream maintainers.
- Accept issues/PRs that improve packagability (e.g., deterministic builds, PREFIX support), but not requests to own or prioritize any one packaging ecosystem.

This ensures broad accessibility without privileging any single distribution channel and keeps ownership with downstream communities.

## Decision:
We will use npm as the package manager to declare and resolve all runtime and build dependencies. All dependencies (e.g. express and nhsuk-frontend) will be sourced from the public npm registry and declared in package.json using semver. We will commit package-lock.json to guarantee reproducible installs across environments and use npm ci in CI/CD for deterministic builds.

Versioning policy:
- Runtime dependencies: use caret ranges for non-breaking updates (e.g. ^4.18.0) and review major upgrades explicitly.
- Dev/build tooling: pin with carets and rely on the lockfile for exact resolution.
- Node.js version will be fixed via .nvmrc/engines to ensure compatibility.

NHSUK UI assets will be consumed via the nhsuk-frontend npm package rather than vendoring or git submodules. Frontend assets required at runtime will be referenced directly from node_modules or copied into the app’s public/build directory as part of the build pipeline.

This approach standardizes dependency management, simplifies updates, and ensures secure, repeatable installs for both application code and design system assets.

## Decision:
We will use flutter_downloader to manage single-file downloads across My Space, Received Shares, and Shared Spaces. Each download will be enqueued per file via enqueue(url, saveDir, headers…) and executed in the background, with progress and status observed to update the UI. We will route the saveDir using our platform-specific path decision (path-provider on Android; iOS alternative as defined separately). We will expose cancel and clear operations using flutter_downloader’s APIs to allow users to cancel individual tasks or clear the queue. We will persist task IDs to support resume/restore after app restarts, and configure retries and notification options as needed. This standardizes download behavior, ensures reliable background execution, and simplifies queue management.

## Decision:
Etabler kontinuerlig leveranse med trunk‑basert utvikling og funksjonsflagg for å kunne levere ofte og smått. Modiapersonoversikt leveres som en selvstendig SPA med egen pipeline og kan rulles ut uavhengig av dagens modiabrukerdialog.

- Strangler‑pattern for gradvis migrering: Trafikk til utvalgte sider/funksjoner rutes til den nye frontenden via reverse proxy/edge‑router. Omkopling styres av feature toggles (f.eks. Unleash) og kan gjøres per brukergruppe/andel.
- Skil separate “release” og “exposure”: Kode kan prodsettes trygt bak flagg; aktivering styres dynamisk uten ny deploy.
- CI/CD: Automatisk bygg, tester (unit, integrasjon, e2e røyk), statisk analyse og sikkerhetsskanning. Hver merge til main kan prodsettes.
- Trygg utrulling: Kanari/gradvis eksponering, blue‑green/rollback ved feil, metrikker og logging/alerting på klient‑ og proxy‑nivå.
- Bakoverkompatibilitet: Kontraktstester mot API‑er og versjonering ved behov for å unngå koordinerte releaser.
- Små endringer: Små PR‑er, rask kodegjennomgang, autofrigjøring når kvalitetsporter er passert.
- Observabilitet: Frontend‑telemetri (performance, feil, brukerflyt) for å styre gradvis utrulling og tidlig oppdagelse av regresjoner.

Dette muliggjør hyppige, små, reversible leveranser av ny funksjonalitet til saksbehandlere samtidig som risikoen holdes lav og migreringen skjer inkrementelt.

## Decision:
We will run Prometheus (and related exporters/tooling) on Ubuntu LTS, standardizing initially on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS across environments, with a planned path to 24.04 LTS after validation.

This choice prioritizes operational familiarity within GDS, leverages existing automation, monitoring, and hardening practices on Ubuntu, and provides predictable long-term security updates and kernel stability. It also avoids unnecessary cloud vendor lock-in associated with Amazon Linux while maintaining broad compatibility with Prometheus packaging, systemd, and common observability tooling.

We will:
- Use Ubuntu LTS images for all Prometheus hosts and container base images where applicable.
- Install Prometheus and exporters from upstream releases or vetted Ubuntu/Debian repositories, managed as systemd services.
- Apply standard Ubuntu hardening and patch management (e.g., unattended-upgrades) consistent with existing GDS baselines.
- Review and validate upgrade to Ubuntu 24.04 LTS within normal LTS cadence once compatibility and performance are confirmed.

## Decision:
Expose distinct status interfaces that reflect different perspectives and their “good state” criteria:

- /health (liveness): Returns 200 OK if the process is running and can serve basic requests (event loop, thread pool, minimal in-memory checks). Never depends on external systems. Returns 500 on unrecoverable internal failure. Public and unauthenticated, short timeout, no caching.

- /ready (readiness): Returns 200 OK only when the portal can serve requests end-to-end: configuration is syntactically valid and required dependencies (e.g., DB, message broker, critical APIs) are reachable within thresholds. Returns 503 Service Unavailable if any required dependency is down or config invalid. Public and unauthenticated for load balancers, no caching.

- /status (administration): Authenticated endpoint (role-protected) returning detailed, machine-readable JSON with:
  - overall.status: up/degraded/down
  - components[]: name, status, latency, lastChecked, error
  - config: syntaxValid, version, checksum
  - dependencies: required vs optional classification
  - build/runtime: buildId, gitSha, startTime
  - readinessPolicy: description of what contributes to “ready”
  This endpoint can include a simple human-readable HTML view.

Evaluation policy:
- Liveness (/health) = process health only.
- Readiness (/ready) = liveness AND config syntax valid AND all required dependencies reachable within SLOs.
- Admin status (/status) surfaces nuanced states (e.g., config valid but datasource unreachable) without declaring ready.

Operational notes:
- Implement standardized JSON schema and exit codes for probes.
- Keep timeouts low and avoid cascading failures (use shallow checks, connection pools, and circuit breakers).
- Add Cache-Control: no-store on /health and /ready; allow short caching on /status for UI if needed.
- Log check results with structured fields for observability.
- Backward-compatible aliases (/live, /readyz, /healthz) may be provided for orchestration systems.

## Decision:
Adopt SDL2’s logical rendering to support multiple screen resolutions while keeping a fixed internal resolution. We will define a fixed logical size that matches our tile grid (15x13 tiles) plus reserved vertical space for the UI, and render all game logic and drawing against this logical coordinate space. SDL_RenderSetLogicalSize will be used to scale to any actual window/display size; SDL will handle mapping of rendering and input coordinates accordingly.

Key points:
- Single coordinate system: all game logic and rendering use logical (tile/pixel) coordinates; no separate “world” vs “screen” coordinate abstractions.
- Base logical resolution: width = tileWidth * 15; height = tileHeight * 13 + uiHeight. Tile size and uiHeight are constants in the renderer/config.
- Aspect ratio handling: rely on SDL’s letterboxing with SDL_RenderSetLogicalSize to preserve aspect ratio across devices.
- Scaling quality: set SDL_HINT_RENDER_SCALE_QUALITY to “nearest” (default) for crisp pixel art, or “linear” if smoothing is preferred; enable SDL_RenderSetIntegerScale(true) when appropriate to avoid subpixel blurring.
- Assets/UI: sprites and UI are authored for the logical resolution; UI layout is computed in logical coordinates.
- Input: use SDL’s scaled coordinates (e.g., SDL_GetMouseState) which are mapped to the logical space.

We will revisit a dual-coordinate “world” model only if we introduce features like camera movement, arbitrary zoom, or physics that benefit from a decoupled world space.

## Decision:
Adopt a strict layered architecture with explicit dependency rules:
- Layers: Presentation (UI) -> Application (Services/Use Cases) -> Domain (Entities/Rules) -> Infrastructure (Adapters/IO).
- Allowed dependencies flow only downward (UI→Application→Domain; Infrastructure depends on Domain and is accessed via interfaces).
- No lateral or upward calls; no bypassing layers (e.g., UI must not access Domain or Infrastructure directly).
- Domain remains pure and technology-agnostic; infrastructure is replaceable via ports (interfaces) defined in Domain/Application.

Enforcement mechanisms:
- Define module/package boundaries per layer with clear public APIs.
- Use dependency constraints (e.g., ArchUnit, module systems, build graph rules) to prevent violations.
- Code reviews/checklists to uphold layering guidelines.

Testing strategy:
- Unit-test Domain and Application in isolation with mocks for ports.
- Integration tests per adapter in Infrastructure.
- End-to-end tests across layers for critical flows.

Benefits:
- Clear separation of responsibilities, easier maintenance, and controlled access between layers.
- Improved testability and adaptability to change (UI/DB/IO can evolve without impacting core domain).

## Decision:
Implement role-based access control scoped per cohort (each cohort as an OpenID/OIDC client). User identity is federated via the user’s home institution IdP; Armadillo relies on OIDC to authenticate and obtains a stable subject identifier plus attributes. Authorization is enforced by requiring the presence of ROLE_<STUDY>_RESEARCHER in the OIDC token (or via token introspection) to read data in the corresponding shared folder <study>.

Cohort representatives are delegated admin over their cohort’s OIDC client and manage role assignments for study researchers within that scope. Role management is performed via an admin UI/API that updates a central RBAC directory backing the OIDC roles/claims for each cohort application. Just-in-time user provisioning is supported on first federated login; no local passwords are maintained.

Consortium representatives have read-only visibility across cohorts to list users, roles, and cohorts, including audit trails of assignments and changes. All role grants/changes are auditable, time-stamped, and attributable to the acting cohort admin.

Token contents are limited to least-privilege role claims needed for authorization; role-to-folder mapping is deterministic (ROLE_<STUDY>_RESEARCHER -> <study>). No cross-cohort role inheritance is allowed. Revocations propagate promptly by updating the RBAC directory and invalidating/shortening token lifetimes to ensure near-real-time enforcement.

Adopt Locust as the primary benchmarking framework due to its scalability, distributed execution, Python-based test authoring, and operator-friendly web UI. To address its limitations, we will extend Locust with custom instrumentation:

- Capture raw, per-request metrics by subscribing to Locust’s request event hooks and emitting enriched records (timestamps, scenario/test IDs, request/response metadata, success/failure, latency) to a durable sink (e.g., Kafka/S3) and a time-series DB (e.g., InfluxDB/Prometheus) for live dashboards.
- Implement end-to-end timing for non-HTTP or multi-step workflows using Locust’s custom events/record_time_context and wrapper utilities to time arbitrary code sections, enabling accurate business-operation latency measurement beyond the HTTP client’s timing.
- Generate HDR histograms offline from raw samples (via post-processing jobs) and include histogram summaries in benchmark reports; optionally evaluate locust-plugins or a lightweight client-side HDR encoder if it reduces data volume.
- Keep CSV/HTML summaries for quick operator visibility, but treat them as secondary to raw data analysis pipelines and notebooks.

If, during implementation, Locust’s event model or overhead prevents reliable raw capture at target load, we will reassess and consider complementary generators (e.g., k6 or wrk for pure HTTP firehose) while retaining Locust for scenario orchestration and reporting.

## Decision:
- MUST use AndroidX WorkManager as the primary scheduler for all background uploads, downloads, and sync on Android.
- MUST represent each transfer as a OneTimeWorkRequest; use UniqueWork with REPLACE/KEEP policies as appropriate.
- MUST set Constraints per job: at minimum NetworkType.CONNECTED; use UNMETERED for large transfers; optionally requiresCharging and requiresBatteryNotLow for heavy jobs.
- MUST configure retry with exponential backoff and respect transient failures (e.g., network) vs. permanent failures (e.g., 4xx).
- MUST persist and resume work across app/process/device restarts (WorkManager default behavior).
- MUST expose progress and state via WorkManager (LiveData/Flow) and tags for grouping; enable user-driven cancel of tagged work.
- MUST use ForegroundService mode with a user-visible notification for long-running/background transfers and expedited work on API 26+ to meet OS requirements.
- SHOULD chain pre/post steps (e.g., encryption, checksum, metadata update) using WorkContinuation with input/output Data.
- SHOULD support resumable or chunked transfers when backend supports it; otherwise, implement safe retry semantics to avoid duplication.
- SHOULD apply concurrency limits and batching via WorkManager configuration (maxSchedulerLimit) and a custom Executor to control parallelism and bandwidth.
- MUST store file I/O using scoped storage paths and validate/whitelist destinations; never expose raw file URIs.
- MUST provide cancellation, pause/resume semantics via cancel by tag and re-enqueue with persisted state.
- SHOULD emit structured telemetry (enqueue time, start/end, bytes transferred, retries) and logs for observability.
- MUST guard network calls with authenticated requests and TLS; validate checksums on completion where available.

## Decision:
- Implement a strategy-based, pluggable sorting system with two explicit, named comparator strategies (e.g., “methodA” and “methodB”), each encapsulated as its own comparator module.
- Expose the sorting method as an explicit parameter (API/query/config), with a sensible default and strict validation to ensure deterministic selection.
- Use a stable sort algorithm to guarantee deterministic ordering; for ties, include a consistent secondary key (e.g., observation ID and timestamp) to avoid nondeterminism.
- Define a shared Comparator interface (input schema, null/NaN handling, tie-breaking rules) so additional methods can be added without impacting existing clients.
- Centralize normalization of observation attributes (units, missing data policy, categorical encoding) prior to comparison to ensure consistent behavior across strategies.
- Provide comprehensive unit tests and golden-file tests per strategy to lock determinism and detect regressions when data quality or rules evolve.
- Optimize for scale by precomputing/composing sort keys per strategy where possible to reduce comparator overhead on large datasets.

## Decision:
Adopt trunk-based development with short‑lived pull requests as the default workflow.

- No direct commits to main; enable branch protection requiring PRs, up-to-date branch, and passing status checks.
- Require at least one peer review; use CODEOWNERS where applicable.
- Keep PRs small and focused (aim for a single logical change). Prefer opening draft PRs early to enable discussion and CI feedback.
- All PRs must pass automated checks (build, unit/integration tests, lint/format, vulnerability scan) before merge.
- Prefer squash merge to keep a clean, atomic mainline history; the PR title becomes the commit message (follow Conventional Commits).
- Use feature flags/toggles or graceful fallbacks to merge incomplete work safely and avoid long‑lived branches.
- Target lead time for PRs: <48 hours from open to merge; if larger, split into smaller PRs.
- CI runs on every PR and on main; failures block merges. Rollback/restore procedures are documented and tested.
- Exceptions (e.g., hotfixes) follow an expedited PR with the same checks where feasible, and a post-merge retrospective.

## Decision:
Adopt “new ASG per LC revision” to guarantee propagation of Launch Configuration changes. Each LC change will produce a new, uniquely named ASG (e.g., LC version suffix), with lifecycle create_before_destroy to allow zero/low-downtime cutover. Traffic will be shifted via ELB/Target Group health checks and connection draining; desired/min/max capacities will temporarily allow overlap to enable a rolling replacement, then the old ASG will be drained and destroyed.

We will not rely on manual instance terminations or embed CloudFormation. Terraform will:
- Generate a new LC and ASG on LC changes (name/versioned identifiers).
- Attach new ASG to existing load balancers/target groups.
- Use health checks and termination policies to ensure healthy replacement before scale-in.
- Optionally stagger replacements via cooldowns or instance warm-up.

This provides deterministic, automated rollout of LC updates across all instances, avoiding long-lived drift.

## Decision:
Adopt a canonical, version-independent grouping taxonomy and require every kata to reference it via metadata.

- Define a global groups registry (groups.json) with stable slugs, human-readable labels, descriptions, and display order, e.g.:
  - array-api, object-api, string-api, map-set-api, promise-api, iterator-generator, async, class, module, number-math, regex, reflect-proxy, symbols, typed-arrays, language-basics, etc.
- Each kata must declare:
  - ecmaVersion: ES1|ES5|ES6|…|ESNext
  - groups: [list of group slugs from registry]
  - tags: [free-form, optional]
- File location remains versioned (e.g., es10/language/object-api/fromEntries.js); grouping and presentation rely on metadata, not directory names.
- The website (and other tooling) aggregates katas by groups across versions using the registry, enabling pages like “Array API” that span ES levels.
- Consistency rules:
  - Only slugs from groups.json are allowed in groups.
  - One kata may belong to multiple groups if justified.
  - Labels shown to users come from the registry; slugs are stable identifiers.
- CI validation:
  - Lint step checks that all groups exist in the registry and that ecmaVersion is valid.
  - Fails on unknown or misspelled groups to enforce consistency.
- Migration: add groups metadata to existing katas; no mass file moves required.

## Decision:
Continue using Prometheus (metrics) and Fluentd (logs) as forwarders, configured with persistent, bounded, and observable buffering to achieve one order-of-magnitude higher resilience than the monitored workloads, while limiting blast radius from storage issues.

- Prometheus:
  - Use local TSDB (WAL) with on-node PersistentVolume to retain at least 48 hours of scrape data.
  - Forward to InfluxDB via remote_write with a tuned queue_config (high max_samples_per_send, max_shards, and capacity) to withstand at least 12 hours of downstream outage.
  - Enable backpressure (do not drop by default), with selective relabeling/sampling for low-value metrics if saturation persists.
  - Alert on remote_write failures, queue saturation, and local TSDB head-block size.

- Fluentd:
  - Use file-based buffered outputs to Elasticsearch on node-local PersistentVolumes, sized to buffer at least 24 hours at peak throughput.
  - Configure chunking, compression, exponential backoff with jitter, and retry_forever semantics within bounded total buffer size.
  - On buffer exhaustion, prefer backpressure and controlled shedding (drop debug/verbose streams via filters/sampling) rather than indiscriminate loss.
  - Alert on buffer utilization thresholds, retry rates, and disk pressure.

- Storage isolation and protection:
  - Use dedicated StorageClasses for forwarder buffers with per-PV size limits and node-level quotas to reduce risk from “disk full” events.
  - Place forwarder buffers on fast local storage where available; fall back to resilient network storage with IOPS guarantees if needed.

- High availability and operations:
  - Run forwarders as DaemonSets with resource requests/limits; enable pod disruption budgets and priority classes above application workloads.
  - Version-pin output plugins; validate configs via CI; blue/green rollouts to avoid buffer loss.
  - Document SLOs: at-least-once delivery unless buffer limits are exceeded; target zero loss for planned DB maintenance windows within the stated buffer durations.

## Decision:
We will standardize all Java-based services on Red Hat UBI 9 minimal as the OS base and the Red Hat build of OpenJDK LTS (currently Java 17) installed from UBI repositories. We will publish two image flavors:
- Builder image: UBI 9 minimal + OpenJDK (JDK) + build tooling (for multi-stage builds).
- Runtime image: UBI 9 minimal + OpenJDK (JRE/Headless), minimized for production.

Rationale and constraints:
- Clear redistribution rights: UBI and the Red Hat build of OpenJDK are explicitly redistributable, avoiding license ambiguity while allowing customers to mirror internally.
- Enterprise posture: predictable security errata, CVE metadata, FIPS-ready base, SBOMs, and long-term updates suitable for regulated environments.
- Consistency: a single, well-supported base eliminates variability and reduces supply-chain and operational risk versus mixing Alpine/Debian/Ubuntu or ad-hoc JDKs.
- Supportability: aligns with widely adopted enterprise container practices; optional vendor support is available without mandating it.

We will distribute full images and will not rely on init/composite/foreign-layer workarounds. Multi-arch images (amd64/arm64) will be produced. Images will be rebuilt on:
- Red Hat UBI security updates
- OpenJDK CPU/PSU releases
- Critical CVE or configuration changes

We will provide a documented process to pin the JDK major (LTS only), allow minor/patch auto-updates, and offer an alternative slim “distroless-like” runtime variant if/when UBI’s footprint materially impacts startup or size-sensitive workloads.

## Decision:
Define a standardized boot pipeline orchestrated by a Boot Orchestrator that executes a fixed, deterministic sequence of phases with clear contracts and extensibility points. The phases are:

1) Relocate: copy initialized data from ROM to RAM (platform/toolchain-provided implementation).
2) Zero BSS: clear uninitialized data (.bss) to zero (platform/toolchain-provided).
3) Call Constructors: run static constructors/init arrays (platform/toolchain-provided).
4) Initialize RTOS: bring up scheduler, timers, and kernel objects but do not start scheduling until drivers are ready.
5) Set Default Pin States: apply board-defined safe I/O defaults.
6) Create Drivers: instantiate driver objects via generic driver interfaces; platform provides bindings and HAL adapters.
7) Configure System: load and apply system/application configuration; register services; start RTOS scheduling and application entry.

Each phase is represented by an IBootPhase interface with before/execute/after hooks and a well-defined error contract. Modules may register tasks within phases via a registry with priority and optional dependency constraints; cycles are rejected at build-time. Platform-specific work is confined to platform packages implementing the same interfaces. Feature flags (compile-time) determine inclusion of phases or tasks (e.g., bare-metal builds may elide RTOS).

The orchestrator emits structured boot logs/metrics, supports watchdog-friendly checkpoints, and fails fast to a safe error handler if a critical phase fails (e.g., pin defaults or RTOS init). Phases must be idempotent where feasible; non-idempotent phases are guarded. The boot plan is declared in a table (ROM) enabling reproducible startup across hardware variants and simulators.

## Decision:
Adopt a dependency strategy that minimizes runtime risk while leveraging third‑party speed in build/dev:

- Classify dependencies by criticality and run-time path impact. For user-facing critical paths, prefer reducing external calls and/or using managed services with strong SLAs and regional redundancy.
- Runtime:
  - Internalize or replicate functionality when feasible (e.g., in-process libs, managed equivalents we control) for critical capabilities.
  - Cache slow-changing/immutable data (read-through/write-behind as appropriate) and enable periodic background syncs to reduce live dependency calls.
  - Implement resilience patterns: strict timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and graceful degradation/fallbacks.
  - Version-pin APIs/SDKs, wrap third-party SDKs behind an internal adapter/anti-corruption layer, and provide feature flags and provider switchability for failover.
  - Monitor external dependencies with SLOs, health checks, and alerts; define runbooks and error budgets.
- Build and development:
  - Consume third-party tools/services directly (no extra mirroring/independence investment), using lockfiles but refreshing regularly to track upstream changes.
  - Allow faster upgrades in non-production; validate compatibility via CI.
  - Use lightweight mocks/fakes only where required for determinism; otherwise test against real services to surface integration issues early.

This balances availability with delivery speed: minimize and harden runtime dependencies on critical paths, while embracing direct use of third-party components in build/dev to maximize velocity.

## Decision:
Adopt instance-scoped logging with explicit, immutable configuration and no global state.

- Introduce LoggerConfig as an immutable value object describing level thresholds, handlers/appenders, and formatters.
- Introduce LoggerFactory that is constructed with a LoggerConfig (and optional DI container bindings) and produces per-class/per-component Logger instances on demand (e.g., factory.for("MyClass")).
- Pass LoggerFactory (or specific Logger instances) explicitly through application composition (constructors, dependency injection) rather than relying on singletons, class variables, or global configuration.
- Support multiple independent factories/configs within the same process (e.g., app vs. test harness), enabling safe parallel tests and isolated subsystems.
- Allow configuration to be built from environment/CLI/files, validated at startup, and then frozen before loggers are created.
- Provide sensible defaults via a ConfigBuilder but require explicit opt-in to mutate before freeze; after freeze, configuration is read-only.
- Support dynamic context (e.g., request/trace ids) via explicit context propagation APIs attached to Logger instances (not thread/global), with helpers to derive child loggers with extra context (logger.with(context: ...)).
- For integration points that expect global loggers, provide an adapter that delegates to a scoped LoggerFactory, keeping globals as thin shims without mutable state.

## Decision:
Adopt a single, versioned NPM package that exports all components, with per-component subpath entry points and tree-shakeable ESM builds.

Key points:
- Packaging: Publish one package (e.g., @org/ui). Provide ESM and CJS outputs with an exports map that supports:
  - top-level imports: import { Button } from '@org/ui'
  - deep imports for explicitness: import Button from '@org/ui/Button'
- Build: Emit ESM-first builds for optimal tree-shaking, plus CJS for compatibility. Provide type declarations. Avoid bundling peer dependencies (React, etc.).
- Consumption: Rely on consumer bundlers for tree-shaking to exclude unused components. Deep-entry imports remain available for bundlers with weaker tree-shaking.
- Versioning/Release: Use Changesets (or semantic-release) for a single version stream following SemVer. Automate changelog generation and docs publishing per release.
- Interdependencies: Keep internal component cross-imports internal to the monorepo; avoid publishing per-component packages to reduce publication complexity and dependency drift.
- Future-proofing: Re-evaluate splitting into multiple packages only if bundle-size analysis, consumer feedback, or platform constraints demonstrate clear benefits. If needed, the current subpath export structure facilitates a gradual migration to multi-package without breaking changes.

Style guide relationship:
- Decouple the style guide app’s deployment from component releases. On each component release, auto-build and publish a versioned documentation site with a version switcher (e.g., docs/@org/ui/vX.Y.Z).
- The style guide depends on the released package; it can render multiple versions via separate static builds per version rather than simultaneous runtime mixing.
- UMD build is provided for live-playground embeds where bundlers aren’t present.

This approach optimizes developer experience and publishing simplicity while preserving efficient consumption and a clear path to future modularization if required.

## Decision:
We will explicitly model phosphorylation/dephosphorylation as a first-class regulatory layer in the metabolic simulator. Each enzyme will support discrete modification states (e.g., active, phosphorylated-inactive), with phosphorylation state controlling catalytic parameters (Vmax/kcat and/or Km) via state-specific rate-law variants. Kinase and phosphatase activities will be represented as reactions in the network with mass-action or Michaelis–Menten kinetics, enabling endogenous dynamics and signal-driven control.

Key elements:
- Enzyme schema gains a “modificationStates” map and “regulationRules” to bind states to kinetic parameter sets; default rule: phosphorylation deactivates enzyme unless explicitly overridden per enzyme.
- Regulatory reactions (kinases/phosphatases) are encoded in the same stoichiometric graph for unified simulation, supporting cofactors (ATP/ADP, Pi) and compartmentalization.
- Parameterization supports fixed rates, condition-dependent activities, or upstream signaling inputs; users may provide priors/constraints for Bayesian calibration.
- Simulation engine computes fluxes conditioned on current enzyme states; state transitions follow kinetic reactions, allowing time-resolved modulation.
- Observability hooks expose enzyme states and effective kinetic parameters for analysis and debugging; sensible fallbacks maintain prior behavior if regulation data is absent.
- Performance is maintained via state caching and sparse updates; rule evaluation is vectorized.

This approach ensures accurate, extensible regulation modeling without fragmenting the core flux computation pipeline.

## Decision:
Adopt Jest snapshot testing to assert the rendered output of React components and detect unintended UI changes.

- Generate snapshots from the DOM using @testing-library/react (e.g., asFragment) to keep tests user-centric and avoid coupling to component internals.
- Commit snapshots to version control; PR reviewers must inspect diffs to validate intentional changes.
- CI will run Jest and fail on snapshot mismatches. Intentional changes require explicit snapshot updates (jest -u), ensuring conscious approval.
- Scope and guidelines:
  - Prefer small, focused snapshots (individual components or stable subtrees) over large, brittle trees.
  - Avoid snapshotting dynamic or time-sensitive output; mock nondeterminism (dates, random ids, feature flags).
  - Prefer explicit assertions for behavior; use snapshots primarily for structural/markup contracts and presentational components.
  - Use stable serializers/formatters (e.g., DOM pretty-print) to minimize noise.
- Do not use snapshots to verify business logic, API contracts, or interactions—these should be covered by unit and integration tests with explicit expectations.

Adopt the Alfresco Community Benchmark framework as the canonical load/benchmark harness and implement our benchmarks using TAS-based REST scenarios. We will not base our solution on the APS JMeter suite; it may be used only for occasional cross-validation.

Actions:
- Stand up the Management Server and one or more Driver Servers; use the built-in MongoDB result store.
- Define Test Suite Definitions that map directly to REQ workload profiles and SLAs.
- Implement a custom Benchmark Driver:
  - Author scenarios in TAS (Java DSL) reusing/expanding existing REST models.
  - Provide event and load processors wired via test-context.xml.
  - Parameterize data volumes, user mix, think times, and ramp profiles for repeatability.
- Automate end-to-end runs:
  - Schedule via Management Server API and integrate with CI/CD to run against test and pre-prod.
  - Export results to dashboards and artifacts (CSV/JSON) for analysis and audit.
- Establish acceptance gates:
  - Pass/fail based on latency percentiles, throughput, error rates, and resource ceilings per REQ.
  - Persist run metadata (git SHAs, environment, test data seeds) for reproducibility.
- Reuse TAS models for data prep, UI test seeding, and integration tests to minimize duplication.
- Maintain parity across environments (datasets, configs) and include anonymized seeders/resetters.

This decision prioritizes extensibility, reuse of existing TAS assets, distributed load execution, and durable, queryable results, while avoiding lock-in to the APS JMeter suite.

## Decision:
Adopt TypeScript as the default language for all client-side code and for the Vue 3/Vuex rewrite. All new frontend modules will be authored in TypeScript; existing JavaScript will be migrated opportunistically as part of the rewrite to avoid a separate, costly migration. We will enable strict typing (strict: true) to maximize correctness and self-documentation, allowing temporary easing (e.g., any, // @ts-expect-error) behind TODOs where needed during transition.

Tooling and build:
- Use Vite (or equivalent) to transpile; run tsc --noEmit in CI and locally for type-checking.
- Standardize on ESLint with typescript-eslint (TSLint is deprecated) and Prettier for formatting.
- Maintain shared tsconfig bases for app, test, and tooling packages.
- Prefer idiomatic TypeScript over non-standard extensions; target modern ES with polyfills as required.

Developer experience:
- Provide onboarding guides, coding standards, and example patterns (types for Vue components, Vuex stores, API models).
- Invest in type definitions for third-party libs (DefinitelyTyped or local d.ts) to keep strictness high.

This decision prioritizes maintainability, readability, and safer refactoring, leverages Vue 3’s TypeScript-first ecosystem, and builds on the sunk cost of our prototype and tooling setup.

## Decision:
The Voice Assistance Platform is responsible for determining the target VRS from the utterance. It will include a pluggable “Invocation Resolver” that:
- Performs wake-word/brand detection and lightweight NLU to extract the intended VRS (e.g., “Hey <Brand>”).
- Returns {vrs_id, confidence, rationale, spans} to the platform.
- Applies configurable confidence thresholds; only explicit, above-threshold results trigger engagement and a call to the selected VRS.
- Falls back to “implicit” classification when no VRS is confidently detected; no VRS is invoked in that case.
- Supports multiple VRS providers via a registry mapping vrs_id to connector metadata.
- Emits telemetry for detection outcomes and confidence to enable tuning.
- Is versioned and hot-swappable to add new brands or update models without changing downstream services.

VRS backends do not self-identify; they are invoked only after the platform has resolved the target VRS.

## Decision:
- Replace DynamicServiceLocator with a centralized Mapping Service that stores and serves mapping specifications and routing metadata via a well-defined, opinionated model.
- Standardize configuration to a minimal canonical schema (e.g., source, destination, messageType, transform, validate, route), eliminating optional extensibility points that have only a single implementation.
- Make the Mapping Service the single source of truth, managed via UI and API, with versioning, validation, and audit trail. Filesystem lookup (SRC-DST-MSG_TYPE.xml) is deprecated.
- Provide import/export of mappings as YAML/JSON to support GitOps and automated promotion across environments.
- Ship a default, single implementation for transformation, validation, and routing hooks; additional pluggability is disabled by default and reintroduced only with explicit ADRs.
- Deliver a backward-compatible adapter that reads legacy filesystem configs and populates/queries the new service, enabling incremental migration without breaking existing integrations.
- Simplify runtime wiring: clients query the Mapping Service by (source, destination, messageType) and receive a concrete execution plan (transformer, schema, endpoint), avoiding per-client XML or DI complexity.
- Enforce schema validation at publish time and contract checks at runtime; reject ambiguous or overlapping mappings.
- Provide caching with TTL/etags in clients to minimize latency while allowing rapid invalidation on updates.
- Ensure observability: emit mapping version, decision path, and outcomes (hit/miss/fallback) as structured logs and metrics.
- Expose fine-grained RBAC in the UI/API for mapping creation, approval, and deployment, with environment-aware overrides limited to explicit fields only.
